News.title: Family pays tribute to 'warm and engaging' man killed in tiger attack
News.content:
The family of a man who was killed by a tiger after he entered its enclosure at a wildlife park has paid tribute, describing him as "bright, warm and engaging".

William Chapman, 23, visited Yorkshire Wildlife Park near Doncaster on Saturday and was attacked after going into the animal's pen. He was pronounced dead at the scene.

In a statement, his family said that he had suffered from "significant mental illness" over a number of years and had been prescribed "strong medication".

His family added: "It will be for the coroner to decide what part this played in his death. We would ask everybody to respect that process."

City of Doncaster Council has launched a health and safety investigation into Chapman's death and the park remains closed.

"William was a bright, warm and engaging young man whom his family dearly loved - and William loved them back," a statement released on Tuesday evening said.

The family also asked for privacy, saying "the publication and circulation of deeply offensive media content is causing them severe distress at an exceptionally vulnerable time".

"The family are utterly devastated by their loss and are struggling to come to terms with what has happened," the statement continued.

"The family are hopeful that the relevant authorities will do their upmost to get to the bottom of why our amazing son did what he did."

A spokesperson for the South Yorkshire Police said Chapman's family are being supported by specialist officers.

Footage of the incident has been widely shared on social media, including on Tuesday evening by US President Donald Trump.

News.title: One stolen every four minutes - inside the police battle against vehicle thieves
News.content:
It is 01:00 on a Thursday and we are in the back of an unmarked police car on the hunt for vehicle thieves in east London.

A call comes in over the radio about a stolen Ford Transit van. Within 25 minutes officers have found it, chased it down and arrested a suspect.

Officers tell us the night has been successful, with further arrests made, yet across the UK a car is stolen every four minutes.

Despite a recent drop, vehicle thefts are up almost 50% in England and Wales compared with a decade ago, according to Home Office data. Last year, just 3% of vehicle theft offences resulted in a charge or summons.

As well as spending time on the front line in London and Sussex, we have privately spoken to 20 police officers from six forces.

They told us while they have the skills and experience to tackle vehicle crime, they are overstretched, under-resourced and struggling to keep pace with increasingly sophisticated criminal networks.

Thieves are becoming more confident. A man who claims he receives stolen vehicles and breaks them into parts at a so-called "chop shop" told the BBC he does not fear the authorities, because they "couldn't catch a cold".

Once the preserve of joyriders and opportunists, vehicle theft is now a lucrative global criminal business. Cars are stolen to order, and moved across the country or dismantled within hours, say police, making them difficult to recover and suspects hard to track. Many vehicles are sent overseas to places like the United Arab Emirates, The Democratic Republic of Congo and Jamaica.

Victims of car theft have told us they feel frustrated and helpless. One woman said it took car thieves just 35 seconds to steal her BMW, yet police only began investigating a day later. Another man said he feared for his life when masked thieves broke into his home demanding his car keys.

The success criminals are having is also hitting motorists more widely, with insurance quotes having risen by 82% since 2021, according to security think tank the Royal United Services Institute (Rusi).

News.title: Watch: BBC joins police on front line against car theft
News.content:
Vehicle thefts have risen by almost 50% in a decade, yet just 3% of offences resulted in a charge or summons last year, BBC analysis has found.

Organised crime groups are using increasingly sophisticated technology to steal cars to order, while police and manufacturers look to keep pace.

Criminals, the BBC has been told, are able to work out how to steal a car within weeks of a model being launched.

Investigations reporter NJ Convery has been out with police as they hunt for thieves.

Watch Stolen: Chasing Britain's Car Thieves on iPlayer now

News.title: Royal Mail losing 400 postal workers a week, says union
News.content:
About 400 postmen and women are leaving Royal Mail per week, according to the Communication Workers Union (CWU), who claims this number has gone up since the company introduced a new delivery system earlier this year.

The CWU says the firm had been losing about 330 postal staff a week from a workforce of 83,000 before it rolled out DM26, which reorganised routes to improve delivery performance.

The union claims the new system is not working in hundreds of offices, and BBC Your Voice has heard from staff warning of a "nightmare" Christmas ahead as the number of parcels increases.

Royal Mail says the reforms are part of its plan to deliver a more "efficient and financially sustainable" service.

Over the last year we've been in touch with more than 30 postal staff in all four nations of the UK, as they have switched over to DM26.

It allows for second class post to only be delivered every other weekday, and is supposed to guarantee first class mail and parcels are delivered every day, by putting workers into groups of three and changing the walking pattern of rounds.

But posties speaking to us anonymously say parcels are still being prioritised, letters left behind, and time wasted in sorting and dividing mail into first and second class.

"I didn't take any first class mail out on my last shift because I was on a road that's been behind for weeks," a worker in the West Midlands told me. "But I'm sure a manager would have ticked a box to say all first class mail went out."

A Royal Mail spokesperson said the company always worked to ensure all mail - both letters and parcels - were delivered on time.

News.title: World's oldest shipwreck found off coast of Turkey
News.content:
The world's oldest shipwreck has been discovered off the coast of Turkey, archaeologists say.

They have dated it to between 4,400 and 4,700 years old, which is the Early Bronze Age, and is around the same time that the Great Pyramid was being built.

The ship's wooden structure has not survived, but the ceramic storage pots it was carrying were lying on the sea floor and, remarkably, some still contain traces of what they held inside.

The archaeologists who found the ship say it was about 10m in length and was a trade vessel carrying cargo across the Mediterranean Sea.

"The shipwreck is a time capsule at the bottom of the sea," said Prof Hakan Ãniz, from Akdeniz University in Turkey, who led the Mediterranean Archaeology Association expedition.

News.title: Zelensky and Burnham to meet in Downing Street
News.content:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham will host Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky at Downing Street on Wednesday, as the UK announces it will accelerate its delivery of air defence missiles to Kyiv.

Burnham is also expected to set out how his government will draw up further sanctions against Russia.

Speaking ahead of the meeting, Burnham said the UK was with Ukraine "for as long as it takes", adding: "Russian aggression cannot be allowed to succeed on our continent."

The UK will also urge allies to step up pressure on Russia, with Chancellor John Healey using International Monetary Fund (IMF) meetings to call for a ban on Russian liquefied natural gas (LNG).

This will be Zelensky's second visit to the UK since Burnham became prime minister. His first was in late July, days after Burnham entered No 10, when the pair met troops and led a news conference at a naval base in Portsmouth.

Burnham said: "Our rock-solid support to Ukraine is vital for keeping us safe here in the UK and ensuring those on the frontlines have the equipment they need to push back Russia.

"My message to the Ukrainian people could not be clearer, we are with you for as long as it takes, and we will go further and faster in our support to back your courageous fight for peace in Europe.

"It is not just the right thing to do, but it's the necessary thing to do."

Among the measures being announced is the quicker delivery of British Lightweight Multirole Missiles (LMMs), with the UK having already committed to send more than 5,000 worth Â£1.6bn over the next four years.

The UK will also reaffirm its plans to fully implement a maritime services ban on Russian LNG exports.

The meeting between Zelensky and Burnham follows what Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband described as a "very difficult few days" for UK-US relations due to President Donald Trump's decision to ease sanctions on Russian diesel.

Zelensky criticised the US deal with Russia, calling it a "gift" to President Vladimir Putin. Trump, in response, called for new leadership in Ukraine and criticised Zelensky for striking Russian oil refineries.

Meanwhile, Healey will ask partners at the IMF to step up support for Kyiv and ensure Russia heeds the US' call for a full energy ceasefire.

Trump claimed on Sunday that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to an immediate energy ceasefire - but hours later, Zelensky said Russian attacks on energy facilities had continued.

On Monday, Russia's Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov said Ukraine did not deserve the "respite" a ceasefire would bring.

News.title: Ex-gang boss sentenced to 40 years for orchestrating Tupac Shakur's murder
News.content:
Former gang boss Duane "Keffe D" Davis has been sentenced to at least 40 years in prison for orchestrating the murder of Tupac Shakur.

A jury found Davis, 63, guilty in September of one count of murder with a deadly weapon for the rap superstar's death in a drive-by shooting in Las Vegas on 7 September 1996. He has said he will appeal the verdict.

Prosecutors argued that although Davis did not fire the gun himself, he was the ringleader of the group that committed the murder. He admitted in his memoir that he had provided the gun used in the crime.

Davis' conviction was the first in a cold case that has intrigued hip-hop fans for nearly 30 years.

Prosecutor Marc DiGiacomo argued during Tuesday's sentencing hearing that Davis spent years "publicly grandstanding" and bragging about his role on Shakur's death, which he said, "had wide-ranging effects upon the world".

News.title: Actress Selma Blair faces charges for kicking nurse and officer after plane incident
News.content:
US actress Selma Blair has been charged with two additional assault counts over allegedly kicking an officer and a nurse after being removed from a flight.

Blair was arrested late Sunday in New York after she allegedly attacked flight attendants on a Delta plane travelling from Los Angeles to New York. The FBI issued her a federal summons accusing her of assault on board.

While appearing in court over the additional charges, the Legally Blonde star's attorney asked the judge to consider the actress's "body of work", and called Blair the "gold standard." The judge said she should not "get special treatment".

Blair has pleaded not guilty. She has since been released on bail.

She was taken to hospital after the incident on the flight. Her representatives have told the BBC that she had "experienced a medical emergency that led to the alleged conduct".

As the flight landed in New York on Sunday evening, airport officials responded to a call about "a physically abusive passenger" on the flight. Two flight attendants were hurt and one was taken to hospital, the New York Port Authority said.

Audio recorded on air traffic control details a pilot asking for medical help, describing "a bloody nose" and "some bite marks", according to CBS News, BBC's US News partner.

Blair, 54, who also starred in Cruel Intentions and Hellboy, was arrested and taken to hospital. She was issued a federal summons for a charge of assault within the special maritime and territorial jurisdiction of the US.

The two additional charges of assault, filed in state court, came after she was taken off the plane.

One of the alleged assaults happened when she was being transported in an ambulance, where she allegedly kicked a police officer. Once at hospital, prosecutors allege that she also assaulted a nurse.

News.title: Football regulator says he would quit over any political interference in Man City case
News.content:
The head of English football's independent regulator says he will resign if he encounters any political interference over the future of Manchester City.

As chairman of the Independent Football Regulator (IFR), David Kogan has the power to assess the suitability of club owners and executives.

If an independent commission's findings that the club broke Premier League financial rules are upheld, the watchdog could even force a sale.

Last month, the Prime Minister Andy Burnham was criticised for saying he would be "really concerned" if the scandal led to Manchester City's Abu Dhabi owners selling the club.

"They've been such a huge partner in the building of modern Manchester and obviously the building of Manchester City into the global force that it is," he added.

When asked about Burnham's comments, Kogan told BBC Sport: "The Prime Minister is entirely entitled to make his own observations on anything.

"We are independent. That is in the name. I am the chairman of the Independent Football Regulator and independence absolutely runs through everything we're doing.

"And no politician has tried to influence and would try to influence anything we do on that."

When asked what he would do if he did come under political pressure over the case, Kogan replied: "I would resign."

An independent commission found City had broken rules over a nine-year period between 2009 and 2018. Owners Abu Dhabi United Group (ADUG) - a private investment company belonging to United Arab Emirates vice-president and deputy prime minister Sheikh Mansour - are said to have topped up the value of commercial deals as part of a "disguised funding scheme" to the scale of Â£830m.

City insist they are innocent and have appealed.

News.title: Argentina targets UK in legal claim over Falklands oil exploration
News.content:
The Sea Lion oilfield, around 130 miles (209 km) from the Falkland Islands, contains an estimated 1.7 billion barrels of oil.

The Falkland Islands government extended exploration licences last month and the field is expected to start pumping in 2028, potentially generating huge revenues for the roughly 3,500 inhabitants of the islands.

Two oil companies â Britain's Rockhopper Exploration and Israel's Navitas Petroleum â have insisted they have valid licences issued by Britain.

The Argentinian government claims the marine environment of disputed maritime areas is protected by international law.

Its application "seeks to preserve Argentina's sovereign rights over its continental shelf and prevent activities authorised unilaterally and illegally by the United Kingdom".

In a post on X, Argentinian Foreign Affairs Minister Pablo Quirno said the government was requesting the tribunal make a number of orders against the UK, including halting new exploration permits.

But the UK government insists Sea Lion is lawful, located on the Falkland Islands shelf and regulated by the islands' government.

While the Falkland Islands government grants exploration licences, they must be signed off by the UK Foreign Secretary.

Kumaran said the tribunal application "does not invalidate licenses issued by the Falkland Islands government, alter the islands' regulatory authority, or require lawful hydrocarbon development activities to cease".

The tribunal that will consider the dispute is an independent judicial body based in Hamburg which is responsible for the fair application of the United Nations' Convention on the Law of the Sea.

FCDO officials have made clear the UK will engage with the tribunal but resist Argentina's claim firmly.

They said the aim was not to escalate the dispute but respond firmly to Argentina's latest move, and defend what the UK sees as legitimate economic activity.

They also hope to provide reassurance to businesses fearful of Argentine retribution. That is why they are introducing measures under the Protection of Trading Interests Act that would protect firms from any extra-territorial impact of Argentine laws following Milei's sanctions threats.

Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said: "Argentina's attempts to intimidate businesses and individuals engaged in legitimate commercial activity are unacceptable. Companies should be free to make lawful commercial decisions without the threat of political coercion."

The latest move comes after Milei roundly criticised the UN in his speech at the General Assembly late last month for failing to act over the sovereignty of the Falkland Islands.

He said the UN had become "a useless organisation" which only serves "arrogant parasites dressed up as well-intentioned bureaucrats".

On Tuesday Kumaran described Milei's remarks at New York as "inflammatory".

Despite its defeat in 1982, Argentina has always maintained its right to the Falkland Islands. But over the years successive governments have pressed their claim with varying degrees of aggression and diplomacy.

UK officials believes the current Argentine leadership is deliberately picking a fight ahead of elections next year.

News.title: MI5 chief warns against overstating Russian interference in Brexit vote
News.content:
MI5 chief Sir Ken McCallum has said there was Russian interference in the the Brexit referendum, but warned against overstating its impact on the result.

It comes after Prime Minister Andy Burnham provoked a backlash from some Brexit campaigners by saying it was "clear" there had been interference by Moscow in the 2016 vote.

Sir Ken said it was "a matter of public record" that there was interference in the referendum by online trolls and bots.

However, he suggested Russian trolls would be "delighted" to be front page news again, "despite the comparative unimpressiveness" of their efforts.

He added: "There is a really important difference between interference attempted and outcome swayed.

"I am a little bit anxious that we don't play into our adversaries' hands by making these trolls look 10ft tall."

Conservative deputy leader Alex Burghart branded Sir Ken's comments "an extraordinary slap down to the prime minister".

In an interview released on Monday, Burnham told The Rest is Politics podcast, external that upon arriving in Downing Street, he had asked if there had been Russian interference in the 2016 vote, adding: "I've had the clear answer that, yes, there was."

He did not provide details about the extent or nature of Russian activities during the interview, and when pressed on the subject in the House of Commons on Monday afternoon appeared to be less definitive.

The PM denied claims from Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch that he was implying the referendum result was illegitimate because of Russian interference.

He said it was a "matter of record" that Russia sought to interfere in the 2019 general election, adding: "We think it is inconceivable that this was the first time".

A No 10 spokesperson also clarified that while the prime minister believed it was highly likely Russia tried to influence the referendum result, he did not believe those efforts were successful.

The Conservatives accused Burnham of making an "embarrassing retreat" after "being caught out trying question the legitimacy of the referendum result".

News.title: Supreme Court hears church warden murder appeal
News.content:
A former deputy church warden could not have have legally caused a university lecturer's death by giving him potentially sedated whisky, the Supreme Court has been told.

Benjamin Field, 35, was jailed for at least 36 years in 2019 after being found guilty of murdering 69-year-old Peter Farquhar in Maids Moreton, Buckinghamshire.

In April, appeal judges quashed Field's conviction and ordered a retrial, but said the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) could take the case to the Supreme Court first.

And on Tuesday, five justices at the UK's highest court were asked to consider whether Field could have made Mr Farquhar cause his own death without Field legally being responsible.

During his murder trial prosecutors said Field drove Farquhar to believe he was losing his mind, secretly drugging him and spiking his whisky so his death would appear to be suicide or an accident, allowing Field to inherit his home and money.

The case has previously been adapted into Bafta winning BBC drama The Sixth Commandment, starring Timothy Spall and Anne Reid.

Before his murder trial, Field admitted burglary and fraud offences connected with relationships he had formed with Farquhar and his neighbour, fellow pensioner Ann Moore-Martin, to persuade them to change their wills.

He received a concurrent 16-year sentence for those offences. He was cleared of conspiring or attempting to murder Moore-Martin and of possessing an article for use in fraud.

The hearing was due to conclude on Tuesday, with a decision expected at a later date.

News.title: Majority of English football clubs on the edge of financial disaster, report says
News.content:
English football's finances are "dangerously exposed, with the majority of clubs living on the edge of financial disaster", according to a landmark report by the independent football regulator.

Research by the watchdog found 94% of clubs are loss-making, and more than 60% of EFL and National League clubs are technically insolvent.

The regulator (IFR) warns of "a dangerous cocktail of rising debt and an over-reliance on owner funding, leaving clubs and their fans at risk".

The 'State of the Game' report also suggests that despite the economic success of the Premier League, the financial 'cliff-edges' between and within leagues have grown significantly.

The report says:

94% of clubs in the top five English leagues made losses in 2025-26

17 clubs across the EFL and National League would be loss-making even if their players played for free

66% of clubs could not survive for more than 90 days without new owner funding

29% of clubs reported they could not survive more than 30 days without such funding

68% of clubs have no contingency plan if their owner walks away

The IFR claims "the underlying foundations of the pyramid are under intense strain and require urgent reform", and its report "should serve as a wake-up call" for English football.

"Seventeen clubs are now trading in such a way that if their players played for free, their non-playing costs would mean they would go bust," IFR chair David Kogan told BBC Sport.

"Thirty-two clubs are operating on only 30 days' cash. If the owner chooses not to pay cash at the end of the month, those clubs go bust.

"That is a very, very risky scenario. This is the moment of addressing these problems before money starts to dry up.

"We can actually fix the house while the sun is still shining and that's essentially what our role is going to be in this."

News.title: 'Unprecedented' murder cases see police force consider 'zero-hours' detectives
News.content:
An "unprecedented" number of murder investigations this year could see Gwent Police hire detectives on "zero-hour" style contracts to cope with demand.

Chief Constable Mark Hobrough said the force would normally see two or three murder probes a year, but has launched 11 in the past 10 months.

As a result it has had to fund record amounts of overtime payments and take neighbourhood officers away from community policing duties to cope with the demand.

Hobrough said the 1,535 officer-strong force would use the additional detectives if the same trend continues next year, but did not specify where they would come from or how the scheme would work.

Hobrough told Monmouthshire councillors that if demand continued he would consider cheaper alternatives to support investigations such as an "almost zero hours-type situation" to conduct interviews or special investigations outside the force's boundary.

"But that has to be of the same quality," he said, adding that he did not want to risk burnout among his staff.

He said: "They are the same people going to these incidents... They are young officers doing an outstanding job and I want to make sure we are looking after them and they stay with us long term."

The chief constable described one particular dog attack involving a baby as an "absolute tragedy", adding: "Our neighbourhood officers were the first on the scene, it's left trauma, it is bound to.

"They've been to the two murder scenes [in Monmouthshire] which were particularly harrowing incidents. It's about making sure we look after the teams, to support them and keep them in service and healthy and leave healthy."

News.title: Maserati driver given suspended sentence after killing woman in crash
News.content:
The court heard Dowling, from Caerphilly, was driving with his wife and their lifelong friend, who they were taking to a hospital appointment, when the collision happened.

Despite wet and windy conditions, heavy rain and high levels of surface water, he was travelling at 76mph (122 km/h) just three seconds before the crash.

After aquaplaning, the defendant crashed into a stationary black Audi A3 driven by Sharon, who had pulled over because of the weather conditions.

She suffered catastrophic injuries and spent three months in hospital before her death in January 2024.

In a victim impact statement, her son Luke Berry, who is expecting a child, described the family's loss as immeasurable, saying his mother would never get the chance to meet her grandchild.

He said: "She was loving, caring and would do anything to make sure I was OK.

"My family will never be the same without her."

The court was also told Jane Beedell suffered multiple injuries in the crash, including chest and elbow injuries, bruising, wounds to her fingers, bleeding on the brain and multiple fractures to her ribs.

She was placed in an induced coma for weeks, and told the court the crash had left her struggling with "fear, anxiety and depression".

"I used to be confident, strong and an outgoing individual," she said, explaining how she now relies on family and friends for daily support and struggles with everyday tasks, finding it difficult to go out alone.

After 48 years working in the civil service, Jane said she had lost her job and now relied on benefits.

She said she was devastated by the changes to her life, adding: "I sometimes feel guilty I survived".

The court heard how Kim Dowling was left paralysed with a broken back and neck and unable to speak after her voice box was removed following the crash.

Mitigating, Dowling's barrister said the defendant felt "deep regret and remorse for the loss of life", along with "strong feelings of guilt and emotional distress".

The court heard that every time Dowling looked at his wife, he was reminded of what he had done.

The case was initially brought as dangerous driving, but the charges were later changed to careless driving, to which he pleaded guilty.

Dowling had previously been disqualified from driving for six months about 15 years ago after reaching 12 penalty points, the court heard.

However, he had no previous convictions despite years of long-distance driving for work and was described as a man of "good character" who was a full-time carer for his wife.

During the sentencing, Judge Hughes said Sharon Berry had suffered a "senseless death", adding that "no amount of sentence given to Dowling would bring her back".

Dowling was sentenced to 27 months in prison for causing death by careless driving and two counts of causing serious injury by careless driving, suspended for two years.

He was also disqualified from driving for four years, ordered to complete 250 hours of unpaid community work and pay Â£1,630 in prosecution costs.

News.title: Raye hits back at ticket touts who 'overwhelmed' sign-up for Albert Hall show
News.content:
Raye has hit back at ticket touts who she says "overwhelmed" the sign-up process for an upcoming live show by using artificial intelligence (AI) bots to create "hundreds of thousands of fake registrations".

The Where Is My Husband! singer revealed there were 1.8 million sign-ups for her one-off 5,000-seat performance at the Royal Albert Hall on 23 October.

To avoid a pre-sale which she felt scalpers could exploit, Raye said the sign-up list had been manually reviewed to identify a shortlist of people believed to be "real fans".

A spokesperson for the Royal Albert Hall said they "invest heavily" in protecting their ticketing systems from "automated attacks" but the "law needs to catch up".

The award-winning artist said she had "never witnessed bots on this scale" and was changing the process as it is "so important" to her that fans can buy tickets at the face value price.

"I'm not sure what the future holds for ticketing, I do know this experience has really opened my eyes," she said in a statement shared on her social media accounts, external.

"Me and my team are going to think really hard about what we can do in the future."

Raye said the fans manually selected would receive a pre-sale link and code by email at 11:45 BST on Tuesday, and pre-sale opened shortly afterwards.

She added that the remaining tickets would be available to all on general sale.

This Symphony May Contain Hope show will showcase songs from her recent chart-topping second album, This Music May Contain Hope, that fuses old-school jazz with orchestral sound, blues, big band and soul.

The 17-track record is a concept album which explores overcoming heartbreak, self-doubt and internet trolling.

News.title: Raising gaming machine tax could put 3,800 casino jobs at risk, report warns
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Nearly 4,000 jobs in Britain’s casino sector could be at risk if the Chancellor goes ahead with a speculated doubling of taxes on gaming machines in the upcoming Budget, a report has warned.

The Government is reportedly considering an increase in the rate of machine games duty, which is the tax on fruit machines, roulette machines and other slot machines.

Currently, operators typically pay a 20% tax on profits from the machines.

However, the Social Market Foundation think tank previously indicated the Government could increase tax revenues by around £450 million by raising this levy to 40%.

A report by the Night Time Industries Association (NTIA) found increasing machine games duty to 40% could put 34 casinos and 3,800 jobs at risk.

The research, which uses modelling by consulting company EY, also found £100 million of planned investment and £73 million of tax receipts could be threatened.

Some 14,000 people work in the casino sector in Britain, across 108 licensed premises, according to the report.

open image in gallery More than half of casino customers would not otherwise have visited the local area, the NTIA found (Daniel Hambury/PA) ( PA Archive )

The report said: “The modelling is not a prediction that these outcomes will inevitably occur.

“It does, however, demonstrate why the effects of further taxation should be assessed across the whole physical business model.

“A reduction in venue profitability can affect capital investment, staffing, suppliers and the ability to develop the hospitality and entertainment offer that recent regulatory changes were designed to encourage.

“Government should therefore assess future fiscal measures against their cumulative impact on investment, employment, local economic activity and venue viability — not solely their anticipated direct tax yield.”

Joe Brown, head of gaming at Metropolitan Mayfair, said: “For me, the biggest issue is the cumulative effect of regulation, taxation, employment costs and banking restrictions rather than any single measure.”

Casino and bingo hall operator Rank Group previously warned that a third of its venues could face closure if the tax hike went ahead.

The Mecca Bingo and Grosvenor Casinos parent firm also said around 30% of its UK workforce, around 2,000 workers, would be affected.

open image in gallery Some 34 casinos and 3,800 jobs could be at risk if the tax is raised, the NTIA found (Daniel Hambury/PA) ( PA Archive )

The report further found the economic value of casino visits goes beyond the venues themselves, with casinos acting as “anchors” of the local economy.

A survey of 1,442 respondents across two weeks in September and October, included in the research, found 55% of polled casino customers probably or definitely would not otherwise have visited the local area.

It also found 72% of customers used at least one other listed business in the area of the casino, including a restaurant, hotel or parking.

Michael Kill, NTIA chief executive, said: “Britain’s high streets need businesses that give people a reason to leave home and spend time in our towns and cities.

“More than four in 10 surveyed casino customers would otherwise have stayed at home, and almost three-quarters used another local business.

“Modern casinos support jobs, hospitality, entertainment and neighbouring businesses.

“That contribution deserves recognition in the national conversation about high-street regeneration.”

Alex Oswald, managing director at Metropolitan Gaming, added: “Casinos are increasingly part of a much broader hospitality and entertainment experience.

“They attract visitors into town and city centres, supporting neighbouring restaurants, bars, hotels and other local businesses.

“This research demonstrates why we should look beyond the gaming floor when assessing the contribution of modern casino destinations.”

News.title: The Rugby League World Cup is a mess – but offers a vital opportunity
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

In a past that now seems dim and distant, this Rugby League World Cup was bound for North American shore; a bold, ambitious new step for a sport so often accused of parochialism. “It is exciting that our sport is expanding into a new destination for our premier event,” Nigel Wood, the then-chair of the Rugby League International Federation (RLIF), beamed in 2016 of a tournament due to take place in 2025. “The USA and Canada provide world-class stadiums allied to a significant multi-cultural population which made the bid so persuasive."

It did not last, of course. Little more than two years later, the USA/Canada bid was withdrawn over financial concerns – which proved prescient, perhaps, given the Toronto Wolfpack debacle that followed. At the start of 2022, in stepped France as an alternative host and another significant expansionist step.

open image in gallery Australia are the holders of the men's and women's Rugby League World Cups ( Getty )

“The rebirth of international rugby league in France has been a strategic goal for many decades. The dream of this coming to fruition has certainly sustained me. There may have been missed opportunities in the past but there won’t be any in the future,” said Troy Grant, chairman of International Rugby League (IRL), roughly 15 months before France pulled out of hosting the tournament over – yep – financial concerns.

And so it has been left to league’s land of plenty to pick up the pieces. Again utilising a combined model, Australia, New Zealand and Papua New Guinea will essentially host four World Cups in one; 53 matches across 29 competing teams from 14 different nations in the men’s, women’s, wheelchair and physical disability tournaments squeezed into a hectic month.

open image in gallery Papua New Guinea are among the host teams at the men's tournament ( Getty )

It is a venture that shows where the power of the sport lies. While it withers elsewhere, rugby league’s Australasian boom shows no sign of abating – Port Moresby’s presence as a host city is a precursor to the National Rugby League (NRL)’s expansion on to the island of New Guinea from 2028, and the use of Christchurch’s newly-built Te Kaha, officially known as the One New Zealand stadium, may prove likewise as rumours of a second franchise across the Tasman persist.

Despite a men’s tournament shrunk from 16 to 10 teams, relaxed eligibility rules remain to allow the NRL’s best and brightest to proudly represent nations of which they have heritage, befitting a sport deepened by diasporas: Lebanon and the Cook Islands may face a few tough outings but this World Cup is richened by their involvement. Even New Zealand, probably the only team capable of challenging an Australian side that has won nine of the last 10 men’s tournaments, benefit from the presence of Kalyn Ponga, a Queensland regular in State of Origin born to Kiwi parents in Western Australia.

open image in gallery Newcastle Knights full-back Kalyn Ponga will be one of New Zealand's key figures ( Getty )

A few within the sport may hope that they do emerge as genuine challengers. Australian’s hegemony is a problem both on the pitch and off for a sport that hasn’t really ever figured out how best to make the most of the international game. The structure of the men’s tournament is a little tough to comprehend, with one pool of four and one of six split into two sub-pools of three – England vs Tonga in each side’s opener may well prove a decisive game, but both Australia and New Zealand are safe bets for the last four, as organisers surely desired.

open image in gallery The London Broncos look set to play in the English top flight next season to seal a deal with the NRL ( Getty )

The build-up to England’s tilt at the tournament has been dominated with the proposed deal for NRL investment in the now sponsor-less Super League. That agreement would appear to hinge on the inclusion of the London Broncos next season, which would come after the Australian-owned club ranked below the 14 top-flight teams and Barrow in the IMG gradings despite romping to the Championship title this season.

The proposal met typically outspoken opposition from Derek Beaumont, the owner of Leigh Leopards, who said it was “just not right” in a lengthy social media post. His dissenting voice has been drowned out, though, by statements from St Helens, Leeds and the two Hull clubs expressing their support. The truth, sadly, is that it may be a deal that Super League has little choice but to sign as it seeks to safeguard its future by taking a slice of the NRL’s pie amid a challenging television rights negotiation.

open image in gallery The NRL has generally made a success of a bold move to Las Vegas ( Getty )

The worry more broadly for the sport is that this World Cup simply comes and goes without so much as a ripple outside of the already thriving waters of the South Pacific. To that end, the loss of free-to-air coverage in the United Kingdom is a major blow; Premier Sports will provide a platform of sorts but possesses little-to-no stumble-upon value.

There are sound logistical reasons for holding the women’s tournament concurrently with the men’s but there is an argument that it would be afforded more oxygen in a different slot, and maybe even offer another shop window in which to sell rugby league.

Perhaps, though, one could look at it a different way. The buoyancy of the NRL, and NRLW, is to be applauded in a market that has proved challenging for so many leagues across sports in the last decade. The State of Origin series remains a roaring success in Australia and out, while games in Las Vegas have, to some extent, broadened horizons, showcasing the pure athletic talent that is so easy to sell.

open image in gallery Meetings between Australia and New Zealand could well bookend the tournament ( Reuters )

This World Cup may not, in that context, be the sport’s pinnacle event but it could nonetheless prove a spectacular sideshow.

News.title: Why this Champions League campaign feels very different for Manchester City
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Enzo Maresca has an idea of how, to borrow a phrase adapted from an Inspiral Carpets song, this is how it feels to be City. It has changed in the last three weeks, with a guilty verdict returned in the case of 114 Premier League charges, with an official judgment that they benefited from more than £900m in disguised, and thus illegitimate, funding, with the word “sham” attached to their contracts and, for some, their achievements.

Maresca has talked about how he and his players have had to block out the “noise”, as he terms it. They did it very effectively at Anfield on Sunday, shrugging off chants about cheating to beat Liverpool 3-0.

He accepts it is harder for the Manchester City faithful to ignore it, and not merely because the subject matter goes beyond the usual back-and-forth between followers of competing clubs.

open image in gallery It is hard for Man City fans to ignore the barbs of opposition supporters ( PA )

“It probably has been more tough for our fans than for the players or for me because it's probably more complicated,” said the Italian. “Because if I am an Arsenal fan or a [Manchester] United fan and you are a City fan, I can tell you, ‘Hey, my friend, you cheat,’ or this kind of thing.”

And if that creates an image of Maresca not as a manager, but as a rival supporter, calling City cheats, his captain endured a similar soundtrack for 90 minutes on Sunday and sounded unruffled.

“I feel like when you build yourself as a player, you build yourself against any kind of noise. So be it the word you just described, or any other kind,” said Ruben Dias. “Personally, and I really feel like I speak for the whole group, we're very calm.”

open image in gallery Man City impressively beat Liverpool 3-0 at Anfield ( Getty )

How does it feel to be City, though? Top of the Premier League with a 100 percent record, having won the two away games that tend to mean most to their supporters – United and then Liverpool – and with Maresca looking a worthy successor to Pep Guardiola, they face the champions of Europe on Wednesday. Paris Saint-Germain could provided a barometer of the progress of this new-look City side.

Dias was asked if Luis Enrique’s team will win a third consecutive Champions League. “Hopefully they cannot,” he replied, speaking to his own ambitions. Yet this is more than a duel of the nouveaux riches, the last two first-time winners of the competition. They have been bracketed together for other reasons: Middle Eastern ownership from oil-rich states, heavy spending, questions if it fell within the parameters of the rules. It was not City who spent a world record €222m on Neymar.

While PSG seek to cement an era of dominance, City’s spell as Champions League ever-presents could be nearing an end: not because of their Premier League form but because of the possible sanctions for their rule-breaking; deduct enough Premier League points or expel them and their only route back into the Champions League is to win it.

open image in gallery Man City may need to dethrone PSG to return to the Champions League ( Getty )

“If this is the last Champions League for a while, I don't know,” said Maresca. The annual trips to the Bernabeu may be no more. PSG, beaten by City in the quarter-finals in 2016 and the semi-finals in 2021, might not be on the fixture list again for quite some time. Perhaps, after City supporters booed the Champions League anthem for years, they may enjoy its sound this season. They may not hear it again in the immediate future.

City started buying before they qualified for the Champions League – for Yaya Toure, David Silva and Carlos Tevez, their European debuts in sky blue came in lesser competitions – but for many a more recent arrival, it has provided part of the attraction.

And, while the sources of City’s income are a reason why they are imperilled, some of their revenue has come from the Champions League: more than £100m in 2022-23, when they won it. A club has been built with a financial model that entails expectations of competing at Europe’s top table.

open image in gallery Man City have one Champions League trophy to their name ( PA )

“For sure, the Champions League for this organisation is so, so important,” said Maresca. It has formed part of their identity, especially during the long quest to win it. The last couple of seasons have marked a regression, with exits in the round of 24 and 16 respectively.

“We're going to try to improve compared to the last two, three years, where the team struggled a bit,” said Maresca. And if that scarcely feels the main issue confronting the club at the moment, it is the only one he can address. “We know how serious the situation is, but at the same time, it's not something that we can do. Where we can do things is inside the pitch,” said Maresca.

Their fate will be determined elsewhere. “We trust the club, we're very calm,” said Dias. “We have full confidence in the club. We will defend the club. We will fight for it.”

open image in gallery Ruben Dias says Man City’s players will fight for the club ( Getty )

The bigger battle is not to stop Ousmane Dembele, Desire Doue and Khvicha Kvaratskhelia. It is not to secure a top-eight finish in the league phase or even, given City’s 4-2 defeat in Paris in January 2025 that left them 25th, to avoid an ignominiously early exit.

There is the chance that, after 16 successive seasons in the Champions League, City’s time rubbing shoulders with the elite will reach an abrupt end. Because it is not merely in friendly banter that they are being branded cheats.

News.title: New species of dinosaur discovered from fossil ‘overlooked’ for over 100 years
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

A new species of dinosaur has been discovered from a fossil found on the Isle of Wight which has been “overlooked” for study for more than a century, researchers said.

The dinosaur – a long-clawed predator the size of a large tiger – is the first of a group of two-legged carnivores called megaraptorans to be found in Europe, according to the research team led by University College London (UCL).

The fossil from which the discovery was made is a part of a skull which was acquired by the Natural History Museum in 1924.

This new species of megaraptorans, which were closely related to tyrannosaurs including Tyrannosaurus rex, lived in the UK in the early cretaceous period around 120 million years ago.

It has been named Invictibellatrix amberina, with the former meaning “unconquered female warrior”.

open image in gallery The oval hole in the fossil is where the brain would have been (The Trustees of the Natural History Museum, London/PA) ( PA Media )

Dr Cassius Morrison, the lead author of the paper documenting the finding, published in the journal Royal Society Open Science, said: “It was not the apex predator of its time, but for humans this dinosaur would have been more dangerous than a T rex.

“We would have been perfectly sized prey, about a third of their body weight. They definitely would have chased us.

“A T rex would not have bothered, as we would have been too small.

“It is a real mystery that this fossil was overlooked for so long, sitting in a drawer for nearly 100 years.

“Lots of bones are found on the Isle of Wight – who knows what else is waiting to be discovered.”

He said Invictibellatrix would have been three to four-metres long, just over a metre and a half in height, with feathers and claws between 10 and 20cm long.

It would have eaten small dinosaurs, lizards and mammals.

The fossil was originally found at the foot of a cliff on the south-west coast of the Isle of Wight by amateur palaeontologist Reginald Walter Tooley.

Megaraptors are thought to have originated in Asia before migrating through Europe.

The research was funded by the Palaeontographical Society, the Royal Society and UK Research and Innovation.

News.title: Vietnam buries remains of 731 war dead nearly 6 decades after the Tet Offensive
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Thousands carrying white flowers lined the roads in Vietnam’s Ho Chi Minh City Wednesday as the remains of 731 people believed to have been killed during the 1968 Tet Offensive were taken for burial nearly six decades after their deaths.

Vietnamese Prime Minister Le Minh Hung attended the memorial services at Le Thi Rieng Park, where the remains were recovered from mass graves after over three months of excavations. They were laid to rest at Ho Chi Minh City Martyrs’ Cemetery in the city previously known as Saigon.

Generations in Vietnam have spent decades searching for loved ones who never returned from war, hoping to recover their remains, give them a proper burial and finally find some measure of closure.

Hundreds were buried in mass graves after bloody fighting

The Tet Offensive began on Jan. 31, 1968, when North Vietnamese communist forces launched coordinated surprise attacks across South Vietnam during the Lunar New Year holiday, known in Vietnam as Tet. One of the largest campaigns of the Vietnam War, it sparked fierce fighting and heavy casualties, including in the southern capital Saigon, where communist fighters attacked the U.S. Embassy, military installations and government buildings.

Although the communist forces suffered a military defeat, the offensive shocked Washington, undermined U.S. public support for the war, and became a turning point in the conflict. “The resultant conflict has changed the pattern of the war,” The Associated Press reported in February 1968.

The South Vietnamese government collected the bodies of communist fighters and civilians and buried them in mass graves during and after the fighting, according to Vietnamese government news.

The remains at Le Thi Rieng Park, which was previously the site of Do Thanh Cemetery, were discovered during excavations that began on June 23 at the park. Over weeks, excavators painstakingly unearthed bones and fragments, along with weapons, ammunition, military hammocks and personal belongings, said the Vietnamese government’s official news portal.

They discovered a wallet containing a faded military document bearing the name Huynh Van Quen, which helped authorities identify one of the dead as a soldier from the 1st Long An Battalion, a communist unit that fought a fierce seven-day battle at Saigon’s Y-shaped Bridge.

Among the mourners was Vo Huy Thinh, 70, who remembered watching bodies being buried there when he was 12. “The memory of that burial pit has stayed with me,” he told Vietnamese state media.

An AP photograph helped uncover the graves

For years, architect Nguyen Xuan Thang pored over photographs from the Vietnam War, searching for clues to the location of the burial site.

A breakthrough came when he found a color photograph taken by an AP photographer on Feb. 12, 1968, with a caption describing three large burial trenches that each contained about 300 bodies, he told state media.

The photograph shows two men carrying a body as two others look on. Three boys stand nearby, one of them wearing shorts and a short-sleeved shirt and looking directly at the camera. A water tower is visible in the background, providing a crucial clue to the site’s location.

Thang told state media that he spent months riding his motorbike through Ho Chi Minh City, comparing old military maps with present-day landmarks, including the water tower. His research was part of a nearly eight-year effort, from November 2018 to May 2026, involving his team and the military, which helped authorities narrow their search to the park.

Investigators worked with researchers, historians, journalists and witnesses to piece together the location of the mass graves. They examined other wartime photographs, satellite images, military maps and archival records from Vietnam and abroad, comparing them with field surveys and accounts from people who witnessed the burials, said the Vietnamese government’s official news portal.

The long effort to identify Vietnam’s war dead

The recovery is part of a nationwide 500-day campaign running through July 2027 to locate the remains of about 7,000 war dead and identify them.

More than half a century after the war ended in 1975, many Vietnamese families are still searching for relatives who never returned home. The remains of about 175,000 Vietnamese soldiers have yet to be recovered, while hundreds of thousands more lie in graves without confirmed identities, according to government figures.

Of the 731 sets of remains recovered in Ho Chi Minh City, 307 were found with personal belongings, according to state media. Most have not yet been identified.

“Due to the harsh conditions of war and the passage of time, we have been unable to identify the names, ages, or hometowns of the majority of the martyrs in this group,” said Nguyen Manh Cuong, who heads the city's war dead identification efforts.

Samples have been sent to the Vietnam Academy of Science and Technology in Hanoi for DNA testing and comparison with samples from relatives.

Similar memorial and burial ceremonies will be held Thursday in three other parts of Vietnam, with the remains of what are believed to be 93 people to be buried in Tuyen Quang province. Another 65 will be buried in Hai Phong and 120 in Can Tho.

News.title: Texas prosecutor says ICE agent appeared to intentionally strike man with vehicle in Houston
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

A Texas prosecutor says a U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent appeared to use a vehicle to intentionally strike a man who took off running in Houston and that an investigation opened by his office could result in criminal charges.

Miguel Parra Hernandez, 48, needed surgery for a broken leg after being hit by a car Saturday, said Cesar Espinosa, executive director of FIEL Houston, an immigrant rights organization that is helping the man's family.

The encounter has set off new criticism over immigration enforcement in Houston, where local prosecutors have also investigated a July fatal shooting by a federal immigration officer.

Harris County District Attorney Sean Teare, a Democrat, expressed concern over surveillance footage that shows Parra Hernandez and another person jumping out of a white truck and running as a dark SUV pursues them. A vehicle strikes Parra Hernandez, who is seen on the ground seconds later.

“In a case like this, the most obvious criminal charge is aggravated assault with a deadly weapon,” Teare told FOX 26 Houston. “Meaning the car was used as a deadly weapon. And it certainly is what appears to have happened based on the surveillance footage.”

Tim Oberle, a spokesperson for ICE in Houston, said in a statement sent to The Texas Tribune on Saturday that “As ICE officers attempted to apprehend the illegal aliens, Miguel Parra-Hernandez ran in front of an ICE vehicle and was struck.”

Spokespersons for the Department of Homeland Security, which oversees ICE, did not immediately respond to an email seeking comment Tuesday.

Parra Hernandez has been in the U.S. for 34 years and was on his way to work when the encounter began, according to Espinosa. Espinosa declined to share Parra Hernandez’s status.

He said he saw two ICE agents in Parra Hernandez's room while visiting him at the hospital.

“He already had a surgery for the injury under his knee and now we’re waiting for swelling to go down in his ankle to be able to have a reconstructive surgery on his ankle,” Espinosa said.

Teare said ICE and DHS have not cooperated with his office during its investigation.

In July, Teare said DHS also ignored his request for information after an ICE officer fatally shot 52-year-old Lorenzo Salgado Araujo. The shooting was one of at least 10 deaths involving encounters with immigration officers since the start of President Donald Trump’s mass deportation campaign.

News.title: Where is hot in December? Best holiday destinations for winter sun in 2026
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

As the UK’s nights lengthen and temperatures plummet, the allure of sun-drenched shores becomes increasingly strong.

While December ushers in chilly, dark days across Britain, the Southern Hemisphere offers a vibrant escape, trading colder months for glorious summer sunshine.

Destinations such as Sydney and Cape Town boast inviting temperatures in the mid-20s, perfect for beachgoers. Meanwhile, Mexico’s bustling tourism hub, Cancun, emerges from its rainy season, promising year-round warmth.

Even within Europe, certain islands defy the continent's winter chill. Cyprus and the Canary Islands consistently enjoy temperatures in the late teens, providing an ideal climate for exploring their rich natural landscapes and historical treasures.

Here are some of the best winter-sun destinations to head to in December.



1. Gran Canaria, Spain

open image in gallery The Old Town and waterfront of Las Palmas de Gran Canaria ( Getty/iStock )

Average temperature in December: 20C

20C Average sunshine hours: 6

One of the perennially warm Canary Islands, Gran Canaria offers an equally enviable array of potential activities.

Its capital, Las Palmas, is the largest city in the Canaries and acts as a more cosmopolitan alternative to Santa Cruz de Tenerife. The historic Vegueta district is a good starting point, while popular museums include the Museo Canario (for a look into the pre-colonial history of the islands) and the former home of Christopher Columbus, which has now been turned into a museum. Other popular resort towns include Puerto Rico and Maspalomas, most famous for the vast expanse of dunes that lead to its beaches.

Maspalomas isn’t the only natural marvel on the island. Gran Canaria is covered by mountainous terrain and valleys; the Caldera de los Marteles and the barrancos (ravines) of Guayadeque and Azuaje are ideal for hiking, while the Roque Nublo (an 80-metre-tall volcanic rock) is a stunning geographical landmark. There are plenty of beaches worth exploring too, including Las Canteras, Amadores and Gui Gui.



2. Cancun, Mexico

open image in gallery Cancun is one of Mexico’s most popular tourist destinations ( Getty Images/iStockphoto )

Average temperature in December: 25C

25C Hours of sunshine per day: 7

Situated on Mexico’s Yucatan Peninsula, Cancun has a reputation as being a spring break favourite among westerners, but it is far more than just a place for seasonal partying. With December highs of around 30C and miles of white sands meeting emerald waters, it’s the ideal destination for combining winter sun with a vibrant local culture.

Nightlife isn’t hard to find (the Hotel Zone is the main party area), but neither is natural beauty, thanks to the beaches on the Riviera Maya, such as Playa Delfines. There are also great scuba diving spots on the Mesoamerican Barrier Reef. Those who want to explore the history of the area can head to the nearby Mayan Museum and the Mayan ruins of El Rey and San Miguelito.

There is also a wealth of fascinating day trips on offer to places including Merida, Tulum and Chichen Itza. The first, the state capital, is known for its mix of Spanish and Mayan influences, while Chichen Itza is one of the country’s most renowned Mayan ruins. Tulum combines ancient ruins with attractive coastal areas and natural limestone sinkholes known as cenotes.



3. Lanzarote, Spain

open image in gallery Lanzarote lies around four hours from the UK by plane ( Getty/iStock )

Average temperature in December: 19C

19C Hours of sunshine per day: 6

Spain’s Canary Islands are among the few European destinations that remain warm throughout winter, and even in December you can expect average highs of 22C in Lanzarote. This picturesque island is dotted with over 300 volcanic cones, lunar-like black rock formations and golden coastal areas.

The main settlement on the island is the port city of Arrecife, a lively but comparatively small city that is less touched by mass tourism. Lined with sand, palm trees and a long promenade, it has a charming network of pedestrianised streets and plazas that also house some of the island’s best nightlife in its marina area. Other popular resorts include the Costa Teguise and Playa Blanca.

Timanfaya National Park is the island’s main natural site, with plenty of great guided walking routes along the rugged, arid terrain and volcanic landscapes. The volcanic cliffs of Los Hervideros and the Green Caves are other notable spots for a scenic walk, while the Jameos del Agua, a natural space that doubles up as a centre for arts and culture, is an oasis-like landscape built around a series of caves and a volcanic tunnel.



4. Muscat, Oman

open image in gallery Muscat is a blend of modern and old Omani living ( Getty/iStock )

Average temperature in December: 23C

23C Hours of sunshine per day: 9

The Omani capital sits between the Gulf of Oman and the towering Hajar Mountains, with surroundings that are as picturesque as the dashes of colour between the white-washed buildings that form its skyline.

A blend of modern and old Omani living, Muscat is a characterful coastal city that serves as a good base for exploring nearby places such as Sur, Nizwa and the numerous oasis wadis. Its main neighbourhoods include Al Qurum (home to a fantastic beach) and Old Muscat, the old centre that has retained its historic charm and small-town feel. Muttrah is one of the best areas for tourists, beginning with the two-mile-long Corniche and extending to the Muttrah Souq, one of the oldest in the Arab world, where you’ll find a maze of alleyways with vendors selling everything from frankincense to jewellery.

Architectural highlights include the imposing Grand Mosque and the retro-looking Al Alam Palace, with the National Museum – chronicling Omani history back to prehistoric times – sitting opposite the former Sultan’s residence.



5. Tenerife, Spain

open image in gallery Tenerife’s weather allows for days spent on the beach, even in December ( Getty/iStock )

Average temperature in December: 18C

18C Average sunshine hours: 6

The largest of Spain’s Canary Islands, Tenerife has long been a popular holiday spot for Brits, catering to everyone from young families to party-going groups of friends. The Canaries’ location off the west coast of Morocco provides ideal year-round weather for many visitors, with average highs of around 21C even in December.

There are several towns and cities on the island, the largest of which is Santa Cruz (the capital, found near the northeastern tip of the island). The city of over 200,000 people is centred around the magnificent Plaza de España (at the centre of which lies a large, man-made lake). Other options for a resort stay include Los Cristianos and Playa de las Americas, both on the southwest coast of the island.

The island also has an abundance of natural wonders. The centrepiece is the imposing Mount Teide – the highest peak in Spain at 3,715m – and the associated National Park, where visitors can explore volcanic landscapes and hike through hills and forest, with sensational views over the island. On the coast, you’ll find the dramatic cliff faces of Los Gigantes and sandy beaches such as Playa del Duque and Playa de las Teresitas.



6. Sydney, Australia

open image in gallery Sydney is Australia’s largest city ( Getty/iStock )

Average temperature in December: 21C

21C Hours of sunshine per day: 8

Australia’s most famous city, Sydney, is home to several of the country’s most well-known landmarks. The Opera House and Harbour Bridge are synonymous with ‘Down Under’, while Bondi Beach is one of the best symbols of the laidback lifestyle that many envisage when they think of the country.

Ferries journey around the waterfront – Circular Quay to Manly is a popular route – and under the Harbour Bridge, but the city is more than just its harbour and beaches like Manly, Bronte and Balmoral.

Take a stroll around neighbourhoods such as Surry Hills, the Rocks, Newtown and Woolloomooloo, and check out the variety of galleries – such as the White Rabbit or the Art Gallery of NSW – plus other attractions including the Royal Botanic Garden and the Australian Museum.



7. Limassol, Cyprus

open image in gallery The marina in Limassol city ( Getty/iStock )

Average temperature in December: 16C

16C Average sunshine hours: 6

Cyprus is one of the warmest countries in Europe in winter, and the city of Limassol is a busier, more cosmopolitan alternative to the historic sites and sandy beaches of Paphos or the small-town feel of Larnaca.

The second largest city on the island, Limassol offers an attractive marina, where stone and white-washed buildings line limestone streets for a particularly memorable sunset view.

Products of its own ancient history include Limassol Castle and the 2,000-year-old ruins at Amathus, while those in search of nature can find a peaceful oasis at the Municipal Gardens. If you want beaches, Lady’s Mile, Dasoudi Beach and Governor’s Beach are some of the most popular in the area and are all suitable for swimming and water sports.



8. Bangkok, Thailand

open image in gallery Bangkok is among the most visited cities in the world ( Getty/iStock )

Average temperature in December: 27C

27C Hours of sunshine per day: 9

There are plenty of reasons why Bangkok is such a popular destination. Yes, it is a starting point for onward journeys to the beaches of Phuket or the tranquillity of islands such as Koh Lipe and Koh Samui, but many who touch down in the perennially popular Thai capital will stay to experience a frenetic city brimming with things to see and do.

The city’s hectic pace of life is best experienced through trips to Yaowarat Road (located in Chinatown) or Khao San Road – where the neon glow is accompanied by a hum of activity, including street vendors and popular nightlife spots – or the markets of the Chatuchak District and the north of the city, packed with evening shoppers and street food stalls.

For sightseeing, you’ll want to head to the Ko Ratanakosin area. This is where you’ll find Bangkok’s main landmarks, including the ornate Grand Palace – once the royal residence – and the attached Wat Phra Kaew, the spiritual centre of Thai Buddhism. The magnificent, 20-acre Wat Pho temple complex sits just 10 minutes away from the Palace.



9. Madeira, Portugal

open image in gallery Madeira has several great destinations; the village of Câmara de Lobos is pictured here ( Getty/iStock )

Average temperature in December: 17C

17C Average sunshine hours: 5

Madeira is a rugged, volcanic archipelago located in the Atlantic between mainland Portugal and the Canary Islands. This location gives it a pleasant, temperate winter climate, with average highs of around 20C in December.

The capital, Funchal, is a coastal city composed of winding streets that house hundreds of red-roofed, white buildings. Whether walking along the maze of streets and the waterfront promenade or taking in the beauty of the Monte Palace Tropical Gardens or Sé Cathedral, you’ll find a vibrant, friendly city with plenty to see and do.

Away from the hustle and bustle, Madeira is another island where nature is king. Its diverse landscapes include steep, jagged cliffs and rolling green hills, all of which provide ideal opportunities for adventure activities such as hiking, canyoning, mountain biking and even paragliding. For walkers, the island is home to a network of special irrigation channels called ‘levadas’; once a way to transport rainwater from the mountains to the settlements, they now provide man-made walks and hikes across the forests, mountains and valleys of the island.



10. Cape Town, South Africa

open image in gallery December is one of the best months to visit Cape Town ( Getty/iStock )

Average temperature in December: 23C

23C Hours of sunshine per day: 11

South Africa’s legislative capital is entering summer come December, making it one of the best months to visit. Temperatures over 20C make it a good time to while away days on beaches like Camps Bay and Muizenburg, though it won’t be prohibitively warm for those looking to hike Table Mountain or explore its 1,305-acre Kirstenbosch National Botanical Gardens.

Cape Town’s V&A Waterfront district is close to most of the main attractions and houses a range of restaurants, bars, markets and museums such as the Zeitz Museum of Contemporary African Art. To discover more about local culture, head to Bo-Kaap, the historic centre made up of cobbled streets overhanging the slopes of Signal Hill. For something more artsy, head to the aptly named Woodstock, the city’s creative hub.

Most visitors will want to include a trip to Robben Island in their itinerary. Lying a few miles off the coast, this island houses the prison in which Nelson Mandela served much of his sentence, and there is now a museum that offers guided tours from former inmates.



11. Gibraltar

open image in gallery The Rock of Gibraltar is the territory’s most well-known landmark ( Getty Images )

Average temperature in December: 16C

16C Average sunshine hours: 6

This British Overseas Territory at the southern edge of Spain is a truly unique blend of British, Spanish and local influences, from the development of Llanito and Gibraltarian English to the presence of traditional English pubs and the distinctly European old town.

The Rock is the territory’s most recognisable landmark; a cable car journey or hike to the top is a must-do activity to take in sweeping views of the Strait, the city and the shores of northern Africa. Plus, you’ll likely see some Barbary macaques, the only wild monkeys in Europe. For more nature-based adventures, there are an estimated 150 caves to explore within the Rock, including St. Michael’s Cave, an impressive network of caves that are home to dozens of stalactites and stalagmites, and that have previously been used as an auditorium and concert venue.

Away from the Rock, Gibraltar’s small size makes it a manageable, walkable destination. For history buffs, Gibraltar’s previous historical importance is showcased in its Old Town just as much as it is in the Moorish Castle or the Great Siege Tunnels (dug in 1779 when under siege by the Spanish and French). Alternatively, you might want to wander its streets, from Irish Town to the Windsor Suspension Bridge or the Ibrahim-al-Ibrahim Mosque.

12. Paphos, Cyprus

open image in gallery Paphos is a hub of ancient history ( Getty/iStock )

Average temperature in December: 18C

18C Hours of sunshine per day: 6

Though less warm than more far-flung destinations, Paphos is one of Europe’s most reliable locations for some shorter-haul winter sun. Average highs will be around 20C, providing pleasant days for walking by the sea or exploring the area’s ancient ruins. Beaches here are plentiful, with sands surrounded by golden cliffs and turquoise waters at locations such as Aphrodite’s Rock, Coral Bay and the Blue Lagoon.

While Paphos is an undeniably great choice for a relaxing break by the Mediterranean, some will come to explore its wealth of ancient sites. Many are contained in the Kato Pafos Archaeological Park, which houses a Roman Acropolis and Odeon (which still hosts summer music and theatre performances), and ruins of villas, mosaics and the Tomb of Kings, a necropolis dating back to the 4th century BC.

Within Paphos itself, the Old Town and Paphos Castle are good places to walk around, the latter for great views over the harbour and the former for an atmospheric fusion of recently restored period buildings, al fresco restaurants, busy avenues and ideal sunset viewing spots.



13. Hurghada, Egypt

open image in gallery Culture sandwiched between beaches awaits in Egypt ( Getty/iStock )

Average temperature in December: 22C

22C Hours of sunshine per day: 8

This former fishing town is now a major resort with both family-friendly accommodation and fun-filled nightlife. Nearby activities include diving down to Red Sea reefs and boat trips to the Giftun Islands, as well as desert excursions to traditional Bedouin villages.

If it's R&R you’re after, there are a handful of shores like Mahmya Beach to sprawl on a sun lounger, without having to contend with the scorching heat of July and August.

News.title: Where was East of Eden filmed? The New Zealand locations that played the role of 19th-century California
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

John Steinbeck’s most ambitious novel, which traces the lives of multigenerational families in rural California, has been adapted into a seven-part Netflix series.

Before the Netflix series dropped on 1 October, East of Eden’s most famous adaptation to date was the 1955 film by director Elia Kazan. Now, over seven decades later, his writer-producer granddaughter, Zoe Kazan, is creating another version as a mini-series starring Florence Pugh.

While following in her grandfather’s footsteps, Zoe Kazan is taking a different approach to East of Eden.

“The movie isn’t a super faithful adaptation of the small part of the book that it is adapting,” Kazan told Netflix’s Tudum. “What I felt was the whole epic story is an opportunity to explore, to fall in love with all these characters.”

open image in gallery Florence Pugh in 'East of Eden' ( Netflix )

The 2026 adaptation of East of Eden takes a deeper dive into Cathy’s story, and how it weaves with the Trask and Hamilton families, whose members are played by actors including Mike Faist, Christopher Abbott and Ciarán Hinds, as they settle in California’s Salinas Valley.

Yet the Salinas Valley that was described comprehensively in Steinbeck’s novel does not appear the same in the 21st Century, so the production team looked to New Zealand to bring the story to life.

We have run down the breathtaking New Zealand locations used as the backdrop to this retelling of East of Eden.

Where is East of Eden (2026) filmed?

The Netflix series was filmed in New Zealand, more than 6,000 miles away from California where the book is set.

“Not to get too nerdy about the history of New Zealand, but there was a big influx of money because of a gold rush in the Victorian era in New Zealand,” Ms Kazan says. “There’s a tremendous amount of Victorian architecture that never got torn down, and so there were many more locations available to us than there would’ve been easily in one place in the States.”

open image in gallery Ōamaru’s whitestone Victorian architecture ( Getty Images )

New Zealand’s natural, unspoiled landscape also appealed to the series producers, serving as an ideal pastoral stand-in for the Salinas Valley, as it was known between the American Civil War and the end of the First World War.

Setting the scene for the town of Salinas, the production used Ōamaru, a small town in the Waitaki District of the Otago region, a central part of New Zealand’s South Island.

The Ōamaru Historic Precinct has retained buildings from the late 1800s made of limestone, such as Smiths Grain Store and The Criterion Hotel, which can be seen in East of Eden.

open image in gallery A street in Ōamaru ( Getty Images )

The Waitaki tourism board has created an hour-long self-guided walking tour of Ōamaru that takes visitors around part of the town used in East of Eden.

Walkers can step inside The Criterion Hotel, which appears in the film and remains a working pub and hotel today. The hotel’s interior has remained true to its 19th-century heritage, with high ceilings, bars, parlours, a dining room and a Gentleman's Lounge with leather chesterfields. Visitors can eat, drink and stay at the hotel.

open image in gallery The Criterion Hotel in Ōamaru ( Getty Images )

The walk also takes visitors to other historic spots in the town that can be spotted staging the background of the dramatic story, such as the live music venue The Penguin Club and the volunteer-run Oamaru Steam and Rail Society railyard and station, which houses vintage steam engines.

Oamaru Whitestone Civic Trust property manager Jacob Barwick said filming brought excitement to the precinct, and has developed the map and walking tour to help people step into the world seen on screen.

“The production has already been a real drawcard, and we expect even more visitors once the series begins streaming,” he said.

“Visitors will be able to walk in the footsteps of the cast, explore the locations for themselves and experience the atmosphere that made Ōamaru such a compelling backdrop.”

Grant Major, the production designer for the series, told Condé Nast Traveller that scenes set on the Trask family farm were shot in the foothills of the Hawkdun Range in Otago.

The flat-topped Hawkdun Range is the centrepiece of the Oteake Conservation Park, a mountainous backcountry popular with hikers and mountainbikers.

open image in gallery Oteake Conservation Park ( Getty Images )

Much of the interior sets, such as parts of the brothels that play a central role in the story, were built in Auckland.

Mr Major also said the city has got one of the biggest collections of wooden Victorian houses in the world, which came in handy while filming.

News.title: Beaten Man Utd in crisis as Martinez launches lacerating attack on board
News.content:
And United have enough troubles as it is without a senior member of his dressing room turning so squarely against the club’s powerbrokers.

Martínez was probably only giving voice to what many fans have been saying since an underwhelming transfer window closed with more questions than answers. But for a player to talk in such blunt, excoriating terms resonated more loudly than anything a supporter or United’s most caustic critic could say.

The message was simple: you can sack all the managers you want but until you pull together a squad worthy of United’s name and give the man at the helm the tools to compete the club will struggle to escape this cycle of mediocrity.

No one can reasonably argue United’s window was a success. They went into it with the hopes of landing Elliot Anderson and other premium midfielders but ended up going for numbers over proven quality or pedigree. Youri Tielemans, Andrey Santos and Carlos Baleba were not a trio of signings anyone expected at the start of summer, not even the club itself.
