He told the BBC they had no confirmation of the German account: "It's one of the versions."

However, Stefan Meister, of the German Council on Foreign Relations, says successive chancellors in Berlin have done their best to remove the politics from the case.

"They tried to make not a big story out of it, not to give it too much attention, to give it to the institutions, to the judiciary that they will deal with it. This is not a political case. So they tried to depoliticise it," he explained.

In August 2025, Serhii K was arrested after checking into a hotel near the Italian Adriatic resort of Rimini, by police acting under a European arrest warrant issued by federal prosecutors in Germany.

After several weeks of court battles fighting extradition, Serhii K - identified in court documents as Serhii Kuznetsov - was transferred to Germany late last year.

German prosecutors allege that in 2022 he was a serving officer in the Ukrainian army, external, and he had led a group of professional divers, a boat captain and an explosives expert.

While his legal fight was going on in Italy, another Ukrainian man called Volodymyr Zhuravlov successfully challenged Germany's extradition bid in a Polish court.

In a ruling very different from Italy's Supreme Court, the Polish judge ordered Zhuravlov's release in October 2025, stating that the attack on the pipelines was not unlawful, and if Ukraine had organised an armed mission it was "justified, rational and just".

Although he was released by the court in Warsaw, he was arrested last August in Croatia on suspicion of being a suspect who "participated in the dives necessary" for the sabotage.

Last month, Croatia approved his extradition, although it is not clear when that will happen, and if his case could become part of the Hamburg trial.

Despite the difficult nature of the case for Kyiv and Berlin, Ukrainian MP Oleksandr Merezhko does not believe it will spoil relations as "it's in the best national interests of Germany to continue to support us".

World.title: MI5 chief warns of threats to UK from Russia, Iran and AI
World.content:
MI5 is devoting more resource to countering state threats than during the Cold War, the head of the intelligence service has said.

Sir Ken McCallum said threats from foreign adversaries had quadrupled in the last decade, with Russia "aggressor number one" as well as increased Iran-linked aggression against Jewish sites and military bases.

At an annual speech in London, MI5's chief said Russia was waging hybrid warfare at a time when AI was "supercharging the cyber-security contest between attackers and defenders".

He also warned of rising threats from "extreme right-wing terrorism" and said MI5 had "caught terrorists seeking to exploit AI," including by integrating the technology with drones.

He said the biggest threat from the misuse of AI was extremist groups using the technology to harness new and existing bioweapons.

However, he noted that work countering terrorism and state threats was now "pretty much of equal scale" which he described as a "huge shift" in recent years.

Sir Ken said Russia had stopped short of "conventional conflict" against Nato and is instead trying to unsettle European countries while its progress in its full-scale invasion of Ukraine is "minimal and horrifically costly".

Hybrid warfare or hybrid attacks are loose terms which tend to describe non-military methods, for example cyber-attacks, sabotage or misinformation, designed to exert pressure and destabilise an adversary.

These are quite often employed using proxies, but Russia always denies involvement in such attacks despite growing evidence to the contrary.

Sir Ken said MI5 successes in identifying and expelling Russian spies from the UK had left the Kremlin dependent on paying proxies for attempted attacks.

"With its traditional covert footprint eviscerated by almost 1,000 expulsions since the invasion, the Kremlin's global toolkit is weak, he said.

"So we see them scrambling to pay criminals to do their bidding."

He added: "These are not the actions of a great power with the strategic upper hand."

His comments come as a growing number of leaders across Europe have warned Russia may be preparing attacks to test their commitment to supporting Ukraine.

Asked after the speech about Prime Minister Andy Burnham's recent comments that Russia interfered with the Brexit referendum, Sir Ken said it was "not new news" that there had been attempts from Moscow but distinguished between "interference attempted" and "outcome achieved".

He said it was a matter of public record that there were pieces in Russian media and "so-called internet trolls and bot farms" seeking to influence the Brexit debate, but also stressed that the result of the 2016 referendum was "not in dispute".

He added that he was "worried" about the the ongoing debate on Russian interference.

"I am a little bit anxious that we don't play into our adversaries' hands by making these trolls look 10ft tall," he told reporters.

World.title: Missiles intercepted near Riyadh after Saudi coalition hits Yemen fuel depot
World.content:
Missiles and drones have been intercepted over Riyadh after the Saudi-led coalition fighting in Yemen struck a fuel depot near the Houthi-controlled capital, Sanaa, its spokesperson says.

Maj Gen Turki al-Maliki said projectiles targeting the Saudi capital and other cities were intercepted. No casualties have been reported however fires broke out at Saudi oil company Aramco's building in Dhahran after the strike, officials said.

It comes after the coalition struck the Yemen Petroleum Company's al-Sabaha facility on Tuesday night.

The latest tit-for-tat attacks in the conflict "have potentially negative spillovers for everybody, everywhere", the chief of the the International Monetary Fund said.

The Houthis warned they would target the airport and Aramco refinery in Saudi Arabia's capital, Riyadh, and Aramco's headquarters in the eastern city of Dammam.

It came as the Saudi cabinet, chaired by Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, said the Iran-backed group would "bear the consequences" of its recent deadly attacks on the kingdom.

Thirteen people were killed when a missile hit King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh on Saturday, while another person was killed in a similar attack there the following day.

On Tuesday, the coalition said its forces had destroyed three drones north of Riyadh.

The Houthis have said they are targeting airports, oil and gas facilities, and military bases in Saudi Arabia with missiles and drones in response to deadly Saudi strikes on territory that they control in western Yemen, including Sanaa.

The Saudi-led coalition has been providing air support for Yemeni pro-government forces mounting an offensive on Yemen's Red Sea coast and several other front lines.

World.title: Bank of America hit with $1.2bn fine for money laundering failings
World.content:
Bank of America has been fined $1.2bn (Â£910m) for failing to detect potential money laundering and other illegal activity, the US Treasury Department said on Tuesday.

The banking giant failed to report over $5bn in suspicious activity to the government, $1bn of which posed national security and illicit finance risks, the Treasury said.

Those failures included not flagging transactions that possibly involved Chinese money laundering networks or trade-based laundering "with a substantial nexus to the southwest border", according to the Treasury.

"Our team is far along with and committed to completing the work required to address the issues raised by our regulators," Bank of America told the BBC.

The announcement came less 24 hours before Bank of America was due to announce its quarterly earnings on Wednesday morning.

"Our third-quarter results will include a non-tax-deductible charge of $1.2 billion impacting net income by approximately 17 cents per share," the bank said in an emailed statement.

"We have already dedicated substantial personnel and resources to our ongoing remediation efforts, and those costs are in the current expense base," it added.

In announcing the fine, the third-largest the department has ever imposed, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said: "When a bank of this size fails to meet its anti-money laundering and sanctions obligations, the consequences extend far beyond its own walls, exposing the entire US financial system to significant illicit finance risks."

The Treasury said the bank overly relied on inquiries from outside parties like law enforcement and other financial institutions instead of its own internal controls.

This meant that it "effectively outsourced to third parties a substantial portion of its proactive detection and reporting obligations," the department said.

As part of the settlement, Bank of America admitted that it "willfully violated" the Bank Secrecy Act by failing to maintain a compliant anti-money laundering programme, conduct required due diligence on foreign correspondent accounts and file suspicious activity reports, the Treasury said.

The $1.2bn fine included penalties imposed by the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) and the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC).

The OCC's $750m fine marked the biggest penalty it has ever levied.

OFAC said its settlement with the bank was tied to 475 apparent violations of sanctions programmes including those on Russia and Iran, narcotics, and global terrorism.

The settlement amount of $11.6m reflected the determination that Bank of America's apparent violations were "non-egregious", OFAC said.

World.title: Trump ousts Kimberly Guilfoyle as US ambassador to Greece after corruption allegations
World.content:
President Donald Trump's administration has asked Kimberly Guilfoyle to resign from her position as US ambassador to Greece, according to White House Press Secretary Katie Zacharia.

Guilfoyle, a former Fox News host, was facing mounting scrutiny over reports she allegedly asked a Trump donor to pay her hefty credit card bill in exchange for access to the administration and behaved inappropriately while in Athens.

Trump said on Tuesday that she had done a good job, but will "not be there" in Greece any longer. "I didn't like what I read," he said.

Guilfoyle vowed to defend herself, calling the claims false, and said the ambassadorship had been the "honour of a lifetime".

Zacharia announced during her first - and unusually short - media briefing that Guilfoyle "had been asked to resign" without providing more details.

"She has been a wonderful asset to the team, and we wish her well," she said.

Guilfoyle, the 57-year-old ex-wife of California Governor Gavin Newsom, was first nominated as envoy to Athens in December 2024, a month before Trump returned to the White House as president.

Around the same time, news broke that she had broken up with Donald Trump Jr, to whom she was engaged.

In a lengthy post on X on Tuesday, Guilfoyle thanked President Trump, said she would always be a loyal supporter and denied any wrongdoing.

"I intend to vigorously defend my name, my reputation, and my integrity," she wrote, adding she will "not allow false accusations to define my decades of public service".

Her position had become increasingly tenuous as allegations of improper behaviour mounted over the past week.

A series of text messages seen by the BBC - and first reported by The Wall Street Journal - appear to show Guilfoyle asking for the money from Eric Deters, a long-time Trump ally.

"It won't show up anywhere if you wire money to American Express," she wrote in one Signal message.

In another message - dated just days before her US Senate confirmation hearing last July - Guilfoyle wrote: "Honey please I need you to get this done for me today."

World.title: Russian strikes hit key power plant in Kyiv, Zelensky says
World.content:
A key energy facility supplying Kyiv with heating and electricity has been hit in a Russian ballistic missile attack, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has said.

Darnytska CHP-4, or CHPP-4, and a residential building were hit in a strike the president said came with "no early warning from our partners".

Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said two people had been killed and 21 injured in the missile strike on the apartment block late on Tuesday. He said "several energy facilities" in Kyiv had been hit in what he, without giving more detail.

Kyiv has reported multiple Russian strikes since US President Donald Trump said an energy ceasefire had been agreed by Russia and Ukraine two days ago.

In the early hours of Wednesday, Klitschko said the "massive missile attacks" had knocked out power to parts of Kyiv.

Kyiv officials have urged residents to stay in shelters after declaring a red alert due to a "missile threat".

Following the strikes on Tuesday, Zelensky said: "Ukraine supported an energy ceasefire. Russia is targeting yet another power plant and the lives of our people.

"This is absolutely unjust: when they are destroying our energy infrastructure, and Ukraine is not even receiving early warnings about ballistic missile launches," he added.

"It is important that the world does not stay silent about this. And it is important that the United States really see what is happening and who is responsible for this war continuing."

It is the second night in a row Kyiv has been hit by Russian missiles, and comes as Zelensky prepares to meet UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham at Downing Street on Wednesday to discuss accelerating air defence supplies to Kyiv.

Following strikes on Monday night, there was speculation America had cut off access to key intelligence enabling Ukraine to track incoming threats.

Earlier on Tuesday, Trump denied that was the case.

"We are helping them and we are sharing intel," he said.

"We want the war to end. So we're working with them and with Russia on getting the war to end."

Asked about Russian strikes on Ukrainian energy sites, Trump said: "Ukraine hit many sites the day before."

But he demurred when asked if Russia had broken a ceasefire. He said both countries want the war to "come to an end" but "just don't know how to get there".

It comes after Zelensky said on Sunday that a 60-day ceasefire would allow â his country to hold presidential elections, following comments from Trump that "it's time for Ukraine to get a new president".

Following Trump's announcement on Sunday, Russia's Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said Ukraine doesn't deserve the "respite" a ceasefire would bring.

Lavrov added that under any ceasefire, Europe would be able to "pump [Ukraine] with new weapons" for it to continue the war.

CHPP-4, which provides heating and electricity to the Dniprovskyi district and parts of the Darnytskyi district, has been hit multiple times during the war.

It was severely damaged in a separate Russian missile attack in February this year, which forced it to shut down.

That strike left more than 1,000 residential buildings without heating and hot water, along with 47 schools, 72 kindergartens and 18 medical institutions, according to Reuters.

World.title: SPECIAL REPORT: Insecurity exposes Zamfara communities to recurring cholera outbreaks
World.content:
It started with a sharp pain in Musa Saidu’s stomach.

The 20-year-old initially thought little of it. But the pain was soon followed by fever, vomiting and frequent watery stools. Within hours, his condition had deteriorated.

This was August 2025, during a cholera outbreak in Bukkuyum Local Government Area of Zamfara State, where Mr Saidu and his family were living after fleeing their home in Dan Bago village following attacks by bandits.

Like thousands of people displaced by years of insecurity in the state, the family had already lost the stability of home. Now, as Mr Saidu became increasingly ill, they faced another problem: getting medical care.

His parents first tried what they could afford. They gave him some medicines and mixed a local herbal remedy with water, hoping his condition would improve. But it did not.

With the health facility serving their community no longer functional, the family eventually took Musa to the Orphan and Less Privileged Clinic (OLPC) in Bukkuyum town, where he was diagnosed with cholera.

But reaching a health facility did not immediately end their difficulties.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The clinic was struggling with an influx of cholera patients. Only three health workers were on duty, while essential medicines were unavailable.

Many residents affected by the outbreak were brought to the same facility, while some had to seek treatment elsewhere because of shortages of staff, medicines and space.

For displaced families such as Mr Saidu’s, the outbreak exposed a problem that went beyond cholera.

Years of insecurity have displaced many communities across Zamfara, forced health workers away from some rural areas and disrupted access to healthcare, safe water and disease surveillance. These are services that become particularly important during an outbreak of a disease that can kill within hours if severe dehydration is not treated.

When insecurity becomes a health crisis

Zamfara is one of the states hardest hit by the insecurity that has spread across north-western Nigeria over the past decade.

What began largely as cattle rustling has evolved into organised violence by armed groups commonly referred to as bandits. Communities have been attacked, residents killed or abducted and thousands forced from their homes.

The armed groups have also imposed levies on some farming communities, stolen livestock and harvests and carried out kidnappings for ransom.

Data obtained from the Mass Atrocities Tracker show that 28,974 people were killed across Nigeria between 2021 and 2025. Borno recorded the highest number, with 4,539 deaths, followed by Zamfara with 3,936 and Kaduna with 2,811.

Zamfara recorded the highest number of abductions during the same period, with 5,447 people kidnapped. Kaduna recorded 4,050 and Niger 3,331.

But deaths, abductions and displacement are only some of the consequences.

In Bukkuyum LGA, residents and health workers told The ICIR that insecurity has also weakened access to healthcare. Some communities have been deserted, while health workers have stopped providing services in areas they consider unsafe.

Reports in 2025 indicated that only about 200 of Zamfara’s more than 700 Primary Healthcare Centres (PHCs) were functional, with persistent insecurity blamed for the closure or abandonment of many facilities.

For residents of affected rural communities, the closures mean illness can require travelling several kilometres, sometimes through unsafe areas, before reaching a health worker.

For people displaced by violence, the risks are compounded by overcrowding, poor sanitation, poverty and limited access to safe water.

During a cholera outbreak, those conditions can become deadly.

Displaced, then confronted by cholera

Buba Muhammad had already fled his home in Sadawa with his family because of repeated bandit attacks when his son began vomiting and passing frequent watery stools.

The 40-year-old farmer and his family were living as displaced persons in Bukkuyum, where several families shared limited space and sanitation facilities.

Mr Muhammad immediately tried to find medical help.

There was no functioning health facility close to where they were staying.

“My first attempt when my son was affected was to go to a hospital, but there was no facility nearby,” he said. “I had to take him to a medicine shop.”

The medicines he obtained there did little to improve the boy’s condition.

As the vomiting and diarrhoea continued, Mr Muhammad decided to take him to General Hospital Bukkuyum, the nearest facility where he believed the child could receive appropriate treatment.

But another problem awaited them.

The hospital was struggling with patients arriving from communities affected by the outbreak.

“We didn’t receive the proper care we expected immediately because there were not enough staff,” he recalled.

“There was no bed space. We even kept our patient on the floor before a staff member later found us a bed.”

The illness also placed a financial burden on a family already displaced by insecurity.

Mr Muhammad said they spent heavily on transportation and medicines, including drugs they had to buy outside the hospital after receiving prescriptions.

“The only solution to ease the hardship of such unwanted incidents or outbreaks is to provide facilities in our local communities,” he said.

But he said restoring healthcare without addressing insecurity would leave another part of the problem unresolved.

“We need security in our locations because we are not safe; there are attacks every day and night in our locations. The government needs to double its efforts to end the problem.”

A preventable disease finds fertile ground

Cholera is an acute diarrhoeal disease caused by consuming food or water contaminated with the bacterium Vibrio cholerae. Without prompt treatment, severe cases can lead to rapid dehydration and death.

It is also largely preventable through access to safe water, adequate sanitation and good hygiene, while prompt administration of oral rehydration solution and other appropriate treatment can substantially reduce deaths.

Yet cholera has repeatedly affected communities in Zamfara State.

In 2023, a World Health Organisation (WHO) report recorded 907 suspected cholera cases in the state, representing about 28 per cent of Nigeria’s suspected cases during the period covered.

The state was affected again in 2024. WHO reported more than 700 cases and over 30 deaths across Zamfara and neighbouring Sokoto during the period covered by its report.

By 9 July 2025, Zamfara had recorded 1,619 suspected cases, six confirmed cases and 31 deaths across 12 of its 14 local government areas, according to a UNICEF situation report.

UNICEF said suspected cases increased by 30 per cent within one week, with children and young people accounting for 62 per cent of reported cases.

The crisis continued.

In August 2025, an outbreak in communities in Bukkuyum LGA killed at least eight people and affected more than 200 across 11 communities, according to residents and local officials cited by Reuters.

For residents already dealing with displacement, unsafe water and weakened healthcare services, the outbreak exposed how insecurity can magnify an otherwise preventable public health emergency.

The Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (NCDC) identifies unsafe water, inadequate sanitation and poor hygiene as major factors driving cholera transmission.

In parts of Bukkuyum LGA, insecurity has made addressing those risks more difficult. Residents have been displaced into congested settlements, some health facilities are non-functional, and health workers say reaching remote communities for surveillance and other services can be dangerous.

For some patients, simply reaching treatment presents another risk.

For rural residents, treatment can mean a dangerous journey

In Masu community, Salihu Bello returned home one afternoon to find his two sisters seriously ill.

“They had stomach pain, and became very weak,” he recalled. “Later we realised it was cholera.”

With no health facility in the community, the family initially relied on local remedies.

But the sisters’ condition continued to worsen. Seeking treatment meant undertaking a difficult journey to Bukkuyum town. Before reaching the town, they had to cross a river, a challenge that has become even more dangerous since insecurity forced many healthcare workers to stop visiting remote communities.

“Sometimes health workers used to come to our community, but because of security problems they stopped,” Mr Bello said.

As night fell, the family began the trip. Fear of bandits lingered throughout the journey, but Mr Bello said concern for his sisters outweighed every other worry.

“At that moment, we were not thinking about insecurity. We only wanted to save them. It took about three hours before we received attention because we arrived very late at night,” he said.

When a health worker eventually prescribed medicines, he had to wake a medicine vendor before dawn to obtain them.

His sisters remained under observation for about 24 hours before their conditions improved.

For Mr Bello, the experience showed the cost of having no functioning healthcare facility nearby.

“If we have a health facility in our community, things will be easier, considering how quickly the disease can affect the human body,” he said.

“Before a patient from our community gets to the hospital, they suffer a lot. Having our own health facility would make access to treatment much easier.”

But the health facility is only part of what residents say they need.

In Masu and other communities around Bukkuyum, preventing cholera begins with something even more basic: clean water.

Unsafe water keeps the risk alive

In communities around Bukkuyum, residents said access to clean water remains a major challenge.

Some depend on streams for drinking, cooking and other household needs. In Dan Bago, residents said people and cattle sometimes rely on the same water sources.

For a community already vulnerable to cholera, such conditions increase the risk of transmission.

Nigeria’s 2021 Water, Sanitation and Hygiene National Outcome Routine Mapping (WASHNORM) report highlighted the scale of the country’s water and sanitation challenge.

The report, based on a survey of more than 24,600 households, estimated that approximately 179 million Nigerians, about 87 per cent of the population, lacked access to safely managed drinking-water services.

The situation was particularly difficult in northern Nigeria. The Northeast had the lowest access rate at just two per cent, compared with 29 per cent in the Southwest.

Although 67 per cent of the population had access to basic water supply services, about a quarter of Nigerians still relied on unimproved or surface water sources.

Muhammadu Sadawa, a community leader, said insecurity has made the situation worse by forcing residents from their homes and concentrating displaced families in already strained settlements.

“Another major challenge we have in our community now is insecurity,” he said. “Most of our people left the community because of banditry. Where we are now living is too congested and very dirty. That congestion helped the disease spread among us.”

Mr Sadawa said access to healthcare had also deteriorated.

Although there is a health facility in his community, he said it is no longer functional.

“We have a facility, but it is not in existence. There are no staff, no drugs. The building is dilapidated and almost collapsing,” he said.

During the cholera outbreak, residents therefore had to look elsewhere for treatment.

He said some families struggled to obtain care before outside assistance arrived, while others faced delays because of distance and the cost of treatment.

“Many people died, and it took a long time before we received any intervention. Some people were treated, some were not. I have a relative who spent over N50,000 on treatment. Many families went through the same thing,” he said.

For critically ill residents, reaching another health facility can itself be difficult.

Mr Sadawa said residents must cross a river to reach Bukkuyum town, where they can get more comprehensive medical care.

“When someone is sick, we have to cross a river before reaching the hospital. We need the facility renovated, and we also need a bridge or canoes to help us cross,” he said.

He estimated that more than 50 people in and around his community were affected during the outbreak, with some becoming ill in displacement settlements before being taken to Bukkuyum town for treatment.

Health workers struggle to reach vulnerable communities

At General Hospital Bukkuyum, Abdullahi Salihu remembers the pressure as cholera patients arrived from communities across the local government area.

“At the time of the outbreak, it was very tense and hectic considering how patients were being brought to the hospital,” he said.

“Some survived, some were quarantined, and unfortunately some died.”

According to Mr Salihu, insecurity complicated the response.

Patients who could leave affected communities were brought to the hospital. But health workers had limited options for people trapped in settlements that were difficult or unsafe to reach.

“As health workers, we faced a lot of challenges because of insecurity,” he said.

“Some people managed to bring patients from their communities because they had no other option. But for those who could not come out, there was little we could do for them.”

Mr Salihu said government officials, politicians and humanitarian organisations provided intravenous fluids, antibiotics, rehydration supplies and other support during the outbreak.

But insecurity was not the only challenge.

Many of the patients were displaced people who had lost livelihoods and struggled to afford transportation, food and other necessities.

“Most of them were displaced from their communities with nothing to eat,” he said. “Then the outbreak added another difficulty to their lives.”

Zaharadeen Abdullahi, a health worker at the Women and Children Welfare Clinic in Bukkuyum, also described insecurity as a major obstacle to preventing and responding to outbreaks.

“Insecurity is a major contributing factor to outbreaks like this,” he said.

“We have services, vaccinations and awareness programmes, but because of security challenges many health workers cannot reach vulnerable communities.”

Some affected settlements are more than 10 kilometres from health facilities, Mr Abdullahi said. In some areas, insecurity has also limited the transportation options residents can use.

“Some communities cannot use motorcycles because of security threats,” he said. “People have to walk long distances or use donkeys. Because cholera requires urgent treatment, these delays can lead to deaths.”

He said displacement had created additional risks.

“Most of the affected people are internally displaced persons living in congested conditions,” Mr Abdullahi said. “Many rely on unsafe water sources, and stagnant water is still being used for drinking and household activities.”

He acknowledged support from the Zamfara State government, UNICEF and other organisations during the outbreak but said greater investment was needed in health facilities, medical supplies and outreach to vulnerable communities.

Insecurity weakens disease surveillance

Shakir Balogun, an epidemiologist, said recurring cholera outbreaks in conflict-affected parts of Zamfara should not be viewed simply as a disease problem.

He said they also expose weaknesses in healthcare access and disease surveillance created or worsened by years of insecurity.

Mr Balogun said insecurity had affected the health system’s ability to reach some communities even before recent cholera outbreaks.

“When insecurity makes communities difficult to reach, children can be missed by immunisation programmes, cases of Acute Flaccid Paralysis (AFP) can escape surveillance, and cases of acute watery diarrhoea can similarly go undetected or reach treatment late,” he said.

“The pathogen changes; the health-system vulnerability does not.”

Mr Balogun said these weaknesses became particularly evident during the 2025 cholera outbreak.

According to him, the African Field Epidemiology Network (AFENET), with technical and financial support from the US Centres for Disease Control and Prevention, deployed eight Field Epidemiology Training Programme residents and a graduate to support Zamfara’s response between 11 September and 2 October 2025.

The team worked with state authorities in four high-burden local government areas.

Mr Balogun said the response identified cases in inaccessible and insecure settlements. It also identified under-reporting linked partly to weak active case searches and insecurity, as well as delayed reporting and incomplete records.

Other challenges included transporting stool samples to the state reference laboratory, shortages of essential supplies outside initially prioritised LGAs and inadequate personnel in some health facilities.

The findings suggest that insecurity can affect almost every stage of outbreak control, from identifying a sick person and reporting a suspected case to testing samples and getting treatment to patients.

Mr Balogun said strengthening community-based surveillance could help close some of those gaps.

Trusted residents and community structures, he said, can help identify and report suspected cases when conventional health teams cannot safely reach affected settlements.

Treatment also needs to be brought closer to vulnerable communities.

“If insecurity means a severely ill patient has to travel several hours or cross an unsafe area before receiving ORS or intravenous fluids, geographical access itself becomes a determinant of survival,” he said.

He recommended establishing oral rehydration points and treatment units close to vulnerable communities, backed by reliable referral systems for patients who develop severe disease.

Authorities should also use surveillance and previous outbreak data to identify communities repeatedly affected by cholera and position essential supplies there before outbreaks escalate, he said.

“You do not want to begin moving ORS, IV fluids, chlorine and other essential supplies into a hard-to-reach community only after an outbreak has accelerated,” Mr Balogun said.

“We should use surveillance and historical data to identify recurrent hotspots and position supplies before the rainy season.”

Treatment alone will not stop recurring outbreaks

Bringing treatment closer to affected communities could save lives, but Mr Balogun said it would not eliminate the conditions that allow cholera to return.

He said safe water and sanitation remain fundamental.

Vaccination and effective case management can reduce infections and deaths during outbreaks, he said, but communities will remain vulnerable if they continue to depend on unsafe water and inadequate sanitation.

Mr Balogun recommended strategic use of oral cholera vaccines among high-risk populations and in communities with recurring outbreaks, particularly where insecurity makes immediate improvements to water and sanitation infrastructure difficult.

But he cautioned against treating vaccination as a replacement for those investments.

“Vaccination is an additional layer of protection, not a substitute for water, sanitation, surveillance and access to treatment,” he said.

Government turns to community-based response

The Zamfara State government said it has adopted community-based measures to maintain disease surveillance and provide basic cholera support in areas where insecurity makes conventional healthcare difficult.

The state Ministry of Health, working with the World Health Organisation (WHO) and other partners, has also begun developing a Multi-Hazard Incident Action Plan to strengthen preparedness and response to public health emergencies, including cholera.

Ahmad Muhammad, the Zamfara State epidemiologist, acknowledged the difficulty of reaching communities affected by insecurity.

He said one strategy has been to identify community health workers from insecure areas, bring them to safer locations for training and then send them back to support residents.

“We train them, particularly the community health workers there. So we train them and then allow them to go back to their community and support them,” he said.

Mr Muhammad said trained workers are provided with available medical supplies and asked to report suspected cases so health officials can track whether infections are increasing or declining.

He said the approach forms part of the state’s risk communication and community engagement strategy, under which people with health-related roles in affected communities are trained to support local outbreak response.

Patients who can safely be evacuated are moved to accessible areas for further treatment, including general hospitals and the treatment centre at the Infectious Disease Hospital in Gusau, he said.

He attributed the state’s reduced cholera burden this year, compared with the previous year, to interventions including community sensitisation, improved hygiene, and oral cholera vaccination.

“Community sensitisation and improvement of hygiene, oral cholera vaccination campaign last time. The burden of the disease has reduced this year compared to last year,” he said.

He said the government had also intensified water, sanitation and hygiene interventions, including measures aimed at reducing open defecation.

“So I think those strategies have really gone a long way in mitigating the impact,” he said.

But for residents of communities where health facilities remain closed or poorly equipped and safe water remains difficult to obtain, the conditions that make cholera dangerous have not disappeared.

This reporting was supported by the Centre for Journalism Innovation and Development (CJID).

World.title: Shell to sell Nigeria’s domestic gas business to Vaaris Energy
World.content:
British energy giant Shell has signed an agreement to sell its full interest in Shell Nigeria Gas Group to indigenous energy firm Vaaris Energy Limited, marking its planned exit from Nigeria’s domestic gas distribution business.

Shell announced the deal in a statement on Tuesday, noting the transaction forms part of the strategy to simplify its portfolio and concentrate investments on areas of competitive strength.

“Shell Nigeria Gas has served industrial and commercial customers in Nigeria for more than 25 years, supported by the commitment and expertise of its people,” Elohor Aiboni, Shell’s country chair in Nigeria, said.

“We believe this agreement provides a much stronger platform for the business’ next chapter under new ownership. Shell continues to focus on strategic Deepwater and Integrated Gas positions in Nigeria.”

The companies did not disclose the financial terms of the transaction.

The deal is subject to regulatory conditions and approvals, and covers Shell Nigeria Gas Holding B.V., established in 2019, which holds all but one share in Shell Nigeria Gas Limited.

Until the transaction is completed, Shell Nigeria Gas Group will remain part of Shell and continue to serve its customers, while operating as usual.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Established in 1998, Shell Nigeria Gas supplies natural gas to industrial and commercial customers and runs about 170 kilometres of pipeline infrastructure across Ogun, Abia and Rivers states.

The company serves more than 130 connected customers, but is not involved in upstream gas production, liquefied natural gas (LNG) operations or international gas trading.

Vaaris Energy is a privately held Nigerian energy company with interests across the oil and gas value chain.

The divestment reflects Shell’s broader efforts to streamline its global portfolio under Chief Executive Officer Wael Sawan, and focus on businesses and projects offering competitive returns.

READ ALSO: Shell faces trial over alleged misleading evidence in Nigeria oil spill case

In Nigeria, the company said it would continue to prioritise deepwater operations and integrated gas, including its interest in Nigeria LNG.

Last week, Shell reportedly raised its forecast for third-quarter integrated gas production to between 740,000 and 780,000 barrels of oil equivalent per day, up from its previous estimate of 570,000 to 630,000 barrels of oil equivalent per day.

World.title: UN General Assembly adopts pandemic declaration, urges stronger global cooperation
World.content:
The United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) has adopted a political declaration on pandemic prevention, preparedness and response, reaffirming the need for stronger international cooperation and sustained investment to protect the world against future pandemics.

The declaration was adopted on Tuesday following a vote in which 153 countries voted in favour, three against and two abstentions, according to the voting record provided.

The United States, Israel and Argentina voted against the declaration, while New Zealand and Paraguay abstained.

The declaration outlines measures to strengthen disease surveillance, improve national health systems and ensure equitable access to vaccines, treatments and other essential medical products during health emergencies.

It also calls on countries to strengthen their preparedness and response capacities, particularly in addressing weaknesses exposed by the COVID-19 pandemic.

WHO welcomes declaration

The World Health Organisation (WHO) welcomed the adoption, describing it as a renewed commitment by countries to work together to prevent and respond to future pandemics.

WHO Director-General Tedros Ghebreyesus urged member states to translate their commitments into action, particularly by concluding negotiations on the Pathogen Access and Benefit-Sharing (PABS) system.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

“WHO welcomes this strong commitment by UN Member States to continue working together on pandemic prevention, preparedness and response,” he said.

Mr Ghebreyesus said concluding negotiations on the PABS annex would be an important step towards opening the Pandemic Agreement for signature, followed by ratification and its eventual entry into force.

The declaration was considered by member states at the second UN General Assembly High-level Meeting on Pandemic Prevention, Preparedness and Response on 25 September 2026 before being referred to the full General Assembly for adoption.

Priorities for pandemic preparedness

The declaration calls for sustained investment in national, regional and global capacities to prevent, detect and respond to emerging pandemic threats.

It also frames pandemic preparedness as a development, economic and security priority that requires coordinated action beyond the health sector.

Among its priorities are stronger disease surveillance and monitoring systems, improved national preparedness capacities and implementation of the amended International Health Regulations (2005).

The declaration further calls for greater community participation, equitable access to pathogens and benefit-sharing arrangements, expanded local and regional manufacturing capacity, increased investment in research and development, and sustainable financing for pandemic preparedness and response.

These measures are intended to help countries identify emerging threats earlier, respond more effectively to outbreaks and improve the availability of essential health products during emergencies.

The emphasis on equitable access also reflects concerns about disparities in the availability of vaccines, treatments and other medical countermeasures during global health emergencies.

Pandemic Agreement negotiations remain crucial

The declaration identifies the conclusion of negotiations on the PABS annex as an urgent priority for member states.

The outcome of the negotiations is expected to be considered at the next World Health Assembly in May 2027, or earlier through a special session.

Concluding and adopting the annex would clear a key outstanding hurdle in the process towards the Pandemic Agreement’s entry into force.

The agreement is intended to strengthen international cooperation in preventing and responding to future pandemics, including through improved coordination and arrangements for sharing the benefits derived from access to pathogens.

WHO said the declaration provides a framework for strengthening global health security through collective action, solidarity and equity.

However, its impact will depend on countries translating their political commitments into practical action through adequate financing, stronger health systems and sustained cooperation at national, regional and international levels.

READ ALSO: Nigeria elected to UN Human Rights Council

Background

The COVID-19 pandemic exposed significant weaknesses in global health systems, including inadequate disease surveillance, limited emergency preparedness and unequal access to essential medical products.

Many countries, particularly those with limited manufacturing capacity, experienced difficulties obtaining vaccines, diagnostic tools and treatments during the pandemic.

These challenges prompted renewed international efforts to strengthen health security and establish mechanisms for more coordinated responses to future outbreaks.

The WHO Pandemic Agreement was developed as part of these efforts, with a focus on international cooperation, equity and improved preparedness.

Although the newly adopted UN declaration reinforces these commitments, it is a political declaration rather than a legally binding agreement.

Its effectiveness will therefore depend on the steps taken by member states to fulfil their commitments, including increased financing, stronger health systems and sustained international cooperation.

World.title: UCL Roundup: Lookman scores as Atletico beat Man United, Osimhen falls to Barca
World.content:
Ademola Lookman scored nine minutes after coming off the bench as Atlético Madrid defeated Manchester United 2-0, while Victor Osimhen played the full 90 minutes in Galatasaray’s 4-1 home defeat to Barcelona in Tuesday’s UEFA Champions League action.

Lookman seals Atlético victory

Atlético took the lead after just 53 seconds when Pablo Barrios converted Alex Baena’s cutback.

Manchester United threatened through Bryan Mbeumo, but goalkeeper Jan Oblak made key saves to keep the visitors out. Alejandro Grimaldo also came close for Atlético, striking the angle of the post and crossbar with a free-kick.

Johnny Cardoso thought he had doubled Atlético’s lead, but his goal was ruled out after a VAR review found a handball by Marcos Llorente in the build-up.

Introduced in the 70th minute, Lookman struck in the 79th to seal the victory for Atlético, who claimed their first points of the league phase and extended their unbeaten run against United to five matches.

Barcelona punish Galatasaray

At Rams Park, Galatasaray took a surprise lead in the 28th minute when Aleksey Batrakov’s shot deflected off João Cancelo and into the net.

Cancelo made amends by curling in Barcelona’s equaliser shortly before half-time. The visitors then took control, with Lamine Yamal providing two assists in four minutes as Barcelona completed a 4-1 comeback victory.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Osimhen played the full match but couldn’t prevent Galatasaray from suffering a heavy home defeat. The result extended Barcelona’s winning run across all competitions to 10 matches.

Other results

Arsenal beat Lille 3-0 with Bukayo Saka and Eberechi Eze on target for the Gunners. Sporting CP also defeated Lens 2-0 while Villarreal overcame Napoli 3-1.

In a mouthwatering seven-goal thriller, Club Brugge edged Inter 4-3, RB Leipzig beat PSV 1-0, and Sabah Baku defeated Slavia Prague 2-0.

There was plenty of drama and goals in Norway, where Bayern Munich were held to a 3-3 draw by Viking.

World.title: Afrilition: Mental models, By Adéwálé Àjàdí
World.content:
The foundation of all systems is the mental model, and the work ahead of Africa that Afrilition raises will transform our future. Unfortunately, we in the African world function within the current global system in reaction to it and with wider acceptance of its current mental model. Based on history and cemented into our formal socialisation that we call education, we are indoctrinated into different forms of inferiority. We accept a lot without critical review, but it is not just us; the wider world mostly also accepts that Westernisation is the surest and only route to modernisation. The depth of this mental model hides the Janus face of the system, which is White supremacist and based on the pseudoscience of race. It does not stand up to basic scrutiny by its own logical or empirical standards.

I have not practised law for a while, but yesterday I had reason to go to the Supreme Court of Nigeria to honour a friend and son who was being elevated to a senior role. I sat in the Foyer for hours, enduring the ceremony and the pomposity of performance. Intelligent people prancing as caricatures in European wigs and dressed for pageantry in 19th-century faux fashion. There were horsehair wigs; the only missing thing was powdered faces. It exemplified the levels our elites are reduced to. On the other side, as speeches droned on for hours in their monotone, I fell asleep many times, hoping I did not snore. My eyes fixed on the Statue of Lady Justice on the wall. She brought a smile to my face, telling me hope is not lost. She stood black and dignified, resting on the wall, with what were Northern Nigerian features; she had her head wrap solid, holding the sword and scale with an elegant buba that just barely touched the scale.

The sword on the other side expressed the glamour of the abundance of her outfit. She seemed aware of the work that needed to be done to move even herself from an Africanised European symbol as she stood on the Latin words beneath her feet with disdain. At least Lady Justice no longer borrows her robe. There was the crowd of well-wishers, many in the unique cultural refinement of their various people. A wonderful sight: the variety and diversity of ethnic excellence expressed in headgear and outfits from across the variety of people who are Nigerians. If there is a country in which people carry culture with dignity, it is in Nigeria, along with the contradiction of colonial mentality.

World.title: Tinubu can’t handle insecurity: Why does he want another term?, By Ugoji Egbujo
World.content:
A nation that conscripts its graduates cannot lose them on a federal highway, allow exchange of ransom, and call the aftermath a rescue.

A few days ago, thirty prospective corps members left Oyo for the East. Twenty were taken near Owerri, on the Owerri–Onitsha road at Umunoha. Ten escaped. The local people who witnessed the abduction could not stand the apathy of the security agencies, so they blocked the road to force a chase. The situation borders on hopeless.

When the police woke from their slumber, they announced that their drones had located the hostages and their abductors. The impression sold to the public was that they had them surrounded. Perhaps the corps members would be luckier than the Chibok girls, who were taken away without the government knowing which way the terrorists went with them. The Owerri police said they could not immediately exrract the hostages because the area was mined. The story did not instill any hope. The nation listened with resignation.

Youth corps members are supposed to be the babies of the federal government. The government cannot conscript youths into a compulsory national service in far-flung places and fail to protecr them. The mass abduction of citizens, let alone corps members, should provoke any responsible government. But perhaps not a government that cares more about optics than substance, about politics and retaining power than purposeful leadership. The real tragedy is that the government has lost sense of shame .

A few days after the kidnap, the government announced triumphantly that it had rescued the corps members, crediting the rescue to the joint security team and emphasising that no ransom was paid. While the government was basking in glory, pictures emerged of the abducted, frazzled corps members moving furtively on a village street, all alone. Could they have been rescued and allowed to walk bush paths?

The parents then went on television. They had scraped, borrowed, and paid. The demand opened at ₦50 million a head and was bargained down to about ₦5 million or ₦6 million, some of it in dollars. The government that said it was watching captives and captors by drone had not noticed the families negotiating, gathering the money, and flying to Owerri to deliver it. It had not seen the captives leave. The Imo commissioner of police says he is not aware of any ransom. Claiming a rescue while the people who paid are on television is worse than silence. It is complicity.

Orire followed the same script. Only with a worse ending. Forty-four pupils and teachers were taken from Oriire in Oyo on 15 May and held for fifty-six days. The presidency said security forces rescued them, arrested eight, killed some, and paid no ransom. A surviving teacher, Zaccheaus Olatunde, told a different story. Two teachers were killed . Sone negotiatipn happened. No fighting took place. The survivors were shown the way home. No public accounting has yet matched the official version to a captured camp. Yet another ‘miraculous’ release passed off as military rescue .

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The terrorists who carried out the Oriire abduction are not ghosts. The Oyo government insinuated as much. In the case of Owerri, two species of bandits operate in the neighbourhood where the kidnapping happened. Unknown gunmen have a camp and control the left side heading into Owerri, while rogue Fulani herdsmen operate in the forest on the right side. The security agencies are aware of the presence and identity of these groups. The Governor of Zamafara said the same thing. That was why the local people at Uumnoha went irate when the corps members were abducted and the agencies hesitated to give an immediate chase. What exactly is Tinubu’s strategy against the rampaging insecurity?

What, then, is the strategy? Mass kidnapping is now followed by a release, and the release is claimed as a rescue. The exchanges are mediated by ransoms. Kidnappers keep the money and the camp. Security agencies have not learned hostage work, and the public is asked to applaud a story the payers have already contradicted. A trade conducted on those terms can only fatten the crime. Ransom is not rescue. The scourge is festering.

Recently it was reported that NNPC booked ₦11.2 trillion as receivables from the federation for advances and the cost of protecting oil and gas assets. We pay local mercenaries and shadowy folks ungodly sums to do the basic work of the police and the military, which are massively underequipped and miserably understaffed. Why have we made being an outlaw so rewarding? Why is the nation-state so weak? We cant live by random ransoms.

Tinubu’s first tenure has been marred by insecurity. But Tinubu wants a second term even though he has no clue how to tackle it. Nothing in the first term shows a strategy. Mass abduction, a week of tales, a release, a denial of ransom, no convictions: that is the operating model.

Tinubu met this model. He has not broken it. The South-East unknown gunmen and north-west bands are known to local security agencies. But they are not cleared. The police are too thin for the territory. The army is spread across internal duties it was not built for. The pipelines are hired out to mercanaries who are paid hundreds of billions and who it appears are helping the reelection effort. What new idea has Tinubu got?

Tinubu wants a second term anyway. Nothing in the first has shown a plan that would make the second different. Kidnappers cannot keep walking away with the ransoms while the government blows its trumpets. What, exactly, would he come back to do?

Ugoji Egbujo writes from Lagos.

World.title: Wike defends cross-party coalition for Tinubu’s re-election
World.content:
The Minister of the Federal Capital Territory (FCT), Nyesom Wike, has defended the growing cross-party political alliance backing President Bola Tinubu re-election in 2027.

Mr Wike, who made this known during a monthly media chat in Abuja on Tuesday, dismissed claims of internal crisis.

He described the rainbow coalition as “a movement bringing together figures from the All Progressives Congress (APC), All Progressives Grand Alliance (APGA), Peoples Democratic Party (PDP), and other political platforms to support Tinubu”.

He emphasised that support for the presidency transcends individual party cards, adding that he would be leading Tinubu’s re-election campaign in FCT and Rivers despite being in the PDP.

Highlighting key figures driving the coalition across various states, Mr Wike pointed out Governor Charles Soludo of Anambra State, a member of APGA serving as a key campaigner for Tinubu in his state.

“In Osun, Governor Ademola Adeleke (PDP) is supporting the president at the national level while maintaining party identities sub-nationally,” he said.

Replying to critics who see a contradiction in political figures backing the presidential candidate of one party while contesting sub-national seats under another, Mr Wike dismissed the perceived friction as a “problem that does not exist.”

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

“Why would anybody say there is a problem there? Take Soludo—he is supporting Mr. President, but that does not mean his party will not field candidates for the House of Representatives or state assembly.

“It tells you leadership capacity. If you speak to your people and they listen, that is political strength,” the minister said.

READ ALSO: Wike admits working with APC to defeat PDP in 2024 Edo governorship election

Addressing opposition figures and state governors who have publicly acknowledged the president’s performance, Mr Wike singled out the Governor Bala Mohammed of Bauchi State for praising national infrastructure and governance strides despite belonging to an opposition party.

He urged politicians to put national progress above blind partisanship

“Time has come, not because of your political party, to just say the chief manager of the country has done nothing for the sake of politics. Politics must be a do-or-die affair.

“For us, whether anybody likes it or not, Mr. President has done well,” he said.

Earlier on Tuesday, Messrs Wike, Soludo and Adeleke had been named as members of the APC Presidential Campaign Council despite belonging to PDP, APGA and Accord Party. They are to coordinate President Tinubu’s re-election campaign in their respective states.

(NAN)

World.title: The weaponisation of yesterday, By Umar Yakubu
World.content:
If Nigeria is to break this destructive cycle, we must transition from what Nietzsche termed “reactive” history to a critical history — a deliberate practice that scrutinises past structural failures, disarms historical grievances, and prioritises civic nation-building over score-settling… Until we stop using yesterday as a weapon to fight today’s political battles, we will remain trapped in Hegel’s grim reality: a nation that speaks of its history incessantly, yet learns absolutely nothing from it.

An excess of history makes life wither and degenerate – Nietzsche

During the recent presentation of the book, Emirs of Zazzau: A Biographical Study (1808–2025), in Zaria, Professor Usman Bugaje made a compelling case for the imperative of historical knowledge. He reminded the audience of the indispensable need to study history if we are to understand our present and navigate our future.

His call echoes a familiar refrain heard across our public space: we must study history so that we do not repeat it. Yet, as the contemporary state of our country so vividly demonstrates, this moral maxim is flawed in its popular execution. Do we truly learn from history in Nigeria? Or do we absorb the past merely to stock an arsenal of grievances, inciting new hatreds under the guise of remembrance?

When examined through the lens of political philosophy, Nigeria’s fraught relationship with its past reveals a tragic paradox: historical knowledge, rather than serving as a lamp for national building and institutional enlightenment, has too often been transformed into a flame for social division.

The Fallacy of the Lesson

In his Lectures on the Philosophy of History, the German philosopher Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel made a stark observation that remains unnerving in its precision: “What experience and history teach is this — that nations and governments have never learned anything from history, or acted upon principles deduced from it.”

Hegel’s insight was born, not out of structural critique of human governance. States rarely act out of wisdom derived from old textbooks. In Nigeria, this Hegelian paradox is visible in the cyclical nature of our political and economic crises. The structural failures that precipitated the tragic collapse of the First Republic — unbridled regionalism, electoral fraud, state-sanctioned corruption, and the politicisation of everything serious, such as the security and economy — are continuously replicated by successive generations of political elites. Each generation claims to understand the national tragedies of the past, yet each reproduces the exact institutional dynamics that triggered those ruptures.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

We quote history in anniversaries and public lectures, but our approach to governance largely remains unchanged. Some will argue that it is worse. We do not learn from history because we treat historical knowledge as an ornamental academic exercise, rather than an imperative for structural reform.

When history is weaponised…memory becomes a catalyst for retribution instead of being a teacher of reflection, caution and progress. Every new generation is taught whom to mistrust based on acts committed long before they were born.

The Arsenal of Memory

If we do not extract constructive lessons from the past, what then do we do with it? We seem to have turned it into a weapon.

In his essay On the Use and Abuse of History for Life, Friedrich Nietzsche distinguished between historical memory that serves human flourishing and history that poisons the present. Nietzsche warned against an obsession with the past that creates a “reservoir for grievances” — a state wherein a society becomes so intoxicated by old injuries that it loses the capacity to build a viable future.

This, for me, is the central dilemma of modern Nigeria. I have often told a few friends that I sympathise with people who possess retentive memories, because most of them use that gift to remember grievances, rather than the good. The engagement with our past has largely devolved into a competitive accounting of historical injury. The 1966 military coups and the devastating Civil War are rarely examined through an objective, institutional framework meant to foster structural reconciliation. Instead, they are routinely weaponised in daily political discourse to justify ethno-regional marginalisation or to cultivate sub-national resentment.

Across the geopolitical zones, historical narratives of pre-colonial dominance, colonial favour, and post-independence betrayals are invoked not to build empathy, but to validate contemporary prejudice, resource hoarding, and political exclusion. And who benefits from all this chaos? The people or the elite?

As my friend Husein Adeto Bello succinctly observed, the underlying issue lies in why people engage with the past in the first place: many study history merely to acquaint themselves with historic grievances and inherit legacy talking points, without ever pausing to ask what they can do to ensure their generation — and the next — does not perpetuate those same grievances.

When history is weaponised in this manner, memory becomes a catalyst for retribution instead of being a teacher of reflection, caution and progress. Every new generation is taught whom to mistrust based on acts committed long before they were born.

Whose History Are We Learning?

This brings us to a fundamental question in the philosophy of history: Whose history is actually being told?

History is never a neutral recording of facts; it is an interpretive narrative shaped by power and context. In a multi-ethnic federation formed through arbitrary colonial amalgamation, there is no singular, universally accepted “Nigerian narrative.” There exists, instead, a contested marketplace of competing ethnic, regional, and religious memories.

When history is learnt through the narrow lens of tribal insularity, it fails to construct a shared civic identity. Instead, it codifies “us versus them” dynamics, ensuring that the act of remembering directly incites more hatred. And we can’t grow with such history.

The historical decision to remove history from the basic school curriculum for years left a critical void. A generation grew up learning their past not from rigorous, critical academic inquiry, but from informal, highly partisan narratives. These informal histories function primarily as national myths of triumph and victimisation:

One group learns a history in which they are the perpetual victims of systemic betrayal.

Another learns a history framing them as the rightful, historical custodians of power.

Yet another learns a history that regional erasure has rendered almost invisible.

When history is learnt through the narrow lens of tribal insularity, it fails to construct a shared civic identity. Instead, it codifies “us versus them” dynamics, ensuring that the act of remembering directly incites more hatred. And we can’t grow with such history.

Reclaiming Yesterday for Tomorrow

The continuous cycle of political instability, inter-communal conflict, and ethnic polarisation in Nigeria validates the fear that knowing the past can easily degenerate into nursing old wounds.

If Nigeria is to break this destructive cycle, we must transition from what Nietzsche termed “reactive” history to a critical history — a deliberate practice that scrutinises past structural failures, disarms historical grievances, and prioritises civic nation-building over score-settling.

Until we stop using yesterday as a weapon to fight today’s political battles, we will remain trapped in Hegel’s grim reality: a nation that speaks of its history incessantly, yet learns absolutely nothing from it.

Umar Yakubu is the executive director of the Center for Fiscal Transparency and Public Integrity.

World.title: NAFDAC bursts Trade Fair Complex den of fake energy drinks, wine, whisky ‘manufacture’
World.content:
Some of the discovered ‘manufacturing’ tools.

By Chioma Obinna

The National Agency for Food and Drug Administration and Control, NAFDAC, has uncovered a suspected counterfeit drinks production facility at Zamfara Plaza, BBA Trade Fair Complex, along the Badagry Expressway, Ojo, Lagos State.

Read Also: Toxic pesticides in food: NAFDAC warns of health risks, seizes ₦800m banned chemicals

The Agency arrested two suspects allegedly involved in the illegal operation.

The suspects, identified as Okafor and John, were arrested during an enforcement operation in a two-storey building where equipment and materials allegedly used to repackage and produce counterfeit alcoholic and energy drinks where discovered.

The raid, according to NAFDAC, followed credible intelligence and surveillance on suspected counterfeiters operating within the Trade Fair International Market.

Speaking during the operation, the Assistant Director of the Investigation and Enforcement Directorate of NAFDAC, Mr Kunle Ojo, said the agency caught some of the suspects in the act and recovered drums, filters, packaging materials, a heating device and other equipment allegedly used in the illicit production process.

“Gentlemen of the press, as you can see today, when we came, we caught some red-handed producing all kinds of alcoholic drinks,” Ojo said.

“What we have discovered today is a lot, and it’s mind-boggling. We are here to protect the lives of many Nigerians.”

Ojo said the agency intensified its enforcement activities ahead of the festive season, when demand for alcoholic and other beverages typically rises.

He warned that the circulation of counterfeit drinks posed a serious public health concern, urging suspected manufacturers to abandon the illegal trade.

“You are killing Nigerians in order to make money, which is not good,” he said, appealing to those involved to stop the activities.

The NAFDAC official disclosed that the agency would investigate the source of the products, the raw materials used and the individuals allegedly financing or directing the operation.

“Where are they getting the products from? Where are they getting their raw materials? Who is employing them to do this kind of dangerous activity?”

He added that the agency would evacuate the recovered materials and products to its warehouse for further action, including destruction in accordance with applicable procedures.

“Those people that we have arrested today will be dealt with administratively and definitely will face the law,” Ojo said.

Ojo also appealed to Nigerians to support the agency by providing credible information about suspected counterfeit production facilities.

“If you see something, say something,” he said, assuring informants that their identities would be protected.

Confession

One of the arrested suspects, Okafor, who identified himself as a drinks dealer in the market, in an interview with Vanguard at the scene said: “I deal on drinks. I change the bottle of the drink. It’s not that the bottle is not good. It’s the drink in there, because the other one is already damaged. So that’s why we are putting it to the next bottle,” he said.

Also speaking during the operation, Mrs. Christiana Obiazikwor, Deputy Director, NAFDAC Public Relations, said the agency routinely carried out surveillance, seizures, arrests and destruction of unregistered and counterfeit products, despite public criticism that it was not doing enough to tackle the menace.

“NAFDAC is still at work. We are on the streets. We are in the markets. We are everywhere,” she said.

Obiazikwor explained that enforcement teams often conducted operations without publicity to avoid alerting suspected offenders or triggering confrontations.

She said the agency decided to take journalists along on the latest operation to demonstrate its activities and reassure Nigerians that it remained committed to protecting public health.

“Most of the things they do, we don’t publicise them so that we don’t raise alarm,” she said, adding that enforcement officers continued to visit suspected production and distribution points.

She urged members of the public to report suspected counterfeit production and distribution directly to NAFDAC rather than merely posting allegations on social media.

“There’s no point going to social media to create fear. Report to NAFDAC and we’ll do the needful.”

Obiazikwor assured informants that the agency would protect their identities, urging Nigerians to provide credible information that could assist investigations.

Speaking, the Assistant Director, Head Public Relation, Investigation & Enforcement, Mrs. Victoria Jennifer Akudu, explained that the raid was part of the agency’s routine efforts to uncover illegal manufacturing activities and protect consumers.

“Every day, our people are in the field. Our enforcement department, they are on the field trying to uncover this. And they do a lot,” Akudu said.

She explained that the agency routinely confiscated products, carried out seizures and destroyed offending goods, adding that the latest operation was intended to demonstrate the work being done by enforcement officers.

“This is just a routine activity of our enforcement directorate,” she said.

Akudu further disclosed that the suspected operators had allegedly moved from an earlier location after enforcement action, prompting officials to continue tracking their activities.

“We have confiscated and sealed off the place. They moved to another place. This time around, we passed through the back door. And that is how we are able to get them,” she said.

She urged Nigerians to report suspected counterfeit products directly to NAFDAC rather than allow rumours and unverified claims to create unnecessary public fear.

Akudu assured the public that the agency remained committed to its responsibilities, stressing that its enforcement teams were continuing operations against suspected manufacturers and distributors of illegal products.

“I will ask Nigerians not to fear. We are alert and we are alive. We are doing our statutory function the way it should be,” she said.

NAFDAC officials said the operation formed part of continuing efforts to remove counterfeit, adulterated and unregistered products from the Nigerian market.

The agency reiterated that consumers could be exposed to serious health risks when drinks were repackaged under the labels of established brands without proper quality controls or verification of their contents.
