World.title: S’ Court ruling: INEC gives Oct. 24 deadline for parties to submit omitted candidates
World.content:
By Omeiza Ajayi

ABUJA: The Independent National Electoral Commission INEC has given political parties that believe their candidates were wrongly left off the final list for the 2027 governorship election until 24th October, 2026 to notify it.

The deadline follows a Supreme Court ruling that bars parties which failed to submit membership registers from sponsoring candidates.

National Commissioner and Chairman, Information and Voter Education Committee, Mohammed Kudu Haruna, said in a statement in the wee hours of Tuesday said the Commission applied the apex court’s decision in finalising the governorship list.

“The Commission, while finalizing the list of candidates for the Governorship election applied the above decision of the Supreme Court and excluded political parties that failed to comply with Section 77(5)-(7) of the Electoral Act, 2026, in relation to fielding of candidates,” Haruna said.

The judgement, in INEC v. Zenith Labour Party, Appeal No. SC/CV/495/2026, was delivered on 24th September, 2026. It arose from INEC’s appeal against a Court of Appeal decision which “nullified the provisions of Section 77(5)-(7) of the Electoral Act, 2026 requiring the submission of membership registers as a prerequisite for the conduct of valid party primaries.”

The Supreme Court overturned that position. It held that the provisions “are constitutional and mandatory for all political parties.”

The Court also upheld the constitutionality of Item No. 2 of INEC’s Timetable and Schedule of Activities, which required political parties to submit their membership registers between 21st April and 10th May, 2026.

According to the statement, “failure to comply with the provisions of Section 77 (5)-(7), renders the defaulting political parties ineligible to sponsor any candidate for the election.”

Haruna said the Commission acted “in accordance with Section 287(1) of the Constitution of the Federal Republic of Nigeria, 1999 (as amended).”

He noted that the final list of Presidential and National Assembly candidates “had already been published on 12th September, 2026, thirteen days before the Supreme Court delivered its judgement.”

On the window for complaints, the statement said: “Under Section 32(2) of the Electoral Act, 2026, political parties that believe their candidates were wrongly left off the list have 14 days from the date of publication to notify the Commission. The deadline is 24th October, 2026.

“The Commission assures the public of its commitment to transparency, the rule of law and the credibility of the electoral process.”

World.title: 2027: No real tension between Wike, APC governors  -  Morka
World.content:
APC spokesman, Felix Morka.

The All Progressives Congress (APC) spokesperson, Felix Morka, has dismissed reports of a rift between the party’s governors and Minister of the Federal Capital Territory, Nyesom Wike, saying there was no real tension between them.

Morka said the perceived disagreement was a “false battle” because both the APC governors and Wike were committed to President Bola Tinubu’s re-election bid ahead of the 2027 general elections.

He spoke on Tuesday during an interview on Arise Television’s News Day, following Wike’s inclusion in the APC presidential campaign council.

“It was a false battle to begin with. I mean, I don’t think there was any real tension between those positions because they united in their extraordinary commitment to the re-election of the president,” Morka said.

He noted that the Progressive Governors Forum comprised governors elected on the APC platform, while Wike, a former Rivers State governor, was a member of Tinubu’s cabinet and a vocal supporter of the President.

According to him, their shared political interest made reports of a disagreement between them largely insignificant.

Morka said the publication of the presidential campaign council list had also clarified the roles of those involved in Tinubu’s re-election campaign.

He pointed to the inclusion of governors who do not belong to the APC, describing it as evidence of Tinubu’s ability to attract support across party lines.

“Governors, who are not of the APC, now [are] front and centre, coordinating some of our activities in their respective jurisdictions,” he said.

The APC spokesperson described the development as a new phase in Nigeria’s democratic politics, arguing that the President was bringing politicians from different parties together around a common objective.

“What we’re witnessing today in our country is novel. It’s really a new dawn for democracy,” Morka said.

He argued that the collaboration was unusual in a presidential system, where political parties are generally expected to compete against one another.

According to Morka, Tinubu was transcending party differences by building a coalition of political actors to support his administration and re-election campaign.

“We’re seeing a president who is transcending all of the divides and really nullifying what I call the politics of difference between these partisans and bringing them together under the same umbrella to pursue a common agenda for the good of the people,” he said.

World.title: APC drafts PDP, Accord, APGA into Tinubu’s campaign council
World.content:
***Why Tinubu pushed for Wike, Soludo, Adeleke despite internal push-backs

***Rainbow Coalition has come to stay, Wike tells APC govs

By Omeiza Ajayi

ABUJA — To ensure a smooth sail for President Bola Tinubu in the January 16, 2027 presidential poll, the Presidency and ruling All Progressive Congress, APC, have included leading opposition figures and governors in Tinubu’s re-election council, in spite of strong push-backs from sections of the party.

In its expanded Presidential Campaign Council, PCC, that will be inaugurated today in Abuja, the APC

included Minister of Federal Capital Territory, FCT; Nyesom Wike of the Peoples Democratic Party, PDP; Governor of Osun State, Ademola Adeleke of Accord; and his counterpart in Anambra State, Chukwuma Soludo of the All Progressives Grand Alliance, APGA.

Wike was appointed coordinator of the party’s campaign in Rivers and the FCT, Soludo coordinator for Anambra, while Adeleke was named coordinator for Osun.

The revised list also incorporated former Gombe State governor and serving PDP Senator, Ibrahim Dankwambo, who was appointed as adviser to the Campaign Council alongside Obafemi George, who will also advise on media strategy.

Key leadership positions within the campaign hierarchy were also confirmed in the updated release.

Senator Abdulaziz Yari retained his position as Director-General of the re-election campaign.

Former Edo State Governor, Senator Adams Oshiomhole, serves as Deputy Director-General for Mobilization, while Chief of Staff to the President, Femi Gbajabiamila, takes on the role of Deputy Director-General for Administration.

Deputy Speaker of the House of Representatives, Benjamin Kalu, was named Deputy D-G South II, while the Speaker of the Rivers State House of Assembly, Martin Amaewhule, will serve as South-South Deputy Coordinator for State Assemblies

Mobilization.

Minister of Works, David Umahi, was appointed Deputy D-G for Infrastructure and Sensitization.

Delta State Governor, Sheriff Oborevwori, has been named Director of Finance, while Ogun State Governor, Dapo Abiodun, and Chairman of the Nigeria Revenue Service, NRS, Zacch Adedeji, will jointly coordinate fund-raising operations.

Former Kano State Governor, Abdullahi Ganduje, was named Director for Stakeholder Mobilization, while former Lagos State Governor, Babatunde Fashola, serves as the South-West Zonal Coordinator for Stakeholders’ Mobilization.

Chief Ayiri Emami was named Director for Special Duties, while former Super Eagles captain, Joseph Yobo was appointed Deputy Director for Sports Sector Mobilization.

A notable difference in the new list is the appointment of all 32 APC governors as campaign coordinators for their respective states, while Sharafadeen Alli, the party’s governorship candidate in Oyo, was appointed coordinator for the state.

For Bauchi, Mohammed Abubakar, the APC governorship candidate, was appointed campaign coordinator, while Chijioke Chukwu, the party’s flagbearer in Abia, is coordinator for the state.

Minister of Solid Minerals, Dele Alake, continues his role as Official Spokesman for the Campaign Council.

Joining the media communications team are Minister of Aviation, Festus Keyamo, Abdulmumin Jibrin, Lere Olayinka (media aide to FCT Minister Wike), and Segun Sowunmi.

In administrative and operational roles, Imo State Governor, Hope Uzodimma, continues as Secretary of the Campaign Council, supported by APC National Secretary, Senator Ajibola Bashiru, and Hadiza Bala-Usman as Deputy and Assistant Secretaries, respectively.

Representative James Faleke will serve as Deputy Director-General for Election Planning, Coordination, and Monitoring.

Unlike the first list, the new one contains 14 advisers, including Chief Bisi Akande, Aremo Segun Osoba, Secretary to the Government of the Federation, SGF, George Akume, former Cross-River south senator; Florence Ita-Giwa, former governor of Ogun State, Ibikunle Amosun, former APC national secretary, Iyiola Omisore, and former Coordinating Finance Minister, Wale Edun, among others.

The expansion of the campaign structure underlines the ruling party’s strategy to build a broad-based political coalition as momentum builds toward the 2027 general elections.

A statement by the APC National Secretary, Senator Ajibola Bashiru, said the campaign council will be inaugurated today.

Why Tinubu pushed for Wike, Soludo, Adeleke despite internal push-backs

Last night, details emerged on the strategic calculations behind President Tinubu’s decision to formally include non-APC political heavyweights, despite internal push-backs from key party stakeholders.

The move followed concerns raised by a section of APC loyalists who privately urged the President to allow the trio operate and campaign for his re-election bid from outside the formal council structure.

Party sources said opponents of the inclusion argued that integrating non-card-carrying members into official campaign structures could displace dedicated party loyalists, dilute party identity and trigger local friction in states such as Osun, Rivers and Anambra.

Presidency sources and campaign strategists revealed that President Tinubu remained firm on their formal inclusion to ensure an all-inclusive campaign structure and to establish a unified management of campaign resources across non-APC controlled strongholds.

According to insider accounts, the President’s decision was finalised only after receiving firm assurances of direct support and alignment from Wike, Soludo and Adeleke, with the agreement to trade off or retain other positions in their states.

Rather than relying on informal or parallel external support groups, President Tinubu prioritised a consolidated command centre.

“By formally designating the trio as state and regional campaign coordinators, the campaign administration aims to optimise resource allocation by consolidating campaign funding, logistics and grassroots mobilisation under single state-level coordinators to eliminate duplicated efforts and conflicting campaign machineries.

“Furthermore, this approach builds a genuine coalition that transcends traditional party lines, while bringing influential allies into an accountable structure directly overseen by the President and the campaign directorate,” said the party source.

Addressing resistance within APC ranks, party insiders noted that President Tinubu recognised the apprehensions of party stalwarts but viewed the broader electoral arithmetic as the over-arching priority.

“By securing solid guarantees of commitment from Wike coordinating Rivers and the FCT, Governor Soludo coordinating Anambra, and Governor Adeleke coordinating Osun, the Presidency believes that pooling political weight directly within the official campaign council offers a far more effective electoral advantage than managing disconnected outside support movements,” another source added.

President Tinubu is set to officially inaugurate the unified Presidential Campaign Council, PCC, at the Presidential Villa in Abuja today, signaling a firm push towards a broad, cross-party campaign structure.

Why I’m leading Tinubu’s campaign in Rivers, FCT – Wike

Speaking on the issue, during a media chat in Abuja yesterday, Wike said the decision was based on the need to accommodate people outside the APC who are willing to contribute to Tinubu’s re-election bid.

“My thinking is that the president, in his wisdom, said there are those who are not members of our political parties but have something to offer to his re-election, and it’s proper to accommodate them,” he said.

He added that the campaign should bring together people willing to support Tinubu’s continuation in office, regardless of their party affiliations.

Rainbow Coalition has come to stay, Wike tells APC govs

Wike also declared that his Rainbow Coalition backing President Bola Tinubu’s re-election has come to stay, saying there was “nothing anybody can do about it.”

Asked if his inclusion in the APC PCC had silenced his critics, who were mainly APC governors, he said: “I don’t know where you are getting all these from. Problem that does not exist. I don’t know what concerns there are. As far as I am concerned, there is no problem.”

Speaking in his monthly media chat, he dismissed suggestions that the coalition had unsettled APC governors or could encourage defections from the ruling party, and challenged anyone unhappy with the arrangement to take the matter up with him directly.

“If you have any problem against me, come out and face Wike. Don’t go under the Rainbow Coalition. For Rainbow Coalition, it has come. It will stay. There is nothing anybody can do about it,” he said.

Wike, who coordinates the coalition’s activities in Rivers State and the FCT, said the initiative puts APC members and Tinubu’s supporters in other parties on one platform.

“If you see that word, PBAT/APC, it means those who are supporting the president who are not members of the party, together with the party, are working together to achieve that purpose,” he said.

He cited Governors Soludo and Adeleke, as political figures associated with the coalition’s state-level coordination.

The minister, who noted that the coalition was not meant to displace APC, said the party remains the platform on which the president will seek re-election, while supporters outside it could work towards the same goal.

“The major thing is Mr President. Whatever we are going to do, whoever has any idea or anything to contribute is to the success of Mr President. That is the whole thing,” he said.

He pointed to the FCT as proof that the arrangement works, adding that “we are going to vote for Mr. President, and the National Assembly candidates are for APC. Why would anybody say there is a problem there?”

Wike also rejected the idea that the arrangement is new in Nigerian politics, adding that such backing existed before without being formalised.

“But this time, it came out because of the period we are in,” he said.

He accused opposition politicians of misleading Nigerians about Tinubu’s performance, saying “whether anybody likes it or not, Mr President has done well.”

To show that praise for the president could come from outside the APC, he pointed to remarks attributed to the governor of Bauchi State, Bala Mohammed, of the Allied Peoples Movement, APM, acknowledging aspects of Tinubu’s performance.

“Politics must not be played as a do-or-die affair,” Wike said, adding that he had never hidden where he stood.

Only baby politicians’re kicking against Rainbow Coalition

Wike also said only baby politicians were kicking against the Rainbow Coalition, citing Edo State, where he said a similar cross-party alliance defeated the then governor’s preferred successor.

He dismissed claims that backing President Bola Tinubu through the coalition would confuse supporters of other parties.

He said he had told his supporters to back the president, while also telling them their own National Assembly candidates mattered.

“Anybody who says he does not recognise the importance of rainbow coalition is not a politician. Anybody who said that is a baby politician. Is there any conflict? There is no conflict. How does it confuse people?” he queried.

Wike then turned to Edo, where, he said, the then governor, Godwin Obaseki, was determined to install a successor.

He said he supported the APC, though he belonged to the PDP, adding “I did not support Obaseki, even though I was and still a member of PDP.”

He said a PDP faction known as the Legacy group led by the late Chief Dan Orbih had joined hands with APC.

“That legacy group and APC now met to work together, and that was how they defeated Obaseki’s successor. If we did not do that, it would have been difficult for APC to defeat Obaseki,” he explained.

Tinubu will win on first ballot

The minister equally declared that President Tinubu will win the 2027 presidential election on the first ballot, ruling out the possibility of a run-off.

“I have not seen any likelihood of a run-off,” he said.

Asked about the legacy Tinubu will be leaving behind should he lose re-election, Wike said: “It will be wrong for me to even answer that kind of question. He will be returned. Nigerians will return him.”

Wike also denied working against three governors of the APC, including Hope Uzodimma of Imo State; AbdulRahman AbdulRazaq of Kwara State; and Inuwa Yahaya of Gombe State.

According to him, it will be wrong to accuse him of sponsoring candidates against the governors.

“It is very much unfair,” he said.

Wike, who insisted his party is entitled to field candidates, said further: “I am not in their party. So you can’t tell me my party cannot have candidates.”

He said backing the president did not stop him from doing that.

“The mere fact I supported President Tinubu, which I did in 2023, and I am still doing does not mean we cannot field candidates at other levels,” he said.

Wike said he made no deal with the governors, citing Uzodimma as proof of his good faith and invited the governor to say whether he had backed him in his second-term bid.

“Ask Governor Hope. If he is a sincere person, he will tell you the role I played in his re-election,” Wike said.

He said politicians commonly hope their rivals would stumble, adding that every person prayed for his opponent to make a mistake.

“So, I have no hand”, he said of the situation in Kwara between the governor and former Senate President, Bukola Saraki.

Why Fubara isn’t coordinating Tinubu’s campaign in Rivers

The minister said he is coordinating President Tinubu’s re-election campaign in Rivers State because the situation there is peculiar.

Rivers is the only state the campaign is not coordinated by a sitting APC governor, Siminalayi Fubara, adding that the job called for a particular kind of leadership.

“Look, in an election, it takes a lot of leadership, there are a lot of things that are involved. You require somebody who has a buy-in,” Wike said.

Describing the situation in Rivers as “peculiar,” Wike rejected the suggestion that Governor Fubara had been sidelined.

“No, he has not been pushed aside,” he said.

Asked whether Fubara would be involved in the campaign, he replied: “Of course,”, adding that the governor will take part at every level, from the state to the national.

Wike, who noted that Fubara is not an unwilling participant in the president’s campaign, said: “He is happy with the role we are giving him. If he is not happy, why would you hold a meeting in his house? “Do you know what it takes to hold a meeting in his house for everybody to be there? Fubara is fully a member, fully plays his part. What is of concern to Fubara, whether he is running or not, is to keep his political family intact.”

Wike blames ‘some govs’ for rift with Fubara

The minister blamed some governors for the rift between him and Fubara, saying they are now working together and that Fubara is happily working for PresidentTinubu.

He said people who never meant well for the governor were behind the trouble.

“We are all one, we have forgiven each other, we have come together but the truth still remains the evil works of some Nigerians is the cause,” he said.

Asked whether he was positioning Fubara for a ministerial role when he leaves office next year, Wike said the decision is not his.

“I am not the president to choose who will be a minister. I don’t have right to nominate,” he stressed..

World.title: Why many Nigerians spend more on phone repairs than buying new phones
World.content:
By Miracle Onyemuwa

The rising cost of smartphones in Nigeria is forcing more consumers to repair damaged devices rather than replace them with new ones.



This is more so, as inflation and the depreciation of the naira continue to push phone prices higher.



At Computer Village, Ikeja, phone repair shops are seeing increasing numbers of customers bringing in devices with cracked screens, damaged charging ports and faulty batteries.



At a repair centre, Kornerstone Technology, one of the engineers who spoke to TechXtra, said screen replacements currently account for about 80 per cent of the shop’s jobs.



He said: “Eighty per cent of our jobs this month are screen replacements. Today’s screens are more delicate than eggs. I don’t know why phone makers are doing that. iPhone 11, iPhone 12, Samsung A32 and Samsung A23 are among the phones frequently brought in here for repairs and screen replacements.”



Revealing the cost for the screens, he said the shop charges about N25, 000 for a copy screen for an iPhone 11 and N45,000 for an original screen. He also said that battery replacement costs between N10, 000 and N20,000, while charging-port repairs range from N7,000 to N15,000.



For him, the increasing cost of original replacement parts has also encouraged technicians to salvage genuine components from damaged or dead phones to reduce repair costs for customers.



The preference for repairs is also evident among owners of lower- and mid-range smartphones.



At Divine Mercy Enterprises, also in Computer Village, another repairer said charging-port damage, cracked screens and swollen batteries were among the most common faults he handled.



He said Tecno Spark and Infinix Hot models were among the phones customers most frequently brought for repairs.



He explained that children sometimes damage charging ports by forcing USB cables into the phones incorrectly.

Factor fuelling repairs



Other factors fuelling phone repairs, according to the engineers, is the rainy season. Water-damaged phones are also flooding the repair tables .



A lady who introduced herself simply as Aisha who came to repair her phone in one of the shops said her child threw her Infinix Hot 50 into the water.



“I opted to repair this phone because I don’t have the money to replace it. I can’t cough out over N300,000, which I am sure this phone costs now. Even if it costs me N50,000 to repair, I am ready to pay.

Cost of repairs



Repair costs vary according to the phone model and the severity of the fault. Screen replacement for low- and mid-range devices generally costs between N10,000 and N40,000, while repairs for high-end phones can range from N50,000 to N150,000 or more depending on the phone model. Battery replacements cost between N5,000 and N20,000, while charging-port repairs typically range from N3,000 to N15,000.



For many consumers, the difference between repair costs and the price of a replacement phone makes repairing an existing device a more practical option.

Repair culture



Nigeria’s long-standing repair culture has also contributed to the trend, with technicians developing skills in salvaging usable components from damaged electronics and extending the lifespan of devices rather than discarding them.



The growing dependence on smartphones has further increased the importance of keeping existing devices functional. For many Nigerians, phones are used not only for communication but also for mobile banking, business transactions and point-of-sale services.

World.title: E-commerce, championing Nigeria’s digital journey?
World.content:
•Online shopping sector jumps 15 points to 75% in new report

•Customer satisfaction hits 71% despite service quality decline in key sectors

•Power, Public Sector trail at 51%, 53%

By Prince Osuagwu

E-Commerce appears to be one sector in Nigeria where customers are not complaining as much as they used to.

While poor service continues to dog several sectors of the economy, e-commerce appears to be quietly winning the hearts of Nigerian consumers.



The online shopping business emerged as Nigeria’s best-performing sector in customer satisfaction in 2025, scoring 75 per cent — a remarkable 15 percentage-point jump from its 2024 score of 60 per cent.



And that is not all.



The sector’s 2025 performance came against a rather gloomy backdrop in which nine of the 12 sectors measured recorded lower scores than in the previous reporting period.



In other words, while service quality was falling in several parts of the economy, e-commerce was going in the opposite direction.

The finding is contained in the 2025 State of Customer Service in Nigeria Report, released by the Nigeria Customer Service Index, NCSI, in a review of Nigeria’s 66th Independence anniversary and the 2026 Customer Service Week.



The report, powered by the West Africa Association of Customer Service Professionals, WAACSP, is based on 21,387 responses covering more than 1,500 organisations across all 36 states and the Federal Capital Territory.



From the report, the numbers tell an interesting story.



Nigeria’s overall Customer Satisfaction Index, NCSI, benchmark climbed from 61 per cent in 2023 to 67 per cent in 2024 and 71 per cent in 2025.



But beneath that headline improvement lies a curious contradiction.



Despite the national satisfaction score hitting an all-time high, the report says nine out of the 12 sectors recorded lower scores than in the previous reporting period.



So, where did the satisfaction come from?



E-commerce appears to have provided part of the answer.



The sector did not merely retain its position among the better-performing industries. It moved decisively to the top, scoring 75 per cent, ahead of Real Estate at 72 per cent.



Telecommunications also recorded modest improvement, rising by one percentage point.



At the organisation level, Slot emerged number one in e-commerce, followed by Jumia and Konga.



Interestingly, e-commerce has not just appeared suddenly on the customer-service radar. Jumia, Konga and Slot have featured in the NCSI every year from 2023 to 2025, showing that the sector’s major players have maintained visibility in the index over time.

Why online shoppers are now happier



Providing a clue, the report found that customer trust was the number-one priority in every sector, but e-commerce recorded the highest trust rating of all sectors at a striking 90 per cent.



That is significant in an economy where consumers are increasingly demanding convenience, transparency and quick responses from businesses.



For the online shopper, the customer journey is increasingly digital. If they are not searching for products, they are comparing prices, ordering, tracking delivery and raising complaints.



The NCSI says its survey measured customer experiences across areas including trust, professionalism, competence, complaint resolution, ease of doing business, processes and procedures, staff engagement and customer-focused innovation.



The 75 per cent e-commerce score therefore suggests that, despite the complaints that still surround online shopping, customers are finding enough improvement in the experience to give the sector a strong vote of confidence.



But there is also another interesting twist. While Power struggles, e-commerce surges. The contrast with some other sectors could hardly be sharper.



For instance, Transportation suffered the biggest decline, falling 13 percentage points, while Power and the Public Sector each dropped by 10 points.



Power ended the ranking at just 51 per cent, while the Public Sector scored 53 per cent.



Negative public sentiment was also highest in the Public Sector, at 44 per cent, and Power, at 43 per cent.



Yet e-commerce was sitting at the other end of the table with 75 per cent satisfaction and 90 per cent customer trust.



It is a striking picture of two Nigerias: one where customers are still battling service failures, and another where digital platforms are gradually learning how to make convenience part of the service.

The e-commerce climb



The journey becomes even more interesting when the figures are placed side by side.



In 2023, Hospitality was the highest-performing sector at 73 per cent, while the Public Sector was lowest at 47 per cent.

In 2024, Transportation took the lead at 73 per cent, while E-commerce was at the bottom of the table among the reported sector extremes with 60 per cent.



Then came 2025, and e-commerce exploded to the top with 75 per cent.



That 15-point jump is arguably the most dramatic sectoral improvement in the latest report.



And it could be telling Nigerian businesses something important: customers may forgive many things, but they increasingly reward businesses that make their lives easier.



But there is a warning; the e-commerce success story does not mean Nigeria has solved its customer-service problem.



The NCSI and WAACSP are urging organisations to focus on trust-building, faster complaint resolution and consistent service delivery, particularly in the Public Sector and Power.



They also recommend combining digital convenience with reliable traditional customer support.



The report further cautions that the survey had a strong concentration in Lagos and Abuja. Of the 21,387 responses, Lagos accounted for 9,897 responses, or 46.75 per cent, while Abuja contributed 2,994, or 14.14 per cent. Together, the two locations accounted for 60.89 per cent of all responses.



So, while the numbers provide a fascinating snapshot of customer sentiment, the researchers say broader participation outside Lagos and Abuja would strengthen future comparisons.



Still, one message from the 2025 numbers is difficult to ignore.



As traditional sectors struggle with complaints over service quality, e-commerce appears to be showing that Nigerians can still be satisfied when technology, convenience and customer experience come together.



For an economy increasingly moving from the physical to the digital marketplace, that may be the beginning of an even bigger story in 2026 and beyond.

World.title: Subscribers lament hours of disrupted mobile service
World.content:
By Islamiyyah Adekanbi

Subscribers in Lagos have lamented hours of disrupted mobile service, saying the outage affected their studies, businesses and communication with family and friends.

The disruption, which was reported in Lagos, Oyo, Rivers, Delta and the Federal Capital Territory, left some users unable to access mobile data and other network services. Several subscribers said they relied on friends’ and relatives’ hotspots or alternative networks to get online.

Kafayat Kokumo, a Mass Communication student, said the outage began as she was trying to send a WhatsApp message while working on a research assignment due in less than 30 minutes.

She said switching on airplane mode did not restore her connection, so she eventually used a friend’s hotspot. The experience left her anxious about meeting her deadline.

Kokumo said service returned after about an hour. She called for more reliable mobile service, noting that disruptions could affect people’s daily activities.

Memunat Olayemi Omidiya, a student and online store manager in Abulegba, said she was unable to respond to customers after her data subscription expired and she could not buy another one.

She eventually used her mother’s hotspot. Omidiya said she noticed the disruption around 5 p.m. and it continued until she went to bed after 11 p.m. She called for steps to prevent similar outages.

Digital marketer, Joel Okikioluwa also said he had difficulty accessing the internet. He said he was debited after purchasing data but had not received a refund by the time of the interview. He described the experience as horrible and called for network improvement.

Abdur-Rahman Awesu, a student in Lagos, said the disruption cut off his mobile data for about six hours, affecting his communication with friends and family. He relied on an alternative network and called for stronger infrastructure and backup systems, as well as timely updates to subscribers during outages.

Covenant Amaechi, a student living around First Gate, Ikorodu, said he could not communicate when he needed to. Although service returned, he said the connection remained intermittent at times. He also called for better customer care.

Another student, AbdulQayum Jakande, who lives in Surulere, said he lost access to mobile data for more than four hours. He called for stronger network servers.

The subscribers’ accounts highlight the role of reliable mobile service in education, communication and online businesses. They called for improved network reliability and measures to minimise future disruptions.

World.title: Nigeria loses $2bn yearly to cocoa value addition gap — FG
World.content:
Production stuck at 300kg p/htare despite improved seedlings — CRIN

Africa needs climate-resilient cocoa varieties to boost yield — IITA

By Cynthia Alo & Kafayat Kokumo

The Federal Government (FG) has said that Nigeria loses about $2 billion annually in potential value from cocoa because the country’s processing capacity is largely underutilised.



Meanwhile, the International Institute of Tropical Agriculture (IITA), has said that West Africa needs high-yielding, climate-resilient cocoa varieties to improve productivity and protect farmers from the effects of climate change.



The Minister of Agriculture and Food Security, Abubakar Kyari, stated this in Lagos at a two-day Africa Cocoa and Coffee Conference organised by the Cocoa and Coffee Farmers Alliance Association of Africa, COCEFAAA in partnership with the Federal Ministry of Agriculture and Food Security, FMAFS, and the Cocoa Research Institute of Nigeria, CRIN.



Kyari, who was represented by the Deputy Director of Tree Crops at FMAFs, Mr. Ajayi Olutobaba, said Nigeria has an installed cocoa processing capacity of about 2,000 tonnes annually, but only about 30 percent is currently utilised.



According to him, the FG was focused on moving Nigeria from simply producing cocoa to processing it into butter, liquor, powder and chocolate locally, adding that it would continue to position the country as a reliable cocoa exporter.



He stated: “Roughly $2 billion in value addition slips away every year. It is not a shortage of resources; it is an opportunity waiting for the right investors. For cocoa and coffee, it comes down to one idea: value addition, not just volume. Our goal is to add value, not export ban and we’ll make it easy for investors to build the factories to do it’’.



He further said, “We will back the renewal of aging farms and the growth of coffee with better seedlings, extension support, and enough for smallholder farmers. As we’ll make sure Nigerian produce keeps its place in the world best markets.And we must protect the harvest of tomorrow with better inputs, stronger pests and disease management, and climate-smart production.”



Kyari called on stakeholders in Africa to share research, align their standards and speak with one voice in the markets that buy their crops.



He stated: “Africa grows about 70% of the world’s cocoa, yet takes home only a tiny fraction of a chocolate industry worth over $130 billion. In coffee, our share of world production has fallen from 27.2% in the 1970s to about 12.5% today, and yet Ethiopia and Uganda each earned over $1.4 billion and $2 billion respectively from coffee over coffee export in 2025.



“If our neighbors can do it, the continent can do it, but none of us will get there alone.



“The EU deforestation regulation is no threat if we prepare early. We’ve been preparing for it.Traceability is simply how we protect our place at the table from farm to markets.”



Speaking on the theme, ‘Building sustainable value chains for cocoa and coffee across West, Central and East Africa’, acting Executive Director, Cocoa Research Institute of Nigeria, CRIN, Dr. Abiodun Adedeji, said Nigeria’s cocoa productivity remained between 250kg and 300kg per hectare annually despite years of government distribution of improved seedlings.



He called for better prices for farmers, greater local processing, stronger research and improved data to build a sustainable value chain.



He said: “Between 2011 and 2015, we gave out 601,000 pods free to farmers. After that, we had 300,000 seedlings during COVID. Presently, Federal Government has mandated CRIN to produce and give out 1 million improved hybrid cocoa seedlings. But between that 2011 and now, the Nigerian productivity still lies between 250 and 300 kg per hectare per year.”



Adedeji urged African countries to strengthen collaboration on research and development, saying the continent needed better varieties and production systems to address emerging challenges.



According to him, 90 percent of cocoa proceeds and over 70 percent of coffee proceeds go to non-producing countries, while Africa shares less than 10 per cent of cocoa and less than 30 per cent of coffee.



Global President & Founder COCEFAAA, and Convener of the conference, Comrade Adeola Adegoke, said Africa produces 80 percent of the world’s cocoa but captures less than 10 per cent of its value.



Adegoke said the 2023-2024 season recorded the largest global deficit in 60 years, about 490,000 tons, pushing prices above $10,000 before the International Cocoa Organization, ICCO reported a surplus and prices fell by 75 per cent.



“When there is bumper harvest, price goes down. When there is shock, price goes to $12,000, Robusta $15,000. Why should we produce more and earn less?” he said.



Representing the Lagos State Commissioner for Agriculture and Food Systems, Abisola Olusanya, Director, Agribusiness, Lagos State Ministry of Agriculture and Food Systems, Mrs. Aramide Gansallo, said Africa must move from exporting raw cocoa and coffee beans to processing, branding and consuming its own products.



Olusanya said the transformation must also make agriculture attractive to young people by presenting it as a business, technology-driven industry and career.



Managing Director, Sunbeth Global Concepts, Olasunkanmi Owoyemi, who was represented by the Manager, Corporate Affairs & Communication, Abdussamad Abdurrahman said, “We have been content to be the world’s farm while others become the world’s kitchen.”



He said the company is building a 70,000 metric ton processing facility at its industrial park, which will be ready by next year to boost local value addition, stressing that traceability has become critical for market access.

Africa needs climate-resilient cocoa varieties to boost yield — IITA



Also speaking at the conference, the International Institute of Tropical Agriculture (IITA), has harped on the need for high-yielding, climate-resilient cocoa varieties to improve productivity and protect farmers from the effects of climate change.

The Institute disclosed that the region’s cocoa output had dropped by 10 per cent due to climate-related challenges, including extreme temperatures and erratic rainfall.



Senior Researcher at IITA, Ranjana Bhattacharjee, who stated this at the conference, advocated the adoption of alternative varieties, particularly Liberica and Stenophylla, as climate change threatens the sustainability of established varieties.



“The production of Liberica coffee is four times more than Arabica and Robusta. So, if Arabica is going down and Brazil is taking over, then you start growing Liberica and make sure that it becomes the legacy of Africa,” she said.



According to her, the decline highlights the urgent need for African cocoa-producing countries to adopt improved planting materials and farming practices capable of withstanding changing weather conditions while increasing yields.



She noted that ageing trees, unmanaged pests and diseases, high input costs, inadequate access to loans and international price volatility were also affecting cocoa and coffee production across the region.



Bhattacharjee urged West African producers to learn from Indonesia’s rising cocoa output by adopting high-yielding varieties, improving soil nutrition, strengthening crop protection and expanding access to agricultural credit.



She warned that climate pressures were worsening production challenges, particularly in Ghana and Côte d’Ivoire, where drought and cocoa swollen shoot virus disease were occurring simultaneously.



The researcher also called on African policymakers to address the disparity between the income earned by cocoa farmers on the continent and their counterparts in Latin America.



“Somewhere Africa gets $3,200, the farmers, while in Latin America they get $5,000. Why? My question is why? We are the highest producers of cocoa, then why should we not get that price? Farmer income 6 per cent in Africa while 31 per cent in Latin America. Why there is a system? policymakers have to fight for it,” she said.



Meanwhile, stakeholders at the conference stressed the need to strengthen the entire cocoa and coffee value chain.

Representing the governor of Abia State, Alex Otti , Deputy Gov. of the state , Engr. Ikechukwu Emetu said Africa must move beyond exporting raw commodities and retain more value through local processing, branding and exports.



He said, “The transformation of cocoa and coffee must therefore begin at the farm, but must not end there. From improved planting materials and agronomic practice through extension, aggregation, and post-harvest management to processing, branding, and export, everything determines the competitiveness of the final product.”



Also speaking, representative of Ondo State Government, Mrs. Foluke-Tunde Daramola, disclosed that the state had begun moves to revive cocoa production through improved seedlings and the rehabilitation of old plantations, alongside plans to establish 1,000 hectares of coffee at Oke-Agbe.



Meanwhile, Permanent Secretary, Ministry of Agriculture and Irrigation Development, Cross River State,Dr.Joseph Odey highlighted the importance of traceability and deforestation-free production, noting that improved seedlings alone could not build a sustainable industry without reliable nurseries, extension services, processing facilities, finance and dependable markets.



Representing the Cocoa and Coffee Farmers Alliance Association of Africa (COCEFAAA) Ghana, Mr. Nana Reuben challenged stakeholders to examine whether African farmers were benefiting sufficiently from the industry and whether the ageing farming population offered a sustainable future for cocoa production.



The two-day conference brought together policymakers, researchers, farmers, investors and development partners to explore ways of building sustainable and competitive cocoa and coffee value chains across Africa.

World.title: 2027 Presidential Poll: Atiku Brings Tinubu into Policy Debate, Obi Missing
World.content:
Olawale Olaleye

With 13 weeks and three days to the January 16, 2027 presidential election, candidate of the Africa Democratic Congress (ADC), Alhaji Atiku Abubakar, has intensified his policy exchanges with the administration of President Bola Tinubu, particularly on petrol pricing, fiscal accountability and the cost of living.

This gradually evolving debate, and the Presidency’s sometimes elaborate responses, have begun to change the character of the campaign conversation as the nation counts down to the election next January.



Curiously, however, the presidential standard beaer of the National Democratic Congress (NDC), Mr. Peter Obi, appears to be missing in the emerging debate, albeit not totally in the wider conversation.



Beyond the customary political intrigues, partisan recriminations, alliances and campaign rhetoric, an increasingly substantive argument about the direction of the country’s economy is beginning to take shape with the duo constantly sparring.



The recurring disagreement between APC’s Bola Ahmed Tinubu and ADC’s Atiku Abubakar, is neither new nor particularly surprising.

What is noteworthy, however, is the increasing specificity of the questions and policy alternatives being advanced by Atiku, and the detailed responses these have elicited from the Presidency.



And, coming from Tinubu, who is naturally not disposed to a debate as evident during the 2023 presidential election, Atiku might have subtly forced the president and his government into interesting policy debate, and inadvertently changing the tenor of campaigns, based on issues.

From the removal of petrol subsidy to the management of the exchange rate, public borrowing, taxation, government expenditure and the affordability of basic necessities, Atiku has repeatedly challenged the administration to explain not merely why its economic reforms were necessary, but how their benefits are reaching ordinary Nigerians.



In doing so, the former vice-president has sought to shift the political conversation from personalities and partisan loyalties to the actual consequences of public policy.



The government, on its part, has not allowed the arguments to go unanswered. Its statements, campaign interventions and direct responses have defended the logic of Tinubu’s reforms, challenged the financial sustainability of Atiku’s alternatives and questioned whether his proposals are compatible with existing legislation.



This exchange has produced an interesting feature of the emerging presidential contest: a government defending the economic decisions it has already taken and an opposition candidate being pressed to explain the practical implications of the decisions he proposes to take.

Yet, amid this increasingly sustained encounter, another major presidential candidate, Peter Obi of the NDC, has not occupied the same place in the particular exchange between Atiku and the Presidency.



Obi has certainly not been silent on national issues. He has articulated positions on economic production, petroleum subsidy, corruption, electricity and public accountability. Indeed, his party recently criticised the government’s petrol discount.



The distinction is that the recent sequence of proposals, presidential responses, counterproposals and fiscal arguments has developed principally around Atiku’s intervention.



That development offers a useful window into the changing character of the 2027 contest.

From Political Rhetoric to Policy Alternatives



For much of Nigeria’s Fourth Republic, presidential campaigns have frequently been shaped by questions of ethnicity, religion, zoning, personalities and political alignments.



Although economic policy has never been entirely absent, the technical details of proposed reforms have not always received the sustained public interrogation that a country facing serious structural economic challenges requires.



The present circumstances make such an interrogation particularly relevant.



When President Tinubu assumed office on May 29, 2023, he announced the removal of petrol subsidy, setting in motion one of the most consequential economic decisions of his administration.



Changes in the foreign exchange system followed, while the government subsequently introduced far-reaching tax and fiscal reforms.

The administration has maintained that these decisions were necessary to correct distortions, improve government finances, encourage investment and place Nigeria on a more sustainable economic footing.



Atiku’s central objection is solely about the implementation of those reforms, the social protection available to vulnerable citizens and the accountability mechanisms governing the resources released.



The argument became particularly pronounced in August 2026, when the ADC presidential candidate publicly pledged to restore petrol subsidy if elected.

His declaration attracted immediate criticism, partly because Atiku had previously supported subsidy removal and downstream petroleum deregulation.

But as the debate developed, his campaign clarified that the proposed arrangement would not simply revive the old system of subsidising imported petrol.

Instead, Atiku advocated a capped, budgeted production subsidy directed at petroleum products refined within Nigeria, including those produced by modular refineries.



According to his campaign, the proposed programme would be linked to verified domestic production, monitored independently and designed to ensure that the benefits reached consumers through lower pump prices.



The distinction is consequential.



Under the former arrangement, public resources were used extensively to compensate for differences between regulated domestic petrol prices and the cost of supply, much of which involved imported products.



Under Atiku’s proposal, government support would be tied principally to domestic refining, potentially through crude oil supplied to qualifying refineries at preferential prices.



The argument, therefore, concerns whether public intervention in the petroleum market should be eliminated, temporarily permitted or deliberately redesigned to support domestic production and consumer affordability.

It is a question with substantial consequences for government revenue, investment, industrial development and household expenditure.

How Tinubu Entered the Argument



However, the government’s responses have demonstrated how closely the issue has become associated with the presidential campaign.

On August 2, 2026, the Presidency published a detailed response to Atiku’s criticisms of the administration’s economic management.

The statement addressed his concerns about public borrowing, the 2024 budget, subsidy removal, tax reforms and the utilisation of oil revenue.

It argued that Atiku’s criticisms placed insufficient emphasis on the economy’s subsequent performance, pointing to improvements in macroeconomic conditions, government revenue and investment confidence.



The government also defended the removal of subsidy as a structural correction that had improved allocations to states and local governments.

The debate intensified the following month.



On September 20, the APC Presidential Campaign Council publicly challenged Atiku to explain the legal, financial and operational implications of his proposed production subsidy.



Among the questions raised were the subsidy rate, annual expenditure ceiling, eligible crude volumes, funding sources, pricing arrangements, safeguards against diversion and possible amendments to the Petroleum Industry Act.



The council estimated that the proposal could cost between 17 trillion and N21 trillion annually, depending on its design and implementation.

Importantly, those figures were APC’s projections, not an independently established cost of Atiku’s programme. The detailed assumptions necessary to reproduce the estimates have not been fully published.



Nevertheless, the questions themselves were substantial.



They required the opposition candidate to move beyond the broad promise of cheaper petrol and explain how the intended intervention would be financed, regulated and monitored.



Atiku’s campaign subsequently maintained that the proposal would be capped, budgeted and independently audited. It also indicated that amendments to existing petroleum legislation could be pursued if necessary.

However, the actual proposed discount rate, annual funding requirement and complete mechanism for passing savings to consumers remain outstanding.

This is precisely the kind of practical policy interrogation that should accompany presidential proposals involving potentially significant public resources.

The presidency’s engagement has not been confined to technical arguments. Some responses have included strong personal and political criticisms of Atiku.

Yet, underneath the political language, questions of subsidy design, market pricing, public expenditure and the legal authority of government intervention have remained central.

October 1: A Clash of Economic Narratives



The exchange acquired additional significance during Nigeria’s 66th Independence anniversary.



In his October 1 national address, President Tinubu declared that the country was transitioning from economic stabilisation towards what he described as an era of shared prosperity.



The President defended the removal of subsidy and foreign exchange reforms, insisting that they had helped repair structural weaknesses inherited by his administration.



He cited improved economic growth, rising foreign reserves, stronger non-oil exports and moderating inflation.



According to Tinubu, the economy had expanded by more than four per cent during the year, while non-oil exports exceeded $6 billion in 2025.



He also outlined priorities involving agricultural mechanisation, industrial production, transportation infrastructure, power supply, employment and access to finance.



Significantly, the president criticised those advocating a return to subsidies, arguing that the country should not abandon reforms simply because their initial effects had been painful.



Although the statement did not expressly identify Atiku, the timing and substance placed the issue of subsidy at the centre of the president’s economic argument.



Atiku responded that same day with an extensive address disputing the administration’s assessment of national conditions.



His criticism revolved around the difference between improvements in macroeconomic indicators and the purchasing power of ordinary households.

He questioned whether economic growth, higher government revenue and reduced inflation could legitimately be described as prosperity when many citizens continued to struggle with food, transport, electricity, education and healthcare costs.



He also offered specific illustrations.



For instance, Atiku argued that the N30,000 minimum wage in April 2023 could purchase approximately 118 litres of petrol, whereas the current N70,000 minimum wage would purchase only about 50 litres at prevailing prices.



The comparison is instructive, though it depends on the petrol prices and locations used. It illustrates how a nominal increase in wages can coexist with a decline in purchasing power.



The statutory minimum wage has risen by approximately 133 per cent, from N30,000 to N70,000. But if petrol costs approximately N1,400 per litre, the newer wage purchases substantially less fuel than the older wage did at prices prevailing before subsidy removal.



Atiku also raised questions about the administration’s budgeting arrangements, public debt, social intervention programmes and the extent to which increased government resources had translated into tangible improvements in living standards. In effect, the exchange highlighted two different measurements of economic progress.



Tinubu’s emphasis was on macroeconomic stabilisation, structural reforms and the conditions necessary for future growth.



Atiku’s emphasis was on immediate affordability, household welfare and the distribution of the gains arising from those reforms.



These are not mutually exclusive economic objectives. Indeed, a sustainable recovery ultimately requires both.



The disagreement concerns the pace, sequencing and effectiveness of the policies intended to achieve them.

The Petrol Discount That Reopened the Controversy



Perhaps the most revealing chapter of the argument emerged between October 8 and 11.



Against the backdrop of higher international oil prices, the federal government announced measures intended to moderate petrol costs.



The Nigerian National Petroleum Company Limited extended a N66-per-litre discount introduced on October 1 at its retail stations, with the arrangement scheduled to continue until October 31.



The Minister of Finance, Taiwo Oyedele, explained that NNPC Retail would forgo part of its profit margin and sell petrol at cost to provide temporary relief to consumers.



The government also outlined a proposed framework involving a negotiated ceiling of approximately N1,350 per litre on petrol supply costs, with provisions for smoothing temporary price increases.



The N1,350 figure was not a uniform nationwide pump price. It related to proposed supply-cost arrangements, with the eventual price paid by motorists still affected by distribution and retail costs.



NNPC subsequently insisted that the discount did not constitute a restoration of the former petroleum subsidy regime.



But Atiku disagreed with the political and economic presentation of the policy.



His campaign questioned why the administration, having consistently defended subsidy removal and criticised government intervention in petrol pricing, was now supporting a temporary discount.



At the October 9 inauguration of the ADC Presidential Campaign Council in Abuja, Atiku accused Tinubu of borrowing from his production-subsidy proposal without adopting its essential features.



The former vice-president, who constantly referred to the president as “Bola” in his speech, a disposition the presidency considers disrespectful, argued that a short-term retail discount could not substitute for a properly structured arrangement intended to lower the cost of domestically refined petroleum products.

He went on to challenge the government to explain what would happen when the discount expires.

The Presidency answered.



On October 11, presidential adviser, Sunday Dare, issued a detailed rebuttal defending the discount as a temporary market intervention rather than an abandonment of deregulation.



The statement argued that Atiku’s production-subsidy proposal underestimated the commercial and contractual complexities of Nigeria’s petroleum industry.

It maintained that the government could not simply distribute crude oil at discounted prices without considering production-sharing contracts, joint ventures, contractual obligations and the revenue implications for the Federation.



The Presidency also pointed to compressed natural gas, domestic refining arrangements and alternative transportation initiatives as components of its broader response to the cost-of-living crisis.



This was a clear example of the debate moving beyond generic campaign accusations.



Atiku had questioned the adequacy, duration and financial transparency of the government’s relief arrangement.



The administration, on its part, challenged the legality, affordability and sustainability of Atiku’s proposed alternative.



Unfortunately, neither argument can be resolved by political rhetoric alone as they both require published figures, transparent implementation arrangements and evidence of benefits to consumers.

The Arithmetic Behind the Argument



A closer examination of the numbers demonstrates why the ongoing debate matters.



According to the National Bureau of Statistics, Nigeria’s economy expanded by 4.43 per cent in real terms in the second quarter of 2026, compared with 3.89 per cent in the first quarter.



This is evidence of economic expansion and provides a factual basis for the administration’s argument that macroeconomic conditions have improved.

Inflation has also moderated considerably from the exceptionally high levels experienced during the earlier stages of the reform programme.

The NBS reported headline inflation of 15.39 per cent in August 2026, slightly below the 15.43 per cent recorded in July and substantially below the 23.14 per cent recorded in August 2025.



But a decline in inflation does not ordinarily mean that prices have returned to earlier levels. It means that the general price level is increasing more slowly.

Indeed, the consumer price index rose from 145.3 in July to 146.3 in August, confirming that prices continued to increase despite the moderation in the annual inflation rate.



This distinction explains an important part of the disagreement between the government and its critics.



The administration can point to lower inflation and faster growth but the households continue to experience pressure from accumulated price increases.

The International Monetary Fund acknowledged both sides of this reality in its June 2026 assessment of Nigeria. The Fund credited reforms with improving macroeconomic conditions and strengthening resilience.



However, it also estimated that poverty had reached 63 per cent of the population, measured against the national poverty line, while approximately 27 million Nigerians faced food insecurity in the latter part of 2025. Those estimates described specific earlier periods and should not be presented as fresh October 2026 measurements.



Nevertheless, they demonstrate that improvements in macroeconomic indicators had not eliminated widespread economic vulnerability.

Yet, government finances present another area requiring scrutiny.



The Debt Management Office reported that Nigeria’s total public debt reached N166.79 trillion at the end of June 2026, compared with N159.35 trillion at the end of March.



That represented an increase of approximately N7.44 trillion, or 4.7 per cent, within three months. Domestic debt accounted for approximately N91.59 trillion, while external obligations stood at about N75.20 trillion.



The administration argued that borrowing should be assessed against economic output, government revenue, debt-servicing obligations and the purposes for which the borrowed funds are used.



Atiku’s criticism focuses more directly on fiscal discipline, expenditure accountability and the measurable benefits of public borrowing. Both considerations are however relevant.



Debt stock alone does not establish whether an economy faces an unsustainable fiscal position. Equally, an improving debt-to-GDP ratio does not remove the need to account for the cost, utilisation and returns on borrowed resources. The same scrutiny applies to petrol subsidy.



Regulatory data for August 2026 indicated average daily petrol receipts of approximately 50.5 million litres, of which around 35.9 million litres came from domestic sources and 14.6 million litres from imports.



Dangote Refinery accounted for approximately 35.87 million litres of the daily domestic receipts. This means the refinery supplied roughly 71 per cent of the total daily petrol receipts recorded during that period.



The figure raises important questions about competition, market concentration and the effectiveness of any production-linked subsidy.

If the government supplies discounted crude to domestic refiners, how much of the financial benefit will reach consumers? What arrangements would prevent the benefits from being retained entirely within the refining and distribution chain?



Conversely, the current government’s temporary discount also requires scrutiny.



Oyedele disclosed that NNPC Retail sells approximately 70 million litres of petrol monthly.



At a discount of N66 per litre, applying the reduction to that entire volume would amount to approximately N4.62 billion in reduced gross sales revenue over one month.



That is an illustrative calculation, not an established fiscal cost or profit loss. Actual figures would depend on the volume qualifying for the discount and the company’s sales margins. The government says the discount is financed through NNPC’s retail margin rather than direct budgetary expenditure.

But the wider implications for company earnings, the number of beneficiaries and the actual effect on transport fares remain important matters for public disclosure.



These figures demonstrate why subsidy policy cannot be reduced to a simple argument between compassion and deregulation.



The relevant questions concern the fiscal cost, commercial incentives, distribution of benefits and long-term sustainability of whichever arrangement is adopted.

Beyond Petrol: Budgets, Taxes and Accountability



Although petrol pricing has attracted considerable attention, the Atiku–Tinubu exchange has further expanded into other areas of economic governance.

Atiku has questioned the administration’s budget implementation, including the continued operation of earlier appropriations alongside newer budgets.

His October 1 address specifically criticised the extension of the 2025 budget’s implementation period towards the end of 2026.



His broader concern was that overlapping budget arrangements complicated public scrutiny of expenditure, completed projects and outstanding obligations.

The administration, meanwhile, defended its broader fiscal reform programme as part of efforts to improve efficiency and government revenue.

Taxation has produced another disagreement.



The Presidency argued that its reforms were intended to protect lower-income earners and small businesses while strengthening compliance among those with greater taxable capacity.



In an August response to Atiku, the government highlighted protections for individuals earning no more than N1 million annually and smaller businesses with turnover not exceeding N100 million.



Atiku’s criticism has concentrated on the wider effects of government economic policy on household finances and private enterprise.

The substantive public-policy question is whether higher government revenue is accompanied by more equitable taxation, transparent spending and sufficiently visible improvements in public services.



Similarly, the two camps have disagreed over the assessment of social intervention programmes, infrastructure investment and the benefits of subsidy savings.

These questions are especially important in a federation where increased allocations to states and local governments can create additional opportunities for development, but where actual outcomes depend substantially on spending decisions and institutional accountability at different levels of government.

Consequently, the responsibility for translating fiscal improvements into public welfare cannot be examined solely at the federal level.



Governors, local governments, spending agencies and public institutions also have responsibilities that should form part of the broader debate.

Where Is Peter Obi in This Exchange?



The growing prominence of the Atiku–Tinubu policy exchanges inevitably raises questions about Peter Obi’s place in the presidential conversation.

Obi emerged from the 2023 presidential election with considerable electoral support.



According to the Independent National Electoral Commission, Tinubu received 8,794,726 votes, Atiku secured 6,984,520, while Obi obtained 6,101,533 votes on the Labour Party platform.



Those figures explain why the three politicians remain central to discussions about the forthcoming presidential election. However, their approaches to the current policy conversation are not identical.



Obi has consistently emphasised the need to transform Nigeria from an economy heavily dependent on consumption and imports into one that prioritises domestic production, agriculture, manufacturing, investment and human capital development.



His 2027 campaign programme includes proposals to improve agricultural productivity, strengthen industrial capacity, expand infrastructure and address insecurity.



He has also pledged to increase electricity generation and distribution by at least 10,000 megawatts within four years and to improve healthcare financing and access.



On petroleum policy, Obi recently entered the subsidy discussion more directly.



In a BBC interview on October 6, he said he would retain a form of subsidy while removing the corruption associated with the previous arrangement.

That position attracted attention because he had earlier supported subsidy removal, arguing that resources committed to the programme could instead be invested in education, healthcare and other productive sectors. This was after his running matter, Rabiu Kwankwaso has held a different view on the subject.

His supporters subsequently maintained that the proposal did not amount to a return to the former subsidy system.



Furthermore, on October 9, the NDC publicly criticised the federal government’s 30-day petrol discount, describing the intervention as inadequate to resolve the underlying affordability crisis.



Therefore, while it may not be entirely accurate to suggest that Obi has offered no policy alternatives or has been entirely absent from the conversation, the fact that he never really offers clear thought on issues remains concerning.



But the more precise observation is that he is not seriously sold on any idea in particular, often lacking the kind of depth required of a presidential hopeful on issues and policies.



Not only is he shifty on policies as if on default mode, he hardly sounds convincing about his own propositions, largely superficial and often citing quite unrelated instances drawn from other parts of the world.



This is why the sustained sequence of direct challenges and detailed presidential rebuttals have been from Atiku’s proposals. That difference is relevant to understanding the changing public conversation, establishing the relative merit of either opposition candidate’s programme.



Many a time, Obi’s proposals present their own questions requiring clarification, which he hardly explains with lucidity.



Take for instance, his idea on fighting corruption. When asked how he planned to tackle the scourge, his submission that once his family refuses to indulge in corruption, the scourge is half-defeated is disappointing to many.



That response is not only considered shallow in many quarters, it shows his limitation in the understanding of issues and evident inability to sell them, even when they emanate from him.



In another example, Obi was asked how he intended to achieve his proposed 10 megawatts of electricity generation and his response to such a critical question that’s central to many things, the economy especially is: “We are gonna do it”.



This seemingly elusive disposition to leadership, seeking perhaps automatic coronation, is deemed the reason Obi might have consciously elected to be absent in the serious debate on issues and policies in the countdown to 2027, counting strongly on his arguably organic and obviously fanatical support base.

Taken together, if a future administration intends to retain petrol subsidy while eliminating corruption, what specific form would the subsidy take? Who would receive it? How would eligibility be determined, what would it cost annually, and how would the government ensure that consumers actually received the intended benefit?



His electricity target equally invites examination of the generation capacity, transmission infrastructure, distribution investment and financing required to achieve it.

These are questions of policy implementation rather than campaign personality. They, too, deserve the same scrutiny being applied to Atiku’s proposed production subsidy and Tinubu’s existing economic reforms. Yet, Obi never gives clarity about the workings.

A Different Conversation Ahead of 2027



The emerging policy argument reflects a broader development in the presidential campaign.



Nigeria’s major political actors are increasingly being required to distinguish between announcing desirable outcomes and explaining the practical arrangements for achieving them.



For Tinubu, the challenge is to demonstrate how the fiscal and macroeconomic gains recorded under his administration are translating into improvements in purchasing power, employment, public services and household welfare.



For Atiku, the challenge is to establish that his proposed alternatives are legally workable, financially sustainable and capable of producing the benefits he promises.



For Obi, the challenge is to translate his emphasis on production, transparency and human capital into fully specified implementation programmes, with financing arrangements, timelines and measurable targets.



These are distinct but equally legitimate areas of public scrutiny. The petroleum debate offers a particularly useful example because it exposes both the attractions and limitations of different forms of government interventions.



A temporary retail discount can provide immediate relief to eligible consumers without necessarily changing the underlying structure of the market.

A production subsidy may seek to support domestic refiners and reduce input costs, but its success depends on financing, competition and the extent to which savings reach the public.



A transparent subsidy regime, as proposed by Obi, equally requires a design capable of preventing abuse while preserving affordability.

None of these outcomes follows automatically from a campaign declaration. Each requires clear legal authority, credible financial calculations, competent implementation and independent monitoring.

The Larger Significance



Perhaps the most interesting aspect of the recent exchanges is that the arguments have begun to move away from the familiar question of who should occupy the presidency towards the more demanding question of how the presidency should manage the economy. The difference is substantial.



A government seeking another mandate must account for its record. Opposition candidates seeking the same office must explain their alternatives.

Atiku’s recent interventions have created repeated occasions for that comparison, particularly by challenging the government on the relationship between macroeconomic reform and the daily cost of living.



The Presidency’s responses have, in turn, subjected his proposals to questions about law, economics and fiscal sustainability.



That is a legitimate function of competitive democratic politics. It is also a reminder that policy debates are not determined simply by the frequency of official statements or the sharpness of political exchanges.



Their public value depends on whether the competing arguments produce sufficient information for citizens to understand the choices before them.

Thus, as the January 27, 2027 presidential bout approaches, the relevant questions should become more specific.



How much will the different petroleum-pricing proposals cost? What proportion of public resources will be committed to education, healthcare and infrastructure?



What measurable improvements in electricity, transportation and security are promised? How will government borrowing be managed, and how will citizens assess implementation?



These are the questions that turn campaign promises into propositions capable of serious examination.



For now, the sustained exchange between Atiku and the Tinubu administration has placed several of those issues more firmly in public discussion.

Obi has not been absent from the wider policy conversation, but the recent direct argument has been particularly shaped by Atiku’s interventions and the government’s responses.



Whether the broader campaign subsequently develops into an even more extensive debate among all 18 presidential candidates remains to be seen.

Ultimately, the importance of the emerging conversation is not which politician makes the most persuasive accusation or issues the most elaborate rebuttal.

It is whether Nigerians are presented with sufficiently detailed, credible and measurable policy programmes to judge what each candidate proposes to do with the responsibilities and resources of the presidency.



That would be a meaningful development in the country’s electoral politics.



Therefore, as the 2027 contest moves deeper into its campaign phase, the debate over what Nigeria’s economic future should look like is becoming as significant as the contest over who should preside over it.

World.title: Lagos-Calabar Coastal Road: Presidency Disowns Plan to Bypass Some States
World.content:
Emmanuel Addeh in Abuja





The Presidency yesterday dismissed suggestions that President Bola Tinubu had ordered the abandonment of parts of the Lagos-Calabar Coastal Highway to route the project through the existing East-West Road, insisting that the entire 750-kilometre coastal highway would be constructed as originally planned.

The clarification followed public controversy over the proposed use of the East-West Road corridor in parts of the Niger Delta, with concerns that the decision could leave some states and coastal communities outside the original alignment of the flagship infrastructure project.

In a statement posted on the Presidency’s official X handle, the government declared that at no time did the President direct that the 750km dualised Lagos-Calabar Coastal Highway be discontinued to East-West Road from Edo State.

Instead, it said the proposed reconstruction of 400 kilometres of the East-West Road, from Edo State to Cross River State, was an additional project to be executed alongside the coastal highway.

“This additional project, which is the reconstruction of East-West Road, is presently below flood level due to climate change and whose pavement is badly damaged, will not affect the complete construction of the entire 750km dualised Lagos-Calabar Coastal Highway as initially proposed,” the statement said.

The statement, issued following a directive by the Minister of Works, David Umahi, sought to clarify the government’s position amid mounting questions over the route of the coastal highway and the implications of the proposed changes for states along the corridor.

Umahi had earlier said Tinubu directed that the continuation of the coastal highway should use the existing East-West Road in parts of the Niger Delta rather than create an entirely new alignment.

The comments generated controversy, with critics demanding clarification on whether the original route had been altered and which communities would benefit from the project.

The latest statement, however, maintained that the original alignment remained intact and that work was progressing on several sections of the highway.

It identified five sections where work was ongoing in the Niger Delta and adjoining areas, including Sections 3A and 3B in Cross River and Akwa Ibom states, covering 75 kilometres of dual carriageway; Sections 4A and 4B in Ogun and Ondo states, covering 65 kilometres; and Section Five in Akwa Ibom State, covering 62 kilometres.

The government said surveying and design work was continuing on the outstanding portions of the highway, extending from the end of the Ondo section through Edo, Delta, Bayelsa and Rivers states before connecting with Section Five in Akwa Ibom.

It added that procurement and construction of the remaining sections would commence after the survey and design work had been completed.

“As soon as the survey and design of the remaining sections of the 750km of the Lagos-Calabar Coastal Highway are completed, procurement and construction will commence starting from the end of Ondo axis,” the statement said.
