The Presidency also cited the additional route approved for the Akwanga-Jos-Bauchi-Gombe-Biu-Maiduguri highway to explain why the East-West Road reconstruction would not mean the abandonment or alteration of the coastal highway.

According to the statement, Tinubu approved an additional 410-kilometre Wukari-Langtang route under the fourth legacy road project, expanding the planned dual carriageway from 700 kilometres to 1,100 kilometres.

It said the additional route had not affected the original alignment of the project, adding that the same principle applied to the coastal highway and the East-West Road reconstruction.

“All sections of the legacy projects are ongoing as proposed, and the additional projects will not affect the performance of the original alignment nor will it change it,” the statement added.

The Lagos-Calabar Coastal Highway is one of the federal government’s major infrastructure projects, designed to link Lagos with Calabar through Ogun, Ondo, Edo, Delta, Bayelsa, Rivers and Akwa Ibom states.

The controversy over its alignment intensified after Umahi’s comments that the existing East-West Road would be incorporated into the route in parts of the Niger Delta. The minister cited flooding, climate change and the condition of the existing road as reasons for the proposed reconstruction.

However, the reported changes prompted questions about the project’s original objectives, particularly its promise of improved connectivity for coastal communities and economic centres across the southern corridor.

But the latest clarification did not provide a detailed map of the final alignment or explain precisely how the coastal highway and the reconstructed East-West Road would connect along the affected stretches.

The Presidency urged Nigerians to disregard what it described as misinformation about the administration’s commitment to delivering the projects as planned.

World.title: Oil Surveillance: Reps Panel Clears PINL, Okunbo, Petitioners Fail to Provide Evidence
World.content:
A subcommittee of the House of Representatives has found no evidence to support allegations against Pipeline Infrastructure Nigeria Limited (PINL) and its Executive Director, Dr. Osahon Okunbo, and has recommended that the petition against them be thrown out.

Constituted under the House Committee on Host Communities, the panel was set up to examine a petition dated September 5, 2026 from the Niger Delta Oil-Producing Communities Reform Movement (ND-OCRIM), which challenged PINL’s pipeline surveillance contract.

The petitioners made five claims, including that the contract was not properly executed; that contract funds were mismanaged, that PINL’s finances required a forensic review and that the executive director spent money on personal matters.

Besides, the petitioner alleged that the welfare of field workers had been neglected. However, no documents or proof of any kind accompanied them.

The Committee nonetheless referred the petition for a proper hearing. Proceedings followed the rules of the House and the principle of fair hearing, with the Committee’s Deputy Clerk serving as secretary.

ND-OCRIM was invited three times, on September 14; September 22 and October 5, 2026, and failed to turn up on each occasion. It sent no one in its place, gave no reason and brought no evidence. No other stakeholder appeared.

However, PINL did appear. Its representative submitted a written document: “The Impact of PINL Operations on Oil Production and Stability of the Niger Delta,” supported by location-tagged photographs. Nobody challenged it. Hearings closed on October 7, 2026.

The submission set out the conditions PINL met on arrival. By May 2022, according to the company, 97 of every 100 barrels of crude pumped into the Trans Niger Pipeline (TNP) were being lost. Force majeure had been declared, and national output had fallen below 900,000 barrels per day.

PINL, engaged in August 2022, said it now works across all 215 host communities and engages more than 35,600 community members. Its operations are supported by 28 forward bases, 130 boats, 175 vehicles, 25 drones and 454 personnel from government security agencies.

The company reported that the share of crude reaching the Bonny Terminal through the TNP rose from 3 per cent in May 2022 to 98 per cent in September 2026. It said the OML 11 field was restarted within 90 days after an 18-month shut-in, that 2,049 illegal connections were repaired and that 1,010 illegal refinery clusters were destroyed.

It also pointed to its work in host communities, citing more than 5,000 scholarships, skills training for over 4,000 women and girls, and flood relief for more than 10 communities in Rivers State.

In its findings, the panel said PINL’s submission directly answered the claims about how the work was done. It also admitted a gap: the submission did not address the claims about contract funds or personal spending. On those two matters, its findings rest on the petitioners’ failure to bring any evidence.

On welfare, members noted PINL’s palliative and food bank support and found no sign of neglect. They described PINL as a well-organised company with a strong structure, well regarded in its host communities, and said no evidence backs any claim against Okunbo.

Twelve recommendations followed. The panel asked the full Committee to dismiss the petition, end any further investigation, and record the claims against PINL and Dr. Okunbo as unproven, while noting that affected parties keep their legal rights.

Also, it asked the Committee to acknowledge PINL’s work in protecting pipelines and its programmes in host communities, urged the company to sustain that work and look after its field staff, and recommended that the federal government extend PINL’s contract.

Commendation was also sought for President Bola Tinubu, for sustaining security reforms in the oil and gas industry; the National Security Adviser (NSA), for coordinating the protection of pipelines as well as the management of NNPC Limited.

They also lauded the pipeline security firms including PINL and Tantita Security Services Nigeria Limited and further asked the Committee to pass a vote of confidence in all of them.

But the report is not yet final. Dated October 7, 2026, it has been submitted to the full Committee for consideration and adoption, and the signature lines for the Chairman, four members and the Secretary were blank in the copy seen.

World.title: Donald Duke Canvasses Two-Party Political Blocs for Effective Presidential System
World.content:
• Warns opposition division could hand incumbents electoral advantage

Sunday Ehigiator





The presidential candidate of the Peoples Redemption Party (PRP) and former governor of Cross River State, Donald Duke, has advocated an emergence of two dominant political blocs in Nigeria, arguing that a fragmented opposition could give incumbents an electoral advantage under the country’s presidential system.

Duke also called for a review of Nigeria’s constitutional requirements for electing a president, saying the existing electoral framework could produce a winner without the support of a majority of voters.

Speaking in an interview yesterday, the former governor said Nigeria needed to understand the differences between presidential and parliamentary systems and structure its political competition accordingly.

“Those of us in the democratic space in Nigeria today really don’t understand how it works. There are different ways of expressing yourselves democratically. But for the system we run, the presidential, the avenue towards success is different from that of Westminster, for instance.

“The Westminster system, you can have several parties. The ability to form government is, if you’re a minority, if you don’t have all the required number of seats in parliament, you can cobble together an opposition. The presidential is different,” he said.

Duke maintained that a presidential system would function more effectively with two major political blocs representing the incumbent and the opposition, warning that the division of opposition votes among several parties could weaken the chances of challenging an incumbent.

“The important thing is that if you want a proper presidential system of government, you ought to have only two major parties, right? An incumbent and an opposition. Once you, like I said, balkanise or fractionise the opposition, you will lose your ball. The incumbent will always have it,” he said.

Citing the 2023 presidential election, Duke argued that the existing constitutional provisions could allow a candidate to win without securing an absolute majority of votes cast nationally.

“It will still be a minority government. It won’t get the majority of the votes cast on election day. Last time we had about 36–37 per cent,” he said.

He warned that the same scenario could recur in the 2027 general election if opposition parties failed to overcome their divisions.

“So that scenario may replay itself. It may even be less. It may get maybe 25 and all that. But because they are fractured, all you would strive to do is get 25 per cent in two-thirds of the states and a simple majority.

“It doesn’t need to get eight million votes. It could just get 10 votes more, five votes more than every other person. And that is one of the faults with the electoral system. It’s not designed for a presidential system.”

Under Section 134 of the 1999 Constitution, as amended, a presidential candidate must secure the highest number of votes cast and satisfy the prescribed geographical spread requirements.

The Constitution does not generally require a candidate to obtain more than 50 per cent of all valid votes cast nationally.

Duke called for a review of the constitutional framework, arguing that Nigeria needed electoral rules that better reflected the principles and workings of its presidential system.

“This is why we really need to revisit the constitution, because those who put it together probably didn’t understand these fundamentals,” he said.

He also criticised the absence of clear ideological distinctions among political parties, saying this had encouraged politicians to move between platforms without firmly established philosophical commitments.

“We don’t have any ideological stance in our politics. They’re just platforms. We have not developed to the point where we stand for certain ideologies. So, these platforms are not ideologically based. And that’s why you have people swarming back and forth,” he said.

Reflecting on the political arrangement of the aborted Third Republic, Duke said there was some merit in the attempt to establish two broad political platforms through the Social Democratic Party and the National Republican Convention, although he questioned the process through which the military government created them.

“Normally, parties form governments. But in this case, the government formed the party,” he said.

Beyond electoral reform, Duke argued that Nigeria needed to redefine the purpose of government by prioritising citizens’ productivity, economic opportunities and security.

“What I find, the synergy I find with PRP, is it articulates something I always believed in, that the main essence, the main function of government is the optimal productivity of our citizens within a safe and orderly environment.

“I think that’s what the government is all about. Not just for people to administer or supervise over people, but to ensure that they are productive within a safe and orderly environment,” he said.

He said education, healthcare and infrastructure should be viewed as investments in the productive capacity of citizens.

“That’s why we send kids to school. That’s why we send them to hospitals. We build infrastructure. All towards the productivity of our citizens. That is the mission statement of the government. It changes the way we see the dynamics of government.”

The former governor also called for Nigeria’s 36 states to develop sustainable economic bases by identifying and exploiting their comparative advantages, rather than functioning primarily as administrative units.

Recalling his tenure as Cross River governor from 1999 to 2007, he said his administration sought to demonstrate that every federating unit could become an economic centre through agriculture, tourism and other viable sectors.

“We wanted to prove a point that it could happen. We wanted to prove that every federating unit in this country could also be an economic unit.

“So, we took our strengths, right? Agriculture, we have incredible land mass. But beyond that, we took a low-hanging fruit like tourism, which everyone thought wouldn’t work. And it worked spectacularly. It can be done. That can-do spirit has been proven before,” he said.

Duke cited Tinapa, the business and tourism project established during his administration, as part of the effort to expand Cross River’s economic opportunities.

“Tinapa was one thing that we built in Cross River. It was a dream. To the extent that it was commissioned a month before I left office, it was successful,” he said.

He maintained that electoral reforms, viable political competition and economic development should ultimately serve the purpose of improving citizens’ living standards.

“Government is to ensure that they are productive within a safe and orderly environment,” Duke said.

World.title: Speaker Abbas Unveils 100-Day Legislative Plan
World.content:
•Warns lawmakers against abandoning duties for 2027 campaigns

Juliet Akoje in Abuja





Speaker of the House of Representatives, Hon. Tajudeen Abbas, has proposed a 100-day legislative programme to accelerate pending bills, clear outstanding committee reports and strengthen oversight, warning lawmakers against abandoning their constitutional responsibilities for the 2027 election campaigns.

Abbas who announced the plan on Tuesday while addressing members at the resumption of plenary after the 2026 annual recess, said the remaining months of the 10th House must be devoted to completing priority legislation and delivering measurable results for Nigerians.

He also proposed that Tuesdays and Thursdays be dedicated to major bills and urgent national issues, alongside stricter attendance at plenary and committee sittings.

Committees are expected to clear outstanding reports within defined timelines, while the House plans to publish a comprehensive legislative scorecard and legacy report before the end of its tenure.

“Our constituents elected us for a full term, and they deserve a full term of service,” the Speaker said, stressing that political activities must not take precedence over legislation and oversight.

Abbas said the House had received 2,747 bills and passed 363 as of mid-June 2026, with its bill passage rate rising from approximately seven per cent in the first session to about 26 per cent in the third.

The House also processed hundreds of motions and public petitions during the period.

He disclosed that an internal assessment showed the House had completed between 65 and 70 per cent of the principal milestones in its legislative agenda, but cautioned that the number of bills passed was not, by itself, a sufficient measure of legislative performance.

According to him, the effectiveness of the National Assembly must be judged by whether laws resolve public problems, motions lead to action, investigations protect the public interest and oversight improves the management of public resources.

The Speaker identified the conclusion of the constitutional review process as one of the House’s immediate priorities, naming the State Police Bill, the Reserved Seats for Women Bill and other outstanding constitutional alteration bills as proposals requiring sustained engagement with the Senate and state Houses of Assembly.

He also urged the Executive to submit the Medium-Term Expenditure Framework promptly to allow the legislature sufficient time to scrutinise the 2027 budget and facilitate the timely passage of the Appropriation Bill.

Abbas said the House would give prompt consideration to bills and requests transmitted by President Bola Tinubu, including the National Research Development Fund Bill and a request received on Tuesday for the domestication of the Geneva Conventions and their relevant protocols.

He described the Geneva Conventions request as nationally and diplomatically significant, saying its approval would strengthen protections for civilians, wounded persons and prisoners during armed conflicts.

On preparations for the 2027 general elections, the Speaker called for strict adherence to the Electoral Act and adequate lawful support for the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) to discharge its responsibilities.

He said all public institutions involved in the electoral process must demonstrate neutrality, competence and restraint, while lawmakers must ensure that political competition does not undermine their constitutional obligations.

Acknowledging the defections and political realignments recorded across party lines, Abbas said such developments were part of an active democracy but should not distract members from their shared responsibilities.

“Whatever our political affiliations or personal ambitions, we remain members of one House. We are bound by one Constitution and one oath. The campaign must never become more important than the country,” he said.

The Speaker also called for the completion of outstanding committee reports and bills awaiting legislative action, warning that important proposals should not expire simply because they had remained unattended.

Reflecting on developments since the House adjourned on July 23, Abbas acknowledged improvements in key economic indicators but said the gains must translate into better living conditions for Nigerians.

He cited economic growth of more than four per cent, a decline in inflation to 15.39 per cent in August from 23.14 per cent in the corresponding period of 2025, and external reserves of $54.7 billion in September, the highest level since 2009.

He also said Nigeria recorded a trade surplus exceeding N20 trillion in the first half of 2026, almost twice the figure recorded during the same period in 2025.

While describing the figures as encouraging, Abbas said the priority should be to convert economic stability into affordable food, productive employment, accessible credit and reliable public services.

He noted that investor confidence was improving, with new commitments emerging in ports, power, agriculture and industry.

Among the projects he cited was the proposed $7 billion Gateway Deep Seaport and Blue Marine Economic Zone, which he said could create jobs, expand exports and strengthen Nigeria’s position in African trade.

The Speaker further observed that increased public revenues had expanded the financial capacity of federal, state and local governments, placing a greater responsibility on them to demonstrate accountability, particularly at the subnational level.

He said higher revenues should result in better roads, stronger schools, safer communities and more effective healthcare.

Abbas, however, drew attention to security challenges and natural disasters reported during the recess, including the abduction of schoolchildren in Borno State, attacks and displacement in parts of Ondo State, and destructive flooding and erosion in Enugu and Abia states.

He expressed solidarity with families who had lost loved ones, homes and livelihoods, calling for prompt relief and lasting protection for affected communities.

He said security agencies would continue to receive the support required to perform their duties but maintained that they must remain accountable for the resources and authority entrusted to them.

On budget implementation, Abbas recalled that the House, on September 29, extended the capital component of the 2025 Appropriation Act to December 31 to protect ongoing projects and prevent public investment from going to waste.

He said the extension must lead to faster implementation and measurable results, adding that it would not justify further delays.

The House, he said, would continue to scrutinise fund releases, project timelines and performance.

The Speaker said the 10th Assembly had entered its fourth and final phase, making it necessary for lawmakers to assess their achievements and concentrate on unfinished business.

He acknowledged that the House had experienced disagreements, intense debates and considerable political pressure but said members had preserved the institution’s unity and repeatedly found common ground on issues of national importance.

Abbas commended Deputy Speaker Benjamin Kalu, the Majority Leader, other principal officers, committee chairmen and members for their contributions, while acknowledging the Minority Caucus for what he described as a robust and responsible opposition.

He also praised the Clerk to the National Assembly and legislative staff for sustaining the institution, and thanked the media for keeping Nigerians informed.

The Speaker called for continued cooperation among the Executive, the Judiciary and the legislature, in line with the constitutional independence of each arm of government.

He also urged civil society organisations, professional bodies, the media and constituents to continue holding the House accountable.

He said the final months of the Assembly would test lawmakers’ commitment as political interests intensified and attention shifted towards the elections.

Abbas urged members to remain focused until the end of their mandate, expressing the expectation that the House would complete its priority legislation, strengthen oversight and maintain its service to Nigerians.

The plenary resumed following the annual recess and rehabilitation of the House chamber.

However, Abbas thanked members for their patience during the break and commended the Chairman of the Committee on House Services, Hon.Daniel Amos, the Clerk and technical teams involved in restoring the chamber.

World.title: Appeal Court Quashes Free Speech Case Against Saraki
World.content:
Hammed Shittu in Ilorin





The Court of Appeal sitting in Ilorin, the Kwara State capital, yesterday, dismissed the criminal defamation and cyberbullying case filed by Kwara State Government against former Senate President, Dr. Bukola Saraki.

The court, in its unanimous decision, also declared that the charge and the evidence produced disclosed no offence committed by Saraki.

In a judgement read by Hon. Justice Ridwan Maiwada Abdullahi on behalf of two other judges, Hon. Justice Gabriel Omoniyi Kolawole and Hon. Justice Abdu Dogo, the appellate court held that there was nothing in the statement by Saraki being complained of by Mr. Abdulrahman Abdulrazaq, Governor of Kwara State, capable of inciting violence in any part of Kwara State or moving anybody to resort to the breakdown of law and order

The judge stated that all the evidence and witnesses’ statements supplied in support of the charge did not disclose that Saraki’s statement led to any breach of the peace in the state; rather, they merely showed that those who testified felt dissatisfied with the statement.

He added that the Administration of Criminal Justice Act, the Penal Code Law of Kwara State, and the Cybercrime and Cyberbullying law were not enacted for the purpose of protecting individuals against statements that they were uncomfortable with.

He added that while the attorney general of a state and that of the federation had wide powers to institute criminal cases, such powers could not be exercised in a manner prejudicial and oppressive of any individual or to violate the fundamental human rights of citizens.

The judge, therefore, ordered that the case instituted at the Kwara State High Court against Saraki over his statement in which he alleged that Abdulrazaq did not complete secondary education and that his level of education was affecting his judgment, could not be sustained, having not disclosed any offence or included any statutory ingredient of the offence he was being charged for.

In his reaction to the judgement, Saraki’s Press Officer on Local Matters, Abdulganiyu Abdulqadir, quoted his principal as stating that he had once again been vindicated in his unflinching belief that nobody, no matter how powerful, can successfully muffle the voice of dissent, particularly, when those in government fail in their responsibility to the people.

Saraki also expressed his gratitude to the judiciary for once again standing for the truth and defending the cause of justice.

He said he wanted his supporters to know that Abdulrazaq’s oppressive tendencies were mere inconveniences that would soon blow away.

The former senate president stated, “This is because the administration has only seven months to stay in office, and the tendency that it represents will be totally eradicated in Kwara State by the people.

“If the need arises, he will not hesitate to reiterate his position on the level of education of Governor Abdulrazaq and that he will not keep quiet when there are issues of public interest that deserve his comment.”

World.title: IMF Warns Poverty Remains High in Nigeria Despite Economic Growth
World.content:
Raises 2026 growth forecast to 4.2%, retains 4.3% for 2027

•Backs CBN’s data-driven inflation fight, urges stronger banking sector safeguards

•Backs CBN’s data-driven inflation fight, urges stronger banking sector safeguards Oyedele cautions against higher taxes on vulnerable households, calls for policy alignment to unlock AfCFTA

Nume Ekeghe in Bangkok, Thailand

The International Monetary Fund (IMF) yesterday warned that poverty remains high in Nigeria despite resilient economic growth, urging the federal government to provide targeted, temporary support to vulnerable households as rising food and energy costs continue to undermine living standards.

The Fund, however, raised Nigeria’s economic growth forecast for 2026 by 0.1 percentage point to 4.2 per cent, while retaining its projection of 4.3 per cent for 2027, reflecting expectations of continued economic expansion despite persistent domestic and external challenges.

The IMF’s assessment came as the Group of 24 (G-24), chaired by Nigeria’s Minister of Finance and Coordinating Minister of the Economy, Taiwo Oyedele, called on the IMF and the World Bank to make development financing more affordable, warning that developing countries pay an estimated $500 billion more in borrowing costs than developed economies.

At the ongoing IMF/World Bank Annual Meetings in Bangkok, Thailand, Oyedele urged African countries to improve policy coordination, remove barriers to intra-African trade and mobilise private capital to accelerate economic transformation through the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA).

The Fund also acknowledged improvements in Nigeria’s inflation outlook, supporting a data-driven approach by the Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN), while emphasising the need for stronger capital and liquidity buffers, effective banking supervision and timely recognition of bad loans.

IMF: Poverty Remains High Despite Growth

The IMF’s projections were presented in its 2026 World Economic Outlook, titled Resilience Under Strain, Urgent Choices, released during the Annual Meetings.

Speaking on fiscal policy responses to rising living costs in Africa, the Fund’s Research Department Division Chief, Deniz Igan, said policymakers needed to balance immediate household needs with medium-term fiscal stability.

She explained that the disproportionate rise in food and energy prices had intensified the cost-of-living crisis, making it necessary for governments to protect vulnerable citizens without undermining the sustainability of public finances.

“What we are advocating for is for policymakers to balance the near-term needs of the population, and that involves food security.

“That involves energy security. Given that the prices of food and energy are increasing disproportionately, while also keeping in mind medium-term stability, how to do that is, of course, a great question,” she said.

Igan noted that the IMF had examined fiscal policy responses capable of addressing situations in which essential goods become more expensive faster than the broader consumption basket.

Using Nigeria as an example, she said the economy had demonstrated resilience, partly reflecting its position as an energy exporter, but the benefits of growth had yet to sufficiently address widespread poverty and household hardship.

“While growth held up in Nigeria, given that it is an energy exporter, poverty rates are still very high, and we are very mindful that the population is suffering, especially when it comes to food security, with risks also arising from El Niño,” she said.

The IMF therefore recommended targeted and temporary income support, including cash transfers, to cushion the effects of higher living costs on the most vulnerable households.

According to Igan, such interventions could alleviate poverty and improve food security, provided they were consistent with a credible medium-term fiscal framework.

She said governments also needed to improve the quality of public expenditure and strengthen revenue collection to ensure that social protection measures remained sustainable.

IMF Backs CBN’s Inflation Fight, Urges Banking Sector Vigilance

Separately, the IMF acknowledged improvements in Nigeria’s inflation outlook, suggesting that a less restrictive monetary policy stance could eventually become appropriate, provided incoming economic data continued to support such a decision.

The Fund’s Assistant Director in the Monetary and Capital Markets Department, Jason Wu, made the assessment at the launch of the Global Financial Stability Report, titled Resilience, Risk, and Transformation, during the Annual Meetings.

Wu stressed that the progress recorded on inflation made monetary policy credibility, data dependence and transparent communication particularly important as the CBN assessed the appropriate direction of policy.

“We have seen improvements on the inflation front, which suggests that a perhaps not as tight monetary policy stance would be appropriate,” he said.

He cautioned, however, that central banks needed to remain responsive to changing economic conditions and clearly explain the rationale behind their decisions, particularly as renewed inflationary pressures and uncertainty continued to shape the global outlook.

“I think what’s important is credibility. In other words, the central bank has to be data-driven and has to be able to explain the decisions clearly. And so far, based on what we have seen, it seems like the news is on the good front,” he added.

According to him, continued reliance on economic data and clear policy communication would be essential to containing further inflationary shocks.

Beyond monetary policy, the IMF urged regulators to strengthen banking sector oversight, noting that recapitalisation alone would not guarantee financial stability without effective supervision and appropriate prudential safeguards.

Wu said emerging economies needed to ensure that stronger capital positions were accompanied by adequate liquidity requirements and timely recognition of credit losses and non-performing loans.

“On strengthening the banking sector, I think often what we see in emerging economies is, after recapitalisation, starting to impose appropriate regulations to prevent risks from building up in the future,” he said.

He also identified the relationship between sovereign and banking sector risks as a critical concern for African economies, urging regulators to understand financial institutions’ exposure to government debt and related vulnerabilities.

The IMF official said these measures would help strengthen banks’ resilience and reduce the likelihood that emerging risks would undermine financial stability.

His comments come amid efforts by Nigeria’s banking industry to strengthen capital positions following the CBN’s recapitalisation exercise.

Meanwhile, the IMF’s Deputy Director in the Monetary and Capital Markets Department, Athanasios Vamvakidis, said emerging markets had remained resilient despite elevated global bond yields, supported by stronger domestic fundamentals, sound policies and investor appetite for risk.

However, he warned that the combination of high yields and historically narrow credit spreads could leave developing economies exposed if global financial conditions deteriorated.

He said developments in advanced economies and renewed energy price shocks could widen spreads, raising borrowing costs even for countries with relatively strong economic fundamentals.

Vamvakidis urged emerging economies to strengthen financial buffers in anticipation of adverse scenarios, adding that transparency was essential to sustaining investor confidence and access to international capital markets.

He said clear information about countries’ financial obligations could reassure investors and preserve financing opportunities, particularly for African economies that depend on international borrowing.

G-24 Seeks Cheaper Financing for Developing Countries

The G-24 called on the IMF and the World Bank to expand access to affordable concessional financing and accelerate sovereign debt restructuring, warning that high borrowing costs are constraining developing countries’ ability to finance infrastructure, social services and job creation.

Oyedele, who chairs the group, made the appeal at its press briefing during the Annual Meetings, arguing that developing economies faced a disproportionate financing burden estimated at about $500 billion compared with developed countries.

He said borrowing remained necessary to finance development and stimulate investment, but the cost of debt was increasingly limiting governments’ capacity to deliver inclusive growth.

“What we have seen by members of the G-24 and across, particularly the developing countries, such as those in Africa, is the increasing burden of not just high debts or high costs of debts. To the extent that we have some estimates indicating that these developing countries are paying in the region of about $500 billion more than they should be paying compared to developed countries,” he said.

The group urged the Bretton Woods institutions to make short-term concessional borrowing more affordable, particularly for vulnerable countries facing mounting fiscal pressures, while developing frameworks that would attract more private investment over the longer term.

Oyedele said greater access to affordable financing would help governments direct limited public resources towards areas where they were most needed, including healthcare, education and social protection.

The G-24’s intervention comes as developing economies contend with debt vulnerabilities and competing expenditure demands, with debt-servicing obligations threatening to crowd out investments that could support economic growth and improve living standards.

The group also called for more predictable, timely, orderly and coordinated sovereign debt treatment, alongside greater transparency and improvements in credit-rating assessments.

The Director of the G-24 Secretariat, Iyabo Masha, said progress had been made in strengthening the international debt-resolution architecture, including updates to debt sustainability assessments and restructuring procedures.

She cited improvements to the IMF’s debt sustainability framework and developments under the Global Sovereign Debt Roundtable and the Common Framework, which are intended to facilitate more effective responses when countries face unsustainable debt burdens.

However, Masha said further reforms were necessary, particularly to ensure that private creditors participated more effectively in debt-resolution initiatives. Countries with substantial exposure to privately held bonds, she noted, might not benefit fully from existing arrangements.

She also called on advanced economies to support improvements in credit-rating methodologies, arguing that developing countries should not be unfairly penalised when their debt sustainability and financing risks are assessed.

Masha cited the experience of countries such as Sri Lanka as evidence of the weaknesses exposed by previous debt crises, adding that the Borrowers’ Platform, spearheaded by the United Nations Conference on Trade and Development (UNCTAD), could strengthen cooperation among debtor countries and improve knowledge-sharing on sustainable borrowing.

Oyedele Warns Against Taxing Vulnerable Households

Beyond the cost of borrowing, Oyedele cautioned governments against responding to fiscal pressures by imposing additional taxes on vulnerable households and productive sectors of their economies.

He argued that governments needed to improve domestic revenue mobilisation and identify inefficient expenditure while ensuring that fiscal measures did not deepen hardship or weaken economic activity.

According to him, taxation and borrowing both have economic and social consequences and should be assessed according to their implications for household welfare, investment and long-term development.

He noted that higher taxes could deprive low-income households of resources needed for food, healthcare and education, while excessive taxation of businesses could undermine productive activity and employment.

“The way I like to put it is: if you collect taxes, you raise the money now, and that itself has a lot of trade-offs. What taxes are you collecting? Are you collecting taxes from the most vulnerable, and this will deprive them of money to provide food, health, education? They have to be mindful of tax, and debts is future taxes,” he said.

He added that the choice was not simply between taxation and borrowing, but about striking a balance that supported sustainable public finances without undermining citizens’ welfare.

“So it’s not one or the other. It’s to strike a balance, bearing in mind ultimately that the essence of tax and of debts is to cater for the people. If you put people always at the centre of your policies, you will not be perfect, but you are likely to strike a balance that works and is sustainable,” he said.

His remarks highlighted the dilemma facing developing economies as governments seek to raise revenue, contain debt and meet rising demands for public services.

Oyedele also stressed that economic growth needed to create employment and improve living standards rather than be judged solely by headline macroeconomic indicators.

He warned that the adoption of artificial intelligence could complicate employment prospects if governments failed to make deliberate policy choices on its deployment and regulation.

“It’s not only just the World Bank and the IMF. This is a collective responsibility for all of us to ensure that growth is not just for the sake of growth. It has to be job-rich. It has to be inclusive, and at the end of the day, must be able to translate to better living standards for our people,” he said.

Masha, however, maintained that macroeconomic stability remained essential to achieving these objectives, arguing that governments needed a stable economic environment to implement structural reforms, employment policies and infrastructure programmes.

Oyedele agreed, describing stability as the foundation for sustainable growth and prosperity.

“The stability itself is the foundation upon which you can build the growth and the prosperity that you want for your people,” he said.

Oyedele: Africa Needs Policy Alignment to Unlock AfCFTA

On regional economic integration, Oyedele called for stronger policy coordination among African countries, arguing that the AfCFTA could transform the continent’s economic prospects if governments removed trade barriers and established consistent rules and standards.

Speaking at the Africa’s Golden Future panel during the Annual Meetings, he said the agreement offered an opportunity to turn Africa’s fragmented national markets into a larger, more competitive continental market capable of supporting production, investment and trade.

“So we have a lot of small countries, and what AfCFTA is trying to do is to turn 54 countries into one market, so that way it’s easy for us to scale. But that will not happen until we remove the barriers, and many of them are actually non-tariff,” he said.

He explained that effective implementation would require clear standards, predictable regulations and supporting infrastructure, noting that non-tariff barriers remained a major impediment to intra-African commerce.

Oyedele cited Nigeria’s National Single Window initiative as an effort to streamline border processes and improve trade facilitation, adding that technology was being deployed to make the process more efficient.

He also disclosed that Nigeria was developing an economic policy framework incorporating its international commitments, including regional treaties.

According to him, economic integration would remain difficult if countries failed to align their trade, fiscal and monetary policies, even within their own borders.

“If you have trade policies, fiscal policies, monetary policies, and they’re not speaking together even within the same country, you can imagine the nightmare dealing with 54 or 53 other countries,” he said.

The minister also emphasised that policy consistency, institutional strength and public trust were critical to attracting private capital, which Africa needs to close its development financing gap.

“Capital follows trust before it follows returns. They need to be able to plan and predict what you are going to do,” he said.

Reflecting on Nigeria’s economic reforms, Oyedele said governments needed to communicate the reasons for policy changes clearly, demonstrate the consequences of failing to implement them and ensure that reforms were properly sequenced.

He explained that price corrections should be followed by efforts to stabilise the economy before policies to expand growth were pursued.

Institutionalising reforms through legislation and strong institutions, he added, would help ensure that they survived changes in political leadership.

“But most importantly, think about how do you make it sustainable, and that’s by putting it into institutions and putting it into law. So, most of the reforms we did in Nigeria are either enacted into law or embedded into institutions, because you need to be able to do that for sustainability,” he said.

He also cautioned that reform implementation needed to account for the circumstances of vulnerable citizens, particularly in African countries where poverty and limited access to education remained widespread.

Oyedele said governments had to ensure that people could withstand the immediate effects of economic adjustment while waiting for the benefits of reform to materialise.

He cited cash transfers to more than 10 million households in Nigeria and education funding supporting more than 1.5 million students as examples of social protection measures intended to cushion the impact of reforms, according to his remarks.

The minister maintained that Nigeria’s experience demonstrated the possibility of implementing difficult economic reforms, provided governments remained committed to policy consistency, institutional development and measures to protect vulnerable populations.

His position reinforced the broader message from the meetings: economic stability, affordable development financing and regional integration must work together to generate investment, create jobs and deliver tangible improvements in citizens’ living standards.

World.title: Alleged Forgery: Court to Decide If Atiku Can Amend His Suit against Tinubu Nov 20
World.content:
Alex Enumah in Abuja





Justice Inyang Ekwo of the Federal High Court, Abuja, yesterday, adjourned till November 20 for ruling in a motion by former Vice President Atiku Abubakar requesting to amend his suit challenging the eligibility of President Bola Tinubu for the 2027 presidential election.

Ekwo adjourned to the said date after listening to Atiku and Tinubu’s lawyers argue for and against the granting of the motion.

At yesterday’s proceedings, Joseph Onu, who stood for Atiku, adopted his application, praying for permission of the court to amend the originating summons against Tinubu and his party, All Progressives Congress (APC), to accommodate more allegations.

Onu explained that the amendment being sought was to allow the plaintiff to produce more evidence against Tinubu and his party in the certificate forgery allegations.

Atiku and his party, African Democratic Congress (ADC), had on September 10 brought an application seeking leave to amend their originating summons and have the proposed amended process deemed properly filed.

They said they discovered errors in the original suit, including referring to a form of the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) as Form CF001 instead of Form EC9A.

The plaintiffs added that the amendment was necessary to set out the particulars of the alleged fraud, include a written deposition by Atiku, and attach clearer copies of exhibits that were unavailable when the suit was filed.

However, Chief Wole Olanipekun, SAN, who represented Tinubu, opposed the request for amendment, arguing that since both parties have joined issues in the matter, Atiku cannot shift the goal post in the middle of the game.

Similarly, APC, represented by former Attorney General of the Federation (AGF) and Minister of Justice, Akin Olujimi, SAN, opposed Atiku on the same ground and urged the judge to reject the bid.

Counsel to INEC, Dr Alex Izinyon, SAN, also urged the court to reject the amendment request and proceed to the substantive matter.

Ekwo after listening to all sides announced November 20, to rule on the application.

The plaintiffs in the main suit are seeking the disqualification of Tinubu and APC from the 2027 presidential election, over the president’s National Youth Service Corps (NYSC) discharge certificate submitted to INEC for purposes of the presidential poll.

They alleged that APC submitted a forged NYSC discharge certificate to INEC and asked the court to order the electoral commission to remove Tinubu and APC from the list of candidates and parties for the election.

The main grouse of Atiku and ADC was that the NYSC discharge certificate presented by Tinubu bore Bola Adekunle as against the well-known name Bola Tinubu.

Tinubu and APC denied the allegation and asked the court to dismiss the suit.

Tinubu opposed the application, arguing that the proposed amendments went beyond correcting errors and would introduce new reliefs, documents, and facts into the case.

The president’s legal team also argued that the substantive suit was statute-barred, contending that the cause of action arose when Tinubu’s name was submitted to INEC on July 11, while the suit was filed on August 14.

INEC also opposed the amendment, arguing that it would introduce a new cause of action and seek to cure defects in the original suit after the constitutional deadline for filing pre-election cases had lapsed.

World.title: Black Friday 2026: When do South African sales actually start?
World.content:
In 2026, Black Friday falls on Friday 27 November. But when do the sales actually start?

BLACK NOVEMBER IS THE NEW NORMAL

The Black Friday sales have started much earlier in the last few years with deals running throughout the month of November before Black Friday itself, which falls at the end of the month. So, Black Friday has become a month-long “Black November” period with smaller discounts.

Retailers have not yet confirmed their 2026 Black Friday or Black November start dates but we can look at 2025 for an idea.



Makro and Game launched their Black Friday specials on 24 October 2025

Amazon South Africa’s Black November deals began on 31 October 2025

Takealot’s Blue Dot sale ran from 25 November

Hirsch’s, a home retailer, started theur Black November sale on 31 October 2025

HOW DO YOU FIND THE BEST DEALS?

Early specials are worth it if you want to play it safe. However, retailers so tend to offer their best deals in the final weekend of the month, as sales carry over online through Cyber Monday. Deciding on when to “check out” depends on what you are buying. You can start monitoring prices of items you need already for big ticket items like appliances and electronics. So, you would know when it’s the best time to check out.

Retailers often announce their dates ahead of time.

TIPS FOR SHOPPING BLACK NOVEMBER

Track prices before the sales start. Price-tracking sites and retailer apps make this easy.

Price-tracking sites and retailer apps make this easy. Compare across retailers. The same TV or air fryer can differ by hundreds of rand between Takealot, Makro, Game and Amazon SA. Check delivery fees and return terms too, since a cheaper price can vanish once shipping or additional fees are added.

The same TV or air fryer can differ by hundreds of rand between Takealot, Makro, Game and Amazon SA. Check delivery fees and return terms too, since a cheaper price can vanish once shipping or additional fees are added. Set a budget and a list. Black Friday works because it pushes impulse buying. Decide in advance what you need, how much you’ll spend, and don’t go beyond it. December and January are long stretches before payday, so leave room for those.

December and January are long stretches before payday, so leave room for those. Shop smart and stay safe online. Stick to trusted retailers and type in the web address yourself rather than clicking links in WhatsApp messages or emails, as scam sites multiply this time of year. Pay by credit card or a secure online payment method where you can, and enable your bank’s transaction notifications.

Pay by credit card or a secure online payment method where you can, and enable your bank’s transaction notifications. Know your rights. The Consumer Protection Act gives you protection when goods are faulty or not as described, and online purchases generally come with a cooling-off period. Keep your invoices and confirmation emails, and read the returns policy for sale items, as some retailers apply stricter terms to discounted stock.

World.title: When vicious WW2 U-boat battles raged off South Africa’s coastline
World.content:
This deadly WW2 U-boat battle raged along the South African coastline in 1942. And no one talks about it. Image: AI generated from historical images, for illustrative purposes only

In October 1942, a vitally important WW2 U-boat battle took place off the coast of South Africa. While thousands of miles away from the heart of the war in Europe, it was, in fact, one of Nazi Germany’s deadliest naval missions in the war.

Specifically, the WW2 German U-boat sortie went by the name Gruppe Eisbär (Polar Bear). It comprised four Type IXC boats (submarines). Namely, the U-68 (Karl-Friedrich Merten), U-172 (Carl Emmermann), U-159 (Helmut Witte) and U-504 (Hans-Georg Poske). So, why were these naval killing machines traversing South African waters?

WW2 U-BOAT BATTLE: OPERATION EISBÄR

At the height of early Nazi aggression in WW2, it saw the strategic importance of the Cape sea route that carried Allied troops and supplies right around Africa. Therefore, the regime dispatched U-boats to patrol the waters at the tip of Africa, more or less destroying anything they encountered.



Historical records say, between 7-11 October 1942, fourteen ships were sunk within a 90-mile radius of the Cape. Roughly 100 000 tons in five days. Among them were the Danish SS Boringia, the British SS Clan Mactavish and the American SS Coloradan, all sunk by U-159. U-172 sank the Panamanian MV Firethorn and the Greek Pantelis on 8 October.

BATTLES MOVE SOUTH EAST

Cape Town’s harbour and foreshore in 1940s during the period of land reclamation. Image: Wikipedia

After Allied forces encountered massive loses, shipping was diverted to Durban. Therefore, the WW2 U-boat battle moved South East. On 17 October 1942 U-504 sank the SS Empire Chaucer, followed by the SS Anne Hutchinson, the SS Empire Guidon and, on 31 October, the SS Reynolds. In total, Operation Eisbär sank 34 ships: 23 off the South African coastline, and eleven in transit. It is estimated that 2 690 people died in total.

Moreover, the deadliest single loss – and largest maritime disaster in South African history – came a month later. On 28 November 1942, U-177 attacked British troopship Nova Scotia with three torpedoes off the Natal coast. It was carrying Italian prisoners of war and civilian internees from Massawa, alongside British and South African guards and crew. More 1 000 were on board, 858 died, with a Portuguese frigate Afonso de Albuquerque rescuing some 192 survivors.



WHY IS THIS WW2 U-BOAT BATTLE FORGOTTEN?

As a defence, Cape Town and Durban went dark at night to help deter the U-boats. Eisbär’s captains had to abandon plans to attack harbour approaches directly. Eventually the blackout tactic worked. The U-179 was sunk, and U-159 was depth-charged by South African forces.

Historians say this most deadly WW2 U-boat battle is largely forgotten due to deliberate wartime censorship. Many of the attacks took place far offshore, in the dark, and Germany wanted to keep details quiet. And yet, in sheer scale, one of the deadliest submarine operations of WW2 was fought within sight of the South African coastline …

World.title: Doctors attend to Kaizer Chiefs coach after Stellenbosch match at FNB
World.content:
Kaizer Chiefs assistant coach Dillan Shepperd took the reins at the post-match press conference after Da Cruz missed the live on-pitch post-match interview.

Asked to shed light on Da Cruz’s whereabouts, Shepperd revealed that the Frenchman had fallen ill shortly after the final whistle at Soccer City.

KAIZER CHIEFS COACH FERNANDO DA CRUZ’S ILLNESS DESCRIBED

According to Shepperd, Da Cruz suddenly felt unwell before vomiting after the final whistle. “Ya, the coach has fallen ill,” he told reporters. “He was vomitting so ya, he needed the doctors checking on him, to see if he is ok.”



Stellenbosch took the lead just three minutes into the second half when Sinoxolo Kwayiba finished first time inside the box following excellent work from Terence Mashego down the left.

Kaizer Chiefs responded in the 58th minute as Mduduzi Shabalala produced a brilliant finish at the near post to level the score.

Da Cruz remains unbeaten in the Betway Premiership. The result was Amakhosi’s fifth draw in eight matches, alongside three wins. The Soweto giants sit fourth on the log, nine points behind leaders Mamelodi Sundowns, although Kaizer Chiefs have a game in hand.

Meanwhile, Kaizer Chiefs are looking ahead to their trip to Zambia on Saturday. They will kick off their CAF Confederation Cup preliminary second round campaign against Red Arrows at Levy Mwanawasa Stadium at 15:00. The return leg will be played at Moses Mabhida Stadium next weekend.

World.title: ‘Fernando Da Cruz will be fired by January’
World.content:
Former Kaizer Chiefs winger Junior Khanye does not believe head coach Fernando Da Cruz will finish the season at Naturena.

The outspoken analyst has predicted that the Frenchman could be shown the door by January following Amakhosi’s latest disappointing result.

Chiefs were held to a 1-1 draw by Stellenbosch FC at FNB Stadium on Tuesday evening, extending their run of consecutive draws to three.



Speaking on iDiski TV, Khanye blamed Da Cruz’s team selection and tactical approach for the dropped points, insisting that the coach needs to improve his reading of matches.

“Kaizer Chiefs coach must take the blame for tonight’s draw. He must change the way he approaches games and his reading of the match. He needs to improve,” Khanye said.

“He played three consecutive draws, and how he approaches games will be his downfall. By now, he should have his main starting eleven. His team needs to have balance in defence and attack.”



Fernando Da Cruz underpressure

The former winger also believes Chiefs supporters are growing increasingly impatient with the coach, especially given the club’s recent struggles to turn draws into victories.

Khanye questioned whether Fernando Da Cruz would be able to succeed after previously working under former Chiefs coach Nasreddine Nabi alongside assistants Cedric Kaze and Khalil Ben Youssef.

“Personally, I think Nasreddine Nabi, Cedric Kaze, Khalil Ben Youssef and Da Cruz are the same because this coach was Nabi’s assistant. He is under pressure now, and I don’t think supporters will allow another draw,” he said.



With pressure mounting on Da Cruz to deliver results, Khanye believes the coach’s position could become increasingly difficult if Chiefs fail to turn their performances around.

The outspoken analyst has set January as his predicted deadline for the Frenchman’s tenure, warning that matches against title contenders Orlando Pirates and Mamelodi Sundowns could expose the team’s weaknesses.

“I don’t think he’ll survive this season. I give him until January. The likes of Orlando Pirates and Sundowns will expose him,” Khanye said.



Chiefs will need to find greater consistency if they are to ease the pressure on their coach and remain competitive in the Betway Premiership. Fernando Da Cruz will need to have a good cup run in the coming months to buy time with the league slippig away.

Fernando Da Cruz Misses Post-Match Interview

Da Cruz was unable to attend his post-match interview following the draw against Stellenbosch.

His assistant, Dillon Sheppard, explained that the Chiefs coach had fallen ill and was receiving medical attention.



“Coach has fallen ill. He was vomiting, so he is with the doctors, checking on him,” Sheppard said.

World.title: Kaizer Chiefs are out of title race and here’s why
World.content:
Kaizer Chiefs’ Betway Premiership title hopes have suffered another setback following their disappointing 1-1 draw against Stellenbosch FC at FNB Stadium on Tuesday night.

Amakhosi found themselves trailing in the second half but did not take long to respond, with Mduduzi Shabalala restoring parity. Despite pushing for a winner, the Glamour Boys were unable to find a breakthrough and had to settle for a point.

Kaizer Chiefs losing ground on title

The result leaves Chiefs nine points behind log leaders Mamelodi Sundowns, while second-placed Orlando Pirates sit eight points ahead of them on 22 points.



With just eight matches played, Amakhosi already have significant ground to make up in the title race. Sitting fourth on the standings, their focus could increasingly shift towards securing a CAF inter-club competition spot for next season.

For Kaizer Chiefs to get back into serious title contention, they will need to put together a strong winning run while hoping both Sundowns and Pirates drop points in the second half of the campaign.

Under new coach Fernando da Cruz, the Soweto giants have shown signs of promise, with improved organisation offering some encouragement. However, their inability to consistently turn performances into victories remains a concern.

With the gap at the top continuing to grow, Kaizer Chiefs face an uphill battle if they are to challenge for the league title this season.

It looks more likely that they will fight for third spot with AmaZulu once again after dropping points at home against Stellies.

Will Amakhosi bounce back?

World.title: ‘Betray his whole family’: Angelique Gerber shades Jacques Potgieter?
World.content:
Did Angelique Gerber shade her ex, Jacques Potgieter? Images via IG

Angelique Gerber has shared a cryptic post alluding to her ex, Jacques Potgieter. This comes after the actress and the former Springbok fuelled rumours that they had reconciled following a four-year separation.

During that time, Jacques dated another woman, whom he split from in June.

Jacques and Angelique married in 2016 and have three children together: son Jacques Jnr and twin daughters Annabella and Olivia.



ANGELIQUE GERBER THROWS SHADE AT EX, JACQUES POTGIETER?

On her Instagram Stories, Angelique posted several cryptic quotes about “exes”.

One read: “Your ex is running someone else’s life. You are safe”.

Another stated: “If you ever feel stupid….just remember a woman saw a man betray his whole family and still thought, ‘that’s my soulmate”

Angelique Gerber’s IG Stories.

The former 7de Laan actress appeared to be shading her ex, Jacqus Potgieter, and implying that he had moved on to another relationship.

It comes as Jacques has deleted pictures of himself and Angelique, which followers believed alluded to their short-lived reconciliation.

In several since-deleted posts, the former couple are seen embracing each other. In one pic, Jacques carried Angelique in the air, whilst in a third, she sat on his lap.



“I hit the bullseye”, he captioned the post. Referring to his ex, he posted in another: “You make my heart beat fast again”.

Jacques Potgieter deleted pictures of him with his ex.

Images via IG

WHAT WENT WRONG?

Jacques Potgieter and Angelique Gerber wed a decade ago on a wine farm in the Western Cape.

The couple began dating in 2014, when Angelique played the popular character “Clara” on the now-defunct SABC soapie 7de Laan.

In mid 2022, Jacques allegedly admitted to being unfaithful to his Springbok wife, Angelique Gerber in a series of Instagram Stories.

At the same time, Angeliqe posted a cryptic post on her IG Stories that read: “The truth always comes out”.

Jacques later claimed his account was “hacked” and assured the public the accusations about his marriage and alleged affairs were false.

Angelique then posted an apology on her account, implying the same.

By Christmas, it was clear the couple had officially split after removing all romantic posts featuring each other. To further fuel the fire, Jacques began posting pictures with his new girlfriend, Lizane Wagner.

Fast forward to 2023, and Angelique put Jacques Potgieter on blast for failing to financially support their three children.

In June, the retired rugby player – now a head coach for Centurion Rugby Club – split from Lizane.

This followed a four-year relationship with the woman many have accused of being behind his marriage breakdown.

Speaking to an Afrikaans publication, Lizane confirmed their break-up, adding that she was not the “other woman” in her ex’s marriage.

World.title: Suspect hands himself over after deadly Katlehong shooting
World.content:
JOHANNESBURG - A suspect has handed himself over to police following a shooting in Katlehong, Ekurhuleni, that killed two ANC Youth League members and wounded five others.

The victims, aged 21 and 23, were returning from a memorial service for a political party member at Mogobeng Primary School when the shooting occurred.

Five people, including teenagers, were wounded and taken to hospital for treatment.

The motive for the shooting remains unclear.

The case has been handed over to the Gauteng Political Killings Task Team for further investigation.

Gauteng Premier Panyaza Lesufi condemned the shooting, describing it as a “senseless killing”.

Lesufi said the group had been singing in the street after attending the memorial service when a car approached and someone opened fire.

According to the premier, the suspect allegedly abandoned his car, got into a taxi and handed himself over to police.

The investigation is ongoing.

World.title: 'Cat' Matlala seeks bail over alleged Waterkloof lease fraud
World.content:
PRETORIA - Vusimuzi “Cat” Matlala is expected to apply for bail in the Pretoria Specialised Commercial Crimes Court.

The alleged underworld figure faces charges relating to the alleged use of a fraudulent identity document and falsified bank statements to secure a property lease in Waterkloof worth R95,000 a month.

READ | R228m SAPS tender case postponed to 17 November

The State is expected to oppose his bail application.

Matlala’s wife, Tsakane, and two other co-accused have already been granted bail of R20,000 each.

His bail application is expected to be heard over two days.

World.title: Shadrack Sibiya continues bid for bail
World.content:
JOHANNESBURG - Disgraced former Deputy Police Commissioner Shadrack Sibiya is expected back in court on Wednesday as his bail hearing continues.

The proceedings took a dramatic turn on Tuesday when a voice recording introduced serious new allegations into the case.

In the recording, businessman Serge Cabonge allegedly claims that Sibiya received money from alleged crime boss Vusimuzi “Cat” Matlala.

Cabonge also allegedly claims that a judge advised him to leave the country after his name surfaced at the Madlanga Commission.

The inquiry has indicated that it plans to obtain Cabonge’s statement as the allegations come under further scrutiny.

World.title: AKA and Tibz murder trial continues after witness testimony
World.content:
DURBAN - The murder trial of rapper Kiernan “AKA” Forbes and his friend, Tebello “Tibz” Motsoane, continues in the Durban High Court on Wednesday.

Proceedings follow a day of testimony on Tuesday, when four witnesses took the stand, including AKA’s manager and a DJ who was with the pair on the night of the fatal shooting.

The DJ told the court he heard a loud bang as they left a restaurant on Florida Road, initially believing the sound was fireworks.
