World.title: Liberian Senator Warns Washington: Mining Giants and Drug Cartels Are Pushing Liberia Toward ‘State Capture’
World.content:
WASHINGTON, DC — A Liberian senator has told American democracy advocates that his country faces two threats at once: multinational mining companies working through legal deals, and drug cartels working through bribes. He said either one could hollow out Liberia’s democracy from within if it is left unchecked.

By Rodney D. Sieh

Senator Amara M. Konneh is an independent lawmaker from Gbarpolu County in northwestern Liberia and chairs the Senate’s Public Accounts and Audit Committee. He spoke at a private roundtable hosted this month by the National Endowment for Democracy (NED), a U.S.-funded



organization that supports democratic institutions abroad. His remarks are drawn from talking points prepared for the session and reviewed by FrontPageAfrica.

“Liberia is not yet a captured state,” Konneh said, “but we are at the most dangerous point since the war and Ebola.”

The West African nation of about 5.5 million people was founded in 1847 with the backing of freed American slaves. It is still recovering from a civil war that ended in 2003 and from the 2014–2016 Ebola epidemic that killed nearly 5,000 Liberians.

‘Legal, so it’s harder’

Konneh said mining makes up 12 percent of Liberia’s gross domestic product and 65 percent of its export earnings. Yet less than 3 percent of that wealth reaches communities directly.

The problem, he argued, starts with the way concessions are negotiated. Liberian law gives the executive branch wide discretion over Mineral Development Agreements. These 25-year contracts are ratified by the legislature and are very hard to amend later. “Companies negotiate with three or four people in Monrovia, not with the country,” he said.

He pointed out that several major operators are renegotiating rail, port and royalty terms at the same time: steelmaker ArcelorMittal, gold miner Bea Mountain, Hummingbird and Bao Chico. On paper Liberia keeps 48 percent of mining value, he said, but stabilization clauses, tax holidays and transfer pricing push the real share far lower.

He also described a system of off-budget signature bonuses and “social contributions,” often paid around elections. He said legislators from mining districts are offered jobs, scholarships and “facilitation fees” of $5,000 to $20,000 to vote for ratification. “This is legalized state capture,” he said. He did not tie any particular company to these payments.

He also warned that private security forces at some concessions are larger and better equipped than the county police. And he said community activists who protested environmental damage have been charged with “economic sabotage.” His examples included Kinjor in Grand Cape Mount County, the community most affected by Bea Mountain’s gold concession, as well as communities in Grand Bassa and Nimba.

‘Illegal, so it’s faster’

The drug trade follows “the same playbook, different commodity,” Konneh said. Traffickers don’t need to buy the whole state, only key people: “an airport baggage handler, an evidence clerk, a police crime services officer, and a port scanner operator.”

He cited two seizures this year. In June, 237 kilograms of cocaine worth an estimated $19.2 million were seized at Roberts International Airport, the country’s main airport. In July, 3.9 metric tons worth about $317 million were seized in Duazon, outside the capital, Monrovia. He said the July haul had links to Spain, Colombia, Serbia, Croatia and Ukraine, and that its value was four times Liberia’s national health budget.

He also pointed to cases inside the country’s own anti-drug agency. On September 29, a court in Margibi County convicted Joe Logan and Lovette Flowers, two agents of the Liberia Drug Enforcement Agency (LDEA), of colluding with traffickers, and sentenced each to the maximum 20 years. They had resold cocaine seized at the airport. Konneh said a police Commissioner for Crime Services was also dismissed after admitting to taking a $10,000 bribe in the same network.

Konneh also raised the most politically sensitive case. Former Vice President Jewel Howard-Taylor was arrested at the airport and charged on August 19 with conspiracy, facilitation and money laundering. She denies the charges. Konneh criticized the government for destroying the 3.9 tons of cocaine before trial. He predicted the case could collapse over constitutional warrant defects or chain-of-custody problems. If it does, he said, “the public will conclude it’s politics, not justice.”

He placed Liberia within a wider regional crisis. According to the UN Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC), 126.4 metric tons of cocaine were seized in or through West Africa between 2019 and 2024, including 30.8 tons in the Gulf of Guinea corridor along Liberia’s coast. The region has become “a destination market, not just a transit zone,” he said. He also described kush, a cheap synthetic drug blend that first spread in Sierra Leone and now reaches Liberia, Guinea, Guinea-Bissau, The Gambia and Senegal, mostly among unemployed young people.

Why Washington should care

Konneh framed the issue as a test of American credibility. He said Liberia voted with the United States 89 percent of the time at the United Nations last year and hosts the largest U.S. diplomatic presence in West Africa.

“If Liberians conclude that America only cares when there’s a big drug bust but stays silent when a $2 billion mining deal is signed behind closed doors, we lose credibility for democracy,” he said. “China and Russia don’t ask about beneficial ownership. Cartels don’t ask about human rights.”

He noted that Sweden closed its embassy in Monrovia last month. He also urged the European Union to keep its delegation in Liberia fully staffed rather than move its functions to Abidjan in neighboring Côte d’Ivoire.

The asks

At home, Konneh said, the Senate is working on several measures. On mining, it wants to require that all mining agreements, amendments, beneficial owners and payments be published before ratification. It also proposes independent valuation of iron ore transfer pricing, modeled on Botswana’s approach to diamonds, and sending 20 percent of royalties directly to district development funds.

On drugs, the proposals would require that seized evidence be kept until final judgment. Officers at the airport, the Freeport of Monrovia and the security agencies would face polygraphs, lifestyle audits and drug tests. An unexplained-wealth law would allow assets to be seized without a criminal conviction.

From Washington, he asked for help that is “practical, not preachy”:

• Funding to monitor Liberia’s drug court and commercial court

• Forensic audits of the ArcelorMittal rail and port concession and of Bea Mountain’s royalties

• Resumed mentoring of vetted Liberian drug units by the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration, with oversight

• Equipment for scanners and sniffer dogs, including maintenance

• Help from the Treasury Department’s Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) in tracing money in three or four specific cases

• A $10 million pilot program to track large cash donations ahead of the 2029 elections

He also urged that Global Magnitsky sanctions, the U.S. tool for penalizing corrupt officials and human rights abusers, be used “surgically.” Their targets should include enablers in mining licensing who move money into U.S. real estate, he said, and Washington should state publicly why it acts.

“Help us establish transparent regulations before finalizing agreements,” Konneh said, “and support impartial enforcement of laws after confiscation — whether the suspect is an airport baggage handler, a police crimes services director, a former Vice President, or a multinational corporation.”

World.title: Liberia: Saudi Rice Trial: Gbassay Rejects Guilty Verdict, Declares Innocence, Alleges Pressure to Become State Witness
World.content:
The ordained Baptist minister says she refused to testify for the prosecution, and warns that the pursuit of accountability must not become “score-settling masquerading as justice”

MONROVIA — Days after a jury at Criminal Court “C” adjudged her guilty in the Saudi Rice corruption case, former National Disaster Management Agency (NDMA) official Rosetta L. Gbassay Bowah has rejected the verdict, declaring her innocence in a Facebook post.

By Selma Lomax, [email protected]

In the lengthy statement, she thanked family, friends, colleagues and fellow clergy for an outpouring of prayers, encouragement, solidarity and love since Friday. She said the support had “renewed my confidence in the face of circumstances that were clearly intended to break me.” As the legal process continues, she said, she wishes to reassure her supporters of her “absolute innocence” and her confidence that “the truth will ultimately prevail.”



Central to her statement is an allegation that she was pressured to cooperate with the prosecution. Gbassay Bowah said that if she has committed any “crime,” it is that she faithfully performed her lawful duties in accordance with her Terms of Reference and the obligations of her office.

She added that her other “crime” may be that she refused what she described as persistent efforts by her accuser and the prosecutors to persuade her to “cooperate” by serving as a State witness.

The post offers no evidence for the claim, and it has not been independently verified. Her position, however, was unequivocal. “As a servant of the living God, an ordained Baptist Reverend,” she said, she could never conspire to testify falsely against any person or speak of matters about which she has no knowledge. “My conscience is not for sale,” she wrote.

She described the personal cost she believes such a compromise would carry. No temporary advantage, she said, is worth “inviting the curse that follows bearing false witness against the innocent.”

That burden, she said, is one she will not bring upon herself, her children or future generations. Regardless of “pressure, intimidation, or schemes,” she said, she remains steadfast in her conviction that God, “in His own time and according to His perfect will,” will vindicate her.

Her statement reads as much like a sermon as a legal defense. Gbassay Bowah, who is an ordained Baptist Reverend, wrote that her faith is “built on nothing less than Jesus Christ, His blood, and His righteousness,” and that it gives her the courage to persevere “through this difficult chapter.” She framed the ordeal as a season of trial and tribulation.

Her appeal then widened from her own situation to the state of the nation. Addressing her “co-workers in the vineyard of the Lord,” she urged fellow clergy to keep praying for Liberia, noting that “it is one thing to preach about injustice, and quite another to experience it personally.”

She warned that the country stands at a “critical crossroads” and risks a “vicious cycle of bitterness, vengeance, political persecution, and score-settling masquerading as justice.” Liberia, she said, needs healing, redemption and a renewed commitment to the rule of law, fairness and national unity. She called on citizens to resist the temptation to weaponize political differences, and to work toward a future in which justice is impartial, truth is honored and every citizen is treated with dignity and respect.

Her words arrive against a very different reading of Friday’s outcome. In a statement dated Oct. 10, the Asset Recovery and Property Retrieval Taskforce (AREPT) welcomed the verdicts as a “significant milestone” in the Government of Liberia’s efforts to combat corruption and protect public resources.

According to AREPT, the jury adjudged eight of the 13 defendants guilty, including former Foreign Affairs Minister Dee-Maxwell Saah Kemayah and former Internal Affairs Minister Varney A. Sirleaf. Three defendants were acquitted, and the jury returned inconclusive verdicts on two others.

The case arose from AREPT’s investigation into the alleged misappropriation of 29,412 bags of rice, valued at about US$500,000, donated by the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia in 2023 for disaster victims and vulnerable Liberians. The indictment alleged that 25,054 of those bags were unlawfully diverted or misapplied.

According to the jury tally, Gbassay Bowah was adjudged guilty of Theft of Property, Misapplication of Entrusted Property and Criminal Conspiracy. Jurors were hung on the counts of Abuse of Office and Economic Sabotage.

AREPT Chairman Cllr. Edwin Kla Martin said the Taskforce is ready for any appeal. “We are prepared,” he said, adding that if the defendants go to the Supreme Court, AREPT will “equally go there and defeat them there.” The Taskforce also said it respects the judicial process and the rights of all parties, including the right to appeal.

World.title: Liberia: Bishop Kortu Brown Backs Growing Calls for a New Political Force ahead of 2029 Presidential Elections
World.content:
Bishop Kortu Brown Backs Growing Calls for a New Political Force ahead of 2029 Presidential Elections

BREWERVILLE, Montserrado County, Liberia, Oct. 12, 2026 — A prominent Liberian clergyman has backed growing calls for a “third lane” in the country’s politics ahead of the 2029 elections. He cautioned, however, that any new movement must offer genuine change rather than recycle familiar faces.

He said such moves were part of the reason ordinary citizens “still yearn for something else politically,” and he urged Liberians to be honest with themselves. “They must mean it when they say they want real change,” he said.

The bishop also said the credibility of any third force would depend on who leads it. “Liberians will not buy an empty third lane,” he said. “It can’t be a contest of political rivals who are dissatisfied with one another, or people who want revenge against one another or to fool one another.”



Instead, he called for “a new line-up of sincere and professional Liberians who are genuinely interested in promoting the political, economic, social and religious causes of the ordinary people.”

“UP and CDC are now brand names with big followings,” Brown said. “However, people are still politically thirsty.”

World.title: Liberia: House Opens for Third Quarter’s Official Business Today Amid Lawmakers’ Revolt in Demand of Personal Benefits
World.content:
Today marks the first day for official business as members of the Legislature return from their second constituency break, but with uncertainty hanging over one of the chambers – the House of Representatives.

By Emmanuel Weedee-Conway

It all began Friday, October 9, 2026 when the Legislature officially resumed official duty following nearly three months of rest when majority member of the House of Representatives; over 40 numbers, reportedly boycotted and held a separate meeting to discuss grievances against the chamber’s leadership.



What Do They Want?

From inside sources, the aggrieved lawmakers under the banner of “Reformists,” are demanding benefits, legislative support funds and other resources they allege have been withheld under the current leadership.

Representative Frank Saah Foko of Montserrado County District #9 said Friday’s meeting was intended to give lawmakers a collective platform to express their concerns. He indicated that another meeting had been scheduled for Sunday, October 11, when the group was expected to determine its next steps.

Joe described the concerns as recurring and said lawmakers intended to engage the relevant authorities to press their demands. Asked whether the gathering was intended to organize the removal of the Speaker and Deputy Speaker, he said he was unaware of such a plan.

Representative Samuel Enders of Montserrado County District #6 similarly said the discussions concerned benefits and district support, adding that he knew of no effort to remove the House leadership.

Representative Abu Kamara of Montserrado County District #15 described the meeting positively but offered little detail about its outcome.

From afar, this is a precondition set by the Reformists – a group that comprises several of Speaker Richard Nagbe Koon’s own allies.

Worst Case

With the overgrown numbers of nearly 50 or more members – both from the ruling class, opposition and independent, reports also have it that the “Reformists” are also thinking otherwise; they are seeking signatures on a proposed 12-count resolution targeting the House leadership.

Though the precise contents of the proposed resolution have not been publicly established, and the lawmakers who addressed the meeting did not openly confirm that removing Koon and Deputy Speaker Thomas P. Fallah was their objective.

These explanations by lawmakers who openly spoke to the matter leave an important gap between the public grievances and the reported effort to circulate a 12-count resolution.

Deputy Speaker Acknowledges Concerns Are Genuine

Since Friday’s showdown, Deputy Speaker Thomas P. Fallah issued his first public response with acknowledgement that the demands are genuine concerns with regard to the payment of lawmakers’ legitimate benefits, which are overdue.

Fallah Gives Hope

On the heel of the rigmarole, Deputy Speaker Fallah has made a promise that his colleagues can hope on.

In a nutshell, the House of Representatives’ second most powerful man informed his colleagues that the deal for the payment of these benefits is almost done, and such, they should return to conduct the Liberian people’s business.

“Let me assure you that under the leadership of Speaker Richard Nagbe Koon, every legitimate effort is being exerted to engage all relevant government institutions so that these benefits are processed and paid without further delay. The signals we are receiving are positive, and I am confident that this matter will be resolved in the soonest possible time,” wrote T-Five as he is popularly referred to in Liberian politics.

“However, as we have entered the third quarter of our third session, I humbly plead with all colleagues to return to work. The Liberian people entrusted us with a sacred mandate—to legislate, to provide oversight, and to represent their voices. Our absence from the chambers delays the progress of the nation and undermines the very purpose for which we were elected,” he stated.

Lawmakers Called To Order

In a clarion call to order, Deputy Speaker Fallah, who represents Lofa County Electoral District #1 in the 55th Legislature called on members of the House to demonstrate leadership, patience, and unity in times of challenge.

By returning to work, he reckoned, this will send a powerful message to the Liberian people: that while they fight for their rights, they will never abandon their duty to them.

“Let us therefore rise above frustration, stand together in solidarity, and continue the work of nation-building. The benefits will come, but the work of Liberia cannot wait,” Fallah added.

A Test To The Gavel

In the face of the latest drama at the Lower House of Liberia’s bicameral Legislature, and on the heel of the zealous plead by Deputy Speaker Fallah, the First Day Sitting of The Third Quarter of the Third Session of the 55th Legislature poses a stern test to the gable of Speaker Richard Nagbe Koon.

It still remains unclear whether the “Reformists” will turn in their huge numbers to sit under the authority of their boss.

A Rebellion From Within

The lawmakers gathered in Schefflin, Margibi County, on Friday, while Koon and a small group of legislators attended the formal reopening ceremony at the Capitol following the legislative break.

The reported boycott was striking: only 13 of the House’s 73 members reportedly attended the ceremony, including the Speaker.

The gathering outside Monrovia also brought together lawmakers who hold influential committee positions, including chairs and co-chairs responsible for scrutinizing public procurement, government contracts, natural resources, the judiciary and public expenditure.

Among those reportedly associated with the Reformist Movement are Jeremiah Garwo Sokan Sr. of Grand Gedeh County District #1, chairman of the House Committee on Mines, Natural Resources and Environment; Prince K. Koinah of Bong County District #1, chairman of the Committee on Contracts, Monopolies, Public Procurement and Concessions and co-chair of the Public Accounts and Expenditure Committee; and Sam P. Jallah of Bomi County District #3, co-chair of the Hydrocarbon Committee.

Other lawmakers reportedly linked to the movement include Bernard Blue Benson Jr. of Montserrado County District #17, chairman of the Committee on Information, Broadcasting, Culture and Tourism; Anthony Williams of Maryland County District #2, co-chair of the Peace, Religion and National Reconciliation Committee; Augustine B. Chiewolo of Lofa County District #5, chairman of the Committee on Resettlement, Repatriation, Relief and Readjustment; and Johnson S. N. Williams Sr. of River Gee County District #3, chairman of the House Committee on Judiciary.

Their reported involvement gives the agitation institutional significance. These are not merely lawmakers expressing dissatisfaction from the margins of the chamber; several occupy positions that place them at the center of legislative oversight and administration.

Why Koon’s Own Allies Matter

The political significance of the agitation lies partly in the reported involvement of lawmakers who have worked alongside Koon and occupy senior committee positions.

Leadership in the House depends not only on formal authority but also on the ability to maintain working relationships with members, coordinate legislative business and secure cooperation across committees.

When discontent emerges among lawmakers associated with the leadership, it can complicate that process even if no formal removal motion is ultimately pursued.

The reported involvement of lawmakers overseeing procurement, public accounts and other major portfolios also places questions about financial administration at the center of the dispute. Their allegations, however, should not be treated as proof of misconduct without supporting documentation or findings by an appropriate authority.

The movement’s leverage will depend on more than the number of lawmakers attending a meeting. Its members would need to demonstrate sustained coordination, agreement on their demands and a willingness to pursue a common course of action.

The next meeting could therefore be an important test of whether Friday’s gathering was a temporary show of discontent or the beginning of a more organized challenge.

The Koffa-Koon Crisis Offers a Warning

The confrontation inevitably recalls the prolonged leadership dispute that preceded Koon’s emergence as Speaker.

During that earlier crisis, lawmakers aligned with what became known as the Majority Bloc boycotted sessions and held parallel meetings. They subsequently declared Koon Speaker and Fallah Deputy Speaker while Cllr. Fonati Koffa remained the sitting Speaker.

The dispute eventually reached the Supreme Court, which ruled that actions taken outside the House chamber while the Speaker remained in office and present were ultra vires.

Koffa later resigned, clearing the way for Koon’s election as Speaker, while Fallah retained the deputy speakership.

That episode exposed deep divisions within the House and demonstrated how disagreements over legislative leadership can disrupt institutional operations and raise questions about the validity of decisions taken during a political confrontation.

The current agitation does not automatically mean the House is headed for a repeat of that crisis. The circumstances may differ, and the Reformist Movement has not publicly confirmed that removing Koon and Fallah is its objective.

Nevertheless, the earlier dispute provides an important institutional backdrop. Any attempt to change the leadership would have to be assessed against the House’s rules and applicable constitutional requirements, rather than simply the strength of a faction’s public declarations.

The previous crisis also illustrates the risks of parallel meetings and competing claims to authority when lawmakers fail to resolve disputes through established legislative procedures.

The Speaker’s Office Keeps Its Distance

When contacted about the reported effort to remove the Speaker, Vehzelee Sumo, head of communications for the Speaker’s Office, declined to comment, saying the office would respond at the appropriate time.

The office had previously said it was unaware of any plan to remove Koon and would not comment on rumors.

The limited response leaves unanswered questions about the allegations involving benefits, legislative support funds and administrative irregularities.

A substantive response from the leadership could clarify which resources have been requested, what has been disbursed and whether disagreements exist over the procedures governing legislative support. Such information would help distinguish a political dispute from a documented administrative failure.

World.title: Liberia: Climate Change and Liberia: What It Means and What We Must Do
World.content:
When floodwater enters a home, a farmer loses a harvest, or the sea washes away land, families suffer. Children miss school, businesses lose income, and communities struggle to recover. Climate change increases these risks. Understanding it helps us protect ourselves and our country.

By Dr. Emmanuel King Urey Yarkpawolo

Executive Director, Environmental Protection Agency of Liberia

Climate change means lasting changes in the Earth’s temperatures and usual weather patterns. Weather is what happens today: sunshine, rain, or wind. Climate is the pattern we expect over many years, including our rainy and dry seasons.



The Earth is warming mainly because human activities release gases that trap heat in the atmosphere. Burning coal, petrol, diesel, and gas produces these gases. Cutting and burning forests adds to the problem because trees absorb carbon dioxide, one of the main gases warming the planet. These gases act like an extra blanket around the Earth, holding in more heat.

Liberia contributes very little to global emissions, yet we are highly vulnerable. Many Liberians depend on farming, live near the coast, or lack strong roads, proper drainage, and reliable basic services. These conditions make climate pressures harder to withstand.

Along our coast, rising sea levels increase the danger of flooding and erosion, threatening homes, roads, businesses, and livelihoods. For farmers, changing rainfall makes planting decisions harder. Heavy rain, dry spells, and higher temperatures can damage crops and reduce harvests. When farmers produce less, their incomes suffer and food supplies come under pressure.

Health and daily work are also affected. Extreme heat makes outdoor work more difficult. Floods can contaminate drinking water and damage roads, disrupting access to clinics, schools, and markets. Families with fewer resources often have the greatest difficulty recovering.

Not every flood or damaged shoreline is caused by climate change alone. Blocked drains, poorly planned construction, and destruction of wetlands can worsen the damage. We must address both climate change and the local practices that make communities more vulnerable.

We cannot end climate change overnight, but we can slow it down and reduce its harm. This means cutting the gases that cause warming while preparing for changes already happening. Cleaner energy, forest protection, stronger infrastructure, and better weather warnings all have a role.

The Government of Liberia, through the EPA and its partners, is already acting. Coastal protection projects in Sinoe County and metropolitan Monrovia are being implemented to reduce risks from coastal flooding and erosion and protect livelihoods. The Climate Information Systems project is strengthening weather monitoring and early warnings so that farmers, fishermen, and communities can better prepare for dangerous weather.

Government is also turning waste into a resource. Working with the Monrovia City Corporation, the Liberia Water and Sewer Corporation, and international partners, the EPA has helped establish a composting facility in Fiamah. It is designed to turn food scraps and other organic waste into compost that improves soil for farming. This shows how better waste management can support cleaner communities and agriculture.

The EPA is also enforcing environmental laws. Nationwide inspections have covered mining operations, industrial sites, coastal areas, and waste facilities across all 15 counties. Actions include stopping illegal operations, ordering corrections, and imposing fines. Protecting rivers, forests, wetlands, and farmland also helps communities withstand climate pressures. Development must provide jobs without sacrificing people’s health and livelihoods.

However, the needs exceed available resources. Coastal protection, drainage, weather services, and nationwide monitoring require sustained funding, equipment, trained personnel, and maintenance. Families also need affordable alternatives to activities that damage the environment.

Large emitters carry a greater responsibility. Countries and industries that have released the most warming gases, especially over many decades, should make deep and rapid emissions cuts. Financing tree planting elsewhere should accompany real reductions from their own factories, power plants, and transport systems.

Wealthy developed countries also have responsibilities to help poorer countries respond. The Paris Agreement requires developed countries to provide financial support to developing countries for reducing emissions and preparing for climate impacts. Liberia needs accessible funding, useful technology, and training that reach communities most at risk.

Major emitters should also support people facing losses that cannot be prevented, including destroyed homes and lost livelihoods. Liberia should not carry an unfair financial burden for a crisis it contributed little to creating. This is a matter of fairness.

Our small contribution to global emissions does not remove our own responsibilities. Citizens should join government’s efforts by reporting pollution, protecting public facilities, keeping rubbish out of drains and streams, avoiding waste burning, saving electricity, and following official weather warnings. Keeping drains clear will not stop global warming, but it can reduce local flood damage.

Businesses must respect environmental permits, reduce waste, and correct damage from their operations. Schools, religious institutions, traditional leaders, and the media can explain climate issues in everyday language and local languages. Communities should help shape projects affecting their homes and livelihoods, while holding government accountable for results.

Every Liberian deserves a safe home, clean water, dependable food, and a secure future. Government is taking action, but lasting progress requires citizens, businesses, and international partners to contribute. Large emitters must fulfil their responsibilities, and we must fulfil ours. Protecting Liberia is a shared responsibility.

World.title: Liberia: Chief Justice Gbeisay Calls for Unity Among Liberians, Particularly People in Gompa City, Nimba County
World.content:
Liberia’s Chief Justice Yamie Quiqui Gbeisay Sr.

MONROVIA – Chief Justice Yamie Quiqui Gbeisay Sr. has called on all Liberians, particularly the People of Nimba County to remain united and respect the rule of Law.

Speaking during the opening of the Supreme Court October Term on Monday, October 12, he said, “I want to use this occasion to call on all Liberians, especially my fellow Citizens in Gompa City, Nimba County, to unite irrespective of tribe or ethnic background. Tribalism destroys national unity and peace, and further triggers violence and war. Liberia has traveled down that road before and we know where it led us. We must not go there again. The Gbeisay’s Bench will enforce all legitimate judgments without fear or favor and irrespective of its consequences.’’

Chief Justice Gbeisay pointed out that the law is blind and the only tribe recognized before a court of competent jurisdiction is Justice. He expanded on the court’s enforcement of judgments, particularly in Montserrado and Nimba Counties.



He said that as the court works to expand access to justice across the country, enforcing court judgments remains a daunting challenge. The Chief Justice pointed to an incident of the court’s final judgment at the 8th Judicial Circuit Court in 2018, wherein some members of the Mandingo Ethnic Group in Gompa mobilized and violently obstructed the enforcement of judgment against a member of their tribe.

Speaking further, he said the spokesperson of the group, Mark Jabateh, took to the media and openly declared that he could kill the former Chief Justice, Francis Korkpor, if he had laid eyes on him. “The past government took no action; instead, the present government rewarded him with a ministerial position in government.’’

On the recent incident in Gompa City, he said that, in an effort to enforce the final judgment, the former Gompa City Mayor used tribal sentiment, claiming that Mandingo people have no land rights in that city.

Accordingly, the former Mayor of Gompa City mobilized some members of the Mano and Gio Communities against the court and especially against him as Chief Justice.

“Up to and including today, my family remains under threat and subject to constant attacks. Some individuals have vowed to kill me for allegedly giving their land to Mandingo people.’’

Among other things, he added, ‘‘the Judgments of our courts are based on evidence and the applicable laws. This is the oath I took and continue to hold.”

World.title: Chilengi sends 123 officers out of Ndeke House, orders qualifications audit of headquarters staff
World.content:
Health Minister Professor Roma Chilengi has ordered 123 officers out of the Ministry of Health headquarters in Lusaka and back to their original stations. Every remaining post at Ndeke House now faces a qualifications audit, in a clean-up aimed at pushing more staff to the front line of the health service.

An internal assessment found that the 123 officers had been working at headquarters under temporary administrative arrangements. Their positions supported central operations, but they fell outside the ministry’s approved 2021 establishment, which caps headquarters staffing at 403 positions. The ministry described the move as part of a comprehensive institutional clean-up and operational optimisation exercise, aimed at enforcing strict structural compliance and restoring administrative integrity across the healthcare sector.

In a ministerial statement dated 13 October 2026, Prof Chilengi said all the affected officers would be redirected immediately to their substantive stations, where their official pay points and original postings are based. The ministry said the move would eliminate structural redundancies and address critical operational personnel needs across the country.

“This step will immediately bolster healthcare delivery at front-line health facilities and decentralised administrative centres,” Prof Chilengi said.

The return of the 123 officers is only the first phase. Once they have been moved, the ministry will carry out a full qualification and competency assessment of everyone holding a post within the approved 403-member headquarters establishment.

Each position will be measured against established professional standards and job descriptions, to determine whether the officers holding them have the required academic, professional and technical qualifications. Staff who fall short for their headquarters roles will be reassigned to operational stations that match their verified credentials.

“This exercise establishes a vital operational baseline as the ministry of health continues to strengthen governance frameworks, streamline administrative efficiency and deliver high-quality public healthcare across the nation,” Prof Chilengi said.

The ministry said the exercise will strengthen administrative accountability and ensure that staff are deployed in line with approved structures and operational needs. It also expects staffing levels to rise at service delivery points, where patients are seen.

The shake-up comes with the health system under pressure from a cholera outbreak. The Zambia National Public Health Institute (ZNPHI) has recorded 55 new cases and one death in 24 hours, bringing the cumulative number of cases to 874 since the outbreak began.

The cumulative death toll has risen to 23. As of Tuesday, 777 patients had recovered and been discharged, while 74 remained in hospital.

Thirteen districts have been affected. Lusaka has recorded the highest number of cases at 429, followed by Chibombo with 217. Chilanga has 46 cases, Mpulungu 42, Chongwe 36 and Chiengi 33.

Mwansabombwe and Nsama have recorded 20 cases each, Mwense 15 and Nchelenge 11. Chikankata and Monze have two each, and Kalomo has one.

The institute has urged the public to wash their hands with soap and clean water, drink boiled or treated water, cook food thoroughly and use clean toilets. It also stressed proper hygiene when handling food and keeping sanitation facilities clean.

Districts without cases are also preparing. In Lumezi, which has recorded no suspected cases, director of health services Evans Phiri said rapid response teams had been activated at facility and district levels, and health workers had been trained to pick up symptoms early.

Dr Phiri said two facilities had been identified for isolating and managing cases. Rapid diagnostic test kits, medicines and intravenous fluids had been set aside.

“A cholera patient may die just from dehydration, just the loss of fluids in the body. So we have kept fluids just for this cause,” Dr Phiri said.

At Ndeke House, the qualifications review of the 403 approved posts is next. The 123 officers are being returned to their substantive stations, where the ministry says they are most needed.

World.title: Chief Justice condemns Supreme Court attack on Davies Mwila as security is tightened at courts
World.content:
Chief Justice Mumba Malila has condemned the confrontation involving former Patriotic Front (PF) secretary-general Davies Mwila at the Supreme Court in Lusaka, calling it flagrant lawlessness and an assault on the administration of justice. Security has since been intensified at the courts to protect judicial officers and members of the public.

Law enforcement agencies are investigating the incident, the Chief Justice said, warning that those responsible will face the full force of the law.

“Unruly conduct and violence will not be tolerated under any circumstances,” Dr Malila said in a statement issued on Tuesday.

The incident took place shortly after proceedings in the Lima Constituency election petition were adjourned. Mr Mwila had a confrontation with some court attendees as people left the hearing.

The petition was filed by United Party for National Development (UPND) candidate Lee Mukupa, who is challenging the election of National Reconciliation Party for Unity and Prosperity (NRPUP) candidate Kelvin Kaunda as Lima Member of Parliament. Mr Kaunda won the seat with 22,760 votes against Mr Mukupa’s 8,041.

Mr Mwila had attended the proceedings in solidarity with Mr Kaunda. He allegedly angered some people by mocking their “salt sana” slogan and making remarks suggesting that he and his generation would not suffer financially.

Some of those present then confronted the former PF secretary-general, forcing him to retreat into the Supreme Court reception area. He slipped and fell while trying to get away.

The group caught up with him, but Judiciary staff and security personnel stepped in to stop the situation from escalating further.

In his statement, Dr Malila reminded the public that court premises demand a certain standard of conduct. He urged everyone visiting the courts to behave with decorum, respect and dignity.

The Judiciary’s response has gone beyond words. Security at the courts has been tightened to protect judicial officers and members of the public, a measure taken directly in response to the altercation.

The ruling UPND has also condemned the attack. In a statement issued by its Media Team, the party described the assault as unfortunate and unacceptable in a democratic society governed by the rule of law. It called on law enforcement agencies to investigate professionally, impartially and without political interference.

“No political disagreement, personal grievance or ideological difference can justify physical attacks, intimidation or the humiliation of another person,” the UPND said.

The party rejected statements attributed to PF-Pamodzi Alliance National Youth IPS Given Gift Chibale, who linked the incident to suspected UPND cadres. It challenged him to hand any evidence identifying the perpetrators to the police rather than assign political responsibility before investigations had established the facts. The UPND said it would report the matter to the police under the cybercrime laws.

The Lima petition is one of several election disputes now before the courts following the August general election. Its hearing will continue under the tighter security arrangements, while police investigations into the attack on Mr Mwila proceed.

No suspects have yet been named

World.title: ZCTU joins calls for Archbishop Banda to step aside
World.content:
The Zambia Congress of Trade Unions (ZCTU) has joined calls for Lusaka Archbishop Alick Banda to step away from his position until the criminal case he is defending is concluded. The union says church leaders facing court proceedings must act to protect public confidence in their institutions.

The labour movement adds its weight to a widening list of voices on the matter. Catholic-aligned Members of Parliament, among them Nominated MP Noel Nkoma, Kazungula North MP Clement Andeleki and Rufunsa MP Sheal Mulyata, have already called on the Archbishop to step aside. House of Clergy Zambia and the Anti-Voter Apathy Project (AVAP) have since taken similar positions.

Archbishop Banda faces a charge of possession of property reasonably suspected to have been unlawfully obtained, contrary to Section 319 of the Penal Code, Chapter 87 of the Laws of Zambia. The Drug Enforcement Commission arrested him on 28 September 2026.

ZCTU president Blake Mulala said leaders of religious institutions should be seen to uphold high moral standards. In his view, they should consider stepping aside whenever they face investigations or court proceedings.

“In many churches, leaders facing investigations or court cases are expected to step aside on moral grounds until the matter is concluded. As an overseer of the church, it is important to maintain public confidence and integrity,” Mr Mulala said in Lusaka.

The union leader said the Catholic Church should be guided by its own doctrines and disciplinary procedures in deciding how to handle the matter. Church leaders, he added, should remain above reproach while carrying out their pastoral responsibilities.

House of Clergy Zambia took a similar line, grounding its position in the rule of law. National executive director Reverend Jimmy Ng’ambi said accountability applied to all citizens, regardless of position, profession or religious office.

“As a matter of integrity, wisdom and institutional responsibility, it may be appropriate for a member of the clergy facing serious legal proceedings to voluntarily step aside while the legal process takes its course,” Rev Ng’ambi said.

The cleric drew a firm line between the individual and the institution, saying holding religious office does not exempt anyone from personal responsibility.

“No one is above the law, accountability is not persecution, and a legal case involving an individual cleric is not a battle against the Church,” he said.

Rev Ng’ambi described the Church as an important partner in national development, peacebuilding and moral guidance. He said legal proceedings involving a cleric should not be misread as an attack on Christianity or an attempt to undermine the Church’s role in society.

He was careful to stress that a step-aside would not amount to an admission of guilt. The call, he said, was neither a declaration of guilt nor a legal requirement, but a position based on integrity and the need to safeguard the Church’s standing.

A temporary withdrawal, the House of Clergy leader said, would also stop the case from being portrayed as a confrontation between Government and the Church. He urged citizens to exercise restraint, avoid premature conclusions and respect the presumption of innocence throughout the process.

AVAP national director Richwell Mulwani said his organisation supported calls for the Archbishop to temporarily relinquish his duties until investigations were concluded. He acknowledged, however, that the final decision did not rest with outside groups.

“As AVAP, we feel it would be acceptable for Archbishop Banda to step aside while the matter is being addressed. However, the Catholic Church has its own rules and procedures and it is up to the institution to determine the appropriate course of action,” Mr Mulwani said.

He said the Church should reach its decision in line with its doctrines, while respecting the legal principle that a person is presumed innocent until proven guilty.

Not every voice has joined the call. The Southern Africa Centre for the Constructive Resolution of Disputes (SACCORD) urged caution, saying the matter should be handled fairly and without prejudice. Executive director Boniface Muyunda said any call for the Archbishop to step aside should respect both the rule of law and the autonomy of the Catholic Church.

University of Zambia lecturer Professor Bizeck Phiri described the situation as complex. He pointed out that the Catholic Church had not publicly indicated that Archbishop Banda should step aside. The Church, he said, has established doctrines and procedures for matters involving members of the clergy and should be allowed to decide the way forward.

Government has set out its own position. Ministry of Information and Media Permanent Secretary Thabo Kawana has distinguished between the Church as an institution and individual members of the clergy, with Government reaffirming that no person is above the law, whatever their position or religious office.

The case remains before the courts, where the Archbishop is entitled to the presumption of innocence and a full defence. Most of those calling for a step-aside have stopped short of demanding one. Several have left the final word to the Catholic Church, which has not publicly announced any change to the Archbishop’s duties.

World.title: Political parties hail parley speech
World.content:
The ruling United Party for National Development (UPND) says President Hakainde Hichilema’s speech during the official opening of the first session of the 14th National Assembly spelled out clear intent by Government to reduce the cost of living.

UPND Media Director, Mark Simuuwe says the President laid out a blueprint for citizens to be involved in the development agenda of the country.

Mr Simuuwe said there are numerous opportunities that give citizens a platform to improve their livelihood while contributing to the Grow Zambia Agenda, describing the Head of State’s plan as inclusive.

Meanwhile, New Nation Party Acting President, Reuben Samboh says the targets set out by President Hichilema present an opportunity for the private sector to contribute effectively.

And Rev Samboh says the 7 percent economic growth target that Zambia is aiming to attain in three years’ time is realistic.

The opposition leader however called on the Government to instead set a target of 10 percent.

Meanwhile, Rev Samboh urged the private sector to take advantage of the Grow Zambia Agenda, describing President Hichilema’s targets as inclusive.

On Friday, President Hichilema officially opened the first session of the 14th National Assembly, making different pronouncements in various sectors.

World.title: Zambians urged to safeguard peace
World.content:
Nominated Member of Parliament (MP) Mubita Anakoka has called on Zambians to safeguard the unity and peace that enable national development,regardless of political affiliation.

Mr Anakoka notes that Zambia belonged to all citizens and that, following the elections, the country should focus its energies on development.

He said this in Parliament today during debate on the Motion of Thanks to President Hakainde Hichilema’s address to the First Session of the 14th National Assembly, which was officially opened on October 9, 2026.

In his median speech and Mover of the Motion, Mr Anakoka said political differences should not become obstacles to national progress but urged the MPs to engage in constructive debate, work together to resolve challenges and ensure that development opportunities improved people’s welfare.

The MP expressed confidence that the UPND’s second term should build on the foundation by expanding production, creating jobs, growing businesses and improving living standards.

He said Zambia had the resources, productive capacity, entrepreneurial spirit and hardworking citizens needed to achieve its development aspirations, adding that determination, discipline, effective implementation and collective effort were ‘essential to the Grow Zambia agenda.’

Chongwe East MP, Anita Kamanga, called for inclusive economic growth that translates into tangible improvements in people’s lives.

Ms Kamanga, who seconded the motion, said she would focus on social protection, water and sanitation, keeping Zambia Clean, and Information and Communication Technology including Artificial Intelligence.

She noted that the Head of State highlighted the need to expand social protection coverage, strengthen the Social Cash Transfer Programme, improve social security systems and ensure the timely payment of retirement benefits.

Ms Kamanga said such interventions were particularly important for older persons, persons with disabilities, low-income households and other vulnerable groups.

She said social protection should not only provide immediate relief but also be complemented by skills development, agricultural support and opportunities for small-scale enterprises to enable beneficiaries to become economically resilient.

And nominated Lawmaker, Lazarous Hakalebula, has commended constitutional reforms that enabled him to become part of the National Assembly.

Mr Hakalebula said disability should not be equated with inability and thanked the government for introducing Bill 10 during the Fifth Session of the 13th National Assembly.

He called on stakeholders to remove barriers that hinder the participation and advancement of persons with disabilities.

Mr Hakalebula submitted that he would champion for the full implementation of the Disability Act to ensure the meaningful inclusion of persons with disabilities in national development.

Meanwhile, several other parliamentarians had, by press time, taken turns debating the Motion of Thanks.

World.title: Zambezi WDCs urged to embrace transparency
World.content:
Zambezi Town Council has conducted a one-day orientation workshop for Zonal Election Officers ahead of the upcoming establishment of new Ward Development Committees (WDCs) across the district.

Speaking during the training held in Zambezi today, Town Council Acting Director of Planning, who also serves as District HIV/AIDS Coordinator, Mwiinga Chimuka, urged participants to embrace utmost transparency during the formation of the new WDCs.

Mr Chimuka emphasised the critical role that Ward Development Committees play in ensuring that government programmes and community priorities, particularly projects funded under the Constituency Development Fund (CDF), are effectively implemented.

He stated that WDCs serve as vital community-level structures bridging the gap between local authorities and residents, providing a direct platform for citizens to identify development priorities and communicate their needs.

Mr Chimuka cautioned that any malpractice, bias, or lack of integrity during the election process could undermine public confidence and compromise local development efforts.

He, however, stated that the orientation is meant to equip Zonal Election Officers with the necessary knowledge, skills, procedures, and statutory guidelines required to effectively manage and facilitate the election process in their respective zones.

Mr Chimuka further urged the officers to maintain neutrality and strictly follow the established legal framework to ensure that the outcome truly reflects the will of the local communities.

He further mentioned that following the orientation, trained officers who are drawn from various government departments will be deployed across all 91 zones in Zambezi District to conduct the elections.

“The establishment of the new Ward Development Committees follows the dissolution of the previous committees in line with Section 36 of the Local Government Act No. 2 of 2019, which provides for the conduct of WDC elections by local authorities within two months after a general election,” he added.

World.title: Activista Zambia welcomes plan to establish skills training centres
World.content:
Activista Zambia a youth-led Solwezi based organisation in North-Western Province has welcomed President Hakainde Hichilema’s pronouncement that Government plans to establish skills training centres in every district to support the Grow Zambia Agenda.

In an interview with the in Solwezi today, Activista Zambia Provincial Chairperson, Asa Lukamata, called on stakeholders to support the initiative to ensure its successful implementation.

Mr Lukamata said the initiative will also improve access to skills training by reducing the distances young people have to travel to access such services.

He said the establishment of skills training centres will promote entrepreneurship, create employment opportunities and empower young people and other citizens with practical skills.

Mr Lukamata noted that skills training is essential in promoting self-reliance, employment, innovation and economic development.

“Creating skills training centres in all districts will not only improve access to training institutions but also supplement Government’s efforts to create jobs for young people across the country,” he said.

Mr Lukamata added that the initiative will promote inclusion and ensure equitable access to skills training opportunities for citizens across the country.

During his address to Parliament last Friday, President Hichilema announced that the Government will ensure every district has a skills training centre to support the implementation of the Grow Zambia Agenda.

The President also assured the Nation that the Government will continue providing student loans and meal allowances to eligible students in public universities.

World.title: UPND condemns attack on Davies Mwila, dares Chibale to produce evidence
World.content:
The ruling United Party for National Development (UPND) has condemned the reported attack on former Patriotic Front (PF) Secretary-General Davies Mwila at the Supreme Court, while challenging an opposition youth leader who linked the assault to UPND cadres to hand his evidence to the police.

In a statement issued in Lusaka on Tuesday, the UPND Media Team described the incident as unfortunate and unacceptable in a democratic society governed by the rule of law. The party urged law enforcement agencies to investigate professionally, impartially and without political interference, and to bring anyone found to have committed an offence to justice.

The ruling party’s sharpest words were reserved for PF-Pamodzi Alliance National Youth IPS Given Gift Chibale, who had publicly blamed suspected UPND cadres for the attack. The UPND said it would report the matter to the police under the cybercrime laws.

The media team said Mr Chibale needed to separate evidence from political speculation.

“An allegation does not become a fact simply because it is repeated publicly or attached to the name of a political party,” the statement read.

The party said that if the youth leader held credible evidence identifying the perpetrators, he should submit it to investigators and allow the law to take its course, rather than assign political responsibility before the facts had been established.

The warning extended beyond the opposition youth wing. The UPND cautioned members of the public against dragging political institutions into disrepute through unsubstantiated allegations, noting that political parties operate within Zambia’s constitutional and legal framework and have legitimate interests that false or damaging claims can harm. Where the law provides grounds for redress, the party said, legal remedies remain available.

Despite its dispute with Mr Chibale, the ruling party was firm that the assault on the former PF official could not be excused.

“No political disagreement, personal grievance or ideological difference can justify physical attacks, intimidation or the humiliation of another person,” the media team said.

The party described the attack as regrettable and condemned violence against Mr Mwila or any other citizen. It called for those responsible to be identified and brought to book, and urged the public to avoid circulating unverified claims, inflammatory commentary or material that could prejudice investigations.

The statement then turned on the opposition itself. The UPND said the incident raised serious concerns about the opposition’s political discipline and its continued association with allegations of violence and intolerance, even after its electoral defeats in 2021 and 2026.

The ruling party said Zambians had been right to renew their mandate to President Hakainde Hichilema and the UPND, whose leadership, it said, had emphasised peace and respect for the rule of law.

It also pointed to what it called the opposition’s apparent internal challenges, saying these were weakening its capacity to provide the credible checks and balances a democracy requires.

“Zambia deserves an opposition that embraces reform, respects its leaders and senior citizens, and resolves political differences through dialogue rather than violence,” the statement said.

The police have not yet named any suspects in the attack on Mr Mwila, and the UPND’s complaint against Mr Chibale under the cybercrime laws is expected to be lodged with law enforcement.

World.title: Africa: All of Africa Today - October 13, 2026
World.content:
WHO Launches Five-Year Strategy to Detect Health Threats Faster

The World Health Organization (WHO) has launched a new five-year strategy to help every country detect and understand emerging health threats within 24 hours of their appearance by 2030. The strategy builds on the work of the WHO Hub for Pandemic and Epidemic Intelligence, established in 2021 after the COVID-19 pandemic exposed gaps. Since its creation, the Hub has worked with 160 WHO member states, 190 partner organisations and thousands of scientists and policymakers to strengthen global disease surveillance. The plan focuses on five key initiatives, including using artificial intelligence to identify potential health threats, strengthening genomic sequencing to track emerging pathogens and connecting experts in data science and disease modelling. It will also support countries in sharing health data securely and improving cooperation between human, animal and environmental health systems. WHO Director-General Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said the strategy provides a clear path towards a world where countries can respond to health threats before they develop into major crises. The organisation says sustained investment and international partnerships will be essential to achieving this goal.

South Africa's Deputy Police Chief Resigns Amid Criminal Charges



South Africa's Deputy National Police Commissioner, Lieutenant General Shadrack Sibiya, has resigned from the police service three weeks after being charged with sexual offences. His lawyer submitted the resignation letter during a disciplinary hearing. Police spokesperson Athlenda Mathe said his departure would be treated as a dishonourable discharge because he was still facing disciplinary proceedings at the time of his resignation. Sibiya has been in custody since his arrest in September. Sibiya faces several serious allegations, including the sexual grooming of a 16-year-old girl, rape, human trafficking and links to organised crime figures. He denies the allegations of criminal links and sexual grooming. He admits having sex with an 18-year-old woman but maintains that it was consensual. Allegations against him also emerged during the Madlanga Commission, a public inquiry investigating claims of police corruption and collusion with criminal networks. He has been accused of interfering with investigations into political killings in KwaZulu-Natal and receiving cash and 20 impalas from an alleged criminal kingpin in exchange for a police contract. Sibiya has denied the allegations.

Renewed Fighting in Tigray Raises Fears of Wider Regional War

Renewed fighting in Ethiopia's northern Tigray region is raising fears of a wider conflict involving Eritrea and other neighbouring countries. Tensions escalated after reports that Eritrean forces crossed into Ethiopia, prompting Ethiopian forces to launch drone strikes against troops and equipment. Eritrea has denied reports of the incursion, while accusing Ethiopia of using the allegations as a pretext to pursue its ambitions for access to the Red Sea port of Assab. Local sources, however, reported clashes involving Eritrean forces at several locations in Tigray. The renewed violence follows the collapse of a fragile peace agreement that ended the 2020–2022 war. The conflict is unfolding amid shifting alliances between rival armed groups and growing tensions between Ethiopia and its neighbours. Tigray's ruling Tigray People's Liberation Front has vowed to continue fighting after federal forces and a pro-government militia captured the regional capital, Mekelle, on 3 October. The TPLF has also aligned with other opposition groups seeking to challenge Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's government. Analysts warn that the conflict could develop into three possible scenarios: the proliferation of armed groups, a prolonged military stalemate, or a full-scale war between Ethiopia and Eritrea. The humanitarian consequences could be severe, particularly in Tigray, where about one million people remain displaced, and nearly four million need urgent assistance. Drought, food shortages, and difficulties delivering aid are adding to the crisis.

Drought and Conflict Push Sudan Closer to Famine

The risk of famine is growing in parts of Sudan as severe drought worsens the humanitarian crisis caused by ongoing conflict, according to the Integrated Food Security Phase Classification (IPC), a global food security monitoring partnership supported by United Nations agencies. A new alert warns that malnutrition is worsening in several areas, particularly in Greater Darfur and Greater Kordofan. Aid organisations are struggling to reach affected communities because of insecurity, restricted access and a severe shortage of funding. In Eastern Jebel Marra, South Darfur, surveys in two displacement camps found acute malnutrition among children at 38% and 30.8%, both above the threshold associated with famine. More than half of Sudan has been affected by the drought, destroying crops and leaving families without enough food or income. In North Darfur, 64% of cropland is showing poor plant growth and late rains have not managed to save most cereal crops. Food prices are expected to continue to rise. There has also been mass displacement in Greater Kordofan, where since October 2025 more than 300,000 people have been forced to flee their homes. Attacks and insecurity are putting aid workers at risk, while many children are going without life-saving treatment for severe malnutrition. By 8 October, less than half of Sudan's humanitarian appeal had been funded. The IPC has called for an end to the fighting, safe access for aid agencies and a major increase in funding to prevent further loss of life.

Close 

Lagos Court Clears Way for Inquest into Chimamanda Adichie's Son's Death

The Lagos State High Court has cleared the way for a coroner's inquest into the death of Nkanu Esege, the son of renowned Nigerian author Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie. Justice Aishat Opesanwo dismissed an application by Eurapharma Care Services Nigeria Limited, which operates Euracare Multi-Specialist Hospital, seeking to stop the inquiry. The hospital argued that the cremation of Nkanu's body made a post-mortem examination impossible and deprived the coroner of the authority to proceed. Nkanu died on 7 January 2026 following medical procedures, prompting an investigation into the circumstances surrounding his death. In her ruling, Justice Opesanwo said the law requires an inquest when the circumstances of a death meet the conditions set out in the Coroners System Law of Lagos State 2007. She said that the absence of the body did not automatically prevent the inquiry from taking place or make it speculative. The judge also rejected the hospital's arguments concerning the handling of statements and evidence from medical personnel, saying the coroner has discretion over how the proceedings are conducted. She stressed that a coroner's inquest is a fact-finding exercise intended to establish who died, and how, when and where the death occurred. It is not a criminal trial to determine guilt or assign blame. The ruling allows the inquest to proceed.

World.title: Malawi: Malawi Urged to Build Economic Resilience As World Economy Wobbles
World.content:
Malawi cannot afford to rely on external demand or donor support as the global economy slows, according to a senior Reserve Bank of Malawi economist, who has warned that the country is underperforming even by regional standards and must accelerate reforms to strengthen economic resilience.

Analysing the implications of the latest World Economic Outlook projections, economist Kisu Simwaka said the expected moderation in global growth to 3.1 per cent from 3.5 per cent signals a more challenging external environment for African economies, particularly those dependent on commodity exports and foreign aid.

"The message is clear: the world economy is slowing down. But Africa must not slow down. Africa must accelerate. And Malawi must accelerate," Simwaka said.

He argued that weaker global growth, coupled with sluggish expansion in Europe, was already being reflected in Malawi's export performance.



Tobacco earnings, the country's largest foreign exchange earner, reached US$287.1 million by early October 2026, down sharply from US$526.2 million during the same period a year earlier.

According to Simwaka, the decline reflects weakening global demand as major economies lose momentum.

"When the world economy slows, small open economies such as Malawi cannot depend on external demand to drive growth," he said, adding that slower expansion in advanced economies could also translate into tighter aid flows.

Particular concern, he said, lies in Asia, where growth is projected to ease from 5.6 per cent to 4.9 per cent.

As a major engine of global commodity demand, a slowdown in the region could put further pressure on export prices and Africa's terms of trade.

"Weakening growth in Asia is a headwind for Africa because it affects commodity markets and export earnings," he said.

Simwaka also pointed to volatility in the Middle East and Central Asia as a source of uncertainty for fuel-importing countries such as Malawi.

Fluctuating oil prices could either worsen inflationary pressures or provide relief to the country's import bill, depending on exchange-rate stability.

"If oil prices fall, Malawi only benefits if the exchange rate remains stable enough for those gains to be passed through to domestic prices," he said.

Close 

While Sub-Saharan Africa is forecast to expand by around 4.5 per cent, Simwaka argued that the figure masks a deeper problem.

With population growth estimated at about 2.6 per cent, the region's per capita growth rate remains too low to achieve meaningful reductions in poverty.

"Four-and-a-half per cent growth for three consecutive years is effectively stagnation when population growth is taken into account," he said.

Against that backdrop, Malawi's projected growth of 2.7 per cent appears particularly weak. Simwaka noted that neighbouring economies such as Zambia, Tanzania and Rwanda are expected to outperform Malawi, underscoring the need for a stronger domestic growth strategy.

"Malawi is underperforming an underperforming region. The country must catch up," he said.

The economist argued that the policy response should focus on building internal resilience rather than hoping for a stronger global cycle.

He identified the accumulation of foreign exchange reserves, addressing fiscal imbalances and removing structural constraints to productivity as key priorities.

"In a global economy growing at only 3.1 per cent, countries such as Malawi cannot rely on exports and donor assistance alone," Simwaka said. "The challenge is to strengthen domestic foundations for growth and reduce vulnerability to external shocks."

His assessment comes as policymakers grapple with persistent foreign exchange shortages, inflationary pressures and subdued economic growth amid an increasingly uncertain global outlook.

World.title: Malawi: Bushiri Extradition Order Thrown Out As Malawi Court Delivers Final Ruling
World.content:
Prophet Shepherd Bushiri and his wife Mary have won a major legal victory after the High Court in Lilongwe delivered its final ruling crushing efforts to extradite them to South Africa.

In a detailed 175-page judgment, the court laid out the reasons behind its earlier decision to throw out an extradition order issued against the couple, dealing a significant blow to South Africa's long-running bid to bring them back to face legal proceedings.

The latest ruling confirms the court's position that the extradition order granted in March 2025 could not stand because of serious procedural and legal flaws.

Among the most damaging findings was that the Bushiris were denied their right to be heard before the extradition order was made, a development the court found was sufficient to invalidate the process.



The decision cements the couple's courtroom triumph and effectively slams the brakes on attempts to send them back to South Africa under the now-quashed order.

Bushiri's lawyer, Wapona Kita, described the judgment as a definitive victory for his clients, saying the court had now fully explained why it ruled in their favour.

"The court has provided the detailed reasons after considering our submissions and grounds for review," Kita said.

He added that the ruling means the Bushiris cannot be extradited under the order that was set aside by the court.

"Prophet Bushiri and his wife will no longer be extradited to South Africa under the quashed order," he said.

Kita said the legal battle could only return to court if the State decides to challenge the High Court's ruling.

"The only way forward now is through an appeal by the State," he said.

The explosive judgment marks the latest twist in one of Southern Africa's most closely watched legal sagas, which has drawn intense attention since the famous prophet and his wife left South Africa and returned to Malawi in 2020.

For now, the Bushiris have emerged victorious, with the High Court's final ruling delivering a crushing setback to efforts to have them extradited.

Memorial service
