World.title: Zimbabwe: Caine Prize Launches Investigation Into Ai Allegations Against Zimbabwean Winner Kundizeza
World.content:
ZIMBABWEAN writer Simbarashe Steyn Kundizeza, who recently won the 2026 Caine Prize for African Writing, is under investigation by the organisation after allegations of using artificial intelligence in his winning short story, "The Blue Fighter".

The allegations stem from an article published by The Atlantic over the weekend accusing Kundizeza of using AI in writing the award-winning story.

Vauhini Vara, in the article, described Kundizeza's story as "bad--maudlin and full of tired tropes."

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

The article has prompted the Caine Prize to investigate the allegations that have been raised against Kundizeza.

"When claims such as this are made, it is our responsibility to look into them. We aim to do this by taking a human-centred approach, ensuring that writers are supported and cared for during the process. We have initiated that process in this case.

"The Caine Prize celebrates stories that have already been published elsewhere. We are therefore in a bond of trust with the magazines and journals that publish the initial work.

"This connection also makes our role more than the simple labour of administering a prize, but a key part of an ecosystem that validates and supports the writing and publishing of African authors. We are mindful of this and will continue the mission of communally upholding and celebrating African literature," read the statement by the Caine Prize.

Kundizeza's "The Blue Fighter" is a story centred on a Tinashe whose family is beset by hardships after his father leaves his profession to pursue a long-time ambition of building fish tanks.

Should Kundizeza be found guilty by the organisers of using AI, he may be stripped of the award.

After winning the Caine Prize for African Writing, Kundizeza said the award will open up avenues in his career.

"Winning the Caine Prize means a great deal to me. I've been writing for several years, often without knowing where the work would take me, just fitting it around everything else in my life.

"To have a story drawn from my own experiences recognised at this level makes all those everyday compromises feel worthwhile. Most of all, it gives me a little more belief that I can keep making room for this life as a writer," he said.

World.title: Kenya: Court of Appeal Clears Kenya-U.S. Health Deal for Implementation Pending Appeal
World.content:
Nairobi — The Court of Appeal has cleared the way for the implementation of Kenya's health cooperation framework with the United States, overturning High Court orders that had blocked the programme over constitutional concerns.

A three-judge bench set aside conservatory orders issued on December 19, 2025, ruling that the public interest in maintaining essential healthcare services outweighed the risks associated with allowing the programme to proceed while the legal dispute remains unresolved.

The judges warned that continued suspension of the framework could disrupt critical healthcare services, including treatment for HIV, tuberculosis (TB), malaria and other infectious diseases, as well as immunisation programmes.

"The lives of citizens who depend on treatment for HIV, TB, and malaria, provided under the Framework risk being negatively and irredeemably impacted," the judges ruled.



"Some even risk losing their lives which is an irreversible consequence," they added.

The framework was signed by Kenya and the United States on December 4, 2025, and is linked to the provision of essential medicines, healthcare support and other services relied upon by millions of Kenyans.

The government, through the Attorney General and the Cabinet Secretary for Health, had moved to suspend the High Court orders pending the hearing and determination of its intended appeal.

In its application, the government warned that blocking the agreement threatened healthcare programmes serving approximately 1.4 million Kenyans.

It argued that interruptions to HIV and tuberculosis treatment could contribute to drug resistance, exposing patients to further complications and creating broader public health risks.

The government also cited the potential disruption of immunisation services, healthcare staffing, medical supply chains and systems supporting service delivery.

The appellate court agreed that the consequences of maintaining the suspension could be irreversible, particularly if resources allocated to the programme were redirected before the appeal was determined.

"If the applicants succeed on appeal, there will be no Framework to implement which will render the appeal nugatory," the court stated.

The judges consequently found that the balance of public interest favoured allowing the framework to proceed as the government pursued its appeal.

"Public interest favours the implementation of the programme pending hearing of the appeal," the ruling stated.

The decision followed opposition from constitutional activist Okiya Omtatah Okoiti, who argued that allowing the framework to proceed before the constitutional challenge was resolved could undermine fundamental rights and public accountability.

Omtatah raised concerns about data protection, privacy, public finance, devolution and Parliament's role in approving international agreements that impose binding obligations and financial commitments on Kenya.

He argued that the framework could violate Articles 1, 2, 10, 31, 43, 201 and 220 of the Constitution.

Katiba Institute also opposed the government's application, maintaining that constitutional safeguards and parliamentary oversight should not be set aside in the interest of expediency in healthcare delivery.

The respondents further argued that the government had increased funding to address potential shortfalls arising from changes in external health financing.

However, the appellate court emphasised that the framework had not been declared unconstitutional following a full hearing of the petition.

"There has not been any declaration of unconstitutionality of the said Framework," the judges observed.

The court clarified that its decision did not settle the substantive constitutional dispute but addressed whether the orders blocking implementation should remain in force pending the appeal.

The questions surrounding the agreement's legality, including the constitutional concerns raised by Omtatah and Katiba Institute, will therefore remain subject to determination in the substantive proceedings.

Beyond the potential healthcare disruptions, the government challenged the manner in which the High Court proceedings were conducted.

It argued that the application resulting in the conservatory orders had been heard on a date set for directions rather than a formal hearing, without adequate notice to the government.

The government also alleged that the proceedings breached the sub judice rule because similar issues had been raised in Nairobi High Court Petition No. E806 of 2025.

The Court of Appeal found that both arguments raised arguable grounds requiring consideration in the intended appeal.

"The case was indeed heard on a day that was fixed for directions, and whether the Court was correct in proceeding to hear the application before giving a formal hearing date, is an arguable point," the ruling stated.

Close 

The judges also noted the alleged sub judice issue, observing that conservatory orders appeared to have been issued in the other petition.

The court's findings did not amount to a final determination of those grounds but established that the intended appeal raised issues warranting consideration.

The Court of Appeal had previously lifted the High Court orders on May 12, 2026, indicating that the substantive ruling would provide the reasons for its decision.

In its final orders, the appellate court set aside the High Court's December 19, 2025, ruling and the conservatory orders restraining implementation of the framework, pending the intended appeal.

The latest decision allows the government to proceed with the health cooperation programme while the wider legal challenge continues.

The central constitutional questions, including the framework's implications for privacy, public finance, devolution and parliamentary oversight, remain unresolved.

The court's decision was anchored on the potential consequences of interrupting essential healthcare services and the risk that the intended appeal could become ineffective if the programme could no longer be implemented by the time the dispute is finally determined.

World.title: Kenya: Laikipia Confirms Two Suspected Ebola Cases Test Negative
World.content:
Nairobi — Laikipia County health authorities have confirmed that two suspected Ebola virus disease cases tested negative, urging residents to remain calm and avoid spreading unverified information following an outbreak of concern in Nanyuki.

The clarification comes after reports of a suspected Ebola case at Nanyuki Teaching and Referral Hospital triggered anxiety among residents on Monday.

Speaking to the media on Tuesday, Laikipia County Executive Committee Member for Health Albert Taiti said the county had activated precautionary measures after a patient presented with symptoms resembling those of Ebola virus disease.

Taiti said health officials collected samples from the patient and sent them for laboratory testing, with the results confirming that the patient did not have Ebola.



However, he disclosed that the patient died while receiving treatment at the facility.

The county health department subsequently received an alert from a private hospital in Nanyuki concerning a second suspected case.

Samples from the second patient were also submitted to the National Public Health Laboratory for analysis, with laboratory results confirming that the patient had tested negative for Ebola.

Following the two negative test results, Taiti assured residents that the county was prepared to respond to suspected Ebola cases and had taken steps to strengthen its capacity to manage potential infections.

He said healthcare workers had been sensitised on the appropriate procedures for identifying and handling suspected cases of the highly infectious disease.

The county government urged residents to remain vigilant and observe established preventive measures while promptly reporting any suspected cases to health authorities.

Officials also cautioned the public against circulating unverified reports about Ebola, warning that misinformation could trigger unnecessary fear and panic.

Residents were advised to rely on official communication from health authorities for accurate information about suspected cases and the county's response.

The two negative results provide reassurance amid heightened public concern over Ebola, but health officials continue to emphasise the importance of surveillance and preparedness.

The county government reiterated the need for cooperation between residents and healthcare workers to ensure suspected cases are assessed promptly and appropriate measures are taken.

Close 

The death of the patient at Nanyuki Teaching and Referral Hospital was reported separately from the laboratory findings, which ruled out Ebola in the two suspected cases.

The county has urged residents to avoid drawing conclusions from symptoms alone and to allow qualified health professionals to conduct the necessary investigations.

World.title: Trump administration slashes time refugees have to challenge loss of legal status
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

The Trump administration is adopting a new rule that would shorten the time refugees have to challenge the termination of their legal status, marking another restriction on legal immigration pathways as the White House continues its immigration enforcement crackdown.

The new policy, which takes effect Wednesday without undergoing the usual advance public notice-and-comment process, reduces the time refugees have to respond to a notice of intent to terminate their status from 30 days to 10.

According to the new rule, the administration is aiming to "mitigate potential risks" linked to people who were admitted as refugees but were not eligible for refugee status.

The documents pointed to refugees admitted during the Biden administration, claiming there was an "alarming erosion of the integrity" of the refugee program during those years, although refugee advocates dispute that allegation.

TRUMP ADMIN PAUSES VISA APPOINTMENTS WORLDWIDE AMID HEIGHTENED SCREENING FOR APPLICANTS

"A review of refugee processing policies and procedures implemented under the Biden administration indicates an alarming erosion of integrity leading to aliens being admitted to the United States as refugees when their identities, eligibility for refugee classification, and admissibility were determined based on incomplete records," DHS' document reads.

"The priority of expediency over quality encouraged a lack of robust interviews," it added. "Certain questions to ensure that aliens were eligible for refugee status prior to admission to the United States were omitted and this increased the risk of ineligible aliens being approved for refugee classification and subsequently admitted to the United States."

A spokesman for Citizenship and Immigration Services, Zach Kahler, similarly said the agency has found "an alarming erosion of screening and vetting measures" during the Biden administration to "rush processing and maximize the number of refugees admitted."

The Trump administration is "ensuring that refugee status is reserved only for those who were eligible under the law," he said in a statement to The Associated Press.

This comes after the Trump administration ordered the review of at least 185,000 refugees admitted during the Biden administration who still have pending green card applications.

The U.S. refugee admissions program has historically enjoyed bipartisan support since Congress passed the Refugee Act of 1980. Refugees undergo extensive security screenings and background checks before being approved for resettlement. Many spend years waiting in refugee camps before they can be admitted after undergoing multiple rounds of interviews and screenings.

With the Trump administration's new rule, critics argue tens of thousands of people who fled persecution and wars in their home countries could be forced into deportation.

"These families did everything asked of them," Krish O’Mara Vignarajah, president of Global Refuge, said in a statement. "They submitted to interviews, background checks and years of waiting abroad, only setting foot on U.S. soil once government officials approved their applications."

She said the Department of Homeland Security now wants to "revisit those decisions on a 10-day clock, a notice period wholly insufficient to find a lawyer, translate documents or get records out of a country they were forced to flee due to conflict or persecution."

"In some cases, refugees may not even receive the notice before their ten days are up, effectively eliminating their only chance to respond," she added. "If the government’s case for termination is truly strong, it can afford to give people a meaningful chance to challenge it."

HIAS, a major refugee aid group, also warned that refugees who have fled violence, persecution and displacement will be at risk of being deported to countries where they could be subject to persecution and torture.

"They are trying to upend the core principle that refugee resettlement represents permanent protection," HIAS Vice President Naomi Steinberg said in a statement.

FEDERAL JUDGE BLOCKS TRUMP ADMINISTRATION FINES OF UP TO $1.8M FOR MIGRANTS

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

The Trump administration has significantly overhauled the U.S. refugee admissions program, sharply restricting overall admissions while prioritizing the resettlement of white South Africans.

Last month, the Trump administration established a ceiling of 17,500 refugee admissions for fiscal year 2027, with most slots allocated to Afrikaners, a predominantly white ethnic group in South Africa.

During his first term, President Donald Trump reduced the number of refugees approved every year. The Biden administration reversed that trend, setting a refugee admissions ceiling of 125,000 for fiscal year 2025.

When Trump returned to the White House in January 2025, he immediately suspended the refugee program, stranding people around the world who had been set to come to the U.S. The administration later reopened the program but limited it mostly to white South Africans.

The Associated Press contributed to this report.

World.title: Tampa Bay Rays win game two over Guardians thanks to terrible error from José Ramírez, even ALCS at 1-1
World.content:
The American League Championship Series has pitted two of the most unlikely franchises against each other, with a trip to the World Series on the line.

The Tampa Bay Rays entered the 2026 season with one of the three lowest payrolls in baseball, as they usually do. They made few big additions, preferring to trust their farm system, player development staff, and the ability to mix and match players in specific situations.

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

Meanwhile, the Cleveland Guardians found a way to reduce spending even further, running the lowest payroll in Major League Baseball, in order to maximize profits for team ownership. Fast-forward to October, and the Rays and Guardians are the two AL teams, not the Yankees or Red Sox. Not the Astros and Rangers from big markets in Texas. Or the Blue Jays, with their top-5 payroll, or even Detroit, where the Tigers ran the 11th highest payroll in baseball and by far the highest in the AL Central.

DODGERS DYNASTY ON THE BRINK AFTER THE MILWAUKEE BABIP MACHINE DIALS UP ANOTHER WIN FOR BREWERS

As surprising as it comes, if you haven't watched baseball before. But maybe even more surprising? How game one of the ALCS between these two teams played out.

Cleveland, hardly known as an offensive powerhouse, fell behind 2-0 against one of the best run prevention teams in baseball. Then, starting in the sixth inning, they started scoring and never stopped. Home runs from Chase DeLauter and light-hitting catcher Patrick Bailey tied it, and a parade of hits led to a 4-3 lead in the eighth, which they promptly expanded to 7-3 by the ninth.

The team that finished 24th in the league in runs scored, exploding for seven runs in game one of the ALCS against one of the best pitching staffs in baseball. If that doesn't demonstrate the randomness of postseason baseball, it's hard to know what does.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

That set up what amounts to a must-win situation for the favored Tampa Bay Rays in game two, who sent midseason trade addition Freddy Peralta, acquired from the lowly New York Mets, to the mound hoping to even the series. Cleveland countered with Parker Messick, coming off an outstanding season of his own. But on Tuesday, Peralta, despite his struggles in New York, was electric.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

Six shutout innings, with six strikeouts and just four hits allowed, with an average fastball velocity over 2.5 mph higher than his season average. And he got a little help from his defense too, as star third baseman Junior Caminero made a nice play on a liner to his left, and hit the Dikembe Mutombo finger wag afterward.

Just as you'd expect from the Tampa pitching lab, Peralta's start lowered his ERA to just 0.81 over his last eight starts in a Rays uniform. Somehow, they do it every single time.

On offense, the Rays' lineup got to Messick in the fourth thanks to some shaky Cleveland defense. After Victor Mesa Jr. beat out an infield single, overturned on review, Jonny DeLuca struck out and Ben Williamson hit what seemed to be a routine grounder to third. But it took a funny hop and got through Guardians third baseman José Ramírez, scoring Mesa from third. Then Liam Hicks made it really hurt, lacing a line drive single to center to score Williamson and Chandler Simpson and extend the lead to 3-0.



The Guardians, as has become their trademark of late, battled back in the seventh. Patrick Bailey worked a leadoff walk after an ABS challenge, and got to second on a one-out Steven Kwan single. After José Ramírez flew out, Chase DeLauter drove in a run with a 105mph double to right. With the tying run at second base, Cleveland sent up Jo Adell, another impactful midseason acquisition who helped seal the game one win with a two-run single in the ninth inning. But Ian Seymour shut the door, getting Adell swinging on a changeup out of the zone.

OUTKICK IS NOW AVAILABLE ON THE FOX NEWS APP: CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD

The Guardians couldn't get anything going in the eighth, and Tampa went into the ninth inning with their dominant closer, Bryan Baker, looking to finish it out. And he did on just seven pitches, going through a quick 1-2-3 inning to even the series at a game apiece.

Tampa entered the series as big favorites, thanks to their deep pitching staff, and a lineup that's better as a whole than the sum of its parts. Plus Baker, who's followed up his 1.44 ERA in the regular season with four scoreless innings and four saves in the playoffs.

Tuesday's game two was a microcosm of this year's postseason; dominant pitching and timely, often advantageous hitting. Given these two teams' strengths, that's likely to continue for the remainder of the series.

The ALCS now shifts to Cleveland for game three, where Gavin Williams, coming off a dominant ALDS start against the White Sox, is expected to face Tampa bulk pitcher Griffin Jax. Expect a raucous crowd at Progressive Field, as the Guardians look to make progress towards a return to the World Series for the first time since 2016.

World.title: NYC Mayor Zohran Mamdani says he won't fire NYPD Commissioner Jessica Tisch despite socialist pressure
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani said Tuesday he has "no plans" to fire NYPD Commissioner Jessica Tisch, pushing back against calls from his democratic socialist allies to remove the city's top cop following protests over an ICE-involved shooting in the Bronx.

Ahead of a ceremony Tuesday honoring fallen NYPD officers, Mamdani was asked about Tisch's future as head of the department.

"Jessica Tisch is the police commissioner. I have no plans to change that," Mamdani told reporters.

"The reason that I made the decision to have Jessica Tisch as the police commissioner was because of her record of uprooting corruption from the upper echelons of the NYPD while lowering crime across our city," he continued. "And over the last 10 months that we've worked together, we have delivered the lowest recorded number of murders in our city's history, the lowest recorded number of shootings as well as shooting victims."

SOCIALIST SURGE: MAMDANI FLEXES GROWING POLITICAL MUSCLE AS HE TAKES ON DEM ESTABLISHMENT

The mayor's comments came after the New York City chapter of the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) called for Tisch's removal following last week's ICE shooting and demanded that Mamdani use his authority to drive ICE out of New York City.

The demand followed last week's shooting of Oscar Belgal during a federal immigration operation in the Bronx.

According to the Department of Homeland Security, Belgal, a 28-year-old Dominican national, was shot after allegedly refusing to comply with officers' orders during a targeted ICE operation to arrest him.

NYC SOCIALIST CANDIDATE SAYS CRIMINAL RECORD OF MAN SHOT BY ICE 'DOESN'T EVEN MATTER'

But after the team went down 2-0 in the NLCS to the Milwaukee Brewers, with Ohtani struggling at the plate, a decision had to be made heading into Game 3 at Dodger Stadium.

World.title: Saints’ 1-4 start under Kellen Moore prompts warning from owner Gayle Benson: ‘Not our standard’
World.content:
Frustration over the New Orleans Saints’ 1-4 start appears to extend beyond the team’s fan base.

Saints principal owner Gayle Benson voiced her concerns Tuesday, less than two full days after the team dropped its third consecutive game.

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

"That is not acceptable to me," Benson said of the team’s record at the Greater New Orleans Quarterback Club luncheon. Quarterback Tyler Shough showed promise during his rookie season, fueling expectations that the Saints could compete for the NFC South title and make a playoff push in their second season under head coach Kellen Moore.

But a narrow overtime loss to the Detroit Lions in the season opener foreshadowed the difficult road ahead. The Saints bounced back in Week 2 before losing to the Las Vegas Raiders in Week 3 and being dominated by division rival Atlanta Falcons in Week 4. The Minnesota Vikings then defeated New Orleans 23-13 in Week 5.

DREW BREES FEELS TYLER SHOUGH HAS EVERYTHING NEEDED WITH SAINTS TO SUCCEED IN 2026: 'UNBELIEVABLE SITUATION'

"And it falls short of what our fans truly deserve," Benson continued. "I hear the frustration directed towards our team and our organization. It is not lost on me. Our fans invest their time and their hearts in the Saints. They are right to expect more than we have delivered."

During a speech that lasted roughly eight minutes, Benson delivered a rare in-season public critique of the NFL franchise she oversees, making clear that the team’s current direction could not continue. Benson, 79, rarely speaks publicly about the Saints during the season, but when she does break her silence, her comments have typically been supportive.

This week, she directly challenged Moore and longtime general manager Mickey Loomis while also accepting personal responsibility for the team’s struggles.

"Kellen Moore and his coaches are responsible for preparing our players to perform," Benson said. "Mickey Loomis and our football staff are responsible for building a roster capable of sustained success. Our players are responsible for their preparation and execution. I am responsible for holding this organization accountable."

NEW ORLEANS SAINTS PROJECTED UNDER 5.5 WINS AS ROSTER TRANSITION CONTINUES INTO 2026 SEASON

Loomis has been a fixture in the Saints’ front office, playing a key role in the team’s football operations for the past quarter-century. Last year, Benson told The Times-Picayune that suggestions of dismissing Loomis were "ridiculous" and said she believed he did a "great job."

"I am committed to making the decisions necessary to improve this team," she said. "Everyone in this organization understands the urgency. We must prepare better, execute consistently and correct the mistakes that are costing us the games."

Benson also referred back to the Saints’ 45-24 loss to Atlanta, which came during a game commemorating the 20th anniversary of the first game played at the Superdome after it was restored following Hurricane Katrina. "Losing this year’s anniversary game to Atlanta truly disappointed me," she said.

Benson also noted that she would not "accept this level of performance."

Benson acknowledged that the Saints will need to show meaningful progress on the field, not simply talk about it, to restore trust.

TRUMP GRANTS PARDONS TO 'PERSECUTED' MECHANICS IN RIGHT-TO-REPAIR CRACKDOWN: 'I AM SETTING THEM ALL FREE'

BIDEN-ERA ENVIRO RULE ACCUSED OF STRANGLING TRUCKERS, SQUEEZING AMERICANS LANDS ON TRUMP CHOPPING BLOCK

World.title: Trump Energy Department issues emergency order to prevent blackouts across 13 states amid unusual October heat
World.content:

The Trump administration has issued an emergency order aimed at preventing potential blackouts across 13 states as unseasonably warm October temperatures strain the electrical grid serving more than 60 million Americans.

The Department of Energy authorized PJM Interconnection, a regional grid operator, to use additional power generation resources as rising electricity demand coincides with scheduled maintenance at power plants and transmission facilities.

The order, issued Monday under Section 202(c) of the Federal Power Act, takes effect Tuesday and remains in place through Friday, Oct. 16. It allows certain generating facilities to operate beyond normal restrictions if needed to maintain electricity supplies.

WHO PAYS FOR US POWER BOOM? BLUE, RED STATES OFFER STARKLY DIFFERENT WAYS TO LOWER UTILITY BILLS AMID AI SURGE

PJM serves all or parts of Delaware, Illinois, Indiana, Kentucky, Maryland, Michigan, New Jersey, North Carolina, Ohio, Pennsylvania, Tennessee, Virginia, West Virginia and Washington, D.C.

PJM Interconnection told Fox News Digital it does not expect the emergency conditions to affect everyday customers but warned that rising electricity demand and unpredictable weather patterns are creating new challenges for grid reliability.

Jeff Shields, a spokesperson for PJM, said electricity demand is growing faster than new generating capacity can come online, while unpredictable weather is leaving fewer opportunities for critical maintenance and construction.

Shields added that planned maintenance periods now present reliability risks that grid operators previously faced primarily during summer and winter.

LAWMAKERS TARGET ENERGY AFFORDABILITY THROUGH SWEEPING PERMITTING OVERHAUL IN NEW HOUSE BILL

"This order will help ensure millions of American families and businesses across the mid-Atlantic have access to affordable, reliable and secure electricity by making additional power generation, including backup power, available to use as needed," Energy Secretary Chris Wright said.

The emergency action comes as temperatures across parts of the Ohio Valley and Mid-Atlantic are expected to climb into the 70s and 80s, increasing electricity demand while some generating facilities and transmission lines remain offline for maintenance.

Wright also criticized energy policies under former President Joe Biden, arguing that restrictions on conventional energy production have weakened grid reliability.

TRUMP'S EPA REFORMS ARE A HUGE BOOST TO MANUFACTURERS, BUT THERE'S MORE RED TAPE TO CUT: EXPERT

The emergency order comes as the Energy Department pursues separate investments to strengthen the nation's electrical infrastructure.

DOE recently announced plans to support 84 Tennessee Valley Authority transmission and distribution projects across eight states, representing approximately $581 million in planned investments.

The projects, which include $250 million in federal funding, are expected to add roughly 2.5 gigawatts of grid capacity, improve reliability for 2.58 million families and businesses and support approximately 800 jobs.

The TVA initiative is separate from the PJM emergency order, and its final funding and regulatory approvals remain pending.

World.title: Florida executes inmate who killed cellmate because he wanted death penalty
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

A Florida man who said he murdered his cellmate in the hopes of securing a death sentence was executed on Tuesday.

James Robertson, 63, died after receiving a three-drug injection at Florida State Prison. He was pronounced dead about 10 minutes after the lethal injection was administered.

Robertson declined to give a final statement when asked if he had any last words.

"Nah, I’m straight," he responded.

TWO FLORIDA INMATES DIE IN RARE DOUBLE EXECUTION AFTER SCOTUS DENIES STAYS

Robertson's execution was a stark contrast to the botched execution of Christa Pike in Tennessee two weeks ago, when she survived two doses of pentobarbital and was rushed to the hospital. Pike has since been released from the hospital and returned to prison.

"Florida has a sound lethal injection process and protocol," Jordan Kirkland, a state Department of Corrections spokesperson, said at a news conference ahead of the execution.

While he could not speak about Tennessee’s lethal injection protocol, Kirkland said Florida would make sure its process was "humane and dignified."

Florida injects death row inmates with a sedative, a paralytic and a drug that stops the heart when they are put to death, according to the state Department of Corrections.

Robertson had pleaded guilty to first-degree murder for strangling his cellmate, Frank Hart, as he was sleeping in 2008. He waived all appeals and told investigators that he killed the man so he would be given the death penalty and not have to live out the rest of his days behind bars.

Hart was killed just eight days before he was set to be released, according to his daughter, Rebecca Hart, who emphasized that her father was not only a piece of Robertson’s story.

"When someone you love is taken from you in such a violent way, the world keeps moving, even when a part of yours feels like it has stopped," she told reporters outside the prison. "Other people go on with their lives, but you carry your loss into every tomorrow."

Hart was sentenced to prison in 2003 following a sexual battery conviction.

Robertson was only 17 years old when he was sent to prison in 1980 for burglary and assault. Additional convictions for escape, battery and weapons offenses extended his prison sentence.

Florida was initially scheduled to execute two people on Tuesday, but Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis withdrew a death warrant last week for William Lee Thompson, 74, who was sentenced to death for his role in the 1976 kidnapping and killing of 23-year-old Sally Ivester. He was convicted of first-degree murder, kidnapping and sexual battery in connection with Ivester's death.

DeSantis did not provide a reason for stopping the execution but had temporarily stayed the execution last month pending a psychiatric evaluation amid concerns about Thompson's mental competency and deteriorating health. His attorneys said he has dementia and failing health and want him transferred to a medical facility.

This was the first time DeSantis withdrew a death warrant. Thompson will remain on death row, and a new death warrant could be signed in the future.

DeSantis is the third Florida governor to sign a death warrant for Thompson. Former Govs. Bob Graham and Bob Martinez each scheduled executions for Thompson in the 1980s, but he avoided the electric chair, the state's method of execution at the time, after years of appeals and stays.

In July, Florida executed two prisoners in one day, the first time a state has done so in nearly a decade.

Florida has accelerated its pace of executions amid a flurry of death warrants signed by DeSantis since 2025. The governor oversaw a record 19 executions last year, more than any other Florida governor in a single year since the death penalty was reinstated in 1976, accounting for approximately 40% of the U.S. total for 2025.

TEXAS EXECUTES JAMAAL HOWARD DESPITE CONCERNS OVER LETHAL INJECTION DRUG USED IN FAILED TENNESSEE EXECUTION

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Last year, 47 executions were carried out nationwide, the highest annual total since 2009.

Florida has carried out more than half of the 31 total executions in the country so far this year.

Robertson was the Sunshine State's 17th execution of 2026, with two more already scheduled, not including Thompson.

William Reaves, 77, who was convicted of fatally shooting a deputy in 1986, is scheduled to be executed Oct. 20. Jesse Guardado, 64, is scheduled to be executed Nov. 5 for robbing and killing a woman to buy drugs in 2004.

The Associated Press contributed to this report.

World.title: In heated Georgia Senate debate, Jon Ossoff says he won’t run for president in 2028
World.content:
Sen. Jon Ossoff, D-Ga., said Tuesday night during a debate that he will not run for president in 2028.

Ossoff made the statement in response to a question as he faced off with his Republican challenger, Rep. Mike Collins. Ossoff is seeking a second six-year term in Georgia and said he would serve the full term.

“I have zero interest in running for president,” Ossoff said when he was asked directly by one of the moderators. “I’m not running for president. I’m running for re-election to the Senate.”

Ossoff has been regularly discussed as a potential Democratic contender in 2028. If he were to win the presidency, he would have to give up his Senate seat, which he stressed Tuesday night that he would not do.

After the brief remark, Ossoff quickly transitioned to pressing Collins about why he has supported President Donald Trump’s tariffs, a main focus of both his campaign and a debate the two held last week. Tuesday was the second debate in the nationally watched Georgia Senate race, this one organized by the Atlanta Press Club.

Collins quipped that Ossoff was actually trying to run for president and will be “your DSA candidate,” a reference to the Democratic Socialists of America.

The exchange came at the beginning of the hourlong debate, which covered ground including data centers; the economy under Trump, whose approval rating is at record lows; the war in Iran; and the issue of Collins’ son-in-law’s promoting white nationalist posts on social media.

Ossoff asked Collins directly whether he considered himself a “white nationalist.”

“I condemn any sort of hate speech,” Collins said. “Antisemitism, hate of any kind. It’s abhorrent.”

The exchange continued when Collins again asked Ossoff to denounce Reid Hoffman, a major donor to Democratic causes — including Ossoff-aligned political committees — whose name appeared in the Epstein files. Collins brought up Hoffman several times last week and did so again during the second debate.

Ossoff did not directly respond, and he again pointed to the fact that those close to Collins amplified white nationalists’ posts.

“How weak a person do you have to be to be unable to stop someone under your own roof from disseminating neo-Nazi propaganda while you run for Senate?” Ossoff said. “The paper reported it’s still going on today.”

Given a chance to respond, Collins did not address it directly. But he said rhetoric like Ossoff’s had motivated a New York man who is accused of making death threats against him.

“I’m a little tired of this, Jon,” Collins said. “This crazy person is in jail right now because of your rhetoric.”

Neither candidate directly answered the other’s charges.

Collins also, once again, did not answer questions about whether or not Joe Biden won the 2020 presidential election. He was asked about audio of a call Trump made after the 2020 election asking Georgia Republican Secretary of State Brad Raffensperger to “find 11,780 votes” to help overturn the 2020 election.

“You know, Joe Biden went into office, and boy, Georgians paid for it,” Collins said.

World.title: Federal judge issues longer-term decision blocking Trump’s White House media ban
World.content:
A federal judge issued an order late Tuesday blocking the Trump administration from banning CNN, Politico and MS NOW from the White House complex while the organizations’ lawsuit over access proceeds.

U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly of Washington, D.C., issued the preliminary injunction in the wake of a hearing Thursday at which the administration contended it imposed the ban in part because of national security concerns; media organizations said it was because of “viewpoint discrimination.”

Kelly sided with the news outlets, noting that Trump used national security as a reason for the ban after their press passes had already been revoked and ruling that it also likely violated reporters’ freedom of speech and due process rights.

“There is practically nothing national security-related in the record connected to the President’s decision to revoke Plaintiffs’ hard passes to which the Court can defer,” Kelly wrote in his 26-page opinion.

His order will give the outlets access to the White House until the underlying lawsuit challenging the ban is resolved. But it doesn’t require the administration to allow reporters from the outlets access to the Oval Office or Air Force One — locations where the administration has blocked reporters from CNN and Politico in recent weeks.

Trump vowed to appeal on Truth Social before the ruling was handed down. The White House didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment following the ruling.

Kelly had issued a temporary restraining order lifting the ban while he weighed whether to issue an injunction.

Trump announced the bans of CNN, MS NOW and Politico on social media on Sept. 18, saying they were a “result of their constant ‘reporting’ FAKE NEWS!”

“Media Outlets shouldn’t be able to constantly write or report FICTION and LIES when they’re covering the President of the United States, the Trump Administration, or the United States of America. Other Fake News Media Outlets to follow,” he wrote on Truth Social.

In court filings, the three news organizations said the ban affected 78 journalists who had “hard passes,” meaning they had been previously screened and credentialed to work at the White House.

The outlets filed a lawsuit alleging Trump’s action violated their due process rights and First Amendment protections for newsgathering and speech.

“This ban could not be a more direct assault on the First Amendment nor a more blatant violation of our most fundamental constitutional principles,” the suit said.

The White House and Trump then began arguing that the ban was intended to address national security concerns, with Trump saying in another post that the outlets’ reporting was “a threat to our National Security, and must be stopped, NOW!”

The judge was unmoved by that argument.

Kelly said it was clear from Trump’s announcement of the ban and from subsequent remarks that his motivation was content.

“President Trump likely banned Plaintiffs from the White House because he believes that their reporting is generally inaccurate and biased against him,” Kelly wrote, finding this decision violated the journalists’ First and Fifth amendment rights.

He noted, however, that his decision doesn’t concede that Trump’s concerns about accuracy and fairness are unfounded or that the government is “powerless when its true aim is to protect national security when classified information is unlawfully disclosed.”

Kelly cited Trump’s recent remarks to Time magazine that he didn’t like “bad story after bad story” coming from CNN, Politico and MS NOW journalists. It was, Ted Boutrous, the news outlets’ attorney, had argued ahead of the decision, “a confession of what amounts to viewpoint discrimination.”

“President Trump, I’ll give him credit,” Boutrous said. “He’s not hiding it.”

In his previous decision, Kelly also found that the administration had denied the outlets due process under settled law from several cases that have made their way to the D.C. federal appeals court.

The White House argued that the appeals court decisions were wrong.

“Maybe—but this Court is bound by D.C. Circuit precedent, full stop,” Kelly wrote.

At a hearing on the injunction Thursday, the Justice Department lawyer representing the White House, Michael Velchik, asked Kelly to lift his restraining order, calling the White House a “sacred place” that shouldn’t have to give people access just because they “identify as a reporter.”

“Access to the White House is a privilege — not a right,” Velchik said.

Boutrous argued that the administration was engaging in impermissible and unconstitutional “viewpoint discrimination” because the ban was based on Trump’s dislike of the outlets’ reporting and because he has said he hoped the ban would force journalists to “straighten themselves out.”

In court filings, Boutrous urged Kelly to ignore the national security arguments, saying they were manufactured and not what the case is really about.

Boutrous argued that “the President himself has continued telling anyone who will listen precisely what this ban is really about, most recently complaining at length in an interview with Time magazine that he banned Plaintiffs because he feels that he should not ‘be forced to bear’ what he considers ‘constantly bad stories,’ as he ‘won the election’ and has ‘done great things.’”

After Tuesday night’s ruling, Boutrous said he and his clients were grateful to the court for securing their access anew.

“The President has repeatedly, candidly, and consistently admitted in public that he banned our clients from the White House to punish reporting he doesn’t like,” he said in a statement. “The harm this ban did to our clients, the First Amendment, and the public as a whole is profound. The Court was right to enjoin the White House from enforcing this ‘unconstitutional ban.’”

Separately, the Justice Department said last week that it was investigating five major TV networks, including CNN and NBC, for potentially violating federal antitrust laws after the networks temporarily declined to provide pool coverage of Trump as a result of the ban against the three news outlets.

The pool is a rotating group of networks that share the duties of recording a president’s activities during public appearances and travel. The on-duty network then distributes information and media, such as video and audio, to other outlets for their use.

World.title: Texas DA says ICE intentionally hit immigrant with a car and may have withheld evidence
World.content:
HOUSTON — Videos collected by local investigators make it “pretty obvious” that an ICE officer intentionally ran over Miguel Parra Hernandez during an immigration stop Saturday, which could lead to assault charges, the district attorney said Tuesday.

“This was an intentional striking and running over of the person by the vehicle, and in that case, that is an aggravated assault with a deadly weapon in Texas,” Harris County District Attorney Sean Teare told NBC News.

Teare said the federal government is not cooperating with the investigation conducted by his office and the Harris County Sheriff’s Office. He also said ICE may have allowed the erasure of critical data in the vehicle involved in striking Parra, who was on foot.

Teare said that in his seven years as a Harris County vehicular crimes division chief, he has reviewed video from a number of other auto-pedestrian collision cases. He said the video his investigators have gathered in Parra’s case “goes above” the video that was posted online and obtained by NBC affiliate KPRC of Houston.

“My viewing of it, and many other investigators that have viewed it, as well, it’s pretty obvious that this was an intentional striking and running over of the person by the vehicle, and in that case, that is an aggravated assault with a deadly weapon in Texas,” he said.

Harris County District Attorney Sean Teare. Raquel Natalicchio / Houston Chronicle via Getty

Parra, 48, was left with multiple breaks and fractures in his body, according to his attorney and an advocate who has been speaking on his behalf. He had surgery on one leg and faces multiple additional operations, said Cesar Espinosa, co-founder and executive director of FIEL, an immigrant civil rights group.

Video obtained by KPRC shows a white truck headed in the opposite direction of traffic on a busy roadway. It shows a vehicle jumping a yellow median and heading in the direction that Parra is running.

It then appears to show the vehicle, which is not marked, swerving left toward Parra’s path, in front of a truck stopped in a shopping center. The parked truck leaves, and a man can be seen on the pavement behind the ICE vehicle, the video shows.

An ICE spokesman said over the weekend that officers were pursuing the fleeing men and that “Miguel Parra Hernandez ran in front of an ICE vehicle and was struck.”

Teare, a Democrat, announced late Monday that his office had launched an independent investigation.

On Tuesday, an ICE spokesperson who was not identified said in a statement that “allegations that ICE struck Miguel Parra-Hernandez intentionally are RECKLESS and FALSE. The men and women of ICE are entrusted with upholding the rule of law and are held to the highest standards of professionalism, integrity, and ethical conduct.”

ICE said the allegations are “disgusting smears” that are “peddled by the media,” leading to more than a 1,600% increase in assaults and a 3,300% increase in vehicle attacks against its law enforcement officers. It did not offer data behind those numbers.

ICE has said that Parra was not the target of the attempted stop but that he was in the country illegally. Parra’s attorney and family have said he has no criminal record and was on his way to work applying stucco.

Teare said his office and the sheriff’s office determined that the vehicle that struck Parra was a Jeep Cherokee and that it potentially had evidence, including a data crash recorder. He said his office wanted to know whether the vehicle locked in information at the time of the collision that could be downloaded, such as speed, steering and braking. Teare said the way to preserve data from the car would have been to “put it on a flatbed trailer and you take it to forensically download it.”

But he said he believes any data on the recorder related to the incident could have been erased when ICE drove the car away.

He and the sheriff’s investigators told ICE the information needed to be downloaded, but ICE refused, Teare said.

ICE did not respond to questions about a data crash recorder, the erasing of any potential data or any refusal to download it.

“Our office began drafting a search warrant that we were in the process of drafting when the ICE agent in question, the one that had been driving, we believed, at the time of the collision, jumped back into the car and drove it away from the scene,” Teare said. “In my 20-year career, I’ve never heard of anything like that.”

Teare also said two people from “an entirely different operation” were in the back seat of the ICE vehicle when it struck Parra. Those two people are also in ICE custody, along with Parra. Teare said his office is working to ensure all three remain in the country as material witnesses.

“I’ve taught for years at the Houston Police Department Academy, Harris County Department Academy. I’ve worked with law enforcement for 20 years. There is not a single agency in the United States that would teach that once you put people in custody in your car, you then begin to pursue other people,” he said.

Doing so puts “every single person out there in danger again,” he said.

According to Teare, the ICE vehicle should have activated its emergency equipment, such as its lights and siren, as it jumped a median and crossed into oncoming traffic.

A senior official at the Department of Homeland Security told NBC News on Tuesday that multiple ICE officers on the scene at the time were wearing body cameras. ICE is reviewing video of the scene as part of an internal investigation, the official said.

Espinosa said Parra told him that he fled because it was unclear whether there were officials in the vehicles, which he said were unmarked, did not use sirens and had dark, tinted windows.

ICE has said it was targeting another man, Jose Mendoza Cervantes, who was in the country illegally and had committed several crimes. Espinoza and Parra’s attorney Kim Bruno said neither Parra nor the man who was with him when ICE stopped their vehicle has any association with Mendoza.

Miguel Parra Hernandez. Noticias Telemundo

In previous encounters between ICE and targets of its arrests in vehicle stops, including some who have been killed, such as Lorenzo Salgado Araujo in Houston, ICE has alleged the people it tried to arrest weaponized their vehicles.

Parra was struck less than two weeks after the Trump administration issued guidance setting tighter rules for vehicle stops.

The guidance says only agents who have completed specific training should make vehicle stops. The memo also says that vehicles used for traffic stops must have lights and sirens and that all officers on the scenes of vehicle stops must wear and activate their body cameras.

The Harris County District Attorney’s Office has been asking witnesses and people who may have photos or video of the incident to contact it. Teare said that there is a secure portal that goes directly to the district attorney’s office and that no one is asked about citizenship or immigration status.

“All we are interested in is getting the truth, and any shred of cellphone footage, anyone that saw something and really can point us in the right direction, it would be wonderful,” he said.

World.title: Diesel futures jump, signaling higher prices to come despite Trump’s Russia deal
World.content:
Diesel futures traded sharply higher Tuesday, as doubts mounted about the likely impacts of the Trump administration’s latest efforts to push prices down.

U.S. diesel futures were up 5% by midday to their highest level in weeks.

In Europe, diesel futures rose by about 3.8%, while gas futures spiked to levels not seen all year.

A move higher in futures markets typically signals that prices will climb in the coming days.

Already, the average nationwide price of diesel is up 70% since the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran on Feb. 28. The cost of unleaded gas has risen by more than 45% over that period.

Crude oil prices, meanwhile, were mixed. Brent traded around $106 per barrel, while U.S. crude oil neared $95 per barrel. Both of those key energy benchmarks have risen around 70% since the start of the year.

Gas and diesel prices are rising especially fast in parts of the country where President Donald Trump and Republicans can least afford to anger voters ahead of November’s midterm elections.

“Absolutely stunning price spikes in wholesale diesel today,” Gulf Oil adviser Tom Kloza wrote Tuesday on X. “US retail diesel price record of $6.53/gal could be topped by the midterms.”

“Up 18cts/gal Gulf Coast and East Coast; but up 28cts/gal in Southern California and 25-30cts/gal in Great Plains and Great Lakes,” he wrote.

Patrick De Haan, the head of petroleum analysis at GasBuddy, wrote on X that “$6/gal diesel may be here to stay for now.”

“Truckers and farmers not going to see any relief anytime soon,” he wrote.

The broad spike higher in diesel futures came just days after Trump announced a controversial deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin to increase diesel supplies in the United States by buying previously sanctioned Russian reserves.

When Trump announced the deal, he said it would result in millions of metric tons of additional diesel for the world.

While that may sound like a lot, analysts have since crunched the numbers and determined that, at best, the diesel in question would amount to less than two weeks’ worth of U.S. demand.

Tuesday’s higher diesel futures are evidence of the market “clearly not believing that Russian oil is on the way,” Kloza said.

The deal with Putin also required that the Trump administration suspend long-standing sanctions on Russian energy purchases.

The sanctions were put in place after Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022, and the decision to lift them until April has drawn widespread backlash both at home and abroad.

Trump has also applied pressure to European allies in an effort to get them to release more of their diesel reserves.

The president’s Oct. 2 announcement that Europe had bowed to the pressure and would release fuel temporarily cooled prices for a few days. But a lack of additional details about that release gradually erased any price relief.

A subsequent statement from the International Energy Agency confirmed what traders had suspected: Europe would not be releasing any new diesel reserves, merely continuing to fulfill a pledge it made in March as part of a multinational effort to cap rising fuel prices.

Trump also signed an executive order this month that sought to ease restrictions on an off-road formulation of diesel that is dyed red and not subject to federal gas taxes.

But industry groups quickly warned truckers to avoid using “red dye” diesel without more information about how the taxes would work.

As of Tuesday, it was unclear whether Trump’s red dye diesel order had any impact on domestic prices or supply.

World.title: What’s fueling inflation? Fuel.
World.content:
Inflation in America is being powered by diesel.

The price of the fuel, used by farmers and truckers, is up more than 75% since the start of the Iran war in late winter. Diesel costs have become a particular concern for economists, who say higher diesel fuel costs trickle down into “just about everything.”

And the final government inflation report before November’s pivotal midterm elections will most likely reflect how much of a headache it has become for businesses and consumers.

The Bureau of Labor Statistics is set to release its September consumer price index report at 8:30 a.m. Wednesday. It’s expected to show the annual rate of inflation rose to 3.7% from 3.4%, according to a survey of economists from Dow Jones. From August to September, prices are expected to have risen by 0.6%. The monthly jump, if it is confirmed, would also be one of the largest in years.

Since August, oil prices have risen to more than $105 per barrel from about $80. The price of regular gas, which most consumers buy, also remains elevated by more than 45% since late February, when the Iran war was launched.

As early voting kicks off this week, a higher inflation reading would come at a precarious moment for Republicans defending majorities in the House and the Senate. Polls consistently find that inflation and the high cost of living are top issues this year for voters in both parties.

Higher diesel prices this summer and fall have hit agricultural states like Kansas, Iowa and Texas especially hard. Long viewed as Republican strongholds, all three states have Democrats outperforming in Senate races with campaigns focused on the high cost of living.

In response to the outcry over the high cost of gas and diesel, President Donald Trump has pulled several policy levers in recent weeks aimed at pushing down prices. But so far, none of them has made much of a dent.

President Donald Trump signed an executive order to lower the cost of diesel fuel at a campaign rally in Nebraska this month. Win McNamee / Getty

The Trump administration has pressured Group of Seven allies to release more diesel stocks, issued an order to allow more widespread use of tax-free diesel and announced a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin under which Russia would release some diesel supplies and drop some of its export restrictions.

The latest action has drawn global backlash after Trump also eased some sanctions on Russia to facilitate the Russian diesel deal.

Core concerns

Consumers’ wages are still lagging behind the rate of inflation. As of September, wage growth was 3%, and it has not grown faster than inflation since March.

Still, despite the pressure on prices and wages, consumers continue to spend. The CEOs of the nation’s largest banks reported Tuesday that consumers continue to spend at a steady pace.

“While various headwinds, most recently higher energy prices, and tighter monetary policies have been challenging, the global economy has held up remarkably well in the U.S.,” Citigroup CEO Jane Fraser said. “While much has been made of the AI boom, the consumer is still driving much” of the economy’s momentum, she added.

Wells Fargo CEO Charlie Scharf said, “Our data shows that our consumer and business customers are doing well.” JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon said the economy “continued to be fueled by strong business investment and ongoing consumer spending” over the last three months.

Core inflation, which strips out food and energy prices and is more closely watched by the Federal Reserve, is expected to rise, as well, to 2.5%. If it is confirmed, that would be its highest level since June.

Planes take off from Hollywood Burbank Airport on Tuesday. Myung J. Chun / L.A. Times via Getty

One key sector fueling higher core inflation is airfare. “Airfares remain the core category most directly affected by higher oil prices,” said economists at Morgan Stanley. “Airfare CPI is already up 23% y/y, which raises the question of how much further prices can increase.”

They noted that jet fuel prices have risen 90% since this time last year “and typically account for roughly 20-30% of airline operating costs.” As a result, airlines “may already be approaching full pass-through of the increase in fuel costs to consumers.”

iPhones and interest rates

Another major consumer item that could affect September’s inflation rate: pricier iPhones.

Apple’s latest iPhone began selling Sept. 12, and Morgan Stanley’s economists said, “Price increases were generally in the 10%-14% range across models.”

00:00 00:00 Why laptops, tablets and phones are skyrocketing in price 01:45

“Given Apple’s roughly 50% share of the U.S. smartphone market,” that could translate into what they said could be a small upside impact on overall inflation.

But while the higher iPhone prices are likely to be contributing to September’s inflation, they are also the product of inflation earlier this year — inflation that traces back to the ever-expanding buildout of AI data centers.

The race to build data centers and chips for AI has triggered a scramble for memory, in particular. Given that the supply of memory chips is limited, prices have soared at an unprecedented pace.

In June, Apple told NBC News that it has “never seen a component price increase this much, this quickly.”

Economists at Goldman Sachs also expect to see a jump in September in other key consumer categories.

“We expect a pickup in autos inflation, reflecting a 0.5% increase in used car prices, a 0.2% increase in new car prices, and a 0.2% increase in the car insurance category,” they wrote in a note.

Wednesday’s data could also “determine whether the Fed’s next hike is imminent, or simply still ahead,” said economists at UBS. Already, the Federal Reserve has raised interest rates once this year to try to slow inflation. A number of top Fed officials have also spoken about the need to raise rates even higher.

“If the economic data continue to come in as expected, I anticipate additional hikes to support a timelier return of inflation to our two percent goal,” Federal Reserve governor Christoper Waller said Thursday. “But there is some flexibility about when those hikes will occur.”

The Fed is expected to raise rates one more time this year, most likely in December. But an inflation reading Wednesday that comes in hotter than expected could increase that urgency and lead to a pre-Election Day rate hike at the central bank’s Oct. 27-28 meeting.

World.title: Bank of America ordered to pay historic $1.2 billion over alleged sanctions law violations
World.content:
Bank of America was ordered Tuesday to pay $1.2 billion to the Treasury Department, which said it violated anti-money laundering and sanctions laws.

00:20 Bank of America ordered to pay historic $1.2 billion fine 00:00 00:00

The penalty is the third largest ever issued in Treasury history, the agency said. As part of that total, the bank was ordered to pay $750 million to the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, the largest fine it has ever levied.

“Today’s actions send a clear message that even the biggest financial institutions are not above the law,” Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in a statement.

As the second-largest bank in the country, Bank of America has more than 70 million clients and processes about $4.5 trillion in payments for individual customers every year.

In addition, the bank handles $450 trillion in payments for corporate customers, including payrolls, corporate credit cards and supplier payments.

The Treasury Department said Bank of America “admits that it willfully violated” the Bank Secrecy Act and “failed to maintain” an anti-money laundering program that met minimum requirements under the law. The bank also admitted having failed to file mandatory Suspicious Activity Reports.

“Bank of America failed to timely report to FinCEN over $5 billion dollars in suspicious transactions, with over $1 billion of this activity implicating national security-related and other priority illicit finance risks, including suspicious transactions indicative of Chinese Money Laundering Networks, fraud, and potential trade-based money laundering with a substantial nexus to the southwest border,” the Treasury Department said in a statement.

FinCEN is the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network, which combats money laundering, illicit financial activities and terrorist financing networks around the world.

“Financial crime compliance is serious, and we are responsible for getting it right,” Bank of America said in a statement to NBC News.

“We have invested billions of dollars in technology and dedicated thousands of employees to combat financial crime, and our team is far along with and committed to completing the work required to address the issues raised by our regulators.”

“We will continue to support federal and local law enforcement across thousands of investigations and report hundreds of thousands of suspicious activity reports each year.”

In addition to the FinCEN violations, the Treasury Department said Bank of America is also settling “its potential civil liability for 475 apparent violations of multiple sanctions programs” with the Office of Foreign Assets Control, which oversees sprawling U.S. sanctions.

The company “processed millions of dollars in payments in apparent violation of sanctions programs targeting Russia, Belarus, Iran, Burma, Somalia, narcotics, and global terrorism,” the Treasury Department said.

Bessent said, “When a bank of this size fails to meet its anti-money laundering and sanctions obligations, the consequences extend far beyond its own walls, exposing the entire U.S. financial system to significant illicit finance risks.”

Bank of America will report its third-quarter earnings shortly before 7 a.m. ET Wednesday.

World.title: Trump says Greenland oil, gas and mineral exploration "getting ready to begin"
World.content:
President Trump said Wednesday that "massive" oil, gas and mineral exploration is preparing to begin in Greenland.

In a statement posted on his Truth Social platform, Mr. Trump said "Massive Oil, Gas, and Mineral Exploration is getting ready to begin in our new and beautiful Greenland," but did not give more details.

The president added that "there are Experts that are saying that the amount of easily available Oil is far greater than that of almost any land, anywhere in the World."

Mr. Trump also touted Greenland's role in the defense of the United States in Europe, saying that "any future attack" on the U.S. would have to come across the semi-autonomous island, "where our Defense will routinely knock down drones, missiles, or any other form of weapon not yet conceived."

"It gives us time, location, and sightline, like nowhere else in the World!" Mr. Trump added.

Prime Minister of Greenland, Prime Minister of Denmark and President Trump sign a security pact on September 22, 2026 in New York City. Chip Somodevilla / Getty Images

The announcement comes more than four weeks after the U.S., Greenland and Denmark, which oversees the territory, signed a new security agreement to bolster American military and security presence on the island.

That agreement, which gives the U.S. broad access to the island's airspace and territory, largely focuses on using Greenland for military purposes, but also mentions resource extraction and "minerals cooperation" between the two countries, without specifying any details.

The plan allows the U.S. to expand the existing Pituffik Space Base, the northernmost U.S. military installation which serves as an early-warning system for incoming missiles. The agreement also says the U.S. can establish additional bases at the sites known as Narsarsuaq and Mestersvig, which are roughly 950 miles apart. Any of the three parties can propose more "defense areas" as needed, subject to approval by the others.

Map showing main deposits of selected critical minerals in Greenland, according to the Geological Survey of Denmark and Greenland. Jonathan Walter, Valentina Breschi/AFP via Getty Images

The deal, which has no expiration date, also blocks non-NATO countries from establishing bases on the island without agreement from the parties.

Since his first term, Mr. Trump had cited Greenland's strategic location as one of the reasons for greater U.S. control over the semi-autonomous island, and even suggested purchasing the island from Denmark or using military force.

Some industry experts believe mineral resources in Greenland have only been lightly explored and up until now the cost of extraction has not made economic sense for private companies.

World.title: Trump pardons 2 auto workers on stage during rally in Alaska
World.content:
President Trump during a political rally in the state late Tuesday granted onstage pardons to two Alaska auto shop owners who pleaded guilty to violating the Clean Air Act — an unusually public use of the president's clemency power.

The president said the two men — Zachary Czubak and Patrick Fleming — were "wrongly charged," and cast the charges against the two men as an example of how the Biden-era Justice Department "viciously targeted the Alaskan way of life."

Czubak, Fleming and a third man named Michael Hanzuk owned an auto shop that specialized in diesel vehicles called Arm Rippin Toys, according to court records. Federal prosecutors say they offered to remove the emission control systems in customers' vehicles for a fee of $1,140 to $5,445, in part by modifying their physical components and preventing their diagnostics systems from noticing a problem, causing the vehicles to spew more pollutants.

All three men pleaded guilty to conspiracy to violate the Clean Air Act in 2022. They were each sentenced to five years of probation, $66,000 in fines and community service.

During Tuesday's pre-midterm election rally in Wasilla, Mr. Trump called Czubak and Fleming onto the stage and said to an aide: "Bring me the pardons!"

"Think of it: They want to put them in jail for 10 years because they fixed an engine. How sick?" the president said. "Now if you murder somebody, no problem. Unless a Republican does the murdering. Then it's, you know, the electric chair, right?"

Mr. Trump signed the pardons at the podium and handed them to Czubak and Fleming, drawing cheers from rallygoers as the president held one of the pardons up to the crowd.

The president said he was also "taking care of" a third person. He did not name the other person, but the third co-owner of Arm Rippin Toys, Hanzuk, received a pardon last month.

"When you give somebody a pardon, they say that means, and I don't know how this works and why it's an expression, but it's well-used, that means you're as clean as a newborn baby's ass," the president said. "I never understood that. Why is that so clean?"

Czubak and Fleming briefly addressed the crowd, with Fleming saying the charges against the three "really did destroy us."

"We're not criminals. We're not trying to hurt anybody," he said. "We want to help Alaskans. We want to help people with diesel trucks, with vehicles, across the world."

CBS News has reached out to Czubak, Fleming and Hanzuk's attorneys for comment.

Earlier this year, Mr. Trump granted a pardon to Mac Spurlock, another diesel mechanic who was also charged with violating the Clean Air Act by removing pollution control systems — a case that the president mentioned during Tuesday's rally.

Spurlock and his supporters, including GOP Sen. Dan Sullivan of Alaska, argue the engine modifications that he performed were necessary to prevent emissions systems from malfunctioning due to Alaska's frigid weather.

Sullivan applauded Spurlock's pardon in July, calling the charges the work of "overzealous federal prosecutors" and arguing the Environmental Protection Agency's rules should be modified to account for cold-weather states. Tuesday's rally was held in part to help Sullivan fend off a challenge from Democratic candidate Mary Peltola.

The Justice Department announced in January it would "no longer pursue criminal charges under the Clean Air Act based on allegations of tampering with onboard diagnostic devices."

During the Biden administration, officials took a different tack, warning in a statement on the Arm Rippin Toys charges that cutting out emissions controls "results in a massive increase in air pollution from even a single vehicle." Scot Adair, former special agent in charge of the EPA's Criminal Investigation Division in Alaska vowed to "hold accountable those who jeopardize human health and the environment for the sake of profit."

Mr. Trump and members of his administration have railed against other environmental regulations, relaxing fuel economy standards and ending an EPA policy that gave credits to car manufacturers that installed start-stop emissions systems.

The president has also frequently used his pardon power to grant clemency to political allies and people who — like him — argue they were wrongly prosecuted.
