Chile – A Cautious Tape

Chile’s peso lost 0.58% to 982.5 per dollar on Tuesday, while the IPSA stock index slipped 0.21% to 11,020. Copec, the fuel and forestry group, fell 3.8%.

The mood is cautious rather than alarmed, with investors waiting for US inflation data that tends to move emerging-market currencies. For anyone holding Chilean assets, the dollar is the variable to watch today.

Brazil – A Runoff Fought on a Split Screen

The presidential campaign feels like two countries arguing in one room. The latest Datafolha poll puts Flávio Bolsonaro ahead of Lula by 4 percentage points.

Datafolha on 8 October had Flávio at 49% and Lula at 45%, with a margin of error of 2 points. Among valid votes, that is 52% to 48%.

The runoff is on 25 October, and Band and Estadão will host a debate on Sunday 18 October at 8 pm. The Ibovespa fell 1.04% on Tuesday to 206,888, and the real lost 0.81% to 5.0273 per dollar.

Polymarket gives Flávio Bolsonaro 86.0% to win, which shows how differently bettors and pollsters read the race. For a foreign investor, the runoff is closer in polls than in betting prices.

Mexico – A Wary Calm

Mexico’s IPC stock index gained 0.60% to 67,147, though it remains about 6.2% below its February high of 71,601. The peso weakened 0.59% to 18.3705 per dollar.

The mood is a careful one: stocks are holding up while the currency reacts to global rate worries. For a US investor, Mexico trades as a proxy for how the dollar and Treasury yields move.

Colombia – A Quiet Currency

Colombia’s peso firmed 0.25% to 3,195 per dollar on Tuesday, one of two currencies to gain among the five we track. The US Oil Fund rose 1.36%, a tailwind for an oil exporter.

For a foreign trader, the message is that the peso is steady into the US data, though that can change quickly if yields jump.

The Shared Mood

Across the region, investors are waiting. Argentina’s slowing inflation, Brazil’s close race and a firmer dollar tone all point to a day when data may matter more than domestic news.

For anyone living or investing here, the lesson is simple: watch the US inflation number at 09:30 Brasília time, then the debate stage on 18 October, not just the indices.

What Prediction Markets Say

Polymarket prices Flávio Bolsonaro at 86.0% and Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva at 14.5% to win Brazil’s presidential election, with US$181 million traded. A separate market sees Flávio winning the second round by 4 to 8 points at 44.5% and by less than 4 points at 32.5% (US$994,738 traded).

Prices are bets, not polls, and were read overnight on 13 October.

Why we show this: prediction markets turn real-money bets into a live probability that moves within minutes of the news, which is why investors, campaigns and newsrooms in the United States now follow them closely. We show them next to polls and official results, never instead of them.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is driving the mood in Argentina right now?

September inflation came in at 1.9%, a second month below 2%, and the annual rate stood at 33.4%. That gives markets a feeling of progress, though prices are still rising by about a third a year.

Why are Latin American currencies weaker?

On Tuesday the Brazilian real lost 0.81%, the Mexican peso 0.59% and the Chilean peso 0.58% against the dollar, while the Colombian and Argentine pesos firmed. US inflation data due today could move Treasury yields and the dollar.

What does the Brazil runoff mean for investors?

The latest Datafolha poll puts Flávio Bolsonaro ahead of Lula by 4 points before the 25 October runoff, and Polymarket gives him 86.0%. The Ibovespa fell 1.04% on Tuesday, so investors should expect volatility until the vote.

US stocks lost a little ground in a session that felt more like a sharp intake of breath than a flight from risk. The S&P 500 slipped 0.02% to 7,805, 0.2% below its 6 October record close, while the Dow fell 0.35% to 51,670.

The ten-year Treasury yield eased to 5.222%, and the dollar index dropped 0.45% to 102.13, unwinding some recent strength. Gold fell 0.37% to US$4,155 an ounce, showing that investors are not yet rushing into havens.

The VIX, Wall Street’s fear gauge, rose slightly to 15.27. Traders appear to want protection against surprises when inflation data lands.

02 The Fed stares down a hot yield

The 10-year yield at 5.222% remains the central tension for the Federal Reserve. A softer dollar and slightly lower yields overnight suggest markets think the recent rate surge has run ahead of economic reality.

Today’s September consumer price report, due at 08:30 US Eastern time, will test that view. Economists expect inflation of 3.6% a year, up from 3.4%, and a monthly rise of 0.6%, while core inflation is forecast at 2.5% a year.

World.title: Reggae Girlz fall 3-1 to Mexico as El Tri avenge loss
World.content:
Jamaicas defender #7 Mimi Van Zanten and Mexico's forward #11 Lizbeth Ovalle fight for the ball during the women's international friendly football match between Mexico and Jamaica at La Corregidora Stadium in Santiago de Queretaro, Queretaro State, Mexico on October 13, 2026. (Photo: AFP)

Jamaica’s Reggae Girlz were beaten 3-1 by Mexico in the second game of their two-game international series in Querétaro, Mexico on Tuesday as the hosts rebounded after losing 3-4 on Friday.

Jamaica made four changes to the starting team from Friday’s games, bringing in Chantel Swaby, Kayla McKenna, Trudi Cater and Solai Washington. However, the Girlz produced a lacklustre effort, especially in the first half when they conceded two goals.

Team captain Khadija Shaw, who played all 90 minutes on Friday, was not on the match card on Tuesday. To add to the loss, Jamaica’s captain on the night, Allyson Swaby was carted off in the second half after an injury to her right foot.

An own goal in the sixth minute gifted Mexico the early lead, a result of a clumsy mix-up between goalkeeper Rebeca Spencer and her defenders that saw a back pass from Swaby roll under Spencer’s foot and across the goal line.

Spencer was well placed in the 19th minute to block a powerful shot from point blank range taken by Lizbeth Ovalle and a minute later Maricarmen Reyes missed from about three yards, lifting the ball over the cross bar.

Another mistake by the Jamaican defence gifted Mexico the second goal in the 32nd minute as Reyes ran between two defenders to volley a cross from the left flank inside the right post.

Ovalle made the score 3-0 in the 58th minute with a stunning left footed free kick from about 25 yards that gave substitute goalkeeper Liya Brooks no chance.

Kalyssa van Zanten pulled a goal back for Jamaica in the 60th minute, when her well taken shot from just on the edge of the 18-yard box flew high into the far left corner.

-Paul A Reid

World.title: Legend confirmed as new JPL title sponsor in $300 million deal
World.content:
Wisynco Group CEO Andrew Mahfood (second right) and CEO of Professional Football Jamaica Limited, Owen Hill (right) share a toast to Legend’s title sponsorship of the Jamaica Premier League with fellow football stakeholders (from left) Craig Butler, Donovan White, Peter Higgins and Dave Cameron. (Photo: Garfield Robinson)

Wisynco Group brand Legend was officially confirmed as the new title sponsor of the Jamaica Premier League (JPL) on Tuesday, in a long-term deal valued at $300 million – described as the largest investment the company has made in local sport.

Speaking at the launch of the Legend Jamaica Premier League at the AC Hotel on Tuesday night, Wisynco CEO Andrew Mahfood said the partnership represented a significant vote of confidence in the country’s football product, with ambitions extending beyond branding to greater fan engagement, stronger club visibility and more opportunities for young Jamaicans.

“This partnership — Wisynco’s largest investment in Jamaican sport — is a long-term vote of confidence in local football,” Mahfood said, to rounds of applause.

“Let me be clear, we are not here for one season. We are here to help build something meaningful and lasting,” he added.

The announcement marks a major commitment by the Jamaican-owned manufacturer and distributor to the local game, with Mahfood insisting that Wisynco’s involvement is about helping to build a stronger and more sustainable football product.

He said the partnership with the Jamaica Football Federation (JFF), Professional Football Jamaica Limited and the league’s clubs builds on Wisynco’s existing support for the Women’s Premier League, the Reggae Boyz and the Reggae Girlz.

“At Wisynco, we believe in the power of sport to unite communities, inspire young people, create opportunity, and bring out the best of the Jamaican spirit,” Mahfood said. “Football is part of our DNA and we see how it strengthens communities and opens doors for the next generation.”

Mahfood believes there is a natural connection between Legend, a Jamaican brand produced by Wisynco, and the ambitions of the country’s footballers, clubs and supporters.

He pointed to the qualities of passion, authenticity, determination and pride associated with the brand as characteristics that also define Jamaican football.

“Every player is pursuing a dream. Every club represents a community. Every supporter believes in something greater,” he noted.

He continued: “That relentless pursuit of excellence is what being a Legend is all about.”

While Legend assumes the title sponsorship, Mahfood explained that the partnership would extend across several Wisynco brands, each expected to contribute to different aspects of the league experience.

Worthy Park Rum Mix will support the adult matchday experience, while Mamba Stout is expected to connect with supporters. M.POWA will target ambitious young Jamaicans, and Powerade will focus on preparation, hydration and recovery.

“Together, our brands will help take the JPL from good to great,” Mahfood said.

However, the Wisynco chief executive stressed that the company’s ambitions were not limited to having its brands displayed at matches and around league venues.

He said the focus would be on improving the overall football experience, creating stronger connections between clubs and their communities, and giving the competition greater visibility.

“Our ambition goes beyond signage and branding,” Mahfood said. “We want stronger fan engagement, greater visibility for clubs, and deeper community support.”

Most importantly, he said, the partnership should help younger Jamaicans view football as a genuine pathway to opportunity.

The investment comes at a time when stakeholders continue to look for ways to strengthen the domestic game, improve its commercial appeal and create a more compelling product for supporters, sponsors and players.

“Jamaica has the talent. The clubs have the passion. And our players have the ambition to take Jamaican football even higher,” he said.

Mahfood described the launch as more than the unveiling of a new title sponsor, saying it represented an opportunity to elevate Jamaican talent and communities through a stronger league.

“Tonight, we launch more than a league — we launch a bigger stage for Jamaican talent, Jamaican communities, and Jamaican dreams,” he said.

“The whistle is about to blow. The next chapter starts now. Welcome to the Legend Jamaica Premier League. Let’s make it Legendary,” he concluded.

World.title: Seprod shareholders approve stock split, share issuance
World.content:
The Seprod corporate offices in Kingston.

Seprod Limited is set to split its shares in the coming weeks, preceding a potential new equity offer to raise fresh capital to reduce its debt balances.

All three resolutions at the company’s virtual extraordinary general meeting (EGM) were approved by shareholders on Monday. As a result, the company’s authorised share capital will be adjusted from one billion ordinary shares to 1.9 billion ordinary shares, effectively lifting the ceiling of how many shares can exist.

Subsequently, the company’s directors will set a date for its ordinary shares to be split five-to-one. This will result in the authorised share capital rising to 9.50 billion ordinary shares while the existing share count will move from 910,945,538 ordinary shares to 4,554,727,690 ordinary shares.

If an investor holds 12,500 ordinary shares of Seprod at Tuesday’s closing price of $79.82, those shares are worth $997,750. A five-to-one stock split would increase the number of shares held to 62,500 ordinary shares with each share valued at $15.96. As a result, an investor holds more shares at a lower nominal price while retaining the same value of shares.

This reduced share price will benefit the company which has hinted at re-entering the markets for fresh capital. The third resolution empowered the directors to allot and issue new ordinary shares for an additional public offer (APO), rights issue or private placement at price(s) deemed fit. The resolution spoke to the net proceeds being applied as the directors see fit, including the repayment of debt by the company and its subsidiaries.

Chairman Paul B Scott reiterated the debt reduction strategy at Monday’s EGM, a point which Seprod has emphasised during 2026. At the company’s July 29 annual general meeting, Scott explained that the group aims to cut its consolidated debt load from $51.21 billion to $47 billion by year end.

The focus on debt reduction was recently rewarded by CARICRIS (Caribbean Information & Credit Rating Services Limited) which revised its outlook on the manufacturing and distribution conglomerate from negative to stable. The ratings agency reported a negative outlook in October 2025 based on the group’s financial flexibility being constrained due to the growing debt levels to fuel the acquisition-led growth. At the time, CARICRIS expected Seprod’s debt service coverage ratio (DSCR) to remain challenged over the next 12 to 15 months.

“The stable outlook is premised on the high likelihood that Seprod’s financial flexibility will continue to improve over the next 12-15 months. This is underpinned by the refinancing of short-term debt into a longer-tenor bond, stronger cash balances, improved capitalisation and an increased focus on deleveraging,” CARICRIS noted as it expects the group’s effective DSCR to remain above 1.0 times.

Seprod’s standalone debt has moved from $13.92 billion in 2022 to $15.88 billion in 2025, with $8.45 billion of this debt in the form of bonds maturing between December 2027 to July 2031. Seprod’s core Jamaican operations and subsidiaries have seen their aggregate debt balances move from $17.13 billion to $19.46 billion.

Meanwhile, subsidiary Musson International Dairies Limited refinanced an $854.35 million bond in December 2025 through the issuance of a new $3 billion bond in November 2025. This included a $1.53 billion tranche with a 9.75 per cent interest rate and a $1.47 billion tranche with a 10.25 per cent interest rate.

However, Seprod’s consolidated debt balance has moved from $33.01 billion in 2022 to $51.21 billion in 2025. The higher debt load is due to its subsidiary A S Bryden & Sons Holdings Limited (ASBH) which has been the vehicle used to expand Seprod’s presence across the English-speaking Caribbean over the last four years.

Aside from ASBH taking on US$60.72 million debt facility for the amalgamation process in June 2022, it has also consolidated the debt load of the various subsidiaries it has acquired over the years. As a result, ASBH’s consolidated debt has risen from $15.88 billion in 2022 to $26.24 billion at the end of 2025.

Despite the relatively large, consolidated debt load, Seprod’s financial risk profile continues to be recognised as good by the ratings agency based on operating revenue growth, improved capitalisation and adequate liquidity. Management also intends to avoid new debt for the remainder of 2026 as it cuts the debt on its balance sheet. The report noted that Seprod is expected to repay $8 billion in maturing debt from internal cash flows over the next year.

“Notably, Seprod has consistently met its debt obligations in full and on time. Moreover, should the need arise, the Group can comfortably utilise its portfolio of liquid assets which includes short-term marketable securities of circa J $4.9 billion as at December 2025,” the CARICRIS report noted.

Seprod sold its stake in subsidiary International Biscuits Limited (IBL) in February 2026, with an inflow of $1.71 billion from the sale. That sale formed part of its portfolio optimisation strategy as it retained distribution rights for IBL products up to February 2031, with the option to renew. According to documents from the Companies Office of Jamaica, Kevin Donaldson, Wade Mars and Ravi Rochlani were appointed directors of IBL on February 28.

“So, we didn’t consider it sensible over the long term to be in a market that we are competing with our customers. So, strategically we felt divesting it would be a good choice,” Scott explained at Seprod’s July 2026 AGM.

Seprod is now moving to integrate its latest Barbadian acquisitions while leveraging its larger distribution platform across the region to improve product penetration and cross-selling opportunities. The company has implemented artificial intelligence (AI) driven analytics to enhance real time monitoring of the business while ASBH moves towards warehouse consolidation in Trinidad & Tobago. It is also set to benefit from the efficiencies from the recent introduction of its new Benhill machine for its dairy business.

With Seprod receiving shareholder approval at Monday’s EGM, the board is also empowered to issue new Seprod shares as consideration for acquisitions in the future. Seprod previously received permission from shareholders to issue new shares as the directors saw fit at its September 2023 AGM.

Seprod increased its stake in ASBH from 50 to 80 per cent in July 2026 by issuing new Seprod ordinary shares in exchange for the ASBH shares tendered by investors. This move resulted in Seprod director Anthony Mark Hart becoming the 10th largest shareholder in Seprod. Hart was previously issued ASBH shares in December 2024 as consideration for his shares in Caribbean Producers (Jamaica) Limited (CPJ).

“CariCRIS expects continued good performance from Seprod over the next 12 to 15 months supported by continued revenue growth from recent acquisitions, planned new product launches, expected benefits from its operational modernization initiatives and broadly stable macroeconomic conditions across its key markets,” the ratings agency noted.

Seprod’s stock price remains down five per cent in 2026 as of Tuesday, resulting in a market capitalisation of $72.71 billion. It has paid $1.21 in dividends totalling $1.10 billion during 2026.

World.title: Ophthalmologist visit under microscope as Ruel Reid and Co fraud trial continues
World.content:
Former Caribbean Maritime University President Professor Fritz Pinnock (left) and former Education Minister Ruel Reid (second left) about to enter the Corporate Area Parish Court in Half-Way-Tree, St Andrew, in October 2019 for a bail hearing. Both men, along with Reid’s wife Sharen and daughter Sharelle, as well as Jamaica Labour Party Councillor Kim Brown Lawrence, are facing multiple charges in a multimillion-dollar fraud case.

KINGSTON, Jamaica — The court is expected to hear details of an August 2018 eye doctor visit by former Education Minister Ruel Reid when his fraud trial resumes on Wednesday as prosecution witness Connie Williams Champagnie continues her testimony on the stand.

Williams Champagnie, during examination-in-chief at the Kingston and St Andrew Parish Court, detailed the payment and record-keeping systems at her business, Optical Smart Limited, before telling the court that Reid had entered the establishment on August 15, 2018, for an eye exam with another customer known to her. She said he also bought two pairs of eyeglasses using two health cards and a debit card.

When asked how she knew Reid, Williams Champagnie said she had never met Reid prior to that day, but described him as a public figure, telling the court that she had recognised him from the news, as he was the education minister at the time of his visit in 2018.

Reid, his wife Sharen Reid and daughter Sharelle Reid, along with former head of the Caribbean Maritime University (CMU) Fritz Pinnock and Councillor Kim Brown Lawrence are on trial, accused of siphoning off around $25 million from the Ministry of Education and CMU between March 2016 and October 2019.

Williams Champagnie told the court that she, from about arm’s length on the day of his visit, had an unimpeded view of Reid for between five and 10 minutes.

When asked if she saw that same individual in the courtroom, she responded that she did, pointing out a man in the dock in a grey suit, glasses and a blue and red tie. The individual stood and identified himself as Ruel Reid.

The five defendants have pleaded not guilty to a litany of charges including that the former education minister and his family members instructed a domestic worker to set up an account in which millions were deposited.

It is alleged that money was funnelled through transfers to various accounts either owned or controlled by the accused, or handed over in cash, with the recipients either knowing, or reasonably should have known, it was criminal property, resulting in charges of acquisition of criminal property.

Pinnock and Reid are accused of using their roles as public servants to mastermind and effect a scheme in which individuals were being paid on a regular basis by CMU, without knowledge that they were being paid; and in which invoices for goods and services were generated, but not by the individuals being paid, who did not at any time provide the stated services or goods to CMU, resulting in charges of conspiracy to defraud.

The two are also charged with acts of corruption under Section 15 of the Corruption Act — Pinnock for allegedly facilitating the payment of monies from CMU by authorising fraudulent vouchers, and Reid, in his capacity as a minister, for causing money to be paid out from the ministry and CMU for work, goods, and services not provided.

— Dana Malcolm.

World.title: Jamaica’s Kaheem Parris makes history for Sabah in Champions League
World.content:
Sabah FK's Jamaican midfielder #11 Kaheem Parris celebrates after scoring the team's first goal during the UEFA Champions League match between Sabah and Slavia Praha at the Baku Olympic Stadium in Baku on October 13, 2026. (Photo: AFP)

Jamaican winger Kaheem Parris made history for Azerbaijani champions Sabah on Tuesday as he scored the opening goal for the club in their first-ever Champions League win, a 2-0 victory over Slavia Prague.

Parris fired home the opener in the 49th-minute from the edge of the box after latching on to a cutback by Ivan Lepinjica. It was the club’s first-ever goal in European competition.

Joy-Lance Mickels clinched victory for the hosts late in comedic fashion, as his weak effort from distance should have been easily cleared by Slavia defender David Moses, but the Nigerian tripped and the ball found its way home.

The victory sees Sabah bouncing back from a heavy 4-0 defeat against Manchester United in their opening match.

Meanwhile, the defeat extends Slavia’s winless run in the Champions League to 21 matches.

World.title: JC booted from Walker Cup for fielding ineligible player Jamone Lyle
World.content:
Jamaica College forward Jamone Lyle (third left) gets away from St Catherine High School’s Caiden Yen (on ground) while his teammates Jaquan Brown and Davill Jarrett (right) look on during their ISSA Manning Cup game at Ashenheim Stadium in St Andrew on Wednesday. (Photo: Naphtali Junior)

Jamaica College (JC) have been booted from the Walker Cup for fielding an ineligible player, bringing their championship hopes crashing down just days before a highly anticipated final showdown against rivals Kingston College (KC).

Additionally, the ‘True Blues’ have been banned from next year’s edition of the knockout tournament, and must forfeit the Manning Cup second round match against St Catherine which they had won 3 – 2, which means the result has been reversed to hand St Catherine a 3 – 0 win over the many-time champions.

The decision was made at an Inter-Secondary Schools Sports Association (ISSA) emergency meeting on Tuesday, following the revelation that JC star Jamone Lyle has a professional contract with Waterhouse Football Club, making him ineligible for schoolboy football under ISSA regulations.

Waterhouse, in a disciplinary letter dated October 9, said it had fined Lyle $60,000 for unauthorised participation in a Manning Cup match on October 7. The club alleged that Lyle ignored instructions from head coach Donovan Duckie and General Secretary Richard McCallum not to take the field for JC, in breach of his professional contract and the club’s rules.

ISSA’s decision to boot JC from the Walker Cup means that KC will now face Mona High in the final set for Friday. Mona had lost to JC in the semi-final via a penalty shootout.

World.title: BZR delayed! Concert postponed to December; patrons offered refunds
World.content:
File Photo BZR Weekend logo Cardi B

KINGSTON, Jamaica — BZR WKND Jamaica 2026 has been postponed from October 18 to December 20, following news that American rapper Cardi B will not be headlining the event as originally promoted.

In a statement issued to patrons and supporters, organisers attributed the postponement to circumstances beyond their control, while extending condolences to Cardi B and her family following the death of a loved one.

“First and foremost, we extend our heartfelt condolences to Cardi B and her family on the passing of their loved one. Our thoughts, prayers and deepest sympathies are with Cardi during this difficult time,” the statement read.

It followed days of speculation after the rapper’s publicly announced cancellation on October 8 and a follow-up video in which she maintained she was not at fault for the cancellation.

READ: ‘Just know it wasn’t me’: Cardi B addresses cancelled BZR WKND performance

However, on Tuesday, the promoters insisted they had fulfilled their financial and contractual obligations and made every effort to deliver the highly anticipated event.

“From the outset, BZR WKND has approached this event with the utmost professionalism, good faith and commitment, including fulfilling our financial obligations in full and honouring our contractual commitments,” they said.

Acknowledging the disappointment likely to be felt by patrons, particularly those who had already secured tickets, accommodation and travel arrangements, organisers apologised for the inconvenience.

Despite the setback, the promoters have assured fans that the show will go on, promising an even bigger, star-studded experience when the event returns in December.

“One thing is certain: we will not let you down. A show will happen. Our vision has always been bigger than one artiste,” the statement said.

“BZR WKND is about bringing world-class entertainment, music, culture, and an unforgettable festival experience to Jamaica,” it added.

All tickets purchased for the original October 18 date will remain valid for the rescheduled event on December 20.

However, patrons who are unable to attend on the new date or who no longer wish to attend may request a refund by emailing eventsteamjamaica@kanoopays.com. Refund requests must include the purchaser’s full name, ticket purchase confirmation, order or transaction reference number, and the email address used to purchase the tickets.

Organisers said further instructions regarding refunds and the rescheduled event will be communicated through official channels.

A press conference is also expected to be held later this week to address questions surrounding the postponement and provide additional details about what patrons can expect in December.

“We are using this additional time to build an even bigger, star-studded experience worthy of our fans and the Caribbean stage,” the organisers said.

They thanked supporters for their patience and continued confidence in the event, reiterating their commitment to delivering a world-class entertainment experience in Jamaica.

World.title: TCN deal takes flight
World.content:
NEW YORK, United States — Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents stand guard at the New York ICE field office at the Jacob K Javits Federal Building on July 31, 2026. (Photo: AFP)

THE first batch of third-country nationals (TCNs) should be arriving in the island today, highly placed sources told the Jamaica Observer late Monday evening after the Government signalled the imminent start of the controversial programme agreed between Kingston and Washington.

It was not immediately clear what time the flight carrying the TCNs would arrive or the number making up the first batch; however, Observer sources said they are mostly South Americans and the country will be updated at this week’s post-Cabinet press briefing.

The Government had previously stated that under the agreement Jamaica would accept no more than 25 per fortnight.

A release from the Ministry of National Security and Peace and the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Foreign Trade on Monday said that “the first flight transporting third-country nationals under the agreement is expected to arrive in Jamaica shortly”.

According to both ministries, the release was issued to provide a further update on the implementation of the memorandum of understanding (MOU) signed earlier this year between Jamaica and the United States.

The release also stated that the International Organization for Migration (IOM) has agreed to commence support services.

Under the agreement signed in June this year, up to 25 asylum seekers who have unresolved migration cases in the US will temporarily transit through Jamaica en route to their home countries every two weeks.

The MOU was inked amidst US efforts to manage regional structured migration.

According to National Security Minister Dr Horace Chang, the people covered under the MOU are not being permanently settled in Jamaica and would only remain on the island while arrangements are made for their onward movement.

But the programme has attracted flak from various quarters, including the Opposition People’s National Party, which has demanded that the Government table the full MOU in Parliament.

In their release on Monday, the national security and foreign ministries reiterated that both Kingston and Washington “had finalised the operating procedures governing the arrangement, including the necessary safeguards and parameters to ensure its implementation in a safe, orderly, and lawful manner”.

“The Government reiterates that this is a transit arrangement intended to facilitate the return of third-country nationals to their countries of origin or other receiving countries, with the support of the IOM, which has been formally engaged to provide assistance to the individuals while they are in Jamaica and to facilitate their onward movement,” the release said.

The ministries also restated that “the arrangement will not be funded by the Government of Jamaica, that no third-country national with criminal antecedents will be permitted to transit through Jamaica under this programme; and further, that the number of persons anticipated will be a maximum of 25 persons per fortnight”.

The ministries also reminded that the MOU provides for its suspension if 10 third country nationals apply to remain in Jamaica through asylum applications or other humanitarian processes.

“The Government of Jamaica will continue to work closely with the Government of the United States and the IOM to ensure that the implementation of the programme is appropriately managed in accordance with the principles of safe and orderly migration, and consistent with both domestic and international law,” the release stated, adding that the Government “will continue to keep the public informed of significant developments as the programme progresses”.

World.title: Europe’s development aid dilemma
World.content:
The Commission is grappling with two goals that may be counterproductive: cutting migration and slashing development aid.

The EU executive’s argument is that a slash in development funding will likely result in people showing up at European borders in search of a better life. And that’s a problem for the bloc, since it’s looking to decrease migration numbers. On the show, hosts Zoya Sheftalovich and Ian Wishart explain how the dilemma will be unpacked at the upcoming European Council this week.

Next, a shooting near the European Parliament in Brussels has EU officials — and everyone else, for that matter — on edge.

Finally, the U.K. under Andy Burnham is at a big inflection point when it comes to redefining its relationship to the EU. But the bloc doesn’t even seem to care.

World.title: Schaffe, schaffe, Rentenreform: Merz und sein neuer Arbeitsminister
World.content:
Share on LinkedIn

Ein verschnupfter und heiser Kanzler im Angriffsmodus – wohl auch heute bei der Regierungserklärung am Nachmittag im Bundestag. Beim Arbeitgebertag gestern hat der Regierungschef Merz gut ausgeteilt und seinen neuen Arbeits- und Sozialminister Alexander Schweitzer öffentlich unter Druck gesetzt. Die Rentenreform soll im Eiltempo durchs Kabinett, doch in der SPD brodelt es gewaltig. Die Analyse von Rasmus Buchsteiner zeigt, warum der Kanzler jetzt auf diese harte Tour setzt und ob die Koalition da mitzieht.

Im 200-Sekunden-Interview fordert der Chef der Jungen Union, Johannes Winkel, erneut ein schnelles Ende der politischen Hängepartie. Er macht klar, an welchen konkreten Punkten der Rentenreform sich Schweitzer nun messen lassen muss und warum reine Strukturdebatten nicht mehr ausreichen.

Eine Hufeisen-Allianz formiert sich derweil in Sachsen-Anhalt: AfD und BSW machen bei der Russland-Politik gemeinsame Sache und wollen die CDU in die Enge treiben. POLITICO-Expertin Pauline von Pezold von „Inside AfD“ ordnet ein, wie die Alternative schnell wortbrüchig werden könnte, wenn es um die Neutralität des Parlaments-Präsidiums geht und wie die CDU-Fraktion im Landtag den Ministerpräsidenten-Kandidaten Ulrich Siegmund in ein Dilemma drängen könnte.

World.title: Ukraine brings war effort to football’s Champions League
World.content:
“At this point we are not representing just Shakhtar Donetsk. We are representing the whole country,” said Palkin, ahead of four matches in London this fall and winter. “For us, it’s also to support Ukrainian people who left their homes and moved to London, to England. And therefore, these games completely change context. It’s very important every time to send messages to support Ukraine.”

Shakhtar’s survival among Europe’s elite is emblematic of Ukraine’s own endurance against Moscow’s bombardment. Forced out of Donetsk in 2014, the club has spent more than a decade moving between temporary host cities while keeping its Champions League ambitions alive throughout the war, despite the difficulty of attracting top European signings while based in a war zone.

Since Russia’s full-scale invasion began in 2022, Shakhtar Donetsk has played “home” matches in Poland and Germany. Club bosses are thrilled to be based in England for this season’s games against Greece’s AEK Athens, Portugal’s Sporting CP, Turkey’s Fenerbahçe and Spain’s Real Madrid. “[London] is the capital of the football world,” Palkin said.

“We don’t have pressure. We want to play football. We are 24/7 under stress in Ukraine. And we want to just go out and play for our fans, for Ukraine,” added Srna, a former star defender for Shakhtar Donetsk and the Croatian national team.

Invest in Ukraine

Large white letters adorn Shakhtar Donetsk’s orange and black jersey bearing the name of SCM, the country’s biggest private financial and industrial investment company, owned by Ukraine’s richest man and the club owner, Rinat Akhmetov.

Russian President Vladimir Putin’s unabating assault has cost tens of thousands of lives in Ukraine, and also caused hundreds of billions of dollars worth of damage to infrastructure across the country. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has crisscrossed the globe in recent months trying to maintain Western support for Kyiv, as it runs short on cash and critical air defenses.

World.title: How Europe can increase resilience to global shocks — live updates
World.content:
Follow updates from inside the room at our European Resilience Summit, where we’re discussing how Europe can strengthen its ability to prosper in an increasingly fragmented world.

Europe needs to find a new way of working.

In an increasingly fragmented and unpredictable world, the policy choices it makes in the years ahead will determine how well Europe competes, prospers, and protects its citizens’ interests.

Leaders face difficult questions. How can Europe finance its ambitions? Can it build globally competitive industries while preserving its social and economic model? How can it secure the technologies, energy, and defense capabilities needed to remain resilient in a more uncertain world? And what tradeoffs will Europeans be willing to accept in pursuit of greater strategic autonomy?

Stay with us to follow the action from POLITICO’s European Resilience Summit as senior policymakers, business leaders, investors and experts explore the policy choices that will define Europe’s next chapter.

See the full program here and follow along here from 9 a.m. CET.

World.title: Corruption could become harder to catch under new EU budget, watchdog warns
World.content:
The warning comes as EU leaders continue fighting over the price tag for the EU’s post-2027 budget in Brussels this week — and as the auditors document an increase in misspending of taxpayer funds.

Yet separate from the budget’s bottom line is the debate over how that money gets divided. As a spending cycle marked by the pandemic, wars and climate-fueled disruption comes to a close, the Commission wants to make the next seven-year budget more agile by assigning about half of it — almost a trillion euros over seven years — to a single pot of money that countries can spend on objectives ranging from migration to agriculture and regional development.

Those agriculture and regional development funds — often delivered in the form of subsidies to farms and local projects — have long been vulnerable to fraud and misuse.

According to Murphy, giving capitals more leeway to shift spending would make spending even harder to track.

“There will be some flexibility, but at what cost?” he said in an interview. More of the oversight will depend on the checks each country has already put in place.

As it stands, misspending of the EU budget was on the rise last year, with errors affecting transactions for an estimated €5 billion according to the ECA’s latest report.

World.title: Burnham pledges ‘rock-solid support’ for Ukraine as Zelenskyy makes UK trip
World.content:
“My message to the Ukrainian people could not be clearer, we are with you for as long as it takes, and we will go further and faster in our support to back your courageous fight for peace in Europe. It is not just the right thing to do, but it's the necessary thing to do. Russia's aggression cannot be allowed to succeed on our continent.”

Downing Street said the U.K. prime minister has asked ministers to draw up proposals for further sanctions, military aid, and fiscal packages to support Ukraine in the coming weeks.

Britain will deliver £45 million of surface-to-air missiles and implement a ban on Russian liquefied natural gas (LNG) exports.

Britain will also accelerate deliveries of more than 5,000 Lightweight Multirole Missiles to Ukraine over the next four years with £1.6 billion funding, Downing Street added.

Chancellor John Healey will use meetings at the International Monetary Fund (IMF) in Bangkok to urge other countries to impose an equivalent LNG ban, arguing it would “curtail the war chest funding Putin so desperately wants.”

European leaders are expected to use a European Council summit Thursday to back stronger sanctions on Moscow after Trump struck a deal with Russia to ease restrictions on its diesel exports.

World.title: Europe’s leaders abandon the race for frontier AI
World.content:
“Striving to build a competitive frontier lab right now feels like very wishful thinking,” said Max Junestrand, CEO of Swedish AI company Legora, a €6 billion company that provides an AI tool for law firms. “I would rather see us put more thinking cycles into how do we capitalize on the technology rather than how do we try to catch up.”

The suggestion that frontier AI models are now out of reach for European AI labs comes as the most advanced models become a major global security issue.

American leaders OpenAI and Anthropic this summer had to disclose incidents in which AI agents broke out of testing. This led the companies to slow-walk and tread cautiously with the release of their latest models, just as Chinese open-source models are emerging as a credible alternative to U.S. proprietary models.

For Europe, relying on U.S. or Chinese models is not without risk, as the bloc is already dependent on both for all the technology underpinning AI, such as chips and cloud services.

But leaders, including European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, say Europe should focus more on helping its industrial and corporate base benefit from AI. They argue that building homegrown tech champions that can deliver those tools is a smart strategy that could help Europe win this next phase as America remains focused on staying ahead of China.

As politicians and industry meet Wednesday in Dublin for an international AI summit, the Irish governmental organizers have sought to focus the talks largely on how AI is used.

World.title: From no cards to many: Europe warns Trump not to waste Ukraine’s leverage
World.content:
Trump’s recent demand that Zelenskyy “better damn well stop” Ukraine’s refinery attacks, and his call for Ukraine to install a new leader, amount to a recognition that Kyiv does indeed have significant leverage in the fight.

Kyiv’s refinery campaign is helping create a growing fuel shortage across Russia and is also harming the Kremlin's ability to finance the war. But European leaders fear that Trump's desperation to lower fuel prices ahead of next month's U.S. midterm elections by pressuring Kyiv to stop its attacks could weaken Ukraine’s hand without persuading Russia to end the war.

Sybiha’s comments drew loud applause at the Warsaw conference and underscored growing tensions among Kyiv, Washington and Ukraine's European allies after Trump said the U.S. had agreed with Vladimir Putin to buy Russian diesel.

The dispute between Washington and Kyiv overshadowed a Warsaw event that is normally strongly pro-American, given Poland's status as a key U.S. ally.

"Ministers and heads of state won’t say so outright what they think about the Americans, but they certainly think a lot of things — the negotiations with Putin are yet another stab in the back for the Ukrainians," said a French lawmaker, speaking on condition of being granted anonymity.

"You end the war by persuading the aggressor to limit his level of ambition, not by asking the victim to capitulate," said Polish Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski.

World.title: Money laundering failures land Bank of America with a $1.2 billion fine
World.content:
The US Treasury Department said on Tuesday that it had imposed a $1.2bn (€1.07bn) fine on Bank of America for anti-money laundering failures.

 

"When a bank of this size fails to meet its anti-money laundering and sanctions obligations, the consequences extend far beyond its own walls, exposing the entire U.S. financial system to significant illicit finance risks," Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in a statement. "Today's actions send a clear message that even the biggest financial institutions are not above the law."

Treasury said Bank of America, the country’s second-biggest bank, also reached an $11.6 million (€9.9mn) settlement with the department's Office of Foreign Assets Control over "apparent violations of numerous sanctions programs, including on Iran, Russia, narcotics, and global terrorism."

In a statement, Treasury said its Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) imposed the $1.2bn penalty for Bank of America's "failure to mitigate and report priority national security risks, including Chinese Money Laundering Networks and illicit finance along the southwest border."

Treasury said the bank failed to report more than $5bn (€4.27bn) in suspicious transactions on time, including over $1bn (€853mn) linked to national security and other priority financial crime risks.

The penalty includes a $750 million (€640mn) fine imposed by the US Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, the largest fine ever imposed by the federal banking regulator.

Treasury said that Bank of America "admits that it willfully violated" the 1970 Bank Secrecy Act, which requires banks to help the government detect and prevent money laundering.

"Financial crime compliance is serious, and we are responsible for getting it right," Bank of America said in a statement. "We worked with regulators to reach these penalty resolutions stemming from violations cited in the previously reported 2024 (Comptroller of the Currency) Consent Order and FinCEN's investigation.

"We have invested billions of dollars in technology and dedicated thousands of employees to combat financial crime, and our team is far along with and committed to completing the work required to address the issues raised by our regulators."

The latest action is the third-largest penalty ever issued by the Treasury Department, behind a roughly $4bn (€3.41bn) settlement in 2023 with Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, and an approximately $3bn (€2.56bn) settlement with Canada-based TD Bank the following year.

Both settlements were part of the Biden administration's efforts to combat money laundering. Its broader push also aimed to improve compliance in the cryptocurrency industry.

In 2024, Binance founder Changpeng Zhao was sentenced to four months in prison after pleading guilty to failing to prevent money laundering on the platform. Prosecutors said criminals had used it to move money connected to child sex abuse, drug trafficking and terrorism.

US President Donald Trump pardoned Zhao in October 2025.

World.title: Brian Cox awarded 2026 Stephen Hawking Medal for Science Communication
World.content:
Cox was presented with the award at a private ceremony at the Royal Astronomical Society in London on 2 October, by co-founders of Starmus, Sir Brian May and astrophysicist Garik Israelian. STARMUS is a global platform for science, art, and human inspiration that brings together some of the most brilliant minds on the planet.

 

The medal, established by Starmus with Stephen Hawking a decade ago, honours outstanding science communicators across disciplines and creative forms – from literature and broadcasting to music, film and art – who are helping bridge the gap between science and society, spark curiosity and make science accessible to all.

“It’s a great honour to receive the 2026 Stephen Hawking Medal from Starmus, and particularly poignant for me because I was there with Stephen when the Medal was first announced 10 years ago,” Cox said at the ceremony.

“Astronomy is the oldest science, and in today’s fractured world I believe that striving to understand the Universe is more important than ever,” Cox added.

“The Stephen Hawking Medal was born from a shared belief that science should inspire people far beyond the scientific community,” May said. He also emphasised this message was particularly important at a time when “truth, evidence, and critical thinking are increasingly challenged”.

Stephen Hawking Medal recognises Cox’s accessible science

Cox is one of Britain’s best-known science communicators. He has presented television series including Universe and The Planets, written books such as The Quantum Universe and delivered lectures around the world. He currently serves as Professor of Particle Physics and Royal Society Professor for Public Engagement in Science at the University of Manchester.

His work attempts to enlighten the public on subjects ranging from the smallest building blocks of matter to the origins and eventual fate of the Universe – ideas that are not always easy to explain while keeping an audience engaged.

Alongside Cox, this year’s medal winners are filmmaker Ridley Scott, the Artemis II crew, Nobel Laureate Geoffrey Hinton, and 17-year-old Valeria Corrales, who receives the Stephen Hawking Medal Junior. Christiana Figueres, a key figure in brokering the 2015 Paris climate agreement, will also be awarded the inaugural Jane Goodall Earth Medal.

Previous recipients of the Steven Hawking medal include broadcaster David Attenborough, astrophysicist Neil deGrasse Tyson, marine biologist Sylvia Earle, filmmaker Christopher Nolan, composer Hans Zimmer and musician Brian Eno. The NASA communications office has also received the award.

The medal’s design reflects the unique mix of science and culture at the heart of Starmus’ vision. One side features a portrait of Hawking by Soviet cosmonaut Alexei Leonov, while the other depicts Leonov during his historic spacewalk, alongside an image of Brian May’s ‘Red Special’ guitar associated with rock band Queen.

During the London ceremony, Cox, May and Israelian discussed astronomy, humanity, music, artificial intelligence and Hawking’s enduring legacy. Cox was also presented with an OMEGA Speedmaster Moonwatch crafted in 18K Moonshine Gold.

SIR BRIAN MAY AND GARIK ISRAELIAN PRESENTED PROFESSOR BRIAN COX WITH THE 2026 STEPHEN HAWKING MEDAL

‘The Search for Truth’ continues at the 8th Starmus Festival

The award will be celebrated as part of Starmus VIII Festival, which takes place on the Canary Islands from 17 to 22 October.

This year’s festival, themed ‘The Search for Truth’, will bring scientists, astronauts, Nobel Prize winners, artists and musicians together across Tenerife and La Palma. The location is fitting for such a celebration, with both islands recognised for the quality of their night skies and astronomic facilities, the latter protected as a Starlight Reserve.

Alongside lectures and discussions, the programme includes music, art, stargazing and a science camp, aiming to take the conversation beyond the lecture hall and inspire real-world curiosity.

Music from Andrea Bocelli, Rick Wakeman and Sarah Brightman will set the tone, alongside more than 40 speakers across the week, including Nobel laureates May-Britt Moser, Donna Strickland and Steven Chu, and astronauts Chris Hadfield, Victor Glover, Reid Wiseman and Jeremy Hansen.

The festival will close in La Palma with a free public performance of Ilan Eshkeri’s Space Station Earth. This live orchestral work is accompanied by footage from space, exploring how seeing Earth from above can reshape human perspective.

Ten years after Hawking helped launch the medal, Starmus is recognising Cox’s embodiment of its original ambition: not only to explain what we know about the Universe, but to inspire us all to look up and wonder.

World.title: France’s emissions are falling as fuel prices soar. Why is it still missing climate targets?
World.content:
France is getting an unexpected boost in its efforts to cut greenhouse gas emissions, but it comes with a catch consumers are feeling at the fuel pump.

 

Soaring fuel prices caused by the war in Iran have prompted people to buy less diesel and cut down on their gas use at home. That has helped bring emissions down 4.1 per cent in the first half of 2026, according to Citepa, a French organisation that measures air pollution and greenhouse gases to track the country’s environmental impact.

France is now on track to cut emissions by 2.8 per cent this year, up from 2.1 per cent in 2025. That would amount to 10 million tonnes fewer emissions than last year.

Even so, it’s still falling short of the pace needed to meet its long-term climate targets. France is aiming to halve emissions by 2030 compared to 1990 levels, but meeting that goal will require annual reductions of around 5 per cent.

Fuel prices hit French consumers

Much of the emissions reduction boils down to the cost of filling up the car. Fuel prices have surged since the start of the year, with diesel climbing 45 per cent after the war in Iran choked off oil supplies through the Strait of Hormuz.

People have simply bought less fuel since then. Diesel sales fell 7.3 per cent in the first six months of 2026. In that same timeframe, transport emissions dropped 4.5 per cent.

Emissions from homes and commercial buildings fell even more, dropping 12 per cent in the first half of the year mostly due to less natural gas use for heating, water and cooking.

But the downward trajectory is unlikely to last. Citepa expects emissions to fall just 1.3 per cent in the second half of the year, partly because France is using more gas-fired power plants to produce electricity for neighbouring countries.

The energy industry’s emissions are expected to rise by 3.6 per cent over the full year, even as transport and other sectors continue to record reductions.

France’s Ecological Transition Minister Monique Barbut called the decline “encouraging” but acknowledged it was “not yet enough to meet our climate targets”, according to AFP.

Global emissions could fall for first time since 2020

Elsewhere in Europe, emissions are on a steady – if slow – decline.

Germany’s emissions fell about 2 per cent in the first half of 2026 as demand for oil dropped. However, the think tank Agora Energiewende has warned the country could still exceed its annual emissions limit by around 10 million tonnes – the first time it will have done so since passing its landmark climate law in 2019.

High energy costs have also encouraged European households to find more affordable alternatives to fossil fuels. Heat pump sales rose 25 per cent in France, Germany and Poland early in 2026, and EV sales have also spiked since the start of the war. Meanwhile, solar power has saved the EU an estimated €37.4 billion in gas imports since it broke out in February.

Outside of Europe, emissions are also going down. In China, oil use fell 9 per cent in the second quarter of 2026, while carbon emissions dropped 1 per cent – the first time a decline in China’s emissions had been linked to oil rather than coal.

A recent report by Carbon Brief based on forecasts from the IEA suggests global fossil fuel CO2 emissions could fall about 0.5 per cent this year, which would be the first annual decline since stay-at-home orders caused them to plummet in 2020.

While the IEA expects oil demand to climb when the war ends, the widespread embrace of solar and wind power, nuclear energy, electric cars and heat pumps could keep fossil fuel use down even after their prices stabilise. Those technologies helped to prevent an estimated 3 billion tonnes of CO2 emissions worldwide in 2025, the agency reports.
