World.title: "Global health is a team sport": World Health Summit in Berlin
World.content:
In recent years the threats have increased, crises have multiplied. Health policy now has to rely on multilateral cooperation, explained Professor Dr Pries at the World Health Summit in Berlin. Global health, he said, is a team sport.

 

For six years, Prof Dr Axel R. Pries has been president of the World Health Summit (WHS) in Berlin. The physician and physiologist previously served as dean and board member of Charité. In this interview with Euronews, Pries outlines one way to strengthen the resilience of the health system at international level.

At the World Health Summit Regional Meeting 2026 in Nairobi in April, you said: "We don't have the virus, but we have a political virus." What exactly did you mean by that?

Prof Dr Axel R. Pries: We are dealing with a global situation in which many countries are looking at health increasingly from a very national, sometimes even nationalist perspective.

And I call it a virus because it is spreading across the whole world. It is a pandemic. You can see it in every region. The problem with this virus is that it is a major obstacle to good solutions. Of course, you need local solutions. You have to stand up for people on the ground and do what they need locally. But this has to be coordinated at a global level.

The Covid pandemic was a clear sign that you cannot tackle problems purely at local level – and that also applies to many other areas, including mental health, NCDs (editor's note: non-communicable diseases) and others. That is why we need to revive multilateral mechanisms and give them fresh momentum.

The partial withdrawal of the US from global health policy has been a talking point for some time, and you have argued that Europe should take on a new leading role. Is Europe really up to it?

Prof Dr Axel R. Pries: I would not say that Europe should be the leader. But Europe should be one of the leading actors – and it absolutely has what it takes.

Europe is a very strong hub for medical innovation, from research through to practical application. Only a few days ago, the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine was awarded to researchers from Berlin and Würzburg for their work on optogenetics. And there are major companies in Europe, from medical technology and pharmaceuticals through to other sectors. In other words, Europe clearly has the right foundations.

Europe also has experience of cooperation between countries with very different political and social systems. That experience can be extremely valuable for international collaboration.

You mentioned that the Nobel Prize went, among others, to German researchers. What role does Germany itself play within Europe?

Prof Dr Axel R. Pries: Within Europe, Germany can certainly send signals and also assume a certain leadership role. As the largest economy in Europe, it is almost predestined to do so, and particularly in the medical sector it has a lot to offer again, from science through to application.

But Germany can definitely only do this as part of a wider ensemble, working on an equal footing with others, for example with France and the United Kingdom.

If you think of Denmark and, say, Novo, these are huge companies based in different European countries which, together, can play a decisive role on the global market.

How do you see this new global order in light of the US stepping back and the dependencies on China?

Prof Dr Axel R. Pries: If we fail now to agree on common strategies, things will become very, very difficult. Europe also suffers from its diversity, because it can sometimes take quite a long time before threats are addressed jointly. But Europe also benefits from the richness that this diversity brings.

The time has come to tackle this vigorously, so that Europe does not allow strategic dependencies to emerge in the health sector whose consequences can only be corrected later at great cost.

In Germany, politicians have for some time been talking about introducing a Health Security Act to close a historic gap in the country's crisis preparedness and security legislation. A draft is due to be discussed in early 2027. Is that a step in the right direction?

Prof Dr Axel R. Pries: Yes, if the aim of such a Health Security Act is to make Germany more resilient in the face of global health crises, then that is, of course, an important step.

It is part of what is known as pandemic preparedness. But here too, it will ultimately become clear that health issues can only be solved in multilateral partnership. If every country tends – as we saw in part during the Covid pandemic – to hold back critical goods exclusively for its own needs and not share them with others, then the entire chain collapses.

No country today can produce medicines or vaccines entirely on its own. It is an international network. This draft law is very important because the work on it forces like-minded countries to reach sensible agreements among themselves and to set themselves up as a network.

And it would be ideal if all of this were to happen under the umbrella of the UN (editor's note: United Nations), in this case the WHO (editor's note: World Health Organization).

One proposal at global level is to conclude bilateral agreements on the exchange of health data – for example, development aid in return for health data. Is that how a network should work?

Prof Dr Axel R. Pries: That is a core element of the America First Global Health Strategy. And in fact, the name of this strategy already highlights a fundamental flaw: you cannot claim on the one hand that you are always first and on the other that you are building partnerships.

The agreements that follow are often not genuinely fair or based on equality, but exploit existing power imbalances. I am therefore extremely sceptical about such arrangements. If two partners sit at the table and one of them is far more powerful than the other, you cannot end up with a truly fair agreement. Trying to solve these issues bilaterally is, in my view, the wrong approach.

The only way to create fair conditions between strong and weaker partners is to develop an overarching common framework, which the WHO can then implement.

This means that the international community does, of course, need data on pathogens and similar information. But the international community should also ensure that the countries providing these data receive resources in return. A fair exchange – data flowing in one direction and resources or vaccines in the other – has to be organised multilaterally.

So you are calling for global health to be organised as multilaterally as possible, ideally under the umbrella of the WHO?

Prof Dr Axel R. Pries: Of course, we also have to make sure that the mechanisms within the WHO work properly. A multilateral institution too has to be constantly renewed and reinvigorated.

A reform of the WHO would certainly be no bad thing, but it should not happen under the influence of the 'virus' I mentioned at the start – the idea that multilateral structures are no longer wanted. Instead, we need to strengthen multilateral mechanisms.

To give an example from a completely different field: when people want to play football together in an orderly way, the first thing they do is appoint someone as referee. Many things in life only work well on a multilateral basis. One-on-one contests exist in sport too. But if you are playing a team sport, you have to organise yourselves. Global health is a team sport.

Given the multiple crises we are currently facing, is the world even capable of taking on this team task – and seeing it as such?

Prof Dr Axel R. Pries: It is not easy, and there are certainly groups that try to play football together but cannot agree and end up at each other's throats. But we have to manage it, because we live on one planet.

We do not want to face a Covid pandemic every five years. We want to live healthy lives. That is something every human being essentially wants. So why should we not be able, in the long run, to overcome the factors that stand in the way of that?

I believe people are capable of learning and will realise that exaggerated nationalism simply does not help here. It is always difficult to hand powers over to higher-level institutions. The last time the UN system underwent major reform was after the horrific experiences of the Second World War.

I hope that this time we will be able to promote multilateralism without such a catastrophe, purely out of a sense of insight. That will require both determination and a certain optimism.

World.title: Ukraine received no intelligence from partners about missiles headed to Kyiv, Zelenskyy says
World.content:
A Russian ballistic missile hit a power plant in Kyiv on Tuesday evening, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said, without Ukraine receiving advance warning from its Western allies and despite US President Donald Trump's claim for an "energy ceasefire" in effect.

 

Ukraine depends heavily on Western intelligence, especially from the US, to detect incoming Russian attacks and identify its own targets.

Kyiv, home to about three million people, has faced intensifying attacks from Russian drones and missiles, with energy infrastructure a key target.

"A Russian ballistic missile attack on Kyiv. Once again, no early warning from our partners," Zelenskyy wrote on Facebook.

"The main target was energy infrastructure, specifically the CHP-4. Unfortunately, it was hit."

AFP journalists also reported hearing several blasts in the Ukrainian capital.

A damaged multi-storey residential building is seen on fire after a Russian missile strike on Kyiv, 13 October, 2026 AP Photo

Zelenskyy said Ukraine's systems detected the missiles only as they neared the city.

"This is absolutely unjust: when they are destroying our infrastructure, and Ukraine is not even receiving early warnings about ballistic missile launches," he added.

At least two people were killed in the same attack, which also struck a residential building in the Desnianskyi district, said Kyiv mayor Vitali Klitschko. Around 20 others were wounded, he said.

Overnight from Monday into Tuesday, Kyiv residents heard explosions from Russian strikes before the air raid sirens sounded, something that has happened only rarely in the past.

On Tuesday, Ukrainian officials said the situation was due to the Russian military's use of hard-to-detect missiles or possible technical issues.

US President Trump caused confusion on Sunday with a surprise "energy ceasefire" announcement on his Truth Social network, saying Russia and Ukraine had agreed to stop their punishing long-range strikes on power plants and oil refineries.

Trump has repeatedly lashed out at Zelenskyy over strikes on Russian oil refineries and on Saturday suggested it was "time for Ukraine to get a new president".

World.title: Cornell University suspends frat parties over gang rape allegations
World.content:
Cornell University in the US has suspended all fraternity parties amid mounting backlash over its handling of an alleged gang rape at a frat house in 2024.

 

In September, a lawsuit filed by a woman known as Jane Doe alleged that she had been "plied with alcohol and drugs to the point of intoxication" by several fraternity members before being sexually assaulted.

Protests have broken out across the US to show support for Jane Doe as the university faces accusations that it did not sufficiently punish the men involved. The fraternity was suspended after Jane Doe initially reported the incident and the college disciplined a number of students, but no criminal charges were filed.

In a statement on Tuesday, Cornell President Michael Kotlikoff said he was "deeply sorry for the harm Jane Doe suffered" and that "this act of sexual violence occurred within our Cornell community."

"All parties and social events in Interfraternity Council (IFC) houses at Cornell will be suspended for the remainder of the 2026-2027 academic year," his statement continued, adding that this would allow time for a "thorough review of fraternity life at Cornell to determine whether and how it can safely continue."

Cornell, which is based in Ithaca, New York, will operate a "zero tolerance" policy for violations of the rule, with any fraternity holding an in-house party or social event to be suspended.

"It is clear that women on our campus continue to question whether they are safe. We must meet this moment by acknowledging where we have fallen short and taking meaningful action," Kotlikoff said.

The university has also appointed former US Deputy Attorney General Sally Yates to conduct a "comprehensive independent review" of the university's response to the rape allegations.

But Kotlikoff said on Tuesday that it was "clear that we cannot wait for these findings to take action."

Other measures to be enacted by the elite Ivy League institution include the appointment of a dedicated case manager to support people reporting sexual misconduct and bringing in New York State Police to allow the force's criminal investigators to investigate any future allegations of sexual assault on campus.

World.title: Violence in Paris as tens of thousands turn out for student protests across France
World.content:
Violence erupted in Paris on Tuesday amid largely peaceful demonstrations across France, as tens of thousands of people joined a student protest movement sweeping the nation.

 

At the Place Vauban, next to Les Invalides in the capital's 7th arrondissement, people threw bottles, fireworks, and stones at police whilst officers fired water cannons and teargas as they sought to disperse the crowds.

French Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said 11 police officers had been hospitalised in Paris on Tuesday, which he described as a "particularly gruelling" day for local law enforcement.

"I wish to reiterate my firm stance against violent individuals who attack the police," he added in a post on social media.

The police also fired stun grenades on Tuesday, as one officer confirmed to Euronews. The use of stun grenades has come under increasing scrutiny in France, with the government suspending the use of a specific type after a 15-year-old pupil lost his hand during a police operation outside a school earlier this month.

According to authorities, an estimated 161,500 people joined Tuesday's rallies across the country, while 41,500 took to the streets of Paris. Unions put the figure considerably higher, at around 480,000 nationwide.

Although many protesters interviewed during previous student demonstrations expressed support for peaceful protests, some questioned on the fringes of Tuesday’s clashes argued that violence could be seen as a legitimate response to police brutality.

"This is the education system rising up, students and teachers. There is absolutely no response, no willingness to engage with our demands. All we get from the police is violence, so there’s violence in response too, because no one is listening to us," one protester told Euronews.

He added that in his view, the fact that rioters had destroyed shop windows or set bins alight was not an issue, arguing that insurances would pay for the cost of these damages.

France's protests and school blockades began in Paris’s suburbs in mid-September before rapidly spreading across the country, with grievances including teacher shortages, poor facilities, and overcrowded classrooms.

Ahead of separate mass demonstrations scheduled for Saturday over the cost-of-living crisis and rising fuel prices, some individuals said they hoped the student movement would unite with a broader social movement.

"Anger which has been building up for years is coming together, and the student movement was the spark that lit the fuse. We’re here now, and we’ll see what happens on Saturday," said a protestor.

Another acknowledged that "masked individuals" had thrown objects including stones at the police on Tuesday, but said that he believed using tear gas was disproportionate.

"I just experienced tear gas and it ripped my eyes out", he said.

Students chant during a march to protest against under-resourced schools in Paris, Tuesday Oct. 13, 2026. Copyright 2026 The Associated Press. All rights reserved

Rights groups have accused police of using excessive force as they have responded to protests around France.

Anne Savinel-Barras, the president of Amnesty International France, has called for authorities to ensure young people attending the demonstrations are kept as safe as possible.

"Authorities must ensure their safety and security and protect and facilitate the exercise of their right to demonstrate peacefully," she said. "Any policing response must be lawful, necessary and proportionate, and authorities must avoid unnecessary and excessive use of force."

Stanislas Gaudon, national secretary for Alliance Police Nationale, a major French police union, previously told Euronews that police remained focused on ensuring security around the perimeter of schools.

"When there are acts of aggression and the use of force, it's a question of determining the proportionality and the legitimacy of the act," Gaudon said.

"If this is done against individuals who have fired at police officers or thrown acid, then the use of force to disperse is necessary. I don't like using the term 'repression' or 'suppression' of student protests. That's not the issue. If there is no disturbance in the public space, then there is no legitimate use of force by law enforcement," he added.

Greta Thunberg joins Paris protests

Swedish activist Greta Thunberg also made an appearance at a protest in Saint-Denis, in the northern suburbs of Paris, on Tuesday.

Speaking to reporters outside a high school, Thunberg said: "Young people are not being included in the conversation. Our future is being robbed away from us."

"As we've seen here, schools are not getting investment that they need," she continued. "It just gives the signal to young people that you are not prioritised in our society."

World.title: Iran: Political infighting deepens as economic woes mount during war
World.content:
Hardliners are stepping up pressure on Iran's government and calling for Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi's removal. The oil minister resigned, but that's doing little to ease the pressure on President Masoud Pezeshkian.

Hardliners are piling the pressure on Iran’s government and calling for the removal of Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi. Oil Minister Mohsen Paknejad’s resignation is also failing to ease the pressure on President Masoud Pezeshkian.

As the war continues and diplomatic efforts to find a solution make little headway, the internal power struggle is intensifying. President Pezeshkian’s government is the focus of mounting tension.

Hardliners in Iran's parliament are pushing for impeachment proceedings against Araghchi. A trigger for the discontent was Araghchi's meeting with US negotiators on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in New York. Critics accuse the foreign minister of holding the talks without official authorization.

Iran's oil exports have plunged as a result of the US blockade of the Strait of Hormuz Image: Asghar Besharati/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

In a letter, Tehran lawmaker Amirhossein Sabeti informed parliamentary speaker Mohammad-Bagher Ghalibaf that he had registered a motion to impeach Araghchi on parliament’s online portal. Lawmaker Hossein-Ali Haji-Deligani also said parliament could use its oversight powers, including impeachment proceedings.

A structural problem within Iran’s power system

"When the regime is forced to negotiate, as it is in the current situation and in talks with the United States, the supreme leader or the hardline core of power avoids taking responsibility and shifts it onto elected institutions and moderate forces within the government," political analyst Ali Afshari, who lives in the United States, told DW.

Hardliners can use this approach to attack moderate factions over decisions that were previously agreed upon within the power apparatus, Afshari said.

He added that hardliners serve an important function within the Islamic Republic.

"The role of hardliners in the Islamic Republic is to influence public opinion, the political system's traditional supporters and the values of the Islamic Republic in both domestic and foreign policy," he said.

All the Ayatollah's men — ensuring the regime's survival To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Hardliners held a parliamentary majority during the implementation of the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action (JCPOA), the 2015 nuclear deal, and voiced their political opposition. Their resistance, however, ultimately did not affect the signing of the agreement.

"The Foreign Ministry is not a decision-maker. It implements what the government asks of it — and Araghchi is operating within that framework," Afshari said.

Lawmakers must first collect a set number of signatures to move forward with impeachment proceedings.

The lucrative business of oil

The timing of the latest move is significant: Iran's government finds itself under enormous economic pressure. Meanwhile, oil exports, which are one of the country's key sources of revenue, have fallen sharply as a result of the US blockade.

The resignation of Oil Minister Paknejad adds to the pressure. Officially, he stepped down for personal reasons.

Umud Shokri, an energy strategist, geopolitical analyst and energy security expert, casts doubt that a change at the helm of the Oil Ministry would alter the situation. Iran relies on networks that enable it to export oil despite sanctions, Shokri said. Opaque structures have become entrenched, making it harder for the government to control key revenue streams.

Circumventing sanctions has become a lucrative business for certain factions within Iran's political system, he said.

"By law, these revenues should be under state control. But we know that has not been the case for years," Shokri said.

Economic opacity has deepened during the sanctions period, he added, under the pretext of national security and protecting the population.

Fighting Iran war, can US military sustain a long conflict? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Private actors with close ties to the country's centers of power, particularly the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), have developed methods to sell oil to the armed forces through hidden channels. Neither the prices nor the commissions charged or the total sums involved are transparent.

"The government has only limited influence over these transactions. The Revolutionary Guards, in particular, would organize and control such deals," Shokri said.

Analysts have signaled that political and economic situation could likely deteriorate further in the coming days and weeks.

This article was originally published in German.

World.title: India news: 'Cockroach' leaders sent to judicial custody amid protest crackdown
World.content:
Skip next section Cockroach party conveners Ranka, Das sent to 5 days in judicial custody

Three leaders of India's Cockroach movement — Co-Conveners Saurav Das, Ashutosh Ranka and organizer Ajinkya Shinde — have been formally charged with multiple violations by authorities in India's national capital.

It all comes amid their protest against India's election chief over mass deletion of voter names from electoral rolls.

Indian authorities crack down on 'Cockroach' protest To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The trio was detained early Tuesday after they allegedly "sneaked" past police barricades to enter the grounds of Jantar Mantar in central Delhi, which until recently was a designated protest site.

News agency PTI, citing sources, reported that police have now formally charged them with trespassing, violation of prohibitory orders, breach of a peace bond and obstructing a public servant from discharging officials duties.

Meanwhile, Cockroach Janta Party's Founder Abhijeet Dipke said Das and Ranka had been "sent to five days judicial custody."

"Their fault? Unfurling tricolor at Jantar Mantar," Dipke wrote on X on Wednesday morning, referring to the national flag.

"Show some guts, Narendra Modi. If you're so determined to crush dissent, have the courage to officially declare an Emergency instead of hiding behind these cowardly tactics," he said.

Dipke's post suggests the trio have already been produced in front of a magistrate. Under Indian law, a person arrested by police has to appear in court within 24 hours of the arrest. One can only be sent to judicial remand by a judge.

Defending advocate accuses police of making false claims in court

Advocate Abhisht Hela, who is representing Das and Ranka, questioned the grounds for sending the two into judicial remand and accused the police of making false claims in court, Times of India reported.

"They have been sent to five-day judicial custody because of the presumption of the police that they can commit a crime. Police lied in court that they had given a call urging people to come there," Hela said, adding that no such call was made.

Meanwhile, Shinde, who seems to have been released, told reporters that the government was misusing its powers to curtail people's rights. "If the government thinks that sending our two leaders, Ashutosh and Saurav, to jail for five days will frighten them, it is absolutely mistaken," Shinde said, as per PTI.

He further called on "everyone" to "come together to bring an end to this dictatorial government."

World.title: US judge extends media outlets' White House access
World.content:
A federal judge extended the order that blocks the Trump administration from banning three media outlets from the White House. The outlets have reasonable grounds to think they'll win the case, the judge said.

A US federal judge has extended the order to allow three US media outlets to report from the White House, despite the Trump administration trying to ban them.

The three outlets, CNN, MS NOW and Politico, filed a lawsuit against the decision due to constitutional free speech and due process claims.

In September, District Judge Timothy Kelly issued an order to temporarily restore the journalists' access to the White House.

On Tuesday, Judge Kelly rulled that President Donald Trump likely broke the law by trying to ban them. He then issued a preliminary injunction to extend this previous order for the duration of the case.

The judge — who was nominated by Trump — added that the decision should not be interpreted as "claiming that President Donald Trump's claims about accuracy and fairness in the media's reporting are unfounded."

More to follow...

World.title: Houthis launch fresh wave of missiles across Saudi Arabia
World.content:
10/14/2026 October 14, 2026 Aramco offices catches fire after suspected Houthi attack

The complex in Dhahran serves as a major operation for Aramco, which is the world's largest oil company Image: Jiji Press/picture alliance

Saudi Arabia said that an attack on the headquarters of oil state oil firm Aramco sparked a "limited fire."

The fire at the building at Aramco's complex in the eastern city of Dhahran resulted in no casualties or deaths, the country's Energy Ministry said.

A company source told the Reuters news agency that a ballistic missile struck the top floors of an office building.

The complex in Dhahran serves as a major operation for Aramco, which is the world's largest oil company.

Hours earlier, Saudi authorities said they had intercepted several missiles, including over the capital city Riyadh.

World.title: Cornell suspends frat parties after gang rape case
World.content:
Cornell said no parties will be held at frat houses until the end of the academic year. The university is trying to mend its reputation following its handling of a gang rape case in 2024.

Cornell University has suspended all parties at frat houses until the end of the 2026/27 academic year, the university announced on Tuesday.

This comes after the case in which a woman alleged to have been drugged and sexually assaulted by multiple members of the Chi Phi fraternity in October 2024, with the university's reaction to the gang rape allegations now attracting criticizm from around the nation and overseas.

The new measures include a new "zero tolerance" policy for violations, which would result in an immediate suspension of a chapter.

University President Michael Kotlikoff said these measures were to "provide time for a thorough review of fraternity life" at Cornell, while also determining how it can safely continue. The university has more than 20 active fraternities that are organized under its Interfraternity Council.

It is not clear whether the suspension also includes parties that take place outside the campus.

More support for victims

As part of the measures, Cornell is to hold talks with students and faculty experts about the "the development of safe social alternatives" to Greek life party culture, as well as investing the money needed to support the initiatives' establishment, Kotlikoff said.

The Cornell president also said the institution will be adding a case manager to its Office of Civil Rights to support people that report sexual misconduct to help in navigating the process.

Campus police, which has full law enforcement authority but is controlled by Cornell, are largely the ones responsible for looking into crimes committed at the university. However, Kotlikoff announced that Cornell will work closely with New York State Police to allow an investigation independent of the school.

The case triggered widespread protests across the US Image: Melissa Bender/NurPhoto/picture alliance

Decision not to prosecute criticized

The 2024 gang rape allegations were initially investigated by the campus police, which then passed its initial findings to the Tompkins County district attorney, who did not prosecute — a decision that was lader met with widespread criticizm.

The woman filed a lawsuit in September, in which she claimed she had been drugged and sexually assaulted by several fraternity members after attending a party at the Chi Phi house in October 2024.

According to the lawsuit, messages saying she was sexually available were sent among fraternity members without her knowledge.

The Chi Phi fraternity house, where the woman was allegedly assaulted Image: Heather Ainsworth/AP Photo/picture alliance

After learning about the case, Cornell closed the fraternity chapter and disciplined several students, without any criminal charges being filed.

All seven men mentioned in the lawsuit have denied the allegations.

After the case was made public and triggered wide-scale criticism, the investigation is now in the hands of New York Attorney General Letitia James. The university's response will be reviewed by former Deputy US Attorney General Sally Yates.

Edited by: Zac Crellin

World.title: OpenAI says employee caught planting listening device
World.content:
A Saudi national employed by the artificial intelligence lab has been arrested after a listening device was planted in a company conference room.

OpenAI, the company behind ChatGPT, said Tuesday one of its employees was arrested after a "sophisticated recording device" was found in one of its San Francisco offices.

A 35-year-old Saudi national working as an engineer was arrested on Friday, a week after the device was discovered in a conference room, according to a criminal complaint filed in federal court in San Francisco.

After the device was discovered, the company reported the finding to the FBI and fired the employee. A federal investigation is ongoing.

The US Justice Department released photos of the hidden recording device Image: US Department of Justice/REUTERS

The suspect, who appeared in court on Tuesday, has been charged with using or endeavoring to use an electronic, mechanical, or other device to intercept oral communications.

The criminal complaint did not specify what the suspect might have wanted to do with the recordings. It did add, however, that the suspect used a tool to inquire about the company's building addresses, meeting rooms, meeting-room capacities and calendars.

How was the device found?

OpenAI said the device was discovered a few days after it was allegedly planted by the suspect.

"We used our models to understand the device and where it had come from, identifying that a specific employee had planted it a few days earlier," a spokesperson for the artificial intelligence company told the Associated Press.

"At this time, we have no indications of this individual inappropriately accessing or exfiltrating model weights, source code, or customer data," the spokesperson added.

Will AI destroy humanity? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

According to the US Justice Department, the suspect wrapped a USB device in toilet paper and hid it inside a television located in an "executive conference room."

He was seen on camera near the room several times despite not having authorization to sit in meetings there. After this was noticed, another camera was installed in the room that captured the suspect on film checking on the stashed device.

World.title: Vatican confirms Pope Leo underwent surgery for lung cancer
World.content:
The pope has had part of his lung removed and is recovering after surgery. Leo has been unusually candid for a pontiff about his health issues, disclosing the surgery to thousands of people in St. Peter's Square.

Pope Leo XIV underwent surgery on Tuesday to remove a nodule from his lung that later was reported to be cancerous, the Vatican said, adding the pope "woke up normally" after the procedure.

"The procedure was completed successfully, within the expected timeframe and as planned," said a brief Vatican statement.

The Vatican ​said in a medical bulletin that he lower lobe of Leo's right lung was removed, and he was diagnosed with lung adenocarcinoma, a common ​form of lung cancer.

The Vatican said the diagnosis had been suspected by preoperative tests and was confirmed during surgery.

The surgery at Rome's prestigious Gemelli hospital, which has been the main site of treatment for popes for decades, lasted about three hours. Leo's recovery is expected to ​take about a week, the statement added.

According to oncologists, Leo has an excellent prognosis since the cancerous nodule was caught so early.

A Vatican source cited by AFP news agency said further tests were being carried out to determine if the cancer had spread further.

Shift in transparency

Leo, 71, disclosed the health issue to thousands of worshippers at a prayer service on Sunday, making a marked shift in the level of transparency about his health compared to his predecessors.

In the past, the Vatican has often been accused of making confusing or extremely vague statements about popes' health, if revealing at information at all.

All of the pontiff's engagements have been cancelled through October 20. He is still likely to take a planned trip to South America in November.



Pope Leo to undergo lung nodule surgery To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Edited by: Jenipher Camino Gonzalez, Wesley Dockery, Zac Crellin

Correction: An earlier version of this article incorrectly stated that the pope underwent surgery for seven hours. The duration of his surgey was actually three hours.

World.title: Tupac Shakur murder trial: Former gang leader Duane Davis sentenced to 40 years
World.content:
Former Los Angeles gang leader Duane "Keffe D" Davis was found guilty of ordering the killing of hip-hop icon Tupac Shakur

Duane "Keffe D" Davis was sentenced by a Las Vegas court on Tuesday to 40 years to life in prison for orchestrating the murder of rap icon Tupac Shakur over 30 years ago.

Shakur was wounded in a drive-by shooting on September 7, 1996, and died in a hospital six days later at the age of 25.

Davis, 63, was convicted in August of first-degree murder with the use of a deadly weapon.

"You don't get to take a man from his family. You don't get to take his very life, his whole future from him, and just walk away from it. Especially when that man is Tupac Shakur," Judge Carli Kierny told a Las Vegas court while handing down the sentence.

What happened the night of the shooting?

On the night of the shooting, the rapper and his entourage got into a brawl with members of a rival Los Angeles street gang at the MGM Grand Casino during a boxing match. One of those beaten in the brawl was Davis's cousin.

Davis said he sought retaliation, and hours after the fight while riding around Las Vegas in a Cadillac, he located Shakur at a red light in the passenger seat of a BMW.

Davis handed the gun to someone sitting in the back seat of the Cadillac and ordered that person to shoot Shakur.

Tupac Shakur was killed at 25 during the height of his career as a hip hop artist Image: Death Row Records/dpa/AFP/picture alliance

The question of who actually pulled the trigger has never been conclusively decided. Davis is the only person who was in the Cadillac that evening who is still alive.

The killing went unsolved for years until Davis gave interviews and wrote about his role in the shooting in a 2019 tell-all memoir.

Prosecutor Marc DiGiacomo said Tuesday that Davis was trying to profit off the killing, and deserved the maximum sentence.

Davis' lawyer said he plans to appeal the verdict.

Shakur was an award-winning rap artist, activist and actor who sold over 75 million records worldwide, many posthumously.

World.title: La anomalía de la orden del Supremo que solo permite votar a los nacionalizados por la ‘ley de nietos’ que viven en España
World.content:
La decisión del tribunal divide los derechos de familias, como la de las hermanas Pérez, españolas por su abuelo emigrado a Cuba: Mabel no podrá votar porque está inscrita en el CERA y Lourdes mantiene el derecho al sufragio porque vive en Sevilla

La decisión de Tribunal Supremo de suspender el derecho al voto de los nacionalizados por la ley de nietos deja un reguero de situaciones anómalas a mes y medio de las elecciones generales del 29 de noviembre. La primera y fundamental, la existencia de 163.020 españoles inscritos en el censo a los que se les ha retirado el derecho a votar por un procedimiento en el que no se les ha dado audiencia. Pero de esa medida general brotan otras situaciones paradójicas como la de españoles nacionalizados por la Ley de Memoria Democrática de 2022 que votaron en las generales de 2023 o en cualquiera de las autonómicas celebradas desde entonces y que ahora se les prohíbe hacerlo; hijos o nietos de exiliados por razones políticas a los que el propio Supremo reconoce el derecho al voto, pero que no van a poder participar en las elecciones porque los consulados no tienen medios para expedir el certificado que requiere el tribunal; y también hay una paradoja sobre el que ni el PP ni Vox ni el Supremo han puesto el foco: españoles que obtuvieron la nacionalidad por la ley de nietos, pero viven en España y votan en cualquiera de las 52 circunscripciones españolas.

Esa anomalía la sufre Mabel Graciela Pérez, que admite sentirse “rara” al ver cómo sus hermanos, sobrinos y primos, que viven en España, pueden votar, mientras que ella, que decidió quedarse en Cuba, tiene suspendido ese derecho. Le duele la distinción entre ciudadanos que pertenecen a una misma familia y considera que la situación es “injusta”. Al otro lado del Atlántico, en Sevilla, su hermana Lourdes Nelba Pérez sí podrá acudir a las urnas el próximo 29 de noviembre. Su sobrina, Annia Rosa Pérez, de 28 años, que lleva cuatro años viviendo en España, califica la decisión del Tribunal Supremo como un “retroceso”. Después de ver cómo la misma familia queda dividida ante las urnas, resume la contradicción en una frase: “Somos iguales, pero no somos iguales”. “Si les dan la nacionalidad y no les dejan votar, no están reconociendo que realmente tienen la nacionalidad”, argumenta.

Annia y Lourdes en su barrio de Sevilla. Alejandro Ruesga

La suspensión del derecho al voto dictada por el Supremo solo afecta al Censo Electoral de Residentes Ausentes (CERA). El tribunal ha dejado sin posibilidad de participar en las elecciones a los nacionalizados por la ley de nietos que ya estuvieran inscritos en el CERA y ha ordenado frenar la tramitación de nuevas inscripciones de personas que hayan obtenido recientemente la nacionalidad por esa vía, una medida que abona la tesis que ha aireado desde hace meses la derecha y la ultraderecha para sostener que el Gobierno prepara un pucherazo electoral a través del censo de extranjeros con nacionalidades otorgadas por la ley de nietos.

Pero ninguno de esos partidos ha cuestionado las inscripciones en el Censo de Españoles Residentes en España (CER) derivadas de esa misma ley, por lo que la Sala de lo Contencioso no cuestiona el voto de los españoles que hayan adquirido la nacionalidad con la Ley de Memoria cuando vivían en el exterior y luego se hayan instalado en España ni los de personas nacidas fuera ue emigraron a España antes de que se aprobara la ley y se han acogido a ella para obtener la nacionalidad. Todos están incluidos en el CER y podrán votar el 29-N.

Toda la familia Pérez obtuvo la nacionalidad española en 2023 al amparo de la ley de nietos. La historia de ese vínculo con España se remonta al abuelo de Lourdes y Mabel, que tuvo que abandonar el país cuando todavía era un niño. “Eran de Lugo, pero cuando empezó la guerra, su papá lo montó en un barco junto a su mamá y el resto de sus hermanos y se fueron para Santiago de Cuba”, cuenta Lourdes. Huyeron para ponerse a salvo del conflicto, pero el exilio no les ahorró las dificultades. “Mandó a sus hijos a Cuba para que se salvaran de la guerra y, cuando llegaron, tuvieron que trabajar mucho, aunque eran unos niños”, recuerda.

El bisabuelo de Annia, José María Pérez Valcarcel, junto a su mujer Parmenia y sus hijos José Manuel, Luis, Denis y Arquímedes. Cedida por la familia

El abuelo nunca regresó a España. Tampoco lo hizo su hijo, el padre de Lourdes y Mabel, que había heredado de él la nacionalidad española. La distancia no borró, sin embargo, el vínculo con el país que había quedado atrás. “Mi abuelo siempre quiso regresar a España. Ha sido un sueño que él tenía y que no se pudo hacer realidad”, señala Annia. Su madre retoma el recuerdo: “Mi papá vivió muy orgulloso de su padre, porque él nunca quiso renunciar a su nacionalidad española”. Tampoco perdió el amor por un país que nunca tuvo la oportunidad de conocer, ni dejó de sentirse español, subraya la joven. Ese sentimiento también se manifestaba en su interés por la política española. Elección tras elección, el padre de Lourdes ejercía su derecho al voto desde Cuba. “Recuerdo que a mi padre siempre le llegaban cartas del consulado y así es como votaba. Él rellenaba la papeleta y decía: ‘Llevadla al correo para que llegue a tiempo’. Se sentía muy orgulloso, para eso él era fundamental”, cuenta.

El Supremo argumentó en septiembre su orden en que el incremento “excepcional” del censo en el extranjero es fruto de una instrucción dictada por el Ministerio de Justicia que “no parece ajustarse” al contenido de la Ley de Memoria, ya que esta solo regulaba el derecho a la nacionalidad de los hijos y nietos de exiliados por razones políticas o de orientación sexual que hubieran perdido o renunciado a la nacionalidad, mientras que la instrucción presupone esa condición a todos los españoles que salieron del país entre 1936 y 1955. El abuelo de Lourdes y Mabel Pérez no perdió la nacionalidad, pero ambas pudieron optar a ella porque su caso sí encaja en los recogidos en la instrucción de Justicia. Paradójicamente, Lourdes va a poder votar porque vive en Sevilla, mientras que los hijos y nietos de exiliados por razones políticas que se acogieron a la ley pero residan en el extranjero, a quienes el Supremo sí reconoce el derecho a ejercerlo, tienen el voto suspendido y solo podrán recuperarlo si consiguen un certificado del consulado.

El abuelo de Annia, José Manuel Pérez Fontela, en su casa de Cuba. Foto cedida por la familia. Cedida por la familia

Annia piensa en cómo habría vivido su abuelo la situación que afrontan ahora sus descendientes. “Ya no está vivo, pero si le hubieran suspendido el derecho al voto, como está ocurriendo ahora, se habría sentido muy traicionado”, afirma. Para una familia marcada por el exilio, la suspensión del voto ha abierto una nueva fractura: la que separa a quienes pueden participar en las elecciones de quienes, aun compartiendo la misma historia familiar y la misma nacionalidad, se han quedado fuera de las urnas.

“Mi padre votó siempre”, cuenta Mabel desde Cuba. Leía los resúmenes biográficos de los distintos candidatos y estudiaba la trayectoria de cada uno antes de decidir su voto. “No votaba por lo que alguien dijera, sino por lo que él entendía que podía ser mejor para el pueblo español. Lo hacía de manera consciente”, explica. Ella, asegura, haría lo mismo. Aun así, Mabel lo tiene claro, no acudirá al Tribunal Supremo para recuperar su derecho al voto, aunque insiste en que “no hacer nada no significa que esté contenta con la decisión”.

World.title: ¿Influirá el veto del Supremo a la ‘ley de nietos’ en el resultado electoral?
World.content:
Según los datos, los españoles descendientes de exiliados que ejercen su derecho a voto en el extranjero no llegan al 1%

Ilustración web de Cinta Arribas para la tribuna ‘Ley de nietos’ y suspensión de derechos fundamentales en las elecciones del 29-N, de Tomás de la Quadra Salcedo, 8 de octubre de 2026. Cinta Arribas
