World.title: 29 countries, including Hungary, condemn Iran over recent incident in England
World.content:
Hungary has joined 28 other countries in condemning Iran over a recent incident near a British airbase in Fairford, western England, with the signatories warning Tehran against hostile acts on their territory.

The joint statement, published by the UK Foreign Office on Monday, was signed by Hungary, the United Kingdom, the United States, Canada, France, Germany, the Czech Republic, Slovakia, Romania and 20 other countries.

The signatories condemned a wider range of hostile activities allegedly carried out by the Iranian regime against the participating countries, including violent attacks, plots to commit murder, cyberattacks, arson, sabotage and other forms of hybrid warfare.

They said it was unacceptable for Iran to attempt to threaten, silence, intimidate, harass, harm or coerce anyone on their territory.

Countries vow to identify and prosecute those responsible

The joint statement warned that anyone carrying out hostile acts on behalf of Iran or any other country should understand that the signatories would work to identify them, investigate their activities and bring criminal proceedings against them.

Iran should have no doubt that the 29 countries are committed to defending their sovereignty, strengthening international coordination in response to hostile actions, improving national resilience and ensuring that those responsible are held accountable, according to the statement released by the UK Foreign Office.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official WhatsApp channel!

What happened near the RAF base in Fairford?

The signatories specifically referred to an incident at the Royal Air Force (RAF) base in Fairford two weeks earlier, noting that the British government had concluded that Iran was involved.

On the final Sunday of September, armed police detained five British men near the base in Gloucestershire, western England. The suspects had arrived in three vans in the early hours of the morning.

The vehicles were searched by British Army bomb disposal specialists trained to deal with and remove explosive devices. Although no explosives were found, Counter Terrorism Policing (CTP), which is leading the investigation, said that officers had seized “a quantity of petrol”.

Seven people have so far been detained in connection with the case. Although they have been released under strict conditions, the investigation is continuing.

Reports suggest Iran may have been planning a drone attack

Unconfirmed intelligence reports published by the British and American media suggested that the Iranian regime may have been preparing a drone attack against the airbase used by the US Air Force in England.

According to these reports, the alleged preparations followed the involvement of US heavy bombers stationed at the base in military operations against Iran launched by the United States and Israel in early February.

Citing a threat that it did not specify in detail, the US Air Force recently withdrew all its strategic bombers from the British base.

Speaking to Parliament on Monday, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the incident was almost certainly the work of Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.

World.title: Hungary passes new child protection law: Magyar slams Fidesz and Mi Hazánk for voting against it
World.content:
Hungary’s parliament has approved a grand child protection bill, including measures addressing children left in hospitals and access to harmful sexual content. Prime Minister Péter Magyar branded the opposition parties’ votes against the legislation a “disgrace”, while Mi Hazánk called on President András Baka not to sign it into law.

Hungary’s parliament has passed a new child protection bill aimed at strengthening safeguards against sexual exploitation, violence and harmful content accessible to minors. The legislation was approved on Tuesday by 139 votes to 51, according to the Hungarian News Agency (MTI).

The bill was submitted by the government in September and introduces several measures, including new rules on protecting children from inappropriate media content, changes to access to criminal records and procedures for children left in hospitals despite no longer requiring medical care.

However, the vote has sparked a political row. Fidesz and Mi Hazánk both voted against the legislation, prompting Prime Minister Péter Magyar to accuse them of opposing measures designed to protect vulnerable children.

Magyar calls opposition vote a “disgrace”

In a Facebook post following the vote, Magyar criticised Fidesz and Mi Hazánk for rejecting the bill, highlighting its provisions concerning children left in hospitals and protection against violence.

“Fidesz and Mi Hazánk voted together against a law strengthening the protection of children. They voted down assistance for babies left in hospitals and the protection of children against all forms of violence. A disgrace!” the prime minister wrote.

When the government submitted the proposal in September, Magyar said he hoped that, despite political disagreements, no MP would vote against legislation intended to provide stronger protection for children.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official WhatsApp channel!

What does the new child protection law change?

The legislation is based on the principle enshrined in Hungary’s Fundamental Law that every child has the right to protection and care necessary for their physical, intellectual and moral development. According to the bill’s justification, effective regulation is needed to prevent, identify and address threats to children. The measures focus on several areas.

Protection from harmful content: The legislation seeks to shield minors from pornography, age-inappropriate material and violent sexual content, as well as other material considered seriously damaging to their development.

Safeguards in public spaces: Children would also receive protection against visual and audiovisual communications in public places that could adversely affect their physical, intellectual, emotional or moral development.

Access to criminal records: The rules governing the criminal records system will also change. Access to information intended to help protect children will remain possible, but it will be subject to prior official checks and additional data protection and technical safeguards.

Children left in hospitals: The bill also addresses cases in which children remain in hospital even though their medical condition no longer justifies their stay. In such cases, the guardianship authority must act within eight days to establish why the child has not been discharged and determine the measures that best serve the child’s interests.

Mi Hazánk accuses government of giving in to EU pressure

Mi Hazánk has strongly criticised the legislation and announced that it would write to President András Baka, asking him not to sign the bill approved by parliament.

Speaking to journalists in the Parliament building after Tuesday’s vote, party vice-president and deputy parliamentary group leader Dóra Dúró described the legislation as a change made in the interests of paedophiles under pressure from the European Union.

Dúró argued that the changes would make it more difficult for parents to access the register of convicted paedophiles and would allow what she called “LGBTQ lobby organisations” back into the education system.

She also indicated that, as the party’s parliamentary group member responsible for the issue, she would most likely draft the letter to the president.

If you missed it: Hungary’s new child protection bill to scrap controversial anti-LGBTQ provisions

The legal and political legacy of Hungary’s previous child protection law

Originally presented as a measure against paedophilia, the child protection law was amended in 2021 to include provisions restricting the portrayal and promotion of homosexuality and gender reassignment to minors. The changes prompted criticism and became the subject of legal proceedings at EU level.

The European Commission launched infringement proceedings in 2021 and referred Hungary to the Court of Justice of the European Union in December 2022.

In April 2026, the EU court ruled that Hungary had breached its obligations under EU law, Telex wrote. In a landmark finding, the court also identified a separate breach of a treaty provision setting out the common values on which the European Union is founded.

The dispute has also had financial consequences. Since late 2022, around EUR 500–600 million in cohesion funding has been blocked in connection with the issue, under the EU’s horizontal enabling conditions. This sum is separate from the EUR 16.4 billion discussed in a political agreement reached in May 2026 between Magyar and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen concerning the release of EU funds.

The EU’s Article 7 procedure against Hungary, launched in 2018 over concerns about the country’s compliance with the bloc’s fundamental values, also remains unresolved. EU affairs ministers and state secretaries were due to hear from their Hungarian counterpart on Tuesday as part of that process, according to Telex.

World.title: Bosnia’s New Government was Being Built as Votes Were Still Being Counted
World.content:
People in Bosnia and Herzegovina voted in elections on October 4, but even as the count went on, the politicians had stopped waiting.

Only three days after the election, the chairmen of the Party of Democratic Action, SDA, the Party for Bosnia and Herzegovina, SBiH, and the Democratic Front, DF, in Sarajevo Canton announced that they would form the cantonal government in the capital. Power was being assembled before the final results were even in.

Other leaders were assembling alliances on the road. On October 9, Dragan Covic, leader of the Croatian Democratic Union, HDZ BiH, the main Bosnian Croat party, was in Mostar with Nermin Niksic, leader of the Social Democratic Party, SDP.

Covic then went on to Sarajevo, where Bakir Izetbegovic, leader of the SDA, received him. On Saturday, Izetbegovic welcomed Semir Efendic, leader of the SBiH, at SDA headquarters. On Monday, Covic was in Banja Luka, in Republika Srpska, sitting across from Milorad Dodik, leader of the Alliance of Independent Social Democrats, SNSD, the main Bosnian Serb party.

Dodik is currently barred from holding public office because of a court conviction. Yet he emerged from the meeting as half of a partnership, already issuing joint conditions to everyone else. Thanks to the good election results their parties enjoyed, both Covic and Dodik are now key to making the government at any level.

It was a striking contrast with the dull election campaign. “This campaign is very anaemic,” Adnan Huskic, a professor at the Sarajevo School of Science and Technology, told BIRN before the vote.

World.title: Albanian Student Protesters Clash with Police Outside Ministry of Education
World.content:
Albanian police at the students’ protest in Tirana on October 13, 2026. Photo: BIRN/Fjori Sinoruka.

A student protest outside the Ministry of Education in Tirana erupted into serious clashes with police officers on Tuesday, as protesters threw rocks and eggs at the building and police used tear gas and water cannon to disperse them.

The rally was called as part of the ongoing ‘Flamingo Revolution’ anti-government protests. As well as chanting slogans against Prime Minister Edi Rama’s administration, students voiced demands for better conditions at educational establishments and adequate financial support.

“We come to Tirana to study, and we are forced not to study but to work,” one student said at the protest.

Police announced that 23 protesters were apprehended while six police officers sustained injuries.

“During the rally, a group of participants committed violent acts, damaging the external fence and then, in order to enter the courtyard [of the ministry building], they also damaged the entrance gate. They also continued to break and damage the windows and facade of the building with stone slabs and hard objects,” police said in the statement.

“Police officers called on them to stop the attack on the institution, but they continued to attack the police officers with Molotov cocktails, cans, stones and hard objects,” the statement added.

The Association of Journalists of Albania reported that a journalist sustained physical injuries at the hands of the police and a crew was prevented from reporting from the protest.

“The Association calls on State Police to immediately stop attacks on media and journalists… This is unacceptable and requires urgent addressing from the Police Oversight Agency and prosecution,” the Association of Journalists said in a statement.

Albana Kociu, Albania’s Deputy Prime Minister, posted a video on Facebook showing a protester clashing with a group of police officers during the protest, with a message saying that “violence has not been, is not and will never be the solution”.

The ‘Flamingo Revolution’ demonstrations have seen large numbers of people protesting against planned construction projects in protected environmental areas and demanding the resignation of Prime Minister Rama, accusing his government of institutional corruption and lack of transparency.

The protests in Tirana began on May 31, a day after a member of the public was assaulted by private security guards during a demonstration in Zvernec against the construction of a luxury tourism project in a protected area linked to US President Donald Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner.

World.title: Romanian Far-Right Politician Georgescu Put Under House Arrest
World.content:
A supporter of independent politician Calin Georgescu attends a protest in front of metropolitan police arrest headquarters in Bucharest, 12 October 2026. Photo: EPA/ROBERT GHEMENT.

The Bucharest Tribunal on Tuesday replaced far-right former presidential candidate Calin Georgescu’s 30-day pre-trial detention with house arrest in a case in which he is accused of defrauding a businessman of more than one million euros.

The ruling is not final and is not immediately enforceable. Anti-corruption prosecutors are expected to challenge the decision within three days, according to media reports.

Dozens of Georgescu’s supporters gathered outside the Tribunal early on Tuesday to show their support for the former presidential candidate. Authorities erected security barriers and deployed gendarmerie units in the area.

His supporters greeted the court’s decision with cheers and shouts of approval. Fellow right-wing leader George Simion of the Alliance for the Union of Romanians, described the house arrest ruling, in a post on X, as “still an abuse of power, but a victory for the protests – a small victory for the Romanian people”.

Prosecutors allege that from September 2021, a group allegedly led by Georgescu convinced the businessman that he could obtain a loan of 6 million euros in exchange for providing a guarantee. The victim then allegedly transferred some 1 million euros.

Subsequently, the suspects allegedly told him that the loan could be increased to 15 million euro, but an additional guarantee was required, after which the businessman allegedly transferred another 100,000 euros. The promised loan never materialised.

Georgescu has not issued any statement on this issue but has previously claimed he was being investigated by the authorities because of his political activities.

This would be the third criminal case against Georgescu. He is already under investigation for endorsing fascist ideas in interviews, online posts and public appearances and also faces trial for complicity to undermine the constitutional order, spreading false information and founding an anti-Semitic organisation.

He denies all the charges.

After he unexpectedly won the first round of the presidential elections in November 2024, the Constitutional Court ordered a rerun of the vote, citing alleged manipulation of public opinion by a “foreign state”, likely referring to Russia.

Georgescu was banned from participating in the re-run in May 2025, which was ultimately won by centrist Nicusor Dan.

World.title: Bulgaria Summons Russian Envoy Over New Black Sea Drone Attacks
World.content:
Prime Minister Rumen Radev convened an emergency meeting of the Security Council after a fresh wave of drone strikes hit two commercial cargo ships on two locations near the Bulgarian coastline overnight into Tuesday, leaving one damaged and causing another to sink.

He also summoned Russian ambassador Eleonora Mitrofanova, and scheduled urgent discussions with NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte.

“We don’t have solid evidence to blame either side [Ukraine or Russia] but the logic points that the strikes have been of benefit to the Russian Federation,” Radev said on Tuesday morning.

Radev previously downplayed Russia’s role when another two ships were targeted in the Black Sea on October 6.

During his presidential terms and now in his first mandate as Prime Minister, Radev has kept up a balancing act, often resisting criticism of the Kremlin and expressing scepticism about Ukraine.

The workers on the damaged ship near the town of Byala – the Malta-flagged, Odesa-registered Chelsea 3 – have been evacuated and some are being treated in the city of Varna. Seven Ukrainian citizens and eight Azerbaijanis were on board. The vessel was travelling from the Turkish port of Giresun to Giurgiuleșsti in Romania.

There is less information about the sunken ship, which was located near Krapets. Radev confirmed that one sailor managed to survive. According to further reports, there were five survivors and 11 more are missing.

The two ships were located 17 and 18 miles from the coast, closer to the shore than the first ships that were targeted.

One of the survivors from the Chelsea 3 said the drone attack came from Russia, speaking when surrounded by local journalists in Varna.

Ursula von der Leyen, president of the European Commission, warned on Tuesday that the Black Sea “has become another front of escalation of the Russian war in Ukraine” and called the attack “unacceptable”.

“I strongly condemn the drone attacks on merchant ships near Bulgaria’s coast. Putting the lives of the crew in grave danger and threatening security in the Black Sea. We stand with Bulgaria and thank its rescuers for their swift response,” von der Leyen said on X.

The previous attack a week ago occurred in a similar part of Bulgaria’s exclusive economic zone in the Black Sea, in the north-east, and with almost identical results – one ship was damaged and another was sunk. Both Ukraine and Russia denied involvement.

On October 12, Bulgaria’s Ministry of Defence confirmed that rescue operations over the first attack have been halted and no further operations are planned, leaving many unanswered details around the sunken ship on which at least ten sailors died.

While authorities said one of the two ships on October 6 was carrying Ukrainian cargo, its nature remains unconfirmed, although speculation points to grain.

On October 12, opposition MP Ivaylo Mirchev, of Democratic Bulgaria, alleged another instance of Russian interference, claiming unknown masked perpetrators had damaged Space-X antennas near Sofia to disrupt Starlink connections to Ukraine.

On Tuesday, Democratic Bulgaria called on Bulgaria’s national security directors to address parliament, in which Radev’s MPs have a majority, over the recent threats.

World.title: Hungary’s Memory Politics: Who Defines the Communist Past?
World.content:
The fight over 1956

The records about informers that are set to be published cover a broad swathe of Cold War history. Their symbolically charged release dates (both the original October 22 and revised November 4), however, link them inextricably to the 1956 revolution and its crushing.

Competing interpretations of 1956 have characterised political identity since Hungary’s democratic transition in 1989-90. The 70th anniversary looks set to continue that trend.

Post-1990, Hungary’s left-wing parties emphasised the revolution’s social-democratic features, including the prominence of grassroots workers’ councils in decision making. The discourse of the Fidesz party, conversely, crystallised around emotive stories of personal heroism, especially concerning the “Lads of Pest” – teenage (and younger) volunteers who faced down the invading Soviet tanks with rifles and Molotov cocktails.

Fidesz also benefitted from the recollections of former prime minister Viktor Orban’s emergence into the public consciousness with his speech at the reburial of prime minister Imre Nagy (and other revolutionary leaders) in June 1989, when he demanded, to much acclaim, the immediate withdrawal of Soviet troops.

In October 2006, around the revolution’s 50th anniversary, Orban’s Fidesz party had, as today, also just lost a parliamentary election. Fidesz’s communication at the time highlighted the connection between the governing MSZP (Socialist Party) and its MSZMP (Communist Party) predecessor, and the persistent need for national liberation.

Violent street clashes in September and October 2006 between far-right extremist groups, normal Fidesz supporters and the police were presented as reiterations of 1956. Those clashes – and with them Fidesz’s claim to be the true heir of the revolution – subsequently became a touchstone of the party’s political identity.

On September 18, 2006, police failed to prevent far-right protestors storming, and setting alight, the national television broadcaster in response to a leaked closed-door speech by the MSZP prime minister of the time, Ferenc Gyurcsany, in which he admitted that his party had “lied morning, noon and night” on the economy. Allegations of Fidesz’s co-operation with extremist groups remain disputed.

Conversely, on October 23, 2006, police responded with excessive force when confronting a gathering of far-right activists in Budapest that had blurred into an adjacent anniversary rally of Fidesz supporters. Many ordinary participants, and some onlookers, were seriously injured.

Past and present converged when protestors hot-wired a Soviet T-34 tank of the sort used in 1956 (part of a nearby street exhibition) and drove it at police lines, only for the vehicle to splutter to a halt due to a lack of fuel.

Police violence, and subsequent official investigations, received considerable criticism, not only from Fidesz but also from independent human rights groups. The current prime minister, Peter Magyar, (then a Fidesz sympathiser), has repeatedly referenced the importance of those events to his political development through his work representing victims as a young lawyer.

Exactly what narrative his Tisza party will promote in relation to the upcoming anniversary remains to be seen. Fidesz, however, has already begun implicitly to frame it in relation to current politics, describing the recently established National Asset Recovery and Protection Office (NVVH), which is looking into corruption during Orban’s 16 years in power, as “AVH” – the name of the secret police at the time of the 1956 revolution. Likewise, Orban has characterised the recent arrest of former ministers in his government, Balazs Hanko and Miklos Sesztak, as exemplifying “neo-communist tactics”.

According to Andrea Peto, professor of history at Central European University in Vienna, Fidesz will likely “continue developing a narrative that reframes 1956 from an anti-Soviet, anti-communist revolution into a broader story of national sovereignty”.

Such reframing, Peto tells BIRN, allows Fidesz “to avoid the uncomfortable contradiction between its historical anti-Soviet rhetoric and its current Russia-friendly foreign policy” – shifting the focus from specific anti-Russian resistance to “protecting the nation from external actors, whether Brussels, migrants or geopolitical pressures”.

University College London’s Bede believes that Fidesz will struggle to mobilise around the anniversary in a way comparable to 2006. This time, Fidesz “were planning to organise a ‘peace march’, but it was cancelled a few days after it was announced,” he notes.

This, he thinks, was “likely because they knew they would not have the numbers.”

World.title: Letter from Brussels: EU’s 15-Year ‘Probation’ Plan is an Unfair Deal for Balkan States
World.content:
Most big Brussels documents have one sentence that matters more than all the rest. In the pre-enlargement package Marta Kos presented in Strasbourg on October 6, it comes near the end, in the chapter on safeguards in future accession treaties. The new institutional safeguard clause, it says, would apply for up to 15 years after accession.

If Montenegro joins the club in 2028, as Podgorica still hopes, it would, therefore, stay on probation until 2043. A child born in Cetinje on accession day would be almost halfway through high school before the country became a member like any other.

Albania, Moldova and Ukraine, the other frontrunners the paper obviously has in mind, would face the same rules, although their accession is still further away.

World.title: Buried in Case Files, Lacking Security: Albania’s Courts Struggle in Dilapidated Buildings
World.content:
On Monday morning, the lobby of the Court of Appeals of General Jurisdiction in Tirana is packed with people waiting for their court proceedings. Defendants, family members and lawyers first pass through security checks before being ushered into the waiting room, where the start of hearings is announced.

Built in 1957 to serve as a police precinct, the old three-storey building housing the Court of Appeals has extended its jurisdiction across the whole of Albania following the approval of the new judicial map in 2023.

But instead of resolving the backlog of cases, the situation at the Court of Appeals is now bordering on the impossible, due to a lack of space for its doubled staff and the files that have accumulated from across the country.

The court’s narrow corridors have now been turned into labyrinths crammed with case files, stacked in cabinets, on shelves and even on chairs. The air reeks of mould and damp.

World.title: NATO’s Top Commander Unveils Plan for Victory Against Russia
World.content:
General Alexus Grynkewich, NATO’s Supreme Allied Commander Europe (SACEUR), presented his so-called “Theory of Victory” at the Warsaw Security Forum on Monday afternoon, bringing into public view a concept previously discussed only within the alliance’s senior military leadership. He warned that NATO would destroy “anything and everything” involved in a potential attack against an allied state.

The announcement comes amid heightened tensions between NATO and Moscow, following Russian airspace violations, cyberattacks and acts of sabotage. Western intelligence officials have warned that Russia could seek to test NATO’s resolve with a limited, deliberately ambiguous attack on its eastern flank in the coming months.

“If someone is foolish enough to attack us, we will fight. We will stop the attack and deny them the ability to achieve their objectives, whatever those may be,” the US general and former US Air Force pilot said. “We will, in short, ensure an attack against any ally proves utterly futile.”

The strategy takes its cues from Ukraine, where relatively inexpensive drones have upended conventional assumptions about military power. Under it, NATO would first seek to repel a Russian incursion using ground troops backed by low-cost drones, minimally crewed systems and AI-assisted targeting.

Once the Russian advance was repelled, the alliance would then seek to cripple Russia’s military command structure and bring the conflict to a swift conclusion. The concept also addresses hybrid warfare, including sabotage and cyberattacks, while emphasising the need to avoid unnecessary escalation.

“My theory of victory is simple: we will block the initial attack. If the attack persists, we will blunt it and prevent enemy advance. And if required, we will break the enemy’s forces and the operational warfighting system that is arrayed against us,” Grynkewich explained.

The choice of Warsaw for the announcement is significant. Poland, one of NATO’s biggest defence spenders, borders Ukraine, Belarus and Russia’s heavily militarised Kaliningrad exclave, placing it on the alliance’s frontline in any confrontation with Moscow.

Yet NATO leaders have played down the prospect of a direct Russian attack. “I do not assess that conflict is imminent or inevitable. It isn’t,” Grynkevicz said. “But deterring conflict also requires warfighting readiness. And readiness requires planning against what is possible, not just what is probable.”

NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte too said on September 30 there was “no imminent threat” to allied territory, stressing that the alliance would detect any Russian military buildup.

When asked why go public with the plan now, Grynkevich said it was due to the heightened scale of Russian activity, and added that it is meant to send a message both to allies and their adversaries: “We’ve got this.”

“We are prepared now,” he said. “Could we be better prepared? Absolutely. But I’m very comfortable with what we have today.”

On the elephant in the room, however – the question of whether American troops would join the fight if Russia attacked NATO’s eastern flank – Grynkewich was less forthcoming. “Ultimately, it will be a political decision,” he said.

The presentation was a centrepiece of the two-day security conference in the Polish capital, attended by more than 2,500 politicians, military officials, diplomats and experts from 90 countries. Among the participants are Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk, Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store and senior NATO representatives, while Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky addressed the gathering remotely.

World.title: Huge Croatian Tourism Projects Are Springing Up, But There’s a Big Problem…
World.content:
October the 14th, 2026 – Some huge Croatian tourism projects are springing up, but with that come some major problems that don’t point quite towards sustainable tourism…

Thousands of new beds are planned across southern Croatia. Although those in power like to say that the country is moving towards sustainable tourism, what is happening on the ground paints a different picture. Paula Klaic Saulacic reports for Dnevnik that from the Dubrovnik littoral all the way down to Konavle – over a road distance of 60 kilometres, around 5,000 new beds are planned. They’re all connected by one single road, the Adriatic Highway, which during the summer months is bursting at the seams – and all roads ultimately lead to Dubrovnik. That city is still teeming with tourists even in October, and precisely by those visitors who come at that time because they want to avoid the summer crowds.

ecological, technological and workforce issues…

“One road, yes, we drove for a long time. It’s nice here, but any more would be too much,” commented Toby from Australia. Thousands of new beds from the Dubrovnik littoral to Konavle are not only a problem when it comes to crowds and the number of guests; the problem is with infrastructure, the workforce, and also with ecology. Some experts believe that even drinking water is under threat. Civil engineer Tomislav Paviša, in an open letter to local leaders as well as the Government, warns that projects such as Tri Sestrice, the Resort in Cavtat, Kupari and others are endangering the water supply.

“We’re witnessing that dry periods are getting longer and longer and that, consequently, there will be less and less water at the springs for a regular water supply. In order for the Dubrovnik region to approach the realisation of these projects ready, it is necessary to form a competent institution composed of hydrogeologists, hydrologists and hydraulic engineers that would deal with this vitally important problem, as well as with protection against water pollution due to accelerated urbanisation in the neighbouring country,” he said.

the water supply

Dubrovnik Mayor Mato Franković was not available for comment today, while the mayors of Konavle and Dubrovačko primorje earlier said that for Cavtat and Doli they see no concern for the water supply.

“There were three important conditions that had to be met, which the Municipality requested from the investor. The first is to enable the western entrance to Cavtat, the second to secure a water reservoir that will be sufficient for the next 30 or so years so that Cavtat and all the hotels have a secure water supply. The third is that all ecological standards be respected to the utmost,” said Božo Lasić, Mayor of the Municipality of Konavle (HDZ), at the end of September. “As for water, water comes from three directions: one is Doli itself with its wells, from Ston via the Oko spring, and the third from Slano via Banići, so water should not be a problem either,” said Nikola Knežić, Mayor of the Municipality of Dubrovačko primorje (HDZ), a few days later.

When asked whether, given the dry summer, golf courses and new capacities, he thinks this can be infrastructurally sustained in the future, he replied: “It can.”

The Mayor of Župa dubrovačka says that restrictions are necessary. In a municipality that is home to 8,000 inhabitants and the same number of beds, tourism has reached its peak. “These are all real and objective questions and we have to seek answers from the profession; in spatial plans all tourist zones need to be revised,” said Marko Miloslavić, Mayor of Župa dubrovačka (ŽUPKA). There are many questions, and the answers are urgent because all these projects, at least according to the investors, are proceeding according to plan – some are even of national interest. Nevertheless – water, the environment, space and the quality of life of the local community should be the only real national interest.

World.title: Natural Disaster Declared for Municipalities of Milna and Nerežišća
World.content:
October the 14th, 2026 – A natural disaster has officially been declared for the municipalities of Milna and Nerežišća on the island of Brač after the recent fire.

Split-Dalmatia County Prefect Blaženko Boban has issued a Decision on the declaration of a natural disaster caused by fire for the area of the municipalities of Milna and Nerežišća. Morski reports that all affected people and legal entities are invited to report any and all damage to their properties as soon as possible, and no later than the 20th of October.

The Prefect issued the Decision on the declaration of a natural disaster caused by fire for the area of the Municipality of Milna and the Municipality of Nerežišća on Monday the 12th of October, according to a statement from Split-Dalmatia County.

By the Prefect’s decision, the municipal commissions for assessing damages in the affected municipalities are tasked with urgently carrying out all actions prescribed by law, processing the reports and entering the data into the national Register of Damages.

The fire that struck the wider Milna area caused extensive damage and directly threatened human and animal lives, homes, cars and other property, not to mention hotels and resorts who were forced to evacuate their tourists. It marked a summer in which the Croatian coast burned in a way that was deeply concerning.

Despite wildfires being the unfortunate norm in the tinder dry, scorching hot Dalmatian landscape in summer, the situation both on the island of Brač and across the channel on the mainland in Omiš stood out in all the wrong ways. Fires up in Zadar which were deliberately caused also threw a new angle onto an already tragic summertime reality.

World.title: Total Renovation Coming for Zagreb Railway Station
World.content:
October the 14th, 2026 – A total renovation is on the cards for the iconic Zagreb Railway Station, with new facilities and much needed modernisation coming as part of it.

Zagreb Main Railway Station is one of the most recognisable places in Zagreb. It was opened back in 1892, at a time of strong development of railway traffic and modernisation of the city, according to a design by the Hungarian architect Ferenc Pfaff. Poslovni reports that while the beautiful station has served as a backdrop for many series and films, passengers frequently complain about the lack of facilities, as well as the fact that the space should be renovated. That is precisely what is about to happen.

“HŽ Infrastructure, together with the consortium of bidders Intekonzalting d.o.o. and PlanAxis d.o.o., has signed a contract for the preparation of technical documentation for the complete renovation of the Zagreb Main Railway Station building. The preparation of the conceptual and main design, including the obtaining of all necessary permits, is currently underway. The preparation of the technical documentation is proceeding according to the planned dynamics, and its completion is scheduled by the end of 2027,” they say at HŽ.

protected cultural property

They note that the project envisages a complete structural, energy and architectural renovation of the Zagreb Main Railway Station building.

“A comprehensive rehabilitation and strengthening of the load-bearing structure will be carried out, and the selected methods will be minimally invasive in order to preserve the structural system, original materials and design elements. The architectural and construction renovation covers the façades, roof structure and interiors under conservation supervision in order to preserve the cultural and historical value of the building, which has the status of a protected cultural property. Special emphasis is on the energy renovation, which includes the replacement of existing windows and doors and the installation of heat pumps with the possibility of using renewable sources,” they explain at HŽ Infrastructure.

a brand new underpass? maybe…

The start of construction works on the Zagreb Main Railway Station building is planned after the completion of the project documentation and the implementation of the procurement procedure for the execution of the works. The planned duration of the construction works is around three years, and completion of the works is expected in 2031.

“During the renovation of the Main Railway Station building it will be necessary to close certain parts of the building, and depending on the organisation and phases of the works it is also possible to close the entire building. The organisation of passenger movement, train traffic and everyday use of the station zone will be adapted to the needs and dynamics of the renovation, taking into account passenger safety and the uninterrupted flow of railway traffic. As part of the project, the possibility has been left open for the construction of a new direct underpass beneath the Main Railway Station building, i.e. beneath the vestibule, which would directly connect the building with Tomislav Square. Further elaboration and possible realisation of the underpass are within the competence of the City of Zagreb,” our interlocutors say.

World.title: Delicious Zagreb: How the Capital’s Food Scene Became an Attraction
World.content:
October the 13th, 2026 – Zagreb is known for its market stands selling fresh, locally grown produce, but it has since managed to merge that perfectly with Michelin mentions and a blossoming international scene. Here’s how Delicious Zagreb can guide you through this impressive gastronomic maze.

Not so long ago in Zagreb (and in Croatia as a whole, if we’re being really honest) a common joke from foreign nationals was that all menus across the country must have been printed in the same factory. You could predict the options with absolute certainty depending on where you were located, and the international culinary scene in the capital was restricted to the odd Chinese restaurant.

Julien Duval/TZGZ

delicious zagreb as the capital’s food map

Sime Modric/TZGZ

Fast forward to 2026, and the food landscape is entirely unrecognisable in comparison. Zagreb has undergone a full-scale culinary revolution in a relatively short time, transforming from a continental gateway into a highly dynamic, self-assured gourmet destination. The home of various food and drink festivals and a growing number of international eateries, the capital’s food scene is no longer just an add-on to its historic architecture or Christmas markets. In fact, for around 37 percent of modern global travellers, the primary motivation for picking a destination is the food on offer at their chosen place.

Sime Modric/TZGZ

Taking this massive shift in traveller mindsets into consideration, the Zagreb Tourist Board (TZGZ) has just revealed a gastronomic offensive of sorts, entirely designed to put the capital city’s culinary identity firmly on the international map. At the heart of this push are two distinct milestones: the launch of the first-ever Gault&Millau guide exclusively dedicated to the City of Zagreb, and a whole wave of fresh, immersive digital content on the Delicious Zagreb platform.

the new gault&millau zagreb guide

Sime Modric/TZGZ

The cornerstone of Zagreb’s new culinary era is the premiere of the standalone, bilingual (Croatian/English) Gault&Millau Zagreb guide. Curating a (very) extensive list of 108 local addresses, the guide spans everything from fine-dining establishments and modern urban bistros to authentic street food stalls and traditional neighbourhood eateries that have resisted any wind of change and remain popular precisely because of that.

Sime Modric/TZGZ

What makes this release so critical for the city is Gault&Millau’s core philosophy: “Luxury lies in quality, not in price.” As Rudolf Štefan, the chef-owner of Šibenik’s Michelin-starred Pelegrini and a collaborator on the project, noted during the presentation at the Tač restaurant: “Nowadays, tourists are travelling with their palates in mind. They want a relaxed atmosphere, genuine local products, and genuine experiences. Above all, they look for honesty.”

Sime Modric/TZGZ

Zagreb’s new food scene delivers exactly that. The Croatian capital is known as a “little big city” where a modern visitors, wherever they come from, can watch a local hand over fresh cheese and sour cream at a wooden stand in the morning, and then see those exact same local ingredients completely re-imagined on a contemporary plate just a street or two away.

the way to a person’s heart is through their stomach, and zagreb has no issues there…

Crochef/TZGZ

The only “problem” anyone could run into in this sense in Zagreb is the sheer choice you have in a relatively small area. That has been taken well and truly into account, and Zagreb Tourist Board’s digital platform, Delicious Zagreb, has rolled out a suite of brand-new thematic content, gourmet routes, and specialised video series to help you work out where to begin. This platform takes everything a step far beyond generic directories, connecting visitors with the actual stories, local wine makers, confectioners, and heritage producers shaping the city’s modern flavours.

Crochef/TZGZ

The platform perfectly complements global trends toward “eat-seeing”, a concept in which dining out replaces traditional sightseeing as the main cultural lens. Through newly curated culinary routes, tourists can systematically explore Zagreb’s unique dual identity. It gives plenty of attention to the heavy, comforting continental traditions of old Zagreb, such as slow-baked štrukli, ajngemahtec (try saying that after a rakija or two) soup, and turkey with mlinci. It also spotlights Croatia’s grill cultures and creative Mediterranean influences that flow steadily inland from the coast and the islands.

Crochef/TZGZ

Zagreb’s global footprints are expanding via strategic partnerships between TZGZ and massive international culinary media. From targeted destination campaigns with Expedia to cultural deep dives in Smithsonian Magazine, not to mention high-profile features across TasteAtlas, Falstaff, and the Michelin Guide, Zagreb is consistently being spotlighted as a capital of diverse tastes.

delicious zagreb will take you seamlessly to old zagreb and into the modern international scene

Crochef/TZGZ

Whether you’re planning a city break in Zagreb or you’ve been on the coast and got a bit sick of fresh fish (it seems unbelievable, but it happens!), Delicious Zagreb is your best friend. You can build your food itinerary through the lens of what the Croatian capital is really all about. To get a true taste of how the old and new school coexist, make sure to add these essential spots to your list.

Crochef/TZGZ

Rome and Italy, the food capital of the world, might lie just across the Adriatic, and Croatia might well be famed for its seafood, but there’s so much more to it than that. Zagreb, once entirely overlooked, is no longer playing catch-up to the coast and the islands or to other European capitals. Powered by an honest culinary identity, top class talent, and excellent infrastructural support from projects like Delicious Zagreb, the quirky Croatian capital has claimed its spot under the sun as a more than worthwhile destination for the modern foodie.

World.title: Why Ancestry.com Is Not Enough to Get You a Croatian Passport
World.content:
October the 13th, 2026 – With the rise of the likes of Ancestry.com becoming a huge social media trend, many are running into an obstacle that surprises them – proof of Croatian ancestry through this service is not enough to apply for a Croatian passport.

For the modern diaspora in the age of (perhaps too much) technology at our fingertips, tracing family history has never been easier. With a few clicks on platforms like Ancestry.com, MyHeritage, or FamilySearch, you can uncover ship passenger manifests from Ellis Island, old federal census data, and digitised draft registration cards. It’s an exhilarating feeling to see your great-grandfather’s name handwritten on a 1910 immigration log, neatly indexed in a searchable digital database.

Very many descendants assume that printing out these beautifully rendered PDF records is the ticket to securing an EU passport. Then begins the imagining of freedom of movement, no endless airport queues and buying a fishing cottage somewhere on a Mediterranean island. They bundle their internet printouts, fill out the basic forms, and head to the nearest Croatian consulate, confident that their lineage is proven… Then comes the cold shower (or rather tsunami) of bureaucratic reality.

why digital records and family mysteries always fail legal standards

The Croatian Ministry of the Interior doesn’t accept internet printouts, digitised screenshots, or family tree charts generated by commercial software. In the complicated world of European Union citizenship law, there is a massive, unforgiving gulf between discovering an ancestor online and legalising a genuine lineage for a citizenship application. If you’re relying entirely on digital databases to claim your Croatian citizenship by descent, here is why you will hit a brick wall, and what it actually takes to cross the finish line.

Croatian citizenship by descent relies on proving an unbroken, entirely legal chain of bloodline from you to the ancestor who once emigrated from Croatia elsewhere. To formally satisfy the strict requirements laid down by law, every single link in that chain must be verified by a certified, physical vital record. Commercial genealogy websites are excellent tools for historical research, but they hold no legal weight. A passenger manifest showing that an otherwise unknown “Ivan Radić” arrived in New York back in 1912 from Dalmatia proves that a man by that name travelled. It doesn’t legally prove that he is your specific biological great-grandfather, nor does it establish his exact birth status or nationality in the eyes of the modern Croatian state, which is much more complex than it seems by today’s standards. In order to build a legally compliant application package, you must transition from online search bars to physical government institutions. You need an array of documents for that.

croatia wants certified, legalised everything

First comes properly, lawfully certified records. These are physical, state-issued birth, marriage, and death certificates for every single generation connecting you to the emigrant. Then comes the chain of international authentication: Every single document issued outside of Croatia (such as an American or Canadian birth certificate) must be authenticated with an Apostille from the appropriate government authority to prove its international validity. Then comes sworn Croatian translations by an executed by a court-appointed translator, ensuring that names, dates, and legal terms align perfectly across languages.

The biggest hurdle for the DIY applicant is obtaining the foundational document: the original birth or baptismal record of the ancestor from Croatia. It simply isn’t enough to have online documents when the most important ones are typically physical pieces of paper. While very many Western countries have digitised a vast portion of their historical records, a significant amount of Croatia’s local history remains locked away in gigantic physical volumes. Millions of vital records are stored exclusively in local municipal registries, regional state archives or historic parish church books scattered all over the country.

If your grandfather was born in a small (likely now totally empty) village somewhere in the Dalmatian hinterland or a town in Slavonia back in 1905, his birth record is highly unlikely to be indexed on a commercial American genealogy site. To find and claim it, someone has to know exactly which local registry office or parish holds the historical volume, communicate with local clerks in Croatian, and physically or administratively extract a certified copy.

For an American applicant sitting in New York, Toronto, or Sydney, navigating this local, ground-level bureaucracy from thousands of miles away and in a language they’re likely unfamiliar with can stretch a DIY project from a few months into endless years of administrative limbo that never budges.

croatian by descent – bridging the gap between online research and physical, acceptable results

If you’ve used Ancestry.com to map out your family tree, it would be wrong to say you haven’t done excellent foundational work. You now have the names, the approximate dates, and the names of the home villages of your ancestors in Croatia. However, in order to turn that complex historical spider’s web into a successful application for citizenship, you need to transition to professional administrative execution.

This is precisely where specialised diaspora services like Croatian By Descent become essential to those unfamiliar with the (often intense) world of Croatian bureaucracy in navigating such choppy waters.

Instead of letting your application stall and begin gathering dust at the digital research phase, their dedicated team acts as the physical bridge to your ancestral homeland. They take your online clues and utilise ground-level access to pull certified vital records directly from Croatian records and archives. They manage the meticulous paperwork, from securing the correct American apostilles to coordinating court-certified translations, ensuring your package meets the exact standards required by the Ministry of the Interior in Croatia and preventing you being ignored and chucked to the back of a long (and dog-eared) queue.

They handle the heavy administrative lifting so you don’t waste years in a loop of consular rejections, turning your internet search history into a verified, bulletproof submission package.

If you’re ready to move past the search bar and secure your Croatian and therefore European Union passport? Explore your options and skip the DIY headaches with comprehensive support from the team at Croatian By Descent who are diaspora members with personal experience with the intricacies of this journey themselves.

World.title: Minor Says Croatian Priest Abused Her in 2021, Bozanić Allegedly Did Not Report Him
World.content:
October the 13th, 2026 – A minor said she was physically abused by a Croatian priest in 2021, yet Bozanić allegedly failed to ever report him.

Index has reported that the Zagreb Archdiocese reported a priest accused of abusing a minor to the police allegedly only five years after receiving the complaint. This occurred only after Dnevnik.hr sent an inquiry about the case. A minor female person accused the priest of abuse back in 2021. The Archdiocese submitted the report to the Zagreb police only on the 9th of October this year, two days after Dnevnik.hr sent them an inquiry about the entire case. They have refused to answer any further questions about the case.

Zagreb police confirmed their receipt of the report. “The police received a report from a church legal entity, following which it has begun a criminal investigation,” they stated in their response. They added that, in accordance with the law, the inquiries are confidential and that they cannot disclose any specific details. According to unofficial information, after the 2021 complaint the priest was relieved of his duties as administrator of one Zagreb parish and banned from public activity. The Archdiocese then appointed a new administrator. It seemed that the priest had indeed been withdrawn from public life for several years.

the case should have been reported immediately – it was not

However, by decision of Archbishop Dražen Kutleša in September 2024 he was appointed parish vicar in one parish, and in August this year as a chaplain in an institution on the territory of the Zagreb Archdiocese. It is interesting that neither the decision on his relief from duties in 2021 nor the later appointments were published in the annual reviews of appointments and dismissals of priests in the Archdiocese. Information about his new duties was found in the parish’s posts on social networks and in the media. The case arose during the term of Cardinal Josip Bozanić, who was Archbishop of Zagreb from 1997 until April 2023, when he was succeeded by Dražen Kutleša.

One priest, who wished to remain anonymous, explained that Bozanić should have been the first to report the case to the police. Since he did not do so, the obligation was taken over by Kutleša, because the new archbishop is at the beginning of his term informed about all open cases, especially accusations of abuse of minors.

whether or not the vatican has been notified is unknown

The guidelines of the Croatian Bishops’ Conference for the protection of minors oblige reporting to the competent state authorities. They state that the church authority, when it receives a report, must inform the victim or parents that they are obliged to report everything to the state authorities. If, after a preliminary investigation it is established that the accusation is credible, the church authority has the obligation to forward the report to the state authorities. Given that the Archdiocese ultimately did submit a report, this suggests that it considers the accusations credible.

According to church laws, the Archbishop of Zagreb, after the preliminary investigation, should also have informed the Vatican’s Dicastery for the Doctrine of the Faith about everything. It is not known whether Bozanić or Kutleša did so. Independently of church regulations, according to Croatian laws everyone is obliged to report suspicion of a criminal offence.

World.title: Environmentalist: Every Country Has a Mafia, in Croatia, the Mafia Has a  Country
World.content:
October the 13th, 2026 – An environmentalist has issued a damning message that while every country has a mafia, in Croatia, the mafia has a country. He added that people are “lobotomised by football” as Croatia slowly disappears into oblivion.

Environmentalist Vjeran Piršić recently spoke about pollution, waste management and habits that harm nature. Index reports that the well known mathematician and computer scientist who has been involved with environmental protection for decades assessed that Croatia is, as a nation, merely turning into a geographical concept and that the Croats will simply disappear as a people if the attitude towards resources does not change. He said that in Croatia, the mafia has the country and that people must wake up, reports HRT.

from maths to ecology…

Piršić’s story about ecology began back in 1980 on the island of Krk, where during the winter holidays in a cold house, he started thinking about energy efficiency. “It was absolutely freezing. I realised I couldn’t heat the house. I was under two blankets for seventeen days, listening to Pink Floyd and dreaming of living in an energy-efficient house, that the bura wouldn’t blow through and that I would be able to produce my own energy,” he said. Four decades later, he realised that idea and today lives in an energy-renovated house that produces more electricity than it consumes. At the beginning of the 2000s, his interest turned into a concrete struggle. The turning point was the Družba Adria project in 2002, which planned the export of Russian oil via Omišalj. Piršić, together with a group of like-minded people, decided to oppose it and founded the association Eko Kvarner.

“That would’ve been five million tonnes of muddy waters, with a heap of dangerous microorganisms and invasive species. A small group of us met at my home and we realised we had three options. The first was to move away, the second was to ignore the problem, but then it would only explode later. Or, we could try to fight. And us six lunatics decided to put up resistance to a project behind which stood Bush and Putin and Mesić and everyone else,” he said. After four years of struggle, with the help of other associations and people, the project was stopped.

“people in croatia are totally lobotomised”

Piršić warned about a system in which environmental impact studies, he claims, often serve to justify projects instead of objective assessment. As one of the hardest examples he cited Vranjic and the remediation of asbestos waste. “Vranjic is the evil of evils. That is the bottom of the bottom. I cried there many times,” he said. He was particularly affected by the absence of a wider public reaction to a problem that directly endangers people’s health. “One hero, Grgo Mandić, stands in front of a truck to stop a vehicle that is not for hazardous waste and is transporting it to a landfill that is not intended for that. And the police arrest him. There were maybe ten citizens, five activists. At the same time, a few kilometres away, at Poljud, thousands of Split residents were celebrating Niko Kranjčar’s transfer from Dinamo to Hajduk. I have nothing against Niko Kranjčar or Hajduk. But that is the madness. What matters is that Kranjčar came to Hajduk,” Piršić said.

Such a disproportion led him to the conclusion that citizens are reacting less and less to important problems, for which he also holds the media responsible. “People in Croatia are completely lobotomised. They are lobotomised by football, Turkish soap operas, Big Brother, by who anointed whom,” he said.

“this poison must be removed from the land”

He also spoke about the waste scandal from Gospić and explained that the proposal for temporary relocation to the area of Udbina arose after consultations with Swedish experts. He believes the first step is to remove the waste from the existing location, and then separate it and seek a long-term solution.

“You have poison under your skin. Those 35,000 tonnes of waste is poisoning this land. And believe me, it is poisoning everything,” he said. According to his proposal, the waste would be moved into appropriate bags and temporarily placed in the area of abandoned military infrastructure in Udbina. After that separation would be carried out, and as one of the options for storing the remainder he mentioned a protected part of the Željava tunnel complex, with appropriate protection and controls.

Piršić said that thermal treatment of waste is often presented as a simple solution, although its effectiveness depends on the whole system. “I don’t understand incinerators, but I have seen that in all countries where a proper waste management system has been set up, incinerators have nothing to burn. Those are huge and expensive facilities,” he said. He emphasised that even after incineration slag and ash remain which also need to be disposed of, and he warned about the importance of technology and supervision, mentioning reports of irregularities in Croatian cement plants. “So an incinerator is not the Joker so that we’ve solved everything,” he concluded.

“croats seem unable to understand very basic, elementary concepts”

He also commented on the problem of illegal dumps. He assessed that such a state shows serious shortcomings of the system, but also insufficient awareness of the general public. “That we are barbarians. That we are heavy barbarians who don’t even understand very basic, elementary things. Secondly, this is the crowning proof of my thesis that the environmental protection system has collapsed,” he said. As key steps he highlighted the education of young people, reduction of consumption, repairing of devices and proper waste separation. “If we really separate waste and teach children that the environment must be protected, then such ‘filth’ will not exist after some time. And there is no other way,” he said.

He also spoke about food waste. He said that this problem can be significantly reduced by better meal planning, thoughtful shopping and proper separation of biowaste. He explained that organic residues in landfills create methane, a greenhouse gas that contributes to climate change. He also shared his own experience, where his family by planning weekly meals and shopping according to a list significantly saves money and reduces waste. He considers food waste an environmental, ethical and financial problem.

“croats will simply disappear as a people”

Using the example of plans for the construction of large poultry farms, Piršić asked the question of who such projects benefit. He believes that development must not be based on megaprojects that neglect small producers, but on the preservation of space and domestic agriculture.

“Every country has a mafia. In Croatia, the mafia has an entire country. The key question is: who needs this? For whom was this Croatia created? Is this country intended for ordinary people with family farms or for big players with mega-projects that will wipe everything and everyone out? Croatia is disappearing. It is turning into a geographical concept. Croatian agriculture is destroyed, even though billions have been invested in it. Now, they will destroy Dalmatia and the Adriatic as well by seizing space and mega resorts. And the Croats will disappear as a people. Demographically, we’re already broken,” he said.

He was asked whether or not there is hope for Croatia, given the clear statement that in Croatia, the mafia has the entire country. Piršić drew a parallel with historical periods of national awakening. “People in Croatia tend to wake up every 100 years. For the protest in Gospić, we gathered in the square where the monument to Ban Jelačić is. So… the Croatian revival did something good. A hundred years after that there was Stjepan Radić. Maybe the time has come for us to finally wake up and realise that the point is not football, Turkish soap operas or Big Brother,” he concluded.

World.title: Air Quality Monitoring Station Installed at Gospić Waste Site
World.content:
October the 13th, 2026 – A new air quality monitoring station has been installed at the shameful Gospić waste site which will assess the potential harmful impacts on the environment above the soil itself.

A measuring station has been installed at the location of PPK Velebit in Gospić, where the scandalous illegally disposed waste is currently located. Index reports that the new station will monitor concentrations of particulate matter PM2.5 and PM10 as well as the presence of metals in the air. Lika-Senj County has revealed that measurements will be carried out during the remediation in order to monitor the state of air quality and the possible impact of the entire situation there on the environment.

The station was installed at the request of the administration in Gospić by experts from the Teaching Institute for Public Health of Split-Dalmatia County. Also involved in the project are Lika-Senj County and the Environmental Protection and Energy Efficiency Fund, which are expected to continue financing air-quality monitoring in the Gospić area.

the station will measure pm2.5 and pm10 levels

The station will measure particulate matter PM2.5 and PM10, and the presence of metals will also be analysed in the collected samples. Two sedimentators have also been installed for collecting total deposited matter, in which the presence of heavy metals will likewise be determined. One sedimentator has been placed next to the measuring station and the other in a nearby settlement. The Institute states that wind directions were taken into account when selecting the sampling sites so that any possible spread of dust and particles can be monitored. Measurements and analyses should be carried out in accordance with regulations on air protection and quality. The County states that the goal is to provide citizens with expert data on the state of the air at a time of increased concern due to the waste at the PPK Velebit location.

the measuring station will remain in place throughout the duration of the large-scale clean up

Deputy Director of the Environmental Protection and Energy Efficiency Fund Mirko Budiša said that air-quality monitoring is part of the process of remediating the illegal landfill. According to him, the station should remain at the location throughout the entire remediation so that its possible impact on the environment and people’s health can be monitored. County Prefect of Lika-Senj County Ernest Petry said that the devices were installed at the invitation of the City of Gospić for an initial period of one month. He announced that the County, in cooperation with the Fund, will ensure the continuation of measurements over the next year, and longer if necessary. Petry stated that the County, the City of Gospić, the Fund and the competent ministries are participating in the monitoring. He highlighted as the goal of the cooperation the enabling of reliable monitoring of air-quality data in the area where waste has been illegally disposed.

daily data

Deputy Mayor of Gospić Ivica Kovačević said that this is a reference measuring station installed by a team from the Teaching Institute for Public Health of Split-Dalmatia County, led by Nenad Periš. He announced daily air-quality monitoring and the availability of relevant data to citizens on an almost daily basis. The measurement results should show the concentrations of particulate matter and metals at the location and serve for monitoring the situation during the remediation of the illegally disposed waste.

World.title: Madise raises presidential chief of staff's monthly salary to €8,000
World.content:
Estonian President Ülle Madise has raised the monthly salary for her chief of staff to €8,000, nearly a third more than his predecessor earned.

Madise, who was sworn in Monday, appointed civil servant and business executive Paavo Nõgene as director of the Office of the President of the Republic (VPK) for the duration of her term, setting his gross monthly salary at €8,000.

Under former President Alar Karis, the role was held by Krista Zibo, whose monthly base salary rose from €5,000 when she took up the post in September 2024 to €6,010 in January.

Madise offered Nõgene the job as her chief of staff in September, citing his experience leading a state agency, serving as secretary general of the Ministry of Culture and heading listed Estonian shipper Tallink.

After eight years at the helm, Nõgene stepped down as Tallink CEO this spring, initially planning to take a year off.

"[Nõgene's] experience should be put to work in service of the Estonian state, to make Estonia an even better place to live, work and do business," Madise said following the announcement last month.

Nõgene described serving the Estonian state as a great honor.

World.title: Isamaa rakes in €229k in 3rd quarter as party donations surge ahead of election
World.content:
Opposition party Isamaa collected by far the most donations among parliamentary parties in the third quarter of 2026 (Q3 2026), taking in €229,301.

The non-parliamentary Parempoolsed raised more than two major parties, the coalition Reform Party and the opposition Centre Party. Reform reported the highest overall revenue in the quarter, at over half a million euros.

Parties' main sources of revenue are donations and state support, the latter issued to all parties who polled above 2 percent at the preceding election, in proportion to votes received. Membership dues make up a smaller proportion of revenue.

According to the Political Parties Financing Surveillance Committee (ERJK), Isamaa's largest donors in Q3 2026 were Bigbank owner Parvel Pruunsild (€100,000), energy and real estate entrepreneur Janek Veeber (€50,000), transport entrepreneur Hugo Osula (€25,000), and Postimees owner Margus Linnamäe (€15,000). Membership fees brought in €3,360. With state funding included, Isamaa's Q3 2026 revenue totaled €326,090.

Reform collected €70,179 in donations and €1,700 in membership fees. Its total revenue was €505,562, the highest of any party. Its largest donors were casino magnate Armin Karu (€25,000), real estate businessman Marek Mägi (€15,000) and wind farm entrepreneur Andres Sõnajalg (€15,000).

Centre took in €64,112 in donations and €14,727 in membership fees. Total revenue came to €266,015. Its largest donation, €3,977, came from Jaak Madison, one of the party's two MEPs.

The opposition Conservative People's Party of Estonia (EKRE) raised €5,791 in donations and €1,103 in membership fees in Q3 2026. Total revenue came to €207,627 once state support is included. Its largest single donation, €1,500, came from Evelin Poolamets, one of the party's MPs.

The other coalition party, Estonia 200, collected €167,633 in total, almost all of it from state funding (€163,383). Donations amounted to €2,132, with the largest, €600, from MP Diana Ingerainen. Membership fees brought in €1,665.

The Social Democrats (SDE), in opposition since spring 2025, received €44,250 in donations and €6,439 in membership fees. Total revenue was €155,722. Their largest single donation, €5,000, came from entrepreneur and local politician Pille-Riin Raidsepp.

The non-parliamentary Parempoolsed does not collect membership dues. It reported €138,043 in donations in Q3 2026, and total revenue of €145,568. Businessmen Rain Lõhmus and Raul Kirjanen each provided €30,000.

The Riigikogu elections take place March 7, 2027, meaning parties will be spending on campaigning in the intervening months.

World.title: Tallinn says no to motorcycles, e-scooters in bus lanes
World.content:
Tallinn is pushing back against plans to let motorcycles and e-scooters use bus lanes, warning they could slow public transport and increase crash risks.

In a submission to the Riigikogu's Economic Affairs Committee, the city reiterated its opposition to a bill allowing motorcycles to use public transport lanes. It also rejects a separate proposal to allow light electric vehicles, including e-scooters, in the lanes.

Deputy Mayor Joel Jesse (Center Party) said adding more traffic would make it harder for buses to stay on schedule and increase the risk of crashes.

E-scooters, he said, pose particular concerns due to the sheer difference in size and mass, and large vehicles' blind spots also increase both the likelihood and severity of collisions.

"In spots where buses share the lanes with rams, there's the added risk of getting caught in the tracks," the deputy mayor continued, adding that wet and icy roads can worsen conditions from fall through spring in particular as well.

Cycle and bus lane in Tallinn. Source: ERR

EV explosion

Tallinn also wants to revoke the existing right under the Public Transport Act for taxis and electric vehicles (EVs) to use public transport lanes, saying fewer vehicles would help public transport run faster and more reliably.

Traffic in public transport lanes has increased significantly, the city said, with the number of registered EVs rising from 1,649 in 2020 to more than 13,000 this year, about two-thirds of them in Harju County.

This rapid increase in EVs has already slowed public transport in the dedicated lanes, making it harder for them to remain on schedule. "This shows that access to public transport lanes should be narrowed rather than expanded," the city added.

World.title: Foreign ministry: The state cannot directly control Silmet's business decisions
World.content:
Although the Ministry of Foreign Affairs says it has pressured Silmet to stop using Russian raw materials, the company has yet to do so.

Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna (Eesti 200) said the ministry has pressured chemical and metallurgical manufacturer Silmet to stop using Russian raw materials. The minister has now promised to set a deadline for the company to end its use of Russian raw materials. Tsahkna believes the company could stop using Russian raw materials as early as the beginning of next year.

ERR asked the Ministry of Foreign Affairs what specific pressure it had exerted, why the company had not complied and whether the ministry or the minister bears responsibility for the fact that, in the fifth year of the war in Ukraine, an Estonian company continues to purchase raw materials from Russia.

In its response, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs noted that the company's dependence on Russian raw materials has been publicly known for a long time. According to the ministry, Estonian media were reporting on the issue as early as 1995.

"However, dependence on Russian raw materials is not only a business risk but also a strategic vulnerability that Russia could exploit for its own benefit. It is therefore important to eliminate this dependence as quickly as possible," the ministry emphasized.

The ministry said it maintains regular contact with Estonian companies, including Silmet, stressing the need to find alternatives to Russian raw materials and end dependence on them.

"Silmet is a privately owned, publicly traded company that belongs to an international group based in Canada. The state cannot directly influence the company's business decisions or continuously monitor the details of its operations. Nor can the state independently assess when and to what extent the company has worked to identify alternative sources of raw materials," the ministry said.

At the same time, the ministry emphasized that it has consistently worked to support Silmet in identifying and establishing supply channels for raw materials from outside Russia. "To this end, we have, among other things, cooperated with the European Commission, which is responsible for the European Union's common trade policy."

According to the ministry, an important step in this direction was taken on October 9 when the European Commission selected Silmet's development project, Silmet 2.0, as one of 46 new EU strategic projects. The project aims to modernize the plant's production capabilities, enable the use of alternative raw material sources and reduce European industry's dependence on Russia.

The ministry noted that strategic project status will put Silmet in a better position to carry out its development plans and reduce its dependence on Russian raw materials.

According to the ministry's information, potentially suitable sources of raw materials for Silmet can be found in Latin America, Asia and Africa. The company itself is best placed to assess the technical suitability of specific raw material sources, taking into account the particular requirements of its production processes and technology.

"Silmet itself should explain to the public as soon as possible how it intends to end its dependence on Russian raw materials," the ministry emphasized.

The ministry also noted that growing international competition is making it more difficult to find alternative supply channels. Major industrialized countries are actively competing for limited raw material resources, affecting both their availability and supply opportunities.

"Estonia's goal remains to support Silmet's efforts to diversify its raw material supplies and reduce its dependence on Russian raw materials. Achieving this goal will require investment and technological changes by the company itself, as well as cooperation at the European Union level to improve access to alternative supply channels and strengthen Europe's security of supply for strategic raw materials," the ministry said.

ERR News reported on Thursday that a Russian company supplying rare earths to Estonia's Silmet was removed from the European Union's proposed 22nd sanctions package at Estonia's request.

World.title: Over 70 unexploded aerial bombs uncovered in Jõgeva nature reserve
World.content:
Dozens of Soviet-era aerial bombs, many of them live, have been excavated and safely disposed of in Jõgeva County, Maaleht reported .

The safety work was planned and covered a known danger zone at a former Soviet military facility.

On the penultimate weekend of September, Rescue Board and Defense League bomb disposal teams removed dozens of explosives from the former Utsali training ground in Jõgeva County.

They recovered more than 70 items from the area over the three days, including explosive devices and their components.

Most of the finds were aerial bombs, including both training and live versions.

The site was selected because the Soviet Air Force had once used it extensively for bombing exercises. Bomb disposal specialists had previously been called to the area, so it was a known danger zone.

Over 30 bomb disposal specialists and assistant specialists, along with more than 50 members of the Estonian Defense League and other support personnel, took part in the search operation.

Hazardous items were transported to a demolition site.

Marti Mereäär, head of the Southern Estonia bomb disposal unit, noted that explosive devices can remain dangerous for many years, and under no circumstances should they be handled. Members of the public should call 112 in such cases.

This is even the case with items of war memorabilia in the home, if there is reason to fear they are explosives. "Calling out bomb disposal specialists is free of charge, and there is no penalty for reporting an artillery shell found at home," Mereäär added.

What should you do if you find suspected explosives?

Under no circumstances should you touch the object

Move to a safe distance immediately

After moving a safe distance away, call the emergency number 112 as soon as you can

Note the location of the found object
