World.title: Estonian court convicts gas station clerk who stole 67,000 liters of fuel
World.content:
A court has convicted a former Olerex employee who, according to the charges, stole a total of 67,000 liters of diesel fuel from storage tanks while working at a gas station in Jüri.

The Ministry of Justice and Digital Affairs announced last week that a court had recently ruled on a case involving the theft of nearly 67,000 liters of diesel fuel from a gas station in dozens of separate incidents.

Toomas Tomberg, a prosecutor with the Northern District Prosecutor's Office who handled the case, told ERR that the thefts took place at the Olerex gas station in Jüri.

Prosecutors accused Igor Sorokin of using his access to the gas station's systems while working as a customer service representative to repeatedly steal diesel fuel from a storage tank.

According to the charges, he committed a total of 51 thefts between December 9, 2022, and January 25, 2024. To conceal the thefts, he switched off the gas station's video surveillance system before pumping diesel fuel into tanks installed in a vehicle he was using. Prosecutors accused him of stealing nearly 67,000 liters of diesel fuel worth almost €108,600.

The court found Sorokin guilty of large-scale, systematic theft and sentenced him to two years and six months in prison, suspended for a three-year probationary period. He was also ordered to compensate Olerex for €108,589 in financial losses. The ruling has not yet entered into force.

"The court proceedings confirmed that this was not an isolated act but a series of systematic thefts committed over an extended period. Although the defendant was caught in the act during one incident in January 2024, work schedules, video surveillance logs, storage tank records, witness testimony and other evidence gathered allowed the court to find that the remaining incidents described in the charges had also been proven," Tomberg said.

He added that the court agreed with prosecutors that the evidence formed a coherent and reliable body of proof establishing the defendant's actions throughout the period covered by the charges.

According to Tomberg, the case is notable both for the amount of fuel stolen and the length of time over which the thefts took place.

"It also demonstrates that prolonged, concealed activity causing financial losses to a company can be proven even when direct evidence relates to only part of the criminal activity, while the remaining incidents are established through a body of mutually corroborating circumstantial evidence," he said.

Recurring fuel theft on the rise

According to statistics from the Ministry of Justice and Digital Affairs, more than 2,000 fuel thefts have been recorded so far this year, nearly 50 percent more than a year ago.

The ministry noted that this does not necessarily mean people across Estonia have suddenly become twice as inclined to steal. Rather, the statistics suggest that thieves have become more systematic in their activities and that some incidents are being classified as criminal offenses because of their repeated nature.

A single theft may constitute a misdemeanor, but when someone repeatedly and knowingly engages in the same behavior, it becomes a criminal offense.

Fuel thefts are largely responsible for the more than 6 percent year-on-year increase in property crimes, the ministry said.

World.title: PPA: Migrants more visible in Tallinn's Nõmme, not more numerous
World.content:
The latest group of illegal migrants apprehended in Tallinn's Nõmme district does not mean that neighborhood has seen more cases than other parts of the city, authorities say.

The Police and Border Guard Board has detained two groups of illegal migrants in recent months, most recently on Sunday evening.

Overall, the PPA has detained 83 migrant groups in Estonia since mid-summer, and 352 individual illegal migrants since July 21, amid heightened migratory pressure on the Belarus-EU border.

In both reported cases in Nõmme, the PPA acted on neighbor tip-offs, as well as in other cases close to the nearby Tallinn University of Technology.

Rainis Sinikas, head of the PPA North Prefecture's border and migration supervision department, noted that the detained migrants are spread across different districts. It is largely Nõmme's character, he said, that makes detentions more likely for those accommodated there.

As a leafy suburb on the southern outskirts of the capital, Nõmme is a place where local residents tend to recognize each other by sight, Sinikas said. Outsiders, still more so those of a different ethnic background from the majority, tend to stand out more than they might in more central areas of Tallinn.

"The point of detention is largely connected to where migrants live. Through a trafficker, they find accommodation somewhere in a Tallinn district. Since Nõmme is a small garden suburb where many neighbors know each other, a number of people of another nationality attracts attention," Sinikas said.

"In the city center, people moving around during rush hour may not be noticed. But in a small garden suburb, far more attention is paid to who is moving around, and so more reports come in," he continued.

Sunday evening's operation in Nõmme began when residents reported what they said were two dark-skinned men outside a building. The men appeared not to be familiar with the area.

PPA officials went to the scene and detained both men. Checks revealed they were Sudanese nationals staying in Estonia illegally. During conversations, it emerged that several other illegal migrants were hiding in the area. Police then launched a search involving patrols, service dogs and the Rescue Board.

This led to eight additional men, also of Sudanese origin, being apprehended. They had been hiding in wooded areas.

"Generally the practice has been that running away and abandoning belongings doesn't happen very often, but this time it did," Sinikas said.

In the July case, it emerged that migrants had congregated at a short-term rental building. The PPA is still establishing the circumstances of Sunday's incident.

"In practically every case we establish whether they have already stayed overnight in Estonia. If they have, we check the accommodation or apartment used as short-term let. We also establish their route in detail: how many came in and where they came from. Through continuous and consistent procedural steps, we establish their background and whether we can apprehend more migrants at that address. Practice has shown that sometimes we do," Sinikas added.

October has so far seen no let-up for the PPA in detaining migrant groups, mainly in Tallinn but also in Pärnu and central Estonia.

On Monday, the PPA detained a group of seven illegal migrants in the city center. Migratory pressure is likely to continue and possibly rise ahead of winter, the PPA said.

The PPA says it receives constant tip-offs about possible illegal migrants. Sinikas denied that tip-offs had been primarily race-based. Actions and behavior stand out, he said — and even dirty clothing in the autumn weather.

"Since the weather is muddy, many of the detained groups get muddy too," Sinikas said.

Not only the PPA but other agencies are coming under heavy pressure. Over 250 people are now in the Tallinn detention center. The courts are overworked too, since detaining people is a legal process, on top of sentencing human traffickers caught in Estonia.

"The situation is difficult and could turn into a crisis situation. Various institutions, including administrative courts and local governments, are overloaded. We order interpretation and our entire network of cooperation partners is under great strain," Sinikas said.

The situation is complicated by the fact that different nationalities are placed in the detention center together, which has led to conflicts.

"It doesn't take much — there have been disagreements and pushing, even over a TV remote. So far we have managed to prevent and avert larger conflicts, but there are still such scuffles and quarrels," Sinikas said.

Sunday's group consisted of Sudanese nationals. The group apprehended Monday in central Tallinn were Somalis. "There are a lot of Bangladeshi, but also Pakistani and Afghan citizens. The circle is quite wide, and people from Ethiopia and Eritrea have also been detained," Sinikas said.

Regardless of country of origin, the migrants mostly arrive in Estonia from Belarus via Latvia, which it borders. They then make their way northwards.

Processing the return of one migrant usually takes over a month, including establishing that they did indeed cross the border illegally from another state. Estonia has so far sent 105 migrants back to Latvia.

The migrants themselves have said during proceedings that their intended destination was a western EU country, for instance Finland, Germany or Spain.

Sinikas said that while some have stated a desire to remain in Estonia, it is not clear whether this is their genuine wish or a script they have been taught.

That "also has to be established during proceedings," Sinikas noted.

Interior Minister Igor Taro (Eesti 200) discussed the Belarus-backed migration pressure on Latvia's border with his Polish counterpart Marcin Kierwiński at the ongoing Warsaw Security Forum. Taro said the migratory pressure should be treated as an attack on the whole EU, and that escalation must carry a cost beyond the existing sanctions on Minsk.

"All our allies are ready to support Latvia, just as we have previously stood alongside Poland and Lithuania. Responsibility lies entirely with the Belarusian regime, which supports and incites illegal border crossings and contributes to damage to Latvia's border infrastructure," Taro said.

Taro is set to take part in a panel discussion on Tuesday about government resilience in the era of hybrid attacks.

World.title: Despite Rail Baltica delay, Tallinn's Ülemiste terminal on track for 2028
World.content:
The new Ülemiste passenger terminal in Tallinn is still due to open in late 2028, despite Rail Baltica's completion being pushed back to 2034.

Although Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania agreed to complete Rail Baltica by 2034, making maximum use of the next EU budget period, construction already underway will continue, Infrastructure Minister Kuldar Leis (Reform) said last week.

Work on the main building and outdoor areas at Ülemiste Linda Terminal is progressing as planned, Rail Baltic Estonia communications chief Silvia Pärmann told ERR.

One platform is already in use by passenger rail operator Elron, she noted, and trains to Tartu and Narva will continue serving the terminal via the existing railway ahead of its full completion in late 2028.

"Even before Rail Baltica is completed, the terminal will bring together trams, connecting passengers to destinations including the airport and port, as well as buses and domestic rail connections," Pärmann said.

Render of Tallinn's future Ülemiste Terminal. Source: Rail Baltic Estonia

The structure's concrete frame is due to be completed by the end of this year, making its overall scale and architectural design more clearly visible, she added.

Tallinn's Rail Baltica terminal was designed by Zaha Hadid Architects.

Major urban center plans

This February, Rail Baltic Estonia, Tallinn Airport and Mainor Ülemiste also unveiled plans to develop the area into a new urban center, with nearly €500 million in combined investments over the coming years.

Projects include a new high-rise with a conference center and a European-themed park, while Tallinn Airport also pursues its own more than €66 million expansion project.

The city has also proposed building a 10,000-seat multifunctional arena in Ülemiste.

World.title: Iraq gains new Red Sea trade link as Saudi NEOM port advances Gulf logistics corridor
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) — Iraq may get access to new trade routes connecting Europe, Egypt, and Saudi Arabia after an agreement between Port of NEOM and CEVA Almajdouie Logistics to investigate integrated cargo services linking the Red Sea with Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) nations and Iraq.

The planned logistical corridor comes as the region’s war worsens and shipping via the Strait of Hormuz is disrupted, making other trade routes more important for Iraq and other Gulf nations.

Under a memorandum of understanding, the two corporations will look into methods to optimize the flow of products along the Europe-Egypt-Saudi Arabia-GCC-Iraq corridor by integrating marine shipping with land transport, customs clearing, storage, and cross-border distribution.

The Port of NEOM, situated in Saudi Arabia’s northwestern Red Sea area, is being developed as a logistics hub linking international shipping lines to domestic markets.

The cooperation would use the port’s marine links and CEVA Almajdouie Logistics’ regional transport network to provide companies with better coordinated cargo services between ports and ultimate destinations.

For Iraq, the corridor might offer an extra route for imports and commercial cargo coming from Europe and other foreign markets, thus decreasing dependence on regular Gulf shipping routes.

The effort also emphasizes Saudi Arabia’s expanding importance in linking Iraq to regional and worldwide supply chains, especially as corporations seek alternatives to sea routes vulnerable to geopolitical disruptions.

The company seek to study combined customer service, market growth, and logistical solutions for various sorts of cargo.

The arrangement is still exploratory, with no precise investment value, implementation timeline, or verified cargo quantities stated.

While the planned corridor has the potential to increase Iraq’s economic relations with Saudi Arabia and other GCC nations, its actual effects will be determined by the development of cross-border transportation services, customs procedures, and business demand.

World.title: Iraq’s crude oil exports jump to 2.7 million barrels per day
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Iraq’s crude oil exports have reached approximately 2.7 million barrels per day, according to Salim al-Rikabi, the spokesperson for the Iraqi Oil Ministry.

Al-Rikabi told the state-run Iraqi News Agency (INA) that Iraqi crude oil export volumes have increased significantly, from around 200,000 barrels per day in May to roughly 2.7 million barrels per day today, despite shipping difficulties caused by the crisis in the Strait of Hormuz.

The majority of exports are transported through southern outlets, with northern outlets accounting for around 300,000 barrels per day, according to al-Rikabi.

The Iraqi official indicated that these statistics are considered high rates given the current situation.

The Iraqi Oil Ministry is planning to increase crude oil export volumes through both southern and northern outlets. Al-Rikabi explained that the Iraq-Turkey pipeline’s target export capacity is around 700,000 barrels per day, which the ministry is aiming to reach.

The Iraq-Turkey pipeline has a design capacity of 1.5 million barrels per day, while the minimum capacity stipulated in the agreement signed between the two countries is 750,000 barrels per day.

The current export volumes through the pipeline are roughly 300,000 barrels per day, although the government plans to use a minimum capacity of 750,000 barrels per day, a step that will increase oil exports and create more markets for Iraqi crude, according to al-Rikabi.

World.title: Asian markets mixed as tech firms claw back some losses
World.content:
Hong Kong – Asian stocks stuttered Wednesday as investors fought to claw back the previous day’s steep tech losses, with focus turning to US inflation data and upcoming earnings from key AI-linked firms.

Tech firms took a hammering on Tuesday amid concerns about China’s progress in developing AI chips and following comments by Broadcom’s boss likening the AI buying frenzy to gambling.

The ructions felt in Seoul, Tokyo and Taipei — which have big tech weightings — saw giants SK hynix, Advantest and TSMC suffer huge losses, pushing them back towards levels last seen following their summer rout.

All three markets bounced Wednesday as the same firms provided much-needed support, with Seoul and Taipei both up more than one percent.

There were also advances in Shanghai and Singapore, but Hong Kong, Sydney, Wellington and Manila dropped.

The gains were helped by hopes that the US Federal Reserve could avoid hiking rates further next year, after the bank’s New York boss suggested the policy board could hold off after lifting once more this year.

“I haven’t changed my view that it may be appropriate to have one more rate hike,” John Williams told Bloomberg News in an interview.

“I don’t think at this time I have any reason to believe that we would need to do more” after that.

He said there were signs inflation will come down towards the Fed’s two percent goal next year as the impacts from tariffs and an energy price shock fade.

All eyes are on the release of consumer price data due later Wednesday, which could play a key role in whether the bank decides to hike for a second successive meeting on October 28.

“After another disappointing (non-farm payrolls) report, the third in the last four months, the Fed is stuck between a rock and a hard place,” said Matt Weller at FOREX.com.

“The labour market is showing signs of deteriorating, while price pressures have remained above the central bank’s target for more than five years.

“Markets are currently pricing in about a one-in-four chance that the central bank will raise interest rates at its meeting… setting a relatively high bar to tip the FOMC (Federal Open Market Committee) toward another rate hike.”

Also in view this week are earnings from Dutch giant ASML and Taiwan’s TSMC.

ASML is a critical cog in the global economy and a key bellwether for the semiconductor sector, while TSMC makes advanced processors for companies including Nvidia and Apple.

“After a strong first half (of 2026), semiconductor stocks have come under pressure as higher bond yields, geopolitical uncertainty and concerns about the scale of AI capital expenditure have prompted investors to reassess valuations,” said Saxo Markets’ Charu Chanana.

“The recent selloff across US and Asian chipmakers suggests that strong demand alone may no longer be enough to sustain the rally.”

The results of ASML and TSMC “offer a useful health check on the AI investment cycle”.

“TSMC tells us whether demand for advanced chips continues to accelerate, while ASML tells us whether chipmakers are investing in enough equipment to meet that demand.”

Crude prices rose more than one percent as worries swirled over the Middle East crisis, with Iran stepping up attacks in the Strait of Hormuz and Houthis pressing ahead with their strikes on oil kingpin Saudi Arabia.

UK Maritime Trade Operations said four tankers were struck in the waterway on October 11, which Bloomberg said was around double the average the agency had seen the week before.

Meanwhile, Saudi Arabia and the Houthi anti-government forces in Yemen exchanged attacks following deadly strikes on Riyadh’s international airport and energy sites in recent days.

World.title: Advanced economies must ‘act now’ to lower debt as bond yields spike: IMF
World.content:
Bangkok – The International Monetary Fund on Wednesday called for advanced economies to “act now” to address ballooning debt, with spiking bond yields at multi-decade highs and pressure growing on central banks to hike interest rates.

Global public debt is at its highest level since the Second World War and on track to soon exceed 100 percent of global gross domestic product, and the Fund lamented the lack of any major progress in reversing the trend.

“The fundamental message (is) that countries need to act now, particularly if you have high levels of debt, in order to create that room for higher spending pressures,” said Era Dabla-Norris, the Fund’s deputy director at the Fiscal Affairs department, referring to spending on defence, ageing populations and other priorities.

While rises in debt have been broad-based, advanced economies have seen their debt-to-GDP ratios skyrocket since the global financial crisis in 2008, the pandemic and the wars in Ukraine and Iran, as they increased spending to deal with the series of economic shocks.

Since late February, yields have increased by an average of around 110 basis points, especially on longer maturities, Dabla-Norris told AFP on the sidelines of the IMF’s Annual Meetings in Bangkok.

On Tuesday, US 10- and 30-year Treasuries were trading at their highest yields since around 2002, with other G7 bonds following similar trajectories.

The spike has been driven by a combination of factors, including heightened inflation expectations caused by skyrocketing energy prices caused by the Iran war.

That, in turn, has caused many central banks to step in to address price stability, with authorities hiking borrowing costs to curb prices.

The rise in rates has contributed to increases in bond yields on the short end of the curve, which has been seeing issuances in greater numbers, Dabla-Norris said.

“High debt and shorter maturities definitely makes the interaction between fiscal and monetary policy more complex than it did in the past,” she said.

“What that really means is that if short-term interest rates change — so say monetary policy tightens — that can quickly spill over into government borrowing costs much faster than if the maturity structure was longer.”

– Communication is key –

In that situation, existing high debt levels act as an “amplification mechanism” for the effect on yields.

Worldwide, governments’ average interest payments are projected to rise from 2.3 percent in 2021 to 3.7 percent in 2031, research released by the IMF on Wednesday showed.

In the United States, interest payments are projected to climb from about 2.8 percent of GDP before the pandemic to 5.7 percent in 2031, or “roughly equal to projected expenditure on Social Security,” the report said.

In low-income countries, the situation is even more dire, with interest payments taking an average of 15 percent of tax revenues.

The solution, the IMF says, is that governments need to undertake fiscal consolidation now.

“Countries will now have to increase primary balances much more than they did in the recent past in order just to stabilise debt ratios,” said Dabla-Norris.

She warned that higher benchmark yields in advanced economies could also spill over to emerging markets by tightening global financial conditions.

Dabla-Norris said governments needed to communicate clearly why consolidation — which can mean painful spending cuts — needs to happen.

“What’s important beyond just having the right credible strategies in order to bring that down is to be communicating what the trade-offs are to the public.

“I think this is really absolutely crucial because the trade-offs mean that the governments have much less room for manoeuvre within budgets,” she said.

“By not starting on the consolidation path today, you’re just kicking the can down the road.”

World.title: Iraq’s foreign exchange reserves hit $85 billion
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Iraq placed 28th out of 30 countries in terms of foreign exchange reserves, with around $85 billion, according to Canada-based Visual Capitalist, citing recent data from the International Monetary Fund (IMF).

According to the report, Iraq ranked 28th with approximately $85 billion in reserves, placing it just behind France, which held 27th with $86 billion. Iraq was ahead of Romania, ranked 29th with $78.2 billion, and Turkey came in last with $76.6 billion.

China led the list with $3.41 trillion of reserves, followed by Japan with $1.259 trillion, Switzerland with $932.3 billion, Taiwan with $602.5 billion, and India with $543 billion.

Saudi Arabia placed sixth internationally with $458.6 billion in reserves, the UAE ranked 12th with $251.4 billion, and Iraq rated third among the Arab countries.

The ranking, which is based on data from the IMF’s International Reserves and Foreign Currency Liquidity (IRFCL) database, shows that foreign currency reserves are an important tool for dealing with economic shocks, maintaining currency stability, financing imports, and servicing external debt.

Director of the Central Bank of Iraq’s (CBI) Statistics and Research Department, Samir Neama, said that the country’s foreign currency reserves can cover Iraq’s imports for a whole year.

Speaking at the MERI 2026 forum in Erbil, Neama clarified that the CBI is in a very comfortable situation in terms of foreign reserves.

While IMF reports indicate a capability to finance imports for three to six months, Neama confirmed that the reserves are sufficient to cover the country’s needs for more than a year.

World.title: Saudi employee arrested for allegedly bugging OpenAI office
World.content:
San Francisco – A Saudi employee of OpenAI was arrested after allegedly planting a recording device in one of the company’s San Francisco offices, the AI firm and federal prosecutors said Tuesday.

“We discovered a sophisticated recording device that was hidden inside one of our offices” and “referred the matter to the FBI,” OpenAI told AFP in a statement.

OpenAI’s security team found the device late last month and the employee, Saudi national Abdulrahman Alfozan, was arrested on October 9, the US Justice Department said.

Alfozan, a 35-year-old engineer who had worked for OpenAI since July 2025, allegedly wrapped a USB device in toilet paper and inserted it into a television located in an “executive conference room,” according to a Justice Department statement.

He was allegedly caught on camera “near” the conference room multiple times but was not authorized to participate in meetings located there.

He used a “productivity tool” to search for more information about OpenAI’s office buildings, meeting rooms, calendars, schedules and people’s locations, according to the statement.

A chatbot account connected to Alfozan’s spouse also allegedly contained queries related to remote audio recording and encrypting memory cards.

“This serious situation underscores why winning the global super intelligence race is a national security prerogative,” Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton said in the statement.

“The intelligence community remains committed to safeguarding America’s cutting-edge intellectual property from foreign threats,” Clayton added.

The arrest and allegations come amid a fierce global race to dominate in artificial intelligence, which the Trump administration has pushed to be rebranded as “superintelligence.”

Saudi Arabia’s state-backed AI firm Humain invested $3 billion in Elon Musk’s xAI shortly before the American billionaire’s space company, SpaceX, acquired the AI division in February.

Now known as SpaceXAI, the division announced last year that it was teaming up with Humain to build a 500-megawatt data center in Saudi Arabia.

– Multiple devices –

It was not immediately clear what, if any information the recording device was able to collect.

“At this time, we have no indications of this individual inappropriately accessing or exfiltrating model weights, source code, or customer data,” OpenAI told AFP in a statement.

A second device was found by OpenAI’s security team when they searched an unattended bag that belonged to Alfozan, according to the Justice Department.

Alfozan was caught on security footage from inside the restricted conference room where he appeared to look behind the television where the recording device had been placed, the Department said.

A LinkedIn account matching Alfozan’s name and resume show that he previously worked at Facebook-owner Meta, as well as an AI startup and a venture capital firm.

He was also a student at University of California at Berkeley and the Massachusetts Institute of Technology.

The Justice Department said Alfozen had been charged with “using or endeavoring to use an electronic, mechanical, or other device to intercept oral communications,” for which he could face up to five years in prison and a $250,000 fine.

It did not accuse Alfozan nor Saudi Arabia, which is a close US ally, of spying activity in its statement on Tuesday.

Alfozan is expected to appear at a federal court hearing on October 19.

In 2022, a former Twitter worker, Ahmad Abouammo, was found guilty of spying for Saudi officials keen to unmask critics on the platform.

World.title: Atletico sink Man Utd as Viking deny Bayern in Champions League
World.content:
Paris – Atletico Madrid beat Manchester United 2-0 in the UEFA Champions League on Tuesday as the Red Devils continued their poor run, while Bayern Munich were held 3-3 in Norway by underdogs Viking Stavanger.

Elsewhere, last season’s beaten finalists Arsenal eased to victory over Lille while Barcelona came from behind to beat Galatasaray but Inter Milan lost a seven-goal thriller at home to Club Brugge.

Atletico, who lost at Liverpool in their opening European encounter, took the lead inside the opening minute in the Spanish capital through Pablo Barrios. Alejandro Grimaldo struck the woodwork from a free-kick later in the first half.

Johnny Cardoso also had a goal disallowed before the break but Ademola Lookman got Atletico’s second in the 79th minute, just after United defender Leny Yoro had been sent off.

The defeat continued the Old Trafford club’s disappointing start to the campaign and increased the pressure on manager Michael Carrick.

They have gone five matches without a victory and have won only once in seven outings, with a trip to Italy to face Como next up in the Champions League.

“Tonight is a one-off game in judgement, it is the Champions League and a tough place to come. We are doing certain things OK,” Carrick told broadcaster Amazon Prime.

Viking, who are in the Champions League after winning a first Norwegian title in 34 years, appeared to be heading for a famous win over Bayern when they led 2-0 at half-time in Stavanger.

Gianni Stensness headed them in front in the second minute and Peter Christiansen ran away to double their advantage.

– Olise sent off –

Harry Kane pulled one back from a penalty early in the second half and then headed in his eighth goal of the season in nine games in all competitions.

Luis Diaz then converted as the match was turned completely on its head, but Bayern’s Michael Olise was sent off in the 74th minute — the France star was booked and then shown a second yellow seconds later for throwing the ball at his opponent.

He will therefore miss next week’s home meeting with Arsenal.

Viking snatched a memorable draw as Herman Haugen headed home in the last minute.

Speaking to Amazon Prime, Kane said Olise “will be gutted and he has to take responsibility for it. It was a mistake, and mistakes happen. He has to learn from it. It’s a shame because we have important games ahead of us.”

Arsenal were too strong for Lille as the Premier League champions won 3-0 at the Emirates Stadium with goals by Jurrien Timber, Eberechi Eze and Bukayo Saka, in the space of eight second-half minutes.

Barcelona, one of the favourites to win the competition, maintained their 100 per cent record this season with a 4-1 win over Galatasaray in Istanbul.

Russian international Aleksei Batrakov gave the Turkish champions the lead and they then had another goal disallowed, but Joao Cancelo equalised before half-time.

Lamine Yamal then turned on the style, setting up goals for Fermin Lopez and Anthony Gordon early in the second half, before substitute Karim Adeyemi sealed Barca’s victory.

– Tresoldi hat-trick –

Italy-born German striker Nicolo Tresoldi scored a hat-trick, including a penalty, as Club Brugge claimed a remarkable 4-3 win away to Inter at San Siro.

Romeo Vermant got the Belgians’ other goal, with Lautaro Martinez on target twice for Inter as they succumbed to a second straight European defeat.

In other games, Villarreal came from behind to beat Napoli 3-1 in Spain while RB Leipzig beat PSV Eindhoven 1-0 with a Brajan Gruda goal after Ivan Perisic failed to convert a penalty for the Dutch side.

Sporting of Portugal won 2-0 away to Lens in France with goals by Luis Suarez and Issa Doumbia, and it was a night to remember for Sabah as the rank outsiders from Azerbaijan downed Slavia Prague 2-0 in Baku.

Jamaican international Kaheem Parris and Rwanda’s Joy-Lance Mickels secured their first victory in the league phase.

Wednesday’s Champions League games include reigning champions Paris Saint-Germain at Manchester City and Real Madrid at Roma.

World.title: Yamal stays cool at boiling Galatasaray to lift Barcelona to victory
World.content:
Istanbul – Barcelona and Lamine Yamal rediscovered their sparkle after a rocky first-half spell in the cauldron of Istanbul’s Ali Sami Yen stadium to win 4-1 away to Galatasaray in the Champions League on Tuesday.

Halfway through the second round of matches, the victory lifted Barcelona to the top of the Champions League table with two wins. Galatasaray are pointless and near the foot of the standings.

“We’re at a very high level. We have to keep going; the season is very long. We can’t relax,” Barcelona’s Fermin Lopez told Spanish broadcaster Movistar.

Barcelona dominated the early stages. With Yamal vigorously policed on the right by the home defence, many of their attacks flowed through Anthony Gordon on the other flank.

Yet Galatasaray took the lead after 27 minutes. After Gordon went tumbling in the penalty box, the hosts launched a rapid counter-attack through Rafael Leao on the left.

He pulled the ball back to the edge of the area to Russian Aleksei Batrakov whose drive deflected off Joao Cancelo and into the corner of the goal.

“That goal made things a bit strange for us, because we had been dominating. But we knew how to react and come back,” said Fermin.

That ignited a spell of furious home pressure which culminated with Victor Osimhen rising to head a corner past goalkeeper Joan Garcia. Baris Yilmaz toed the ball over the line but was ruled offside.

Barcelona reasserted control. When Yamal went down on the edge of the box, the ball broke to a surprised Davinson Sanchez who gave the ball away immediately. It fell to Dani Olmo who threaded a pass to Cancelo who scored.

At the start of the second half Yamal took over. After setting up Gordon, who spurned the chance, he helped put Barca ahead in the 50th minute, placing a gentle curled cross on the forehead of Fermin who nodded home.

“He’s a friend and a great team-mate,” said Fermin of Yamal. “When he has the ball, I always look for a run. He’s the best in the world. We get along well off the field, and that shows on the pitch, too.”

Three minutes later, Yamal beat Eren Elmali three times, and in three different ways, in a tiny space before rolling a pass to Gordon in front of goal.

This time the England striker made no mistake with Elmali, a Turkey international, lifting his arms to the heavens in an expression of powerlessness.

After 65 minutes Yamal cut in from his wing and fired a pass to replacement centre forward Gabriel Jesus. The ex-Arsenal man could not control the ball but it deflected to Karim Adeyemi who drilled the ball home.

And three minutes later, Yamal should have got on the scoresheet himself but after being quickest to a loose ball he fired his shot over the bar.

The 19-year-old finished the game without a goal which would have taken him closer to Kylian Mbappe’s record for Champions League goals as a teenager, but Yamal, who became Barcelona’s youngest ever captain in the previous round, again took over the captain’s armband when Pedri was replaced.

World.title: Over half of Amaha clients live with mental health concerns for a year before seeking help; 56% report self-harm thoughts
World.content:
NEW DELHI: Mental health concerns can persist for months, sometimes years, before people seek professional help. By then, the distress may be affecting their relationships, work and ability to manage everyday tasks.

More than half of people who eventually sought care had lived with their concerns for over a year, while 56.2% reported thoughts of self-harm before reaching professional support, according to the Amaha Mental Health Report 2026.

The report is based on responses from 13,825 people who answered questions before beginning care with the mental healthcare provider between October 2025 and September 2026. Only 11.3% sought help within a month of experiencing mental health concerns.

Dr Amit Malik, psychiatrist, founder and CEO of Amaha, said, âIndiaâs progress in mental health must be judged by whether people can get timely, effective care, not simply by how openly we talk about it. These are the accounts of people who reached us; they should make us ask who is still unable to access care.â

He added that friends, families and communities were vital to helping people recognise their needs and find care, and said finding treatment should not become âanother test of a personâs resilienceâ.





Nearly 95% of respondents reported at least two concerns, averaging five each. Anxiety was most common (72.1%), followed by stress (67.5%), low mood (58.3%), relationship difficulties (55.6%) and sleep disturbances in over a third. The report also found a gap between self-reported distress and clinical diagnosis: 33% of those initially reporting stress were later diagnosed with depression, while among those reporting repetitive thoughts and behaviours, 32% were diagnosed with depression and 11% with obsessive-compulsive disorder.

Before approaching a professional, many respondents relied on informal support or tried to manage their concerns on their own. More than half (54.5%) had spoken to friends or family, while 44.6% had turned to self-help resources such as books, apps, videos and online communities. Nearly a third had tried therapy previously, and 19.4% had used prescribed medication.

Avoidant coping strategies, including excessive screen time, oversleeping and overworking, were reported by 82.7%.

Another 15.4% said they had turned to alcohol or other harmful substances instead of professional support.

The impact extended to everyday functioning. Only 12.3% said they could manage all their daily tasks, while 27.3% said they could not manage most tasks or any at all.

Young adults and working professionals formed the bulk of the cohort. Those aged 25â34 accounted for 51.3% of respondents, followed by 26.9% aged 18â24.

Working professionals made up 64.3%, while students accounted for 15.3% and unemployed people 7.9%.

Friends were the most frequently named contact in a mental health crisis (33.9%), followed by spouses (20.5%) and siblings (18.1%), underscoring the role of family and social networks in recognising distress and helping people access care.

World.title: Saudi OpenAI engineer arrested for planting hidden device to record executive meetings
World.content:
A Saudi national and OpenAI engineer has been arrested by US federal agents and charged with allegedly installing a hidden audio recording device in an executive conference room at the AI company to capture sensitive discussions about its technology, the US Justice Department said Tuesday.

The employee, identified as 35-year-old Saudi national Abdulrahman Alfozan, was arrested on Friday.

The complaint did not name the company, but OpenAI confirmed in a separate statement that it had discovered a âsophisticated recording device that was hidden inside one of our officesâ. The company reported the discovery to the FBI and fired the employee.

âWe used our models to understand the device and where it had come from, identifying that a specific employee had planted it a few days earlier.

We referred the matter to the FBI, and weâre grateful to the agents and prosecutors who moved quickly to make an arrest. The FBIâs investigation is ongoing and we will continue to support their work,â an OpenAI spokesperson was quoted as saying by AP.

âAt this time, we have no indications of this individual inappropriately accessing or exfiltrating model weights, source code, or customer data. The employee was terminated,â the statement read.





The complaint does not specify what Alfozan intended to do with the recorded conversations. However, OpenAI said the device was sophisticated, designed to evade detection and equipped with advanced encryption and audio-monitoring capabilities.

The company also said it had evidence that the employee planned to install additional listening devices in other parts of the office building to record meetings.

Alfozan appeared in court for the first time on Tuesday. He faces a charge of using or attempting to use an electronic, mechanical or other device to intercept oral communications.

According to the complaint, the recording device was found on September 30, concealed in toilet paper and plugged into a USB port at the back of a television in an executive conference room.

The conference room did not have a security camera when the device was installed. However, CCTV footage from other parts of the office showed Alfozan near the room on nearly a dozen occasions last month, despite having no authority to access the space or attend meetings there, the complaint said.

OpenAI later installed a camera in the room. According to the FBI, footage recorded last week showed Alfozan entering the room and checking behind the television where the device had been placed.

The complaint also alleges that Alfozan used a productivity tool to make multiple inquiries about the company's building addresses, meeting rooms, room capacities and calendars.

Days before his arrest last week, Alfozan allegedly left an unattended bag in another room. When OpenAI personnel opened it, they found his wallet, identification documents and another recording device similar to the one discovered in the executive conference room, the complaint said.

World.title: L Murugan offers to resign, sparks Union Cabinet reshuffle buzz
World.content:
NEW DELHI: Union minister L Murugan on Tuesday offered to resign from the Cabinet and Rajya Sabha, saying he wanted to return to politics in his home state, Tamil Nadu, after being part of govt for over five years.

This rekindled the buzz that PM Modi could be preparing to reshuffle his council of ministers amid a steady exit of its members and some being in the queue.

Murugan has three and a half years left of his RS term, and his exit will allow BJP to pick a new face from Madhya Pradesh, where he was elected from in 2024.

In his five-page letter, Murugan expressed gratitude to the PM for all the opportunities he got and his govt's work for Tamil Nadu.

He said, "I therefore request you to relieve me of my responsibilities as Minister of State and permit me to relinquish my membership of the Rajya Sabha so that I may dedicate myself full-time to strengthening the party in Tamil Nadu."

What stoked curiosity in political circles is that he chose to post the letter offering his resignation on social media, apparently with the consent of the BJP leadership. This suggested a clear signal from the party brass, leaving many within the governing alliance wondering if it was a prelude to more resignations.

Rajya Sabha vacancy may open up possibilities for Puri

L Murugan's exit comes on heels of BJP not renominating ministers Hardeep Puri and B L Verma for another term in RS. Ravneet Bittu and George Kurian have already resigned earlier under similar circumstances.

Two other ministers, Pankaj Chaudhary and Harsh Malhotra, have been made chiefs of BJP units in UP and Delhi, making their departure only a matter of time.

Interestingly, an imminent RS vacancy from MP opens up the possibility for Puri, the lone Sikh face in the govt, to return to Rajya Sabha.

Murugan has been BJP chief in Tamil Nadu, the last one among big states where BJP remains on the margins of electoral politics, and it was given a jolt when K Annamalai, who enjoyed a decent following, quit in June 2026.

World.title: Sensex jumps 1100 after finance minister's remarks spark LTCG cut hopes
World.content:
NEW DELHI/MUMBAI: Finance minister Nirmala Sitharaman Tuesday said the govt was open and keen to "hear" discussions around the long-term capital gains (LTCG) tax as it was "healthy" to have the debate.

The minister, however, declined to be specific on the matter as preparations for the Union Budget in Feb are already underway.

The FM's comments raised investors' hopes of a reduction in LTCG tax and securities transaction tax (STT), a longstanding demand among foreign funds who have been big sellers in the Indian market in the last two years.

As a result, after a steady start, stock prices jumped with the sensex finally settling 1.5% or 1,109 points up at 73,034 points while Nifty closed 1.6% or 359 points up at 22,722 points.

RBI steps to check rupee volatility: FM

While responding to an observation that investors, especially foreign funds, were keen on removal of capital gains tax and streamlining of taxation before they started investing in India, Sitharaman said, "Two years ago, we had bought all the asset classes similarly and people thought that I was increasing the tax. I was not increasing the tax, I was bringing all of them at par, so that an investor is not speculating as to which one gives them greater leverage.





So, these are the things on which there is a lot of debate. It's healthy to have this debate and I will be keen to hear them."

At a Bloomberg event, FM acknowledged that investors, both within and outside, were commenting on LTCG and the question of treating all asset classes similarly has been a widely discussed topic.

So far this year, foreign portfolio investors (FPIs) have bet sold Indian stocks worth a little over Rs 3 lakh crore, NSDL data showed.

In 2025, the corresponding figure was a net outflow of nearly Rs 1.7 lakh crore and just Rs 427 crore in 2024. Since Sept 2024, sensex has lost about 13%.

At the same event, Sitharaman also noted that rupee has depreciated "significantly" over the past year and a half, and RBI will continue its efforts to prevent excessive volatility. "RBI is not trying to fix the rupee, it is trying to stop the volatility, and for that there is a lot of effort from their side.

I am sure RBI will take further steps to make sure that rupee does not become too volatile," she said in response to a query on capital outflows, especially in the equity market due to currency depreciation.

FM stressed that govt has kept the economy on a sound footing and been careful with its spending and borrowings, helping investors looking to diversify away from China. "Fiscal discipline is not going to be a matter which should worry investors," she said, adding that domestic private capital is moving in and is attracting private capital from elsewhere as well.

Join conversation Commentsâ Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines

At a time when foreign funds are taking money out of India at a fast clip, a relook at the taxes related to the markets is a welcome move.

According to Hitesh Sawhney, partner at Price Waterhouse, against the current backdrop of sustained foreign investor selling, elevated global yields and capital moving towards competing markets, revisiting LTCG taxation may be timely.

"A (zero) tax rate on LTCG, linked to a relatively longer holding period, could reward patient capital, encourage investors to remain invested in India and strengthen India's relative capital market attractiveness. It would also reduce foreign investors' dependence on treaty-based exemptions and the resulting uncertainty over treaty eligibility."

World.title: Muslims disproportionately flagged in Delhi SIR
World.content:
An analysis of Delhi’s draft electoral rolls released as part of the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) process showed that the software-driven check for “logical discrepancies” in their records is flagging a disproportionately higher number of Muslims.

Muslims, who form 13.6% of electors on Delhi’s draft roll, made up 20.3% of those flagged for “logical discrepancies”, and 30% of those flagged under five reasons indicative of family size. Who got flagged was decided not by the Electoral Registration Officers (EROs), the statutory custodians of the rolls, but by the Election Commission of India’s (ECI’s) centralised ERONET software.

World.title: Japanese journalist arrested in Russia's Sakhalin region on spying charges
World.content:
A Japanese journalist suspected of spying has been arrested on Russia's Sakhalin Island, the top Russian domestic security agency said Tuesday (October 13, 2026).

The arrest comes amid a spike in tensions between Russia and Japan following Russian President Vladimir Putin's August trip to the Kuril Islands, the Moscow-controlled Pacific archipelago that is claimed by both countries.

The Federal Security Service, or FSB, said in a statement that the Japanese man, who worked for the Hokkaido Shimbun newspaper, was suspected of gathering information related to Russia's defence capability on behalf of a Japanese intelligence agency.

The FSB, the main successor agency to the Soviet KGB, said the Japanese man, whom it didn't name, was arrested as he was preparing to leave Russia. The agency said the suspect was flown to Moscow, where he was put behind bars.

The FSB released a video showing masked agents in black outfits arresting the man in a hotel room and then escorting him to a plane bound for Moscow. He was then shown facing a judge at the Lefortovo District Court, who ordered him to be held in custody for two months pending the probe.

Russia's Sakhalin region includes Sakhalin Island and the four southernmost islands of the Kuril chain, which Japan calls the Northern Territories. Putin visited one of them, Iturup, in August.

The Soviet Union took the Kuril Islands from Japan in the final days of World War II, and the ongoing dispute has prevented the countries from signing a peace treaty formally ending their hostilities.

Japan's Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said Putin's visit, his first to the islands, was “incompatible with the Japanese position on the Northern Territories” and was “absolutely unacceptable.” She said it was a further blow to already-strained ties between the two countries over Ukraine.

Moscow responded by summoning the Japanese ambassador to protest the “anti-Russia” statements by Takaichi and other Japanese officials, emphasising that “Russia's sovereignty and jurisdiction over the southern Kuril Islands are absolutely unshakable.”

Decades of diplomatic efforts to negotiate a settlement haven't produced any visible results. Over the years, Moscow has also bolstered its military presence on the Kurils in moves that appeared to underscore its firm stance in the dispute.

In recent years, Russia has arrested many foreigners -- mainly Americans -- on various criminal charges and then released them in prisoner swaps with the United States and other Western nations.

The largest exchange since the Cold War took place in August 2024, when Moscow freed journalists Evan Gershkovich and Alsu Kurmasheva, fellow American Paul Whelan, and Russian dissidents in a multinational deal that set two dozen people free.

World.title: Mangaluru city glitters for Dasara
World.content:
Mangaluru city has been decked up with colourful illuminations as part of Mangaluru Dasara celebrations.

Major thoroughfares in the city, including M.G. Road, K.S. Rao Road, Mangaladevi Temple Road, Car Street, and Kudroli Temple Road, have been illuminated. Major government buildings, including the Mangaluru City Corporation building and Kudmul Ranga Rao Town Hall, besides commercial complexes and banks, have been lit up.

The major part of the illumination has been provided by the Mangaluru City Corporation. Tiger dance (huli vesha) troupes have installed huge billboards at major circles in the city.

Temple management committees have decorated their respective temples. The Kudroli Sri Gokarnanatha temple, Mangaladevi temple, Urwa Mariyamma temple, Kadri Sri Manjunatha temple, Car Street Venkatramana temple, and Mariyamma temple at Bolar have been decorated with attractive lights.

Mangaluru Dasara illumination

The city is witnessing a heavy rush of people, including tourists, who are visiting the streets and temples to see the illumination in the evening. Most streets are jam-packed between 6 p.m. and 10 p.m. during Dasara days, with people enjoying street food and beverages.

Mangaluru lit up for Dasara 1 / 3

Approximate cost

In October 2023, the Mangaluru City Corporation (MCC) proposed to spend ₹1.39 crore to illuminate the roads leading to Kudroli Gokarnanatheshwara, Mangaladevi, Urwa Marigudi, Bhagawati, Venkataramana and other temples in the city for the 10-day Dasara celebrations. Then mayor Sudheer Shetty Kannur proposed to make permanent arrangements for lighting the streets of the city during Dasara.

Start of celebrations

The Dasara (Navaratri) celebrations in the coastal belt began on October 11, with thousands of devotees thronging temples across Dakshina Kannada, Udupi and Uttara Kannada districts.

Chief Minister D.K. Shivakumar was expected to inaugurate the celebrations at the Kudroli Gokarnanatha temple in Mangaluru and Uchchila Mahalakshmi temple in Udupi district on October 12. However, he cancelled the visit as he had to travel to Delhi to join the protest by the Congress demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over alleged irregularities in electoral rolls and the Election Commission of India’s Special Intensive Revision (SIR) exercise.

Apart from the temples in Kudroli and Uchchila, Mangaladevi temple in Mangaluru, Durgaparameshwari temples in Kateel, Bappanadu, and Kamalashile, Mookambika temple in Kolluru, Mahishamardini temple in Kadiyali and Neelavara, and the Polali Rajarajeshwari temple draw huge crowds during the Navaratri festival.

Most temples serve food to devotees during the celebrations. Tiger dance, or huli vesha, is a major attraction of Dasara. Roads leading to the temples, and the temples too, have been illuminated, adding to the festive atmosphere.

World.title: Why did academics and activists sleep in Telangana schools? | Explainer
World.content:
The story so far

The state of schools and teaching has been in the spotlight nationally. In Telangana, a collective of academics, bureaucrats and activists known as the Telangana People’s Front was on a 12-day tour of districts in the State to understand and highlight the state of schools called ‘Vidya Bus Yatra’.

Why is this being done now?

Budgetary support for education has declined to a single-digit percentage of the State outlay and has remained so over the past decade. After the formation of the Congress government by A. Revanth Reddy, a Telangana Education Commission was formed under former IAS officer Akunuri Murali to suggest measures to improve the sector. After his two-year term with the commission expired, Mr. Murali quit the commission and has take up cudgels for reform and started the ‘Vidya Bus Yatra’.

Is there a road map for improving schools?

The Telangana Education Commission submitted a 354-page report after visiting 305 institutions over 14 months in all 33 districts. The report has four annexures that are draft Bills that lay out a clear map to reinforce and rebuild the education sector in Telangana. Also sketched out was a six-phase plan to upgrade the infrastructure at a total cost of ₹31,600 crores, staggered across five years. It also created a checklist on what constitutes a Telangana Foundation School.

A functioning model of the concept is Telangana Public School at Arutla, about 50 km from Hyderabad. The school is a pre-primary to Intermediate facility and offers English-medium education with airy classrooms, a playground, free transport, three meals a day, and sports facilities.

What the ‘Vidya Bus Yatra’ revealed?

Schools without compound walls. Taps without running water. Locked toilets or dysfunctional toilets. In Gattuguddenapalli village, the government school had fewer than 60 students, where the inspiration was a science and Telugu teacher, but one of the children wanted either salt or jaggery to be given to add taste to “Ragi java (millet broth)”.

What is ‘badi nidra’?

The members of Telangana People’s Front not only visited the schools but also slept in them at night to experience in real time the functioning of amenities in the schools. They discovered that Unified District Information System for Education Plus (UDISE+) data that is being updated almost daily for consideration of national ranking does not match the ground reality.

A drinking water tap may be in the school, but how often it functions is different. This is the same issue flagged by the UN report ‘Progress on drinking water, sanitation and hygiene in schools 2015-2025’. The UN report found that 50 million, or five crore, Indian children still lack access to sanitation service in their schools.

Is the infrastructure the only issue?

One of the academics who was part of the bus yatra says that mismanagement of resources with irrational deployment of staff is a big bugbear. “Some schools have excess classrooms, others without enough rooms. All are under the Education Department, but the head of each institution doesn’t want to share the barely functional infrastructure.”

There are schools with 10 teachers where the number of students is 60, and then there are other schools with 50 students and two teachers, where one of them is either on long leave or absent. In multi-grade classrooms, children don’t have space, and students sit in the verandahs,” she said.

What’s the road ahead?

The Telangana People’s Front wants to mobilise parents and society to force the government to act on its proposals to raise spending on education from the current 8.2% to 18%. Make government schools share resources like playgrounds, classrooms, labs, library facilities, etc. Currently, the government spends ₹1,10,00 on each student, according to an estimate. Once the resources are shared, facilities expanded then this cost will drop to ₹55,000, according to a TPF estimate.

World.title: ‘Immature and counterproductive’: Sheikh Hasina slams Bangladesh PM Rahman for skipping BRICS Summit
World.content:
Bangladesh Prime Minister Tarique Rahman’s decision to skip the BRICS summit in India was “immature” and damaged Bangladesh’s national interest, former premier Sheikh Hasina has said, warning that foreign policy driven by personal reactions or short-term political calculations is inherently counterproductive.

In an exclusive interview with PTI, Ms. Hasina said Bangladesh’s participation at the summit of the influential grouping could have opened up new opportunities for the country’s economic and social development, but that chance was lost.

The former Bangladesh Prime Minister said if her presence in New Delhi was the reason behind Mr. Rahman’s refusal to attend the summit, it was very unfortunate, as relations between two countries cannot be determined by personal considerations or political sensitivities involving one individual.

Questioning Mr. Rahman’s decision, Ms. Hasina said that a responsible government should “open doors for the country, not close them.”

New Delhi had extended an invitation to Bangladesh Prime Minister Rahman for the BRICS summit in his role as the current chair of BIMSTEC (Bay of Bengal Initiative for Multi-Sectoral Technical and Economic Cooperation).

However, Mr. Rahman opted out of the summit, which took place in New Delhi on September 12 and 13.

“It was deeply unfortunate that Bangladesh chose not to participate. In my view, it was an immature decision and one that did not serve Bangladesh’s national interest,” Ms. Hasina said.

“BRICS is not simply a diplomatic gathering. It brings together major emerging economies and creates opportunities for cooperation in trade, investment, infrastructure, technology and development. By participating, Bangladesh could have gained valuable experience and opened new opportunities for its own economic and social development. That opportunity was lost,” she said.

The former Prime Minister said foreign policy cannot be conducted through personal reaction or short-term political calculation.

“India is our closest neighbour and an important historic partner, but BRICS engagement is also about Bangladesh’s own place in the international community,” she noted.

The 78-year-old Hasina, living in Delhi since she left Bangladesh following the collapse of her government in August 2024 in the face of a massive anti-government agitation, also recalled how then-Prime Minister Ziaur Rahman visited New Delhi in 1979 even when she was staying in India.

“After the assassination of the Father of the Nation, Bangabandhu Sheikh Mujibur Rahman, along with members of my family on August 15, 1975, and the killing of the four national leaders inside Dhaka Central Jail on November 3, Ziaur Rahman came to power through an unconstitutional process,” Ms. Hasina said in response to written questions.

“Yet when he visited Delhi in 1979, I was living in Delhi. When he travelled to London in 1980, I was also in London. My presence in either city did not prevent him from travelling there,” she said.

“So why should my presence in Delhi prevent Ziaur Rahman’s son, Tarique Rahman, from coming to India today? What is the real reason behind such a decision?” she asked.

“Relations between two countries cannot be determined by personal considerations or political sensitivities involving one individual,” she stressed.

Ms. Hasina also highlighted how her government’s foreign policy approach helped Bangladesh’s economic growth.

“During my tenure, we maintained strong relations with India while also expanding cooperation with China, Russia, Japan, the United States, Europe and many other partners,” she said.

“Friendship with one country never required hostility towards another.

Bangladesh needs a mature, balanced and confident foreign policy. A responsible government should open doors for the country, not close them,” she said.

The India-Bangladesh relations came under some fresh strain after Ms. Hasina held a virtual media interaction in New Delhi on August 5.

Following the event, Dhaka reiterated its demand for her extradition and even sought to link it with Mr. Rahman’s planned trip to India. New Delhi sought to distance itself from the event, saying it neither played a role in it nor endorsed Ms. Hasina’s comments.

The former prime minister also attacked the Rahman government for its overall foreign policy direction, and said it should be “independent, balanced and guided by national interest.”

“The principle given by the Father of the Nation, Bangabandhu Sheikh Mujibur Rahman, remains the best guide: friendship to all, malice to none. India is Bangladesh’s closest neighbour and historic friend from the Liberation War,” she said.

“China is also an important development partner. Japan, the United States, Europe, ASEAN and the Muslim world are all important to Bangladesh. The problem is not engagement with China or any other country. The problem begins when one relationship is used against another,” she said.

“It begins when anti-India rhetoric is encouraged for domestic politics. It begins when major decisions are taken without transparency,” she added.

The Awami League leader said Bangladesh is passing through a “grave national crisis as democratic space has been “closed”.

“The judiciary has been used for political revenge. Media freedom has been restricted. Law and order have weakened. Minorities feel unsafe. Extremist forces have regained space. The economy has suffered,” she said.

“This is no longer only an Awami League issue. It is a national crisis. One of the country’s largest political forces has been banned. Its leaders are in jail or forced into hiding,” she said.

“Millions of its supporters have been denied normal political rights. A country cannot return to stability by excluding such a large section of its own people. The suffering is being felt across the country, but Awami League leaders, workers and supporters have faced an unprecedented burden of political persecution,” she said.

Ms. Hasina, without divulging specific details of her return to Bangladesh, said she is going back to restore democracy.

“Thousands have been jailed, many more have been forced into hiding, and families have lost homes, jobs, businesses and livelihoods simply because of their political identity,” she said.

“My return is part of the struggle to restore democracy, voting rights and the rule of law. I want to stand beside the people of Bangladesh, fight for their rights, and help restore democracy, security and development in my country,” she said.

“The people of Bangladesh must be allowed to decide their own future through a free, fair and inclusive election. That is why my return will be significant. It will be a step towards returning Bangladesh to its people,” she added.

At the same time, she admitted that her return to Bangladesh could be risky, as she was given a death sentence by a Bangladeshi court, but asserted that she was not afraid.

“This is not the first time death has come close. In 1975, my father, mother, brothers and almost my entire family were murdered. In 1981, despite military rule and intimidation, I returned to Bangladesh. There have been repeated assassination attempts, including the August 21, 2004, grenade attack, as well as imprisonment, conspiracy and political persecution,” the Awami League leader said.

“The greater concern today is not personal safety. It is the destruction of justice in Bangladesh. A death sentence imposed through a politically motivated process, without a genuine opportunity to defend oneself, cannot be called justice,” she said.

World.title: Sheikh Hasina’s activities in India ‘principal challenge’ in planning Bangladesh PM’s visit: Humaiyun Kobir
World.content:
The “principal challenge” in planning a visit of Bangladesh Prime Minister Tarique Rahman to India are the activities of deposed premier Sheikh Hasina and her team who are based in India, said State Minister for Foreign Affairs of Bangladesh Humaiyun Kobir on Monday (October 5, 2026).

Responding to questions from The Hindu on the sidelines of the ongoing Bay of Bengal Conversation organised by Dhaka’s Centre for Governance Studies (CGS), Mr. Kobir emphasised the importance of “strategic autonomy” for Bangladesh and said India has to appreciate the “challenges of a newly elected government” in Bangladesh. He further argued that activities of the exiled leaders of the Awami League will not help India.

Also Read: ‘Immature and counterproductive’: Sheikh Hasina slams Bangladesh PM Rahman for skipping BRICS Summit

‘Destabilising a foreign country’

“The visit will be bilateral but there are challenges and through dialogue we will overcome them. The principal challenge is not too much to ask for. Sheikh Hasina and her team are stationed in Delhi and they are trying to destabilise a foreign country sitting in Delhi. This does not benefit India either,” said Mr. Kobir calling on India to restrain Ms. Hasina and her team.

Mr Kobir accused Ms. Hasina of killing around 2,000 Bangladeshi citizens during the crackdown of the uprising of July-August 2024 and described her as a “terrorist”. He said that Bangladesh’s people need a “clean break” from the past as they have sacrificed lives in the process of overthrowing the previous government of Ms. Hasina that ruled for more than 15 years. He, however, said there are ongoing talks with India that have been welcomed in Dhaka.

“We are seeing some positive signs as India is trying to restrain them. That is the norm between two countries. If they (Hasina and her team) are restrained, then there will be no problem in the [bilateral] relationship,” said Mr Kobir asserting that ties with India are a priority for Dhaka. “The visit of Prime Minister will take place at a conducive time and I am hopeful. PM has never said that he will not visit [India],” said Mr. Kobir highlighting the role of Indian High Commissioner Dinesh Trivedi in this regard.

Indian High Commissioner’s role

“The Indian High Commissioner here is doing a good role. He is trying and hopefully Delhi will be receptive to his opinion and if they give importance to his opinion, then we are ready to engage across the board. We are carrying out our consultations,” said Mr. Kobir describing the Awami League leadership as a “hindrance” to normalisation of Delhi-Dhaka ties.

The State Minister of Foreign Affairs said that Bangladesh is ready to discuss all issues but expects some “reciprocation”. “When two governments sit down to discuss keeping in mind national interests, all issues can be addressed,” he said arguing that Bangladesh will not allow anyone to work against India’s interest sitting in Dhaka and he expects similar action from India.

Earlier, Mr. Kobir delivered a “ministerial address” at the Bay of Bengal Conversation and said Bangladesh seeks “strategic autonomy” in foreign affairs but will maintain strong relation with global and regional stakeholders.

“Our foreign policy must respond to the changes in Bangladesh. We seek engagement with all based on mutual respect and mutual benefit and national interest. We want a strong partnership but we also want strategic autonomy,” said Mr. Kobir delivering his speech where he did not mention India or any other global partners of his country. Later, speaking to The Hindu, he elaborated on his idea of strategic autonomy and said, “Every country likes strategic autonomy. India likes its strategic autonomy. Bangladesh too likes its strategic autonomy. This idea is more about what we require.”

(The correspondent is visiting Dhaka as a guest of the Centre for Governance Studies to participate at the Bay of Bengal Conversation)
