World.title: Social media bans are no cure-all, but governments may still find them necessary
World.content:
SOCIAL MEDIA APPS. Instagram, TikTok, Snapchat, Kick, YouTube, Facebook, Twitch, Reddit, Threads and X applications are displayed on a mobile phone ahead of new law banning social media for users under 16 in Australia, in this picture illustration taken on December 9, 2025.

Experts warn that social media bans may offer short-term safety but push young people to circumvent restrictions, making radicalization harder to detect

BALI, Indonesia – Restricting access to online platforms cannot address all the factors that contribute to the radicalization of young people, but governments have “valid” reasons for imposing bans, said I Gusti Agung Wesaka Puja, executive director of the ASEAN Institute for Peace and Reconciliation (ASEAN-IPR).

“There is no perfect solution, especially when we are encountering this new kind of threat, a new kind of non-traditional security issue,” Puja told Rappler in an interview on October 12.

Puja maintained that while governments may find it necessary to step in and implement social media bans to protect children from harmful content, these measures still require careful assessment.

“The government in this respect has the responsibility to consider the safety and well-being of young people because they are our future leaders, particularly as digital platforms continue to evolve and continue to provide a threat to them,” said Puja.

“However, whether restrictions on social media access will produce positive long-term outcomes, certainly this needs careful assessment,” he added.

Puja leads ASEAN’s think tank on peace and conflict. A recent study by ASEAN-IPR found that traditional security responses are insufficient to prevent violence as young people in Southeast Asia gain greater access to it.

The Philippine Senate has approved Senate Bill 2424 that restricts social media access of children under 16. The House of Representatives approved a similar measure or House Bill 11566. These legislative developments follow three school shootings in the country that occurred this year. (READ: Why Congress should think twice about banning under-18s from social media)

Indonesia also started implementing the ban early this year, and countries across the world are considering social media legislation, following the likes of Australia, the United Kingdom, and Brazil.

“Maybe putting some bans on the use of social media, it could be effective,” Bora Park, security and terrorism expert from Seoul-based Institute for National Security Strategy, told Rappler in a separate interview.

“But in the long term, it might also have a side effect,” Bora said, adding that young people may find ways to circumvent the regulations and create new slang, making it “much harder to detect which one is radicalized and how dangerous that individual would be.”

Proposal to create tiered restrictions

Skeptics of such measures cite their potential effects on young people’s access to information, education and opportunities, as well as their social interactions.

Implementation of the regulation remains uncertain, as it relies heavily on the cooperation of private technology companies.

Senator Risa Hontiveros, the sole Philippine lawmaker who voted against the bill on social media ban for kids, said the priority is how to effectively protect children. Hontiveros advocates for “tiered restrictions for adolescents.”

In her statement, Hontiveros said younger adolescents should have tighter restrictions. As kids age and mature, she proposed they be given “autonomy while protections remain against abuse, exploitation, and harmful content.”

“Taking it away from them all of a sudden without providing adequate ways for them to cope with its absence is not the answer to their needs and it is not the answer to our collective fears,” Hontiveros said.

– Rappler.com

World.title: How did Escudero rule so fast on prosecution’s surprise move?
World.content:
Presiding officer Chiz Escudero addresses the court before the start of the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte on August 26, 2026.

As presiding officer of the impeachment court, Chiz Escudero anticipated and prepared for different scenarios in the course of the trial

There were two surprises during Vice President Sara Duterte‘s impeachment trial on Tuesday, October 13: the bombshell motion of the prosecution to drop three of the four articles of impeachment, and the extensive ruling of presiding officer Francis “Chiz” Escudero delivered less than an hour after the House prosecutors’ request.

So how did Escudero manage to make the ruling in such a short period of time? Senate impeachment court spokesperson Reginald Tongol said that Escudero, with his staff as well as Senate Clerk of Court Renato Bantug Jr., anticipated different scenarios and prepared rulings based on all legal possibilities.

“The presiding officer has prepared rulings for different scenarios but they were in skeletal in form. It still has to be drafted and finalized upon his delivery and formal manifestation in the court,” Tongol in a mix of English and Filipino during a press briefing after the trial on Tuesday, October 13.

Tongol cited the prosecution’s October 6 manifestation signaling its intent to withdraw Article III, which covers bribery, as an example of how Escudero anticipated possible developments.

“For example, the prosecution filed a manifestation to drop Article III on October 6, so with due diligence, the presiding officer prepared and anticipated whatever that is going to be thrown at him at the trial,” he said.

The prosecution ultimately went further, seeking to withdraw Article I, which covers the alleged misuse of confidential funds, and Article IV, which covers grave threats. The court granted the request, leaving only Article II, which concerns Duterte’s alleged unexplained wealth.

Tongol said Escudero continued working on his ruling until shortly before delivering it, incorporating inputs from his fellow senator-judges.

“The presiding officer’s rulings considered the inputs of his fellow senator judges. That’s why up to the last minute, he was actually writing and editing his speech,” said Tongol.

This also explained why Escudero was cautious when Duterte’s defense counsel requested a copy of the ruling. Tongol said the presiding officer wanted the written version checked against the ruling delivered in court and reflected in the journal.

“That’s also the reason when the respondent’s counsel was asking for a copy of the ruling, he said he wanted to be careful and that his written speech should be compared to the delivered speech in the journal. The official ruling was the one delivered during the trial,” he added.

Escudero himself explained during the proceedings that the court had prepared for various possible scenarios to ensure it could address issues raised by either party.

The court sought to know “the same, if not more, than each party or both parties combined,” Escudero said, explaining that the preparation was intended to help the court address potential issues and consider different outcomes. – Rappler.com

World.title: Investigators hunt French supermarket fridge hackers, no claim of responsibility
World.content:
REFRIGERATORS. View of empty refrigerators at the frozen food aisle inside an Intermarche supermarket in Paris the day after a cyberattack targeted refrigeration systems at French supermarket chains, causing food losses and fires at several stores, France, October 13, 2026.

The absence of a claim of responsibility by hacktivists or a ransom demand by cybercriminals puzzles French investigators

PARIS, France – French investigators on Tuesday, October 13, were hunting the hackers who seized control of cooling units at hundreds of supermarkets in a cyberattack that underlined the vulnerabilities of connected systems, with no group publicly claiming responsibility.

The investigation comes as Dutch supermarket company Ahold Delhaize grapples with a separate cybersecurity incident that disrupted online services, although Dutch authorities said they saw no connection between the two events.

The absence of a claim of responsibility by hacktivists or a ransom demand by cybercriminals has puzzled French investigators, according to a source with knowledge of the probe. Typically, such groups tend to quickly seek to monetize their hacks or claim credit for them for political ends.

The cyberattack, which manually overrode the temperatures at fridges in supermarket groups including Carrefour, Monoprix, Intermarche, and Cooperative U, appears to have been easy to pull off, three cyber experts told Reuters.

Staff at some Paris supermarkets threw boxes full of perished meat and frozen goods into giant trash containers on Tuesday. At least 350 supermarkets — a small fraction of the total number in France — were caught up in the strike.

France’s cybersecurity agency has said the breach affected fridges that relied on software by Danish firm Danfoss, as well as Copeland and Dixell software.

Danfoss said on Monday that many of the affected units had “reached end of life and no longer receive software or security updates” or were “running outdated firmware.” It said it had “advised customers to keep supported systems updated with the latest firmware and to migrate legacy systems to current-generation solutions”.

The company declined further comment on Tuesday.

Copeland, which owns Dixell, acknowledged the “vulnerability.”

“We are currently working with impacted customers to mitigate the risk,” the company said, adding that it would strengthen cybersecurity.

In Danfoss’ case, the serious vulnerabilities present in older versions of its firmware have been known for months.

On August 9, cybersecurity firm Claroty detailed weaknesses — since patched — in the Danfoss AK-SM 800A controller that could have allowed intruders to bypass authentication and run code on compromised devices.

‘Basic cyber hygiene’

Although the precise mechanism by which attackers compromised the refrigerators has not been publicly disclosed, cybersecurity experts said all signs pointed to a basic stunt enabled both by the failure to adopt Danfoss’ updates and by exposing device interfaces to the internet.

“This is about basic cyber hygiene,” said Ken Munro, a partner at the British cybersecurity firm Pen Test Partners. “Get it wrong and you get a smelly mess of defrosted food.”

He said the well-known vulnerabilities meant the attackers were essentially pushing at an open door, something that meant the hack could easily be “kids messing around”.

“If this was a nation state, why affect only a subset of French fridges? There are plenty of other nations with fridges on the internet,” he said. “No ransom or demand suggests a lack of appreciation of the potential commercial losses that the fridge owners may experience.”

Problem still exists

Plenty of fridges remain reachable via the internet. Using the internet scanning service Shodan, Reuters found at least 4,500 Danfoss interfaces still viewable on Tuesday.

Reuters could not independently establish how many of them were running vulnerable software, but French internet scanning company Onyphe said only a small minority of the devices appeared to be running the latest version of the software.

Outdated and vulnerable versions were “still widely represented among publicly accessible interfaces”, Onyphe said.

Dutch disruption

Separately, Dutch retailer Ahold Delhaize said on Tuesday it had begun “starting a controlled re-launch of certain systems” following a cybersecurity issue that began on Sunday evening.

The Dutch cybersecurity watchdog NCSC said it did not believe the incident was linked to the French supermarket hack.

Ahold operates the Albert Heijn chain in the Netherlands and several major US chains including Stop & Shop and Giant Food. Websites for stores in both countries remained offline late Tuesday afternoon, with online ordering and delivery services unavailable. – Rappler.com

World.title: TIMELINE: Changes in AFP’s structure since revised modernization law
World.content:
Here’s a breakdown of major changes in the military’s organization and structure since the Revised AFP Modernization Act was signed in 2012

It has been nearly 14 years since then-president Benigno Aquino III signed the Revised Armed Forces of the Philippines (AFP) Modernization Act, a landmark law that enabled the military not only to acquire modern assets but also to review its structure and personnel.

Many of the adjustments reflect the Philippines’ goal of shifting its focus from internal security operations to territorial defense.

Here’s a breakdown of how the AFP’s organizational structure has shifted since then:

February 23, 1995

The first AFP Modernization Act is signed. Aside from acquisition of assets, the plan includes components on force restructuring and organizational development as well as human resource development. The latter puts emphasis on the need for the AFP to transition from an internal security-oriented force to a primarily external security-oriented force.

But reluctance from Congress to fund it, as well as the 1997 Asian financial crisis, prevented the plan from taking off, a 2005 paper by defense expert Renato de Castro said.

The law’s implementation period lapsed 15 years later in February 2010.

January 1, 2011

The AFP’s six-year Internal Peace and Security Plan — more commonly known as Oplan Bayanihan — takes effect. It aims to eventually allow the AFP to transition into a territorial defense-focused force.

From 2011 to 2013, the AFP continued its primary task of fighting internal armed threats. The remaining years — 2014 to 2016 — were focused on handing over the lead role in internal peace and security to appropriate civilian agencies.

October 2011

The Defense Planning Guidance (2013–2018) is released, according to a 2016 study by De Castro. It restructures the AFP into a “lean but fully capable” military to confront the challenges to the country’s territorial integrity and maritime security. The guide emphasizes the importance of naval assets.

The guide also includes the reduction of infantry and marine battalions so limited financial resources could be redirected to key priorities. These reductions would take effect in 2012.

May 4, 2012

The military’s development arm and anti-insurgency unit, the National Development Support Command, is abolished. It was first formed in 2006 under the Arroyo government to handle the military’s development programs in far-flung areas and address insurgency.

July 12, 2012

The AFP National Capital Region Command (NCRCOM) is deactivated. It had mainly served as an anti-coup unit in the capital region.

A smaller joint military task force for Metro Manila is activated to take NCRCOM’s place, called the Joint Task Force (JTF) NCR.

December 11, 2012

Aquino signs the Revised AFP Modernization Act. It effectively restarts the clock on the modernization program, but also amends the language used to describe the components on force restructuring and human resource development.

The revised law says the AFP should be transformed into a “multi-mission oriented force” that has the shifting capability to meet internal and external threats.

February 2014

Responsibility for Bajo de Masinloc (Scarborough Shoal), a high-tide elevation some 120 nautical miles off Zambales, is transferred from the Tarlac-based Northern Luzon Command (Nolcom) to the Palawan-based Western Command (Wescom).

The move is meant to put the country’s external defense efforts under one commander. Wescom also has more ships and aircraft capable of monitoring the shoal.

March 16, 2016

The Philippine Navy activates its Submarine Group to “lay the groundwork for undersea warfare.”

April 6, 2018

Special operations are effectively unified under one command, after then-president Rodrigo Duterte deactivated the Army Special Operations Command and transferred its personnel to the newly activated AFP Special Operations Command (AFPSOCOM).

The AFPSOCOM is tasked with commanding all the military’s elite units: the Special Operations Wing of the Air Force, Naval Special Operations Group of the Navy, Scout Ranger Regiment, Special Forces Regiment (Airborne) and Light Reaction Regiment of the Army, and Joint Special Operations Group of the General Headquarters.

June 2018

The AFP activates the AFP Cyber Group (AFPCyG).

April 13, 2022

Duterte signs Republic Act No. 11709, which sets a fixed three-year term for high-ranking AFP officers, including the chief of staff. The law is said to end a “revolving door” policy that gave rise to military chiefs serving for only a few months before mandatory retirement.

Other provisions in the law intend to strengthen the merit system of the AFP and ensure continuity of programs and policies.

September to November 2022

The 4th Marine Brigade transfers from Sulu to Ilocos Norte. It is now under the command of Nolcom, which means it is also responsible for Scarborough Shoal and the Philippine Rise, key features in the West Philippine Sea. (READ: From Sulu to Burgos, the Marines’ Fourth Brigade comes home)

May 17, 2023

President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. amends the law fixing high-ranking AFP officers’ terms to three years. The AFP chief is given a “maximum tour of duty” of three consecutive years, instead of the “fixed tour of duty” in the previous law.

The maximum tour of duty of the commanding generals of the Army, Navy, and Air Force are also set to two years instead of the three stipulated in the law Duterte signed.

January 11, 2024

The AFP reactivates its counterintelligence group that is tasked with protecting the military against espionage, sabotage, and other intelligence activities.

The unit was first organized in 1989 and disbanded in 1995 to create a presidential task force on intelligence and counterintelligence instead. (READ: Why did the Philippines reactivate its military counterintelligence group?)

January 24, 2024

Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jr. announces that the AFP is embarking on a “comprehensive archipelagic defense concept.” It is the country’s strategy to secure its vast maritime areas.

August 21, 2024

A new AFP Intelligence Command is activated “to enhance the nation’s intelligence capabilities in response to evolving security challenges,” according to AFP spokesperson Colonel Francel Margareth Padilla.

Late 2024

The AFPCyG becomes the AFP Cyber Command sometime in late 2024. Expanding the group into a command allows it to have more personnel and equipment. (READ: AFP chief Brawner eyes ‘Cyber Command’)

February 28, 2025

JTF NCR once again becomes the NCRCOM.

March 31, 2025

The reorganization of the Naval Forces West to the Western Naval Command and the Naval Forces Northern Luzon to the Northern Luzon Naval Command is approved. (READ: Presence is deterrence: The Philippine Navy’s pivot)

May 28, 2025

The AFP reorganizes special operations again, deactivating the AFPSOCOM and simultaneously reactivating the Special Operations Command of the Philippine Army and creating the Joint Special Operations Command of the AFP.

October 27, 2025

The AFP officially activates the AFP Strategic Command. It is described as a “strategic hub where intelligence, operations, and civil-military functions converge,” and is tasked with overseeing and synchronizing joint exercises and engagements with allies and partners.

July 2026

The AFP announces plans for a space force or a space command by 2028. – Rappler.com

World.title: In Philippines’ external defense push, resilience boils down to logistics
World.content:
As the Revised AFP Modernization Act approaches the end of its 15-year horizon, what upgrades are in store for the Philippine military?

MODERN FLEET. The BRP Tarlac (LD-601) sails in waters close to Bajo de Masinloc (Scarborough Shoal) alongside partner navies for an ADMM-Plus joint sail in September 2026.

Hereâs a breakdown of major changes in the militaryâs organization and structure since the Revised AFP Modernization Act was signed in 2012

READ TIMELINE: Changes in AFPâs structure since revised modernization law Hereâs a breakdown of major changes in the militaryâs organization and structure since the Revised AFP Modernization Act was signed in 2012 â

Senior officers of the military are not one to take for granted the relative speed at which modernization has taken place.

The Indonesia-made BRP Tarlac and BRP Davao del Sur, named after the home provinces of the presidents under whom they were commissioned, will soon be joined by the BRP Ilocos Norte and the BRP Leyte. At least four more OPVs of the BRP Rajah Sulayman class will be delivered to the Philippines, and the BRP Diego Silang will eventually be joined by two more sister ships.

Today, more vessels are coming â mostly brand-new ones, although both Japan and South Korea are also set to transfer their existing five and two warships each.

Then-military chief Gregorio Catapang Jr. recalled that in one naval gunfire exercise, rust icicles would fall on the beddings of sailors inside a hand-me-down battleship. At the time, the Navyâs newest vessel was the BRP Conrado Yap, a secondhand corvette from the South Korean Navy. Before her were the secondhand vessels from the US, the Del Pilar class.

Teodoro says Misamis Oriental will be center of Navy ops in Northern Mindanao, Visayas

READ Teodoro says Misamis Oriental will be center of Navy ops in Northern Mindanao, Visayas

This is why the defense department is looking to finally acquire and convert some 300 hectares of the state-owned Philippine Veterans Investment Development Corporation (Phividec) Industrial Estate in Tagoloan, Misamis Oriental, into a naval base that will include drydock facilities. However, over a year since Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jr. confirmed that the department was proceeding with the planned acquisition, talks have yet to wrap up.

The privately owned NOB-Subic is still the largest port facility for the Navy. The waters off the Naval Station Heracleo Alano in Cavite (popularly known as Sangley Point) are far too shallow for the newest assets of the Philippine Fleet.

That the Philippine Navyâs newest and most modern platforms are docked in a private facility in Subic, where the government must pay fees for usage, illustrates the difficulties the AFP continues to face despite strides in modernization since 2012.

On the other side of the lineup was the freshly commissioned BRP Rajah Lakandula, an OPV. It was the first to berth at the Naval Station Jose Andrada in Manila, after dredging work in the area.

Beside Tarlac was the BRP Ramon Alcaraz, a US coast guard cutter commissioned to the Philippines in 2013. Sheâs a senior citizen in human years, but remains a steady and reliable workhorse for the fleet, especially for maritime patrols in all fronts of the countryâs maritime spaces.

The BRP Tarlac, an Indonesia-made landing platform dock, was the first major vessel to be delivered in 2016 under the new modernization program. Beside it stood a similar ship, the BRP Davao del Sur. Both Tarlac and Davao del Sur are the largest of the Navyâs vessels that perform a wide array of tasks â humanitarian and disaster response, as well as resupply missions for features in the West Philippine Sea.

Flanking the frigates were the modern fleetâs first and latest acquisitions.

Silang docked beside her sister ship, the BRP Miguel Malvar, which was commissioned in the summer of 2025. With them were two similar ships, BRP Jose Rizal and BRP Antonio Luna, the first brand-new frigates that the Navy acquired in 2020 and 2021 after a long wait. Before this, the Navy had to live with old ships from other countries which it would refurbish.

In August when we paid a visit one damp and humid evening, we saw the BRP Diego Silang (FFG-07) berth at the shipyard after almost a week out at sea for a maritime patrol and joint drills with Australia and the United States. Already docked beside the spot allocated for her was a fleet of the Navyâs pride â modern frigates that were acquired, in relative rapid succession, under the Revised Armed Forces of the Philippines (AFP) Modernization Act.

Yet, what a sight to behold â a fleet of six modern gray ships now owned by a navy of an archipelago that had, for decades, had to make do with hand-me-downs from its allies.

Despite its ambitions, the Navy does not have its own docking facility to accommodate its brand-new frigates and offshore patrol vessels (OPVs). The big shipyard here that holds the countryâs finest warships is owned by private firm Agila Subic Compass, which assigns its own civilian security at the first two gates that visitors enter.

SUBIC, Philippines â When visiting the Philippine Navyâs newest warships at the Naval Operating Base (NOB) in Subic, most people â including military personnel â go through at least three gates. The long wait at the first gate speaks volumes of how the vision of a modern armed forces turns into reality.

SILANGâS CHIEF. Captain John Percie Alcos is the first commanding officer of the BRP Diego Silang.

But where do they go? Where would they be serviced?

âWe have always been able to perform our mandate with the limited assets that we used to have. Now, with the assets in our inventory, we can do more and perform our mandate,â he told reporters.

At the end of a maritime drill in August 2026, Captain John Percie Alcos was asked about the strides the Navy has made in its modernization plan in over a decade. Alcos was the last commander of the first BRP Miguel Malvar (PS-19) before it was decommissioned in 2021. The first Malvar was a US warship that was transferred to Vietnam before eventually finding her way to the Philippine Navy. Alcos also commanded the BRP Andres Bonifacio (PS-42) of the Del Pilar class, before being appointed Navy spokesperson and eventually, the first commanding officer of the new Silang.

North, west, and everything in between

The AFPâs long-overdue modernization, to a large extent, was spurred by China. In 2012, the Philippine Navy was in a brief standoff with Chinese maritime forces in Bajo de Masinloc (Scarborough Shoal). By June that year, the Philippines eventually withdrew the white-hulled Philippine Coast Guard (PCG) vessel, expecting China to do the same under a deal supposedly brokered by the United States. Beijing stayed. To this day, at least one China Coast Guard (CCG) ship is stationed at the opening of the shoal, with at least one or two more roving within its vicinity. Chinese Maritime Militia serve as force multipliers in Beijingâs sovereignty claim over the shoal. In early December 2012, the Philippine Congress passed Republic Act No. 10349 or the Revised Armed Forces of the Philippines Modernization Program Act, a 15-year plan divided into three horizons. READ FAST FACTS: Big ticket items in the Philippine Navyâs modernization Chinaâs actions and apparent aspirations in the West Philippine Sea, an area that includes the Philippinesâ exclusive economic zone (EEZ) and features where it has sovereignty claims, is the most obvious priority in the military and the reason for the Navyâs shift in focus to external defense. But the western front is only one of five critical spots that the Navy must cover, through its fleet, the Marines, and other units that monitor and detect potential threats. To the east is the Pacific Ocean, with the yet-to-be-tapped Philippine Rise in the northeastern part of the countryâs vast maritime area. The âbigger domainâ east to the Philippines is where the military must âstart building infrastructure and logistical bases,â said Teodoro in an August 2026 budget hearing. Down south are both sea-lanes and porous borders between the southernmost Philippines and neighbors Malaysia and Indonesia.

NORTH Batanes and Taiwan WEST West Philippine Sea EAST Pacific Ocean, Philippine Rise BETWEEN Archipelagic sea-lanes SOUTH Sea-lanes, borders with Malaysia and Indonesia The five critical spots the Navy must cover. Locations are approximate.

Between the major island groups are archipelagic sea-lanes that are vital not only for domestic use but also for international trade and freedom of navigation. The Philippine Archipelagic Sea Lanes Act codified the 2016 Arbitral Award by identifying where foreign vessels, including the military kind, may pass. Up north is where the AFP, non-uniformed experts, and pundits may feel the most anxious. Taiwan, an issue that for China is even touchier than the South China Sea, is a flashpoint for tensions not only between independently governed Taipei and Beijing, but the rest of the region. Self-proclaimed Chinese scholars have claimed that the northernmost Batanes province is part of Taiwan and therefore, also Chinaâs. The Chinese embassy in Manila, in September 2026, claimed âsovereign rightsâ over waters between Batanes and Taiwan. Tensions over northernmost features started after the Philippines and Japan announced maritime delimitation talks. President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. has ruled out offensive attacks from the Philippines, even in the event of a Taiwan conflict. But the sheer proximity of the countryâs northern provinces to Taiwan is also why Marcos has said that Manila would be dragged into the conflict âkicking and screaming.â All of those potential flashpoints and weakpoints are where the Navy â the fleet, the Marines, and special units like the elite Special Warfare Force â is expected to always be on the frontlines and in the forefront. READ Philippines tells China: Leave Panganiban, Zamora reefs in West PH Sea Itâs a tall order when budgets are perennially tight, assets remain limited to serve a vast archipelago, and resource gaps exist. But as one officer once put it, the Navy and the rest of the armed forces have always managed to do the most with even the barest of means.

The western frontier

NAVY WORKHORSE. The BRP Ramon Alcaraz (PS-41) is moored inside Ulugan Bay in Palawan in June 2025. Photo by Bea Cupin/Rappler

On most days, Ulugan Bay in Palawan is a picture of calm. Tucked in the middle of Palawan island, the bay is close to the Western Command (Wescom) in Puerto Princesa City, the site of an air base where American troops may preposition assets under the bilateral Enhanced Defense Cooperation Agreement. Itâs the center of West Philippine Sea operations for the Philippine military. From Ulugan Bay, Pag-asa (Thitu) Island, the Philippinesâ farthest civilian-populated island in the west, is just around a dayâs sail away. It takes under two hours by military cargo plane to fly from Wescomâs Antonio Bautista Air Base to Rancudo Airfield in the remote island. On a rainy June afternoon in 2024, the three vessels of the Del Pilar class â the BRP Gregorio del Pilar, the BRP Ramon Alcaraz, and the BRP Andres Bonifacio â were all moored in the middle of the bay as inclement weather slowly creeped into the Palawan mainland from the West Philippine Sea. The Bonifacio had just narrowly missed bad weather in the West Philippine Sea after a weeklong Maritime Domain Awareness mission with reporters on board. The same weather conditions would cause a Chinese fishing vessel to run aground near Pag-asa (Thitu) Island. The Del Pilar, former US Coast Guard cutters that were launched in the 1960s and commissioned into the Philippine Navy as frigates in 2011, 2013, and 2016, are the senior citizens of the Philippine Fleet. They have since been upgraded beginning in the 2020s to more modern systems, as the South Korea-made frigates started arriving and the Del Pilar ships were reclassified as OPVs. Dotting the shoreline of Ulugan Bay are private and public resorts and secluded homes â that is, until you get closer to Naval Detachment Oyster Bay, where smaller patrol ships, attack craft, and the Navyâs supply vessels are usually docked. The detachment itself is surrounded by vast greenery. In 2002, then-president Gloria Macapagal-Arroyo declared at least 1,838 hectares of land as part of the Ulugan Bay Naval Reservation, with most of it dedicated for what was then the proposed Naval Operating Base Ulugan. More than two decades later, Oyster Bay is the site of major upgrades, thanks in part to the United States, treaty-ally of the Philippines. In 2025, the US announced several plans for the bay â a boat repair and maintenance facility, a fast boat base, and maintenance facility for unmanned surface vessels. These planned upgrades are a huge boost to the capabilities of the Wescom, whose area of operation includes most of the West Philippine Sea â from the BRP Sierra Madre in Ayungin Shoal to Pag-asa (Thitu) Island, located beyond the countryâs EEZ. Theyâre part of the Navyâs âbroader effort to strengthen the Armed Forces of the Philippinesâ external defense capabilities, particularly its ability to sustain maritime operations in the West Philippine Sea,â said Navy public affairs chief Captain Marie Angelica Sisican in a message to Rappler. Sisican, citing Teodoroâs earlier statements from 2024, said naval facilities on the western side of Palawan would âreduce the distance that naval assets would otherwise have to cover in conducting operations.â US-funded projects, including the boat maintenance facilities, are âintended to enhance the [Philippine Navyâs] repair and maintenance capabilities for watercraft, including unmanned surface vessels, while improving existing infrastructure.â The facility will cater to both the AFP and the PCG for âcapabilities related to maritime security, maritime domain awareness, interoperability, and infrastructure development.â Indeed, itâs the Wescom in Palawan and the Northern Command up north that have become the focus of US assistance. Americaâs âonce-in-a-generation investmentâ was first announced in 2024, a total of $500 million in foreign military financing for the Philippines. This has since grown to a $2.5-billion commitment in military aid over five years, from 2026 to 2030, under the US 2026 National Defense Authorization Act signed in December 2025.

US military aid to the Philippines 2024 Â· Foreign military financing $500 million 2026â2030 Â· US 2026 NDAA $2.5 billion

The support for the US-Philippine alliance is one of the bipartisan issues in a deeply divided Washington, an indication not just of shared values but of common strategic interests. Even as US President Donald Trump has signaled a âstrategic stabilityâ with China, America still wants a âfavorable, but durable, balance of power in which no state â including China â can impose its hegemony and hold the security or prosperity of our nation and our allies in question,â said US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth at the Shangri-La Dialogue in Singapore in May 2026. READ No alibis: Retooling and modernizing the Marines But even with bipartisan support for aid to fund the Philippinesâ military upgrades, the White Houseâs message for partners and especially allies is clear: burdens must be shared. âAlliances only work when they are true partnerships. It is a two-way street. You don't have a strong alliance unless everyone has skin in the game. No freeloading,â said Hegseth in Singapore.

The Navyâs latest warship

RADIO CHALLENGE. The BRP Diego Silang (FFG-7) issues a radio challenge to a Chinese warship that was tailing it during an August 2026 multilateral joint sail in the West Philippine Sea. Photo from AFP PAO

World.title: LIVE UPDATES: Impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte
World.content:
WHAT YOU NEED TO KNOW

The impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte — the first Philippine public official to be impeached twice by the House of Representatives — began at 2 pm on Monday, July 6.

There are four articles of impeachment against Duterte involving alleged misuse of confidential funds, unexplained wealth, bribery of Department of Education officials, and grave threats against President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. and his family.

Only 21 out of 24 senator-judges are physically present. Senator Bato dela Rosa remains in hiding as he faces an International Criminal Court arrest warrant over Rodrigo Duterte’s drug war, Senator Jinggoy Estrada has been detained and suspended in connection with a plunder case, and Senator Rodante Marcoleta surrendered to authorities as he also faces a plunder case.

On this page, we bring you the latest updates, analyses, videos, and photos as the trial of the Vice President unfolds.
