World.title: Georgia to raise pensions for under-70s by 45 lari instead of 20
World.content:
Pension increase in Georgia

From 1 January 2027, the Georgian government will increase pensions for people under 70 by 45 lari instead of the planned 20 lari. Their monthly pension will therefore rise to 415 lari (around $160). Meanwhile, Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze argues that setting a minister’s salary below 12,000 lari encourages officials to engage in corruption.

As of August 2026, 905,000 people in Georgia received an old-age pension. Of these, 420,000 were under 70, while 485,000 were aged 70 or older. The initial draft budget for 2027 allocated up to 5.6bn lari (around $2.16bn) for pensions. The announced change will increase this amount by 128m lari (around $49.4m), bringing the total to 5.7bn lari. Under the law, an ordinary member of parliament’s salary, before tax, should rise by 1,080 lari, from 12,800 to 13,880 lari (around $5,359). The Georgian Dream party may decide not to implement this increase.

Kobakhidze said the indexation mechanism under current legislation would have increased pensions by just 20 lari. However, the government decided to raise payments further. The change does not apply to pensioners living in mountainous settlements, where different rules govern pension supplements.

Implementing the decision announced today will require an additional 128m lari in state budget spending.

What did Irakli Kobakhidze say?

According to the prime minister, social spending accounts for more than 33% of the state budget. Available figures show that the government allocated more than 5bn lari for old-age pensions in 2026, while 540m lari went towards co-financing the funded pension system. For comparison, Kobakhidze noted that pension spending totalled 1.065bn lari in 2012.

Kobakhidze said further increases in social spending carry fiscal and macroeconomic risks. He stressed that social spending had already reached the upper limit recommended by international financial institutions. Exceeding that threshold, he warned, could slow economic growth, fuel inflation and undermine Georgia’s access to international financing.

Nevertheless, he promised that the Georgian Dream government would continue looking for ways to increase pensions for people under 70 beyond the statutory indexation rate in the coming years. He added, however, that any increase must remain within acceptable budgetary limits.

Alongside the pension announcement, Kobakhidze addressed public sector pay, linking low ministerial salaries to potential corruption risks.

“Paying a minister less than 12,000 lari means pushing them towards corruption,” he said, explaining that new figures put a minister’s take-home salary at around 12,000 lari.

Kobakhidze argued that a private sector role with comparable responsibilities and workload could pay between 50,000 and 100,000 lari a month. He rejected the suggestion that 12,000 lari was a high salary for a minister.

“Given the work a minister does and the responsibilities they bear, they would earn at least 50,000–100,000 lari in a comparable private sector role. Yet we are expected to accept that 12,000 lari is a high salary for a minister. Is that reasonable? Is it really that high?” Kobakhidze said.

He noted that ensuring public officials receive decent salaries forms part of the government’s anti-corruption policy. In this context, he recalled the previous government’s time in office, saying that Bidzina Ivanishvili, the founder of Georgian Dream, had used his own money to pay salary supplements to public servants. Kobakhidze presented this practice as a measure to combat corruption.

How much will the pension increase cost Georgia’s budget?

Paata Kvizhinadze, chairman of the parliamentary Finance and Budget Committee, said that raising an MP’s salary by 1,080 lari would cost the state budget 1–1.3 million lari. By contrast, increasing the old-age pension by just 1 lari would require 11 million lari.

“MPs’ salaries are not set to increase under the initial draft budget. Even if the increase had been included, it would have added only slightly more than a million lari to budget expenditure — around 1.3 million lari. Meanwhile, raising pensions by 10 lari requires 111 million lari, while an increase of just 1 lari costs 11 million lari. Therefore, we should not link MPs’ salary increases to pension increases,” Kvizhinadze said.

Pension increase in Georgia

World.title: From Uzbekistan to EU: Where Armenian goods are exported after Russia imposes restrictions
World.content:
Changes in the geography of Armenian exports

On 10 October, a preferential trade regime for Armenian goods exported to the European Union came into force. Under the EU decision to apply autonomous trade measures, the bloc will liberalise around 80% of imports from Armenia by removing import duties. The measures will cover a wide range of goods, including agricultural products.

The European Union has decided to support Armenia in response to restrictions that Russia has imposed on Armenian goods. Since May, Russia has banned imports of Armenian fruit, vegetables, fish products, alcohol and many other goods. Russian agencies responsible for enforcing the restrictions cited alleged failures to meet quality standards. However, it later became clear that Armenia’s closer integration with Europe had prompted the measures.

Exports of Armenian-origin goods to EU countries have grown for several months. In effect, this trend began before the preferential trade regime came into force. From January to June 2026, Armenia exported more than $516m worth of goods to the EU. This marked an increase of more than 80% compared with the same period last year.

Exports to EU countries are now expected to grow further. At the same time, Armenia is seeking other markets.

The local outlet Factor TV analysed the results of these efforts. Drawing on data from the Ministry of Economy and the Food Safety Inspection Body, it compiled a list of countries that received significant volumes of Armenian goods. The findings show that products traditionally exported to Russia now go to Uzbekistan, Kazakhstan, Georgia, Ukraine and Iraq.

More than 94% of exports went to three countries

According to data from the Food Safety Inspection Body, Uzbekistan, Georgia and Ukraine accounted for more than 94% of Armenia’s fruit exports in June 2026:

48% of fruit exports went to Uzbekistan,

around 34% went to Georgia,

approximately 12% went to Ukraine.

Georgia took the lead in July, accounting for around 35.3% of exports. Uzbekistan followed with 21%, Kazakhstan with 13%, Ukraine with 10.5% and Iraq with around 8.2%.

By comparison, in June 2025, Russia alone accounted for 86.7% of Armenian fruit exports. The figure rose to 87.2% in July.

State budget compensation for exporters

In response to the restrictions Russia imposed, the Armenian government launched support programmes for local exporters. These include subsidies and cash compensation, including payments to cover export duties in other markets.

In June and July, the government paid around 3.96bn drams ($10.3m) in compensation to exporters of strawberries, apricots, sweet cherries, plums, nectarines and peaches.

Over these two months, the state covered costs associated with around 90% of the export volume:

“The total volume of strawberry, apricot, sweet cherry, plum, nectarine and peach exports reached around 16,752 tonnes. The state budget provided compensation for 15,083 tonnes.”

Support programmes also continued in August. The government allocated around 4.52bn drams ($11.8m) that month to support exports and purchases of agricultural produce. This sum also covered costs for exporters of vegetables and flowers.

How the compensation was distributed

The figures for June and July show that apricots and sweet cherries accounted for 81% of the 3.9bn drams ($10.3m) allocated to fruit exports:

The government allocated around 1.86bn drams ($4.8m) for apricots.

Sweet cherries received around 1.33bn drams ($3.5m).

The government also paid compensation for strawberry, peach, nectarine and plum exports, but the amounts were smaller.

Exporters do not receive compensation automatically for every kilogram of produce they ship abroad. They must apply to the Ministry of Economy and submit customs or transit declarations, along with invoices confirming the exports. The ministry reviews each application and pays the compensation if it finds no discrepancies in the documents.

Under the government’s decision, compensation rates per kilogram stood at 770 drams ($2) for strawberries, 200 drams ($0.5) for apricots, 250 drams ($0.6) for nectarines and 400 drams ($1) for sweet cherries. For some fruits, the compensation came close to the average market price. In June, for example, strawberries sold for an average of 933 drams ($2.4) per kilogram.

Changes in the geography of Armenian exports

World.title: Non-medical support during childbirth in Armenia: who are doulas and what do they do?
World.content:
Doulas in Armenia: non-medical support for pregnant women

The first certified doulas appeared in Armenia six years ago. Yet few women know that they can turn to doulas for support during pregnancy, childbirth and even after giving birth.

Doulas are not medical professionals. They help women manage labour pain through massage and breathing techniques, while also providing emotional support. Women now have a choice about who accompanies them during these hours. Some still prefer to have their husbands, mothers or sisters by their side. Others choose to give birth with a doula.

A doula with a woman in labour in the antenatal ward. Photo: Yvetta Kosyan-Suvorova

Most doulas enter the profession after a negative personal experience

Yvetta Kosyan-Suvorova says women decide to become doulas after giving birth themselves. Sometimes they want to share a positive experience. More often, however, they turn to the profession because of a negative experience.

“I took a long journey to get to this point. I gave birth twice. My second birth was therapeutic and healing. I realised that a woman’s preparation, knowledge and expectations largely determine how childbirth unfolds. The problem is that women often have expectations that do not match reality. This can lead to traumatic consequences,” she says.

Иветта с мужем и сыновьями

Yvetta says her husband stayed by her side during both births. The first was a terrifying experience for both of them. The second went differently because they had both prepared for it. This time, they could talk to each other, joke and even dance during labour. She remembers the birth as “a wonderful process”.

She recalls that seven days before her second child was born, she listened to a lecture by an American doula. She remembers everything that might prove important during childbirth:

“Before that lecture, I was determined not to let anything that happened during my first birth happen again. For eight months, I told my doctor that I refused to give birth naturally. I insisted on a caesarean section. But that one-hour lecture changed everything for me. I realised I could understand my hormones and my surroundings, and that I could control many things. Ultimately, I could simply give it a try.

“My second birth went smoothly, without anxiety, and so quickly that after I was discharged, I kept telling my husband I wanted to offer to help pregnant women during labour and reassure them. Of course, those plans never came to fruition because they were unrealistic expectations.”

Yet the idea stayed with Yvetta for the next ten years. Eventually, she began working with pregnant women and women in labour, but as a photographer. Her family was living abroad at the time, where maternity photography was very popular. When she moved to Armenia, she expected to find plenty of clients for similar photo shoots. However, she says, almost all women in labour there turned down her offers.

“Either they invited me into the maternity ward not to take photographs that would capture this important moment in their lives, but simply because they did not want to be alone. But a photographer cannot intervene; they are like a shadow. Their presence should be as discreet as possible. I realised that, ultimately, I could not help women.”

Immediately after childbirth. Photo: Yvetta Kosyan-Suvorova

Yvetta’s dream of becoming a doula came true during the coronavirus pandemic, when many training centres moved their courses online. Yvetta completed a course, passed her exams and received an international doula certification. She became the first doula in Armenia.

Who are doulas?

Doulas are trained professionals who support pregnant women, women in labour and those who need help during the postnatal period. They prepare women for childbirth and stay by their side throughout labour in the delivery room. Doulas provide informational, emotional and physical support.

During labour, doulas help women through massage, pressure techniques and touch. Sometimes they simply offer encouragement; at other times, they explain what is happening in a woman’s body at that moment. They suggest different positions and help women feel comfortable and safe throughout the process. This can increase the likelihood of a positive birth outcome.

Yvetta helps a woman in labour manage the pain.

According to Yvetta, in countries where many women use doula services, they start looking for a doula in the early stages of pregnancy, sometimes even when planning to conceive:

“Since doulas can take on only a small number of pregnant women each month, women book their services well in advance. They try to avoid complications this way, as there may be no available doulas when they go into labour. The situation in Armenia is different. Women who have given birth before usually contact us earlier in their pregnancy. First-time mothers tend to get in touch later, around weeks 28–30, when they start preparing for childbirth.”

Yvetta believes women should not leave the search for a doula until the final weeks of pregnancy. Sometimes doulas have to turn women away because the medical facility where they plan to give birth does not allow them into the maternity ward.

Armenia’s Ministry of Health has yet to recognise how much the work of a trained doula differs from the support a husband, mother, friend or anyone else can provide. Armenian law also contains no regulations governing their work.

There are only five or six doulas in Armenia

Most trained and received certification through Doula Link, a platform run by Russia’s Institute for Perinatal Support. They thereby became members of the European Doula Network. This allows them to provide doula services in Russia, Germany, Switzerland, Serbia, the Czech Republic, Slovakia, Spain, Italy, Israel and Panama.

In Armenia, people regard doulas as unqualified assistants.

A 2020 order issued by the health minister gives all women in labour the right to have a companion present during childbirth. However, some medical facilities still refuse to let doulas into the delivery room.

Moreover, some maternity hospitals charge a fee for allowing a companion to attend the birth. The Ministry of Health does not regulate this practice.

Why do women turn to doulas?

Yvetta says women in Armenia mainly choose to give birth with a doula because they want someone they trust by their side. They need someone who understands what is happening and what to do, can keep track of the situation and looks after them. They also hope to avoid traumatic experiences, including obstetric violence.

“Of course, having a support person present cannot guarantee that a woman will never experience abuse. But a doula is someone who will listen to her and understand her. I am convinced that in 99% of cases involving abuse, doctors do not intend to cause harm.

“They often intervene to reduce certain risks. Yet they do not answer the woman’s questions or explain why they have decided to intervene, even when the intervention involves surgery. A doula will at least ask why the intervention is necessary and why it needs to happen at that particular moment. Women feel safer when a doula is by their side,” Yvetta says.

A mother with her baby after childbirth. Photo: Yvetta Kosyan-Suvorova

In 2024–2025, the United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA) conducted a study of women’s experiences during pregnancy and childbirth in 16 countries across Eastern Europe and Central Asia, including Armenia.

The study found that 67% of the women surveyed had experienced at least one form of obstetric violence.

In Armenia, around 55% of respondents said medical staff had performed obstetric interventions without their consent or any explanation. Meanwhile, 32% reported mistreatment by medical staff, highlighting a lack of information or pressure to make them agree to certain interventions.

Another 27% reported poor-quality care, such as inadequate staff qualifications. Around 15% of women experienced verbal aggression, while 5% reported physical violence. Eleven per cent of respondents reported various forms of sexual violence, including excessive or inappropriate touching.

Why don’t women turn to doulas?

Yvetta admits that 80% of the pregnant women who contact her are foreigners who, for various reasons, give birth in Armenia. Local women tend to be more cautious. The main problem, in the doula’s view, is a lack of information. Stereotypical attitudes also play an important role. Many people see childbirth as something women must go through on their own, without any need for additional support.

Waiting for childbirth. Photo: Yvetta Kosyan-Suvorova

“But this is the wrong approach, because every woman in labour is vulnerable. It is very important that, by the end, she feels like a winner because she has brought a new person into the world, rather than feeling broken and miserable after enduring unbearable suffering. Unfortunately, most women still prefer to overcome their fears of childbirth and pain not with a doula’s help, but by paying for a caesarean section. They believe this will solve the problem,” she says.

Sometimes women do not turn to doulas because they assume their services will be expensive. Yvetta does not specify how much she charges. However, she says she sometimes helps pregnant women entirely free of charge because she sees this work as her mission.

“Being a doula is a calling. This work is first and foremost about your inner world and your heart, and only then about your skills.”

She recalls that when she first started working as a doula, she sometimes returned home exhausted and upset. She even considered giving it up. Poor working conditions and hostility from doctors and hospital administrators were the main sources of stress. She also felt distressed when her presence created additional difficulties for the woman in labour.

Now she knows which maternity hospitals allow her to do her job most effectively. Some doctors there see doulas not as competitors but as professionals who support their work. Every birth has therefore become a wonderful experience for her.

“Now I come home happy because I no longer suffer alongside a woman during labour; instead, I help her avoid suffering. I can see that my work makes a difference. I see a woman who was screaming in pain and fear stop screaming, get up and start dancing,” Yvetta says.

Yvetta with the parents of a baby born with her support

Doulas in Armenia: non-medical support for pregnant women

World.title: International exhibition on restoration of Karabakh opens in Baku
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 14. The 6th Azerbaijan International Exhibition for the Restoration, Reconstruction, and Development of Karabakh - "Rebuild Garabagh 2026" - is launching in Baku, Trend’s correspondent reports from the event.

The exhibition, held at the Baku Expo Center from October 14 through 16, will address topics such as the restoration of Karabakh and East Zangezur, modern urban planning, construction technologies, eco-friendly materials, agricultural machinery, digital media, education, and industrial cooperation.

By bringing together local and foreign companies, government agencies, experts, and potential investors, the exhibition aims to create new opportunities for cooperation regarding the development of the liberated territories. According to the organizers, the platform's primary objectives are to attract more enterprises to the Karabakh restoration process, expand investment opportunities, and foster collaboration in infrastructure development and the construction of civil facilities.

The exhibition aims to showcase products, services, and solutions across sectors such as energy, ecology, information technology, construction, agriculture, the food industry, mining, transport, healthcare, security, education, tourism and cultural heritage, as well as road construction and infrastructure.

Government agencies, representatives from the architectural sector, and international delegates attending the opening ceremony

In addition to the official opening ceremony, the program for the first day of the exhibition includes sessions on the participation of youth in the restoration of Karabakh, eco-friendly construction materials, modern construction technologies, and a presentation of Russian agricultural machinery.

The opening ceremony is scheduled to be attended by Special Representative of the President of Azerbaijan in Lachin district, Masim Mammadov, Special Representative of the President in Kalbajar district, Bashir Hajiyev, Chairman of the Board of the Karabakh Revival Fund, Rahman Hajiyev, Deputy Chairman of the State Committee for Urban Planning and Architecture, Dovlatkhan Dovlatkhanov, Chairman of the Board of the Union of Architects of Azerbaijan, Elbay Gasimzade, Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary of Italy to Azerbaijan, Luca Di Gianfrancesco, and General Director of Iteca Caspian, Farid Mammadov.

These individuals are listed in the event's official program to deliver welcoming remarks.

Involvement of youth in the development of Karabakh will be discussed

One of the panel discussions scheduled for the first day of the exhibition will focus on the topic "Youth in the revival of Karabakh: Initiatives and Opportunities." The discussion, moderated by Head of the Fundraising and Communications Department at the Karabakh Revival Fund, Parvin Baghirova, will feature the participation of MP Shahin Seyidzade, Deputy Minister of Youth and Sports Farhad Hajiyev, PASHA Bank’s Human Resources Department Director Zibeyda Hajiyeva, and Acting Executive Director of the Youth Foundation Yusif Valiyev.

The panel will serve as a platform for discussing youth participation in the reconstruction process, support for initiatives, and opportunities arising across various sectors.

On the same day, the "Karabakh Hackathon 2026" will also take place as part of the "Year of Urban Planning and Architecture." The hackathon will run throughout the three days of the exhibition.

Eco-friendly building materials and energy efficiency will be in the spotlight

Another session, scheduled for October 14, will focus on discussions regarding eco-friendly building materials and energy-saving solutions. The session, moderated by the Secretary General of the Azerbaijan Construction Materials Manufacturers Association, Shahana Sari, will highlight the importance of construction material production, environmental approaches, and energy-efficient solutions.

Russian agricultural machinery and equipment will be presented

The business program for the first day of the exhibition also includes a presentation of Russian agricultural machinery and equipment.

Representatives from companies such as Yaroslavich, Melinvest, Krasnokamsk RMZ, Rostselmash, Rosspechmash, SALSKSELMASH, SmartC, the St. Petersburg Tractor Plant, and others will participate in the session.

The event will include Deputy Head of the Department for Agricultural, Food, and Construction-Road Machinery Manufacturing at the Ministry of Industry and Trade of Russia, Ilya Orsik; Trade Representative of Russia in Azerbaijan, Adam Khakimov; and Official Representative of the Russian Ministry of Agriculture in Azerbaijan, Nikita Goncharenko.

The session program creates opportunities for establishing connections between agricultural machinery manufacturers and potential buyers and partners.

Digital media and industry-university collaboration will be discussed on the second day

The exhibition will continue on October 15. In addition to visiting the exhibition, the day's agenda includes bilateral business meetings, the Karabakh Hackathon 2026, and a series of panel discussions.

One of the key events of the second day will be a panel discussion titled "Karabakh truths: the potential and social impact of digital media."

Moderated by a representative of the Karabakh Revival Fund, Parvin Baghirova, the discussion will feature MP Hikmat Babaoghlu, Director of ASAN Radio and TV, Emin Musavi, Head of the Department for Work with Media Entities and Journalists at the Media and Broadcasting Council, Natig Mammadli, Head of ASAN AI Hub, Laman Ibrahimova, and a technology journalist and Board Member of the Press Council of Azerbaijan, Farid Pardashunas.

The panel will discuss the potential of digital media and its impact on the dissemination of information regarding Karabakh, public opinion, and the information landscape.

A session titled "Teaching Industrialization: University-Industry Cooperation for a Circular Construction Industry" will also be held on the same day.

Moderated by Deputy Dean of the Faculty of Design and Architecture at ADA University, Leyla Hasanova, the discussion will feature professors Gianluca Pocci and Davide Cerati from Politecnico di Milano and ADA University, CEO of Design Bureau LLC, architect Fizuli Aliyev, and founder and general manager of Glasstech LTD, Elshan Suleymanov.

The discussion will focus on cooperation between universities and the industry, as well as the application of circular economy approaches in the construction sector.

Modern interior and exterior solutions will be presented

Another session, to be held on October 15, is titled "The agile spaces of the future: adapting interiors and exteriors to changing lifestyles."

The session will focus on topics such as adapting spaces to evolving needs and exploring architectural and design solutions.

The day's program also includes a discussion titled "From reconstruction to sustainable development: the role of education in the revival of Karabakh." Participants scheduled for this event include the Head of the Public Relations Department at Garabagh University, Jamila Ismayilzade, Deputy Chairman of the Board of the Economic Zones Development Agency, Agil Azizov, and a representative of the Karabakh Revival Fund, Parvin Baghirova.

The topic provides a platform to discuss the roles of education, economic activity, and various support mechanisms in the development of Karabakh.

Third day’s discussions will focus on architectural policy, cultural heritage, and the future of urban planning

On October 16, the final day of the exhibition, special attention will be paid to issues of architecture and urban planning.

The day's program features a panel discussion on "Architectural policy and cultural heritage preservation in the context of modern construction." Following this, a session titled "Architectural discussions: a new perspective on urban spaces" will be held.

The day's next architectural discussion will focus on the theme "The future of urban planning in Azerbaijan."

The discussions will cover topics such as shaping the modern urban environment, architectural approaches, and preserving cultural heritage.

What sectors will be represented by products and solutions showcased at the exhibition?

"Rebuild Garabagh 2026" isn’t limited to panel discussions alone. According to official information from the organizers, the exhibition covers a wide range of areas related to the restoration and development of Karabakh.

These include energy, ecology, information technology, construction, agriculture, the food industry, mining, transport, healthcare, security, education, tourism and cultural heritage, as well as road construction and infrastructure.

Showcasing innovative products, services, and technological solutions in these sectors, along with establishing new partnerships between companies, are among the exhibition's key objectives.

As the official program does not disclose specific product models or a complete list of all exhibitors, individual... Further details on the products to be showcased are available from the organizers.

The exhibition will run for three days

It will be open to visitors on October 14 from 11:00 to 18:00 (GMT +4), on October 15 from 10:00 to 18:00, and on October 16 from 10:00 to 17:00.

According to the organizers, simultaneous interpretation in Azerbaijani and English will be provided during the event. Visitor entry will cease 30 minutes before closing time each day.

Thus, the three-day "Rebuild Garabagh 2026" event will serve not only as a showcase for construction and infrastructure solutions related to the restoration of Karabakh but also as an international platform for the exchange of ideas on urban planning, industry, education, digital media, and business cooperation.

World.title: Karabakh, East Zangezur emerge as new non-oil growth hubs – minister
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 14. The expansion of production capacity in Karabakh and East Zangezur is turning the regions into new growth hubs for Azerbaijan’s non-oil and gas sector, Azerbaijani Economy Minister Mikayil Jabbarov said in a message to participants of the sixth Azerbaijan International Exhibition for Restoration, Reconstruction and Development of Karabakh (Rebuild Garabagh), Trend’s correspondent reports from the exhibition.

The minister noted that Rebuild Garabagh, held as part of Caspian Construction Week, is an important platform bringing together reconstruction efforts in the liberated territories and investment opportunities being created in the regions.

He said that, under the leadership of President Ilham Aliyev, residential areas being developed in Karabakh and East Zangezur under the “smart city” and “smart village” concepts, along with new transport corridors, green energy initiatives, and social projects, reflect the state’s strategic vision for these territories.

According to Jabbarov, consistent and systematic reconstruction efforts have created broad opportunities for sustainable resettlement and economic development in the regions.

The minister emphasized that tax and customs exemptions, preferential loans, loan guarantees and subsidies, industrial parks equipped with ready-to-use infrastructure, and other incentives introduced to promote entrepreneurship in the liberated territories have created a favorable business environment.

He noted that additional support mechanisms had also been established under decrees signed by the president. These include covering a significant portion of the costs of transporting goods to foreign markets, including new and alternative destinations, from the state budget, as well as compensating exporters for customs clearance costs. These and other measures will help exporters operating in the liberated territories strengthen their positions in domestic and international markets.

Jabbarov said that the launch of new manufacturing facilities in Karabakh and East Zangezur, along with an increase in the number of residents at the Aghdam Industrial Park and the Araz Valley Economic Zone Industrial Park, demonstrates the rapid realization of the regions’ industrial potential.

“These projects will not only meet domestic demand but also enable the export of competitive products and the development of new value chains,” the minister said.

He added that the regions’ abundant natural resources, favorable geographical location, energy potential, transport and logistics capabilities, and tourism prospects offer extensive opportunities for investors.

According to the minister, the regions have substantial geological reserves, and extraction has already begun at several deposits. Intensive projects are also being implemented in agriculture, particularly in horticulture and livestock farming.

Jabbarov emphasized that the launch of the Zangezur Corridor would further enhance the regions’ transport and logistics potential.

He also noted that Karabakh and East Zangezur offer additional investment opportunities in tourism thanks to their ancient history, scenic landscapes, rich cultural heritage, and therapeutic mineral water resources.

The minister called on business representatives to explore the regions’ economic potential and launch new projects.

“We are confident that the Rebuild Garabagh exhibition will help present the regions’ economic potential to the business community, generate new investment initiatives and partnerships, and accelerate regional development,” Jabbarov said.

He thanked all partners involved in organizing the exhibition and wished participants and visitors success, productive meetings, and new opportunities for cooperation.

World.title: Uzbekistan, Franklin Templeton discuss IPO plans for state-owned companies
World.content:
Photo: The Ministry of Economy and Finance of Uzbekistan

BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 14. Uzbekistan and global investment management firm Franklin Templeton discussed plans to transform state-owned enterprises, develop capital markets and prepare selected companies for initial public offerings (IPOs) during a meeting in Tashkent on October 13.

This was reflected in the statement by Uzbekistan’s Ministry of Economy and Finance, following a meeting between Uzbek Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Economy and Finance Jamshid Kuchkarov and representatives of Franklin Templeton.

The delegation included Manraj Sekhon, chief investment officer of Templeton Global Investments and CEO of Templeton Asset Management; Marius Dan, CEO for Central Asia at Templeton Global Investments; and Khurshed Mustafayev, Uzbekistan’s deputy minister of economy and finance responsible for the oil and gas sector.

The parties reviewed Uzbekistan’s ongoing economic reforms, efforts to improve the efficiency of state-owned enterprises, capital market development and opportunities to expand cooperation with international investors.

Particular attention was given to transforming companies in the portfolio of the Uzbekistan National Investment Fund (UzNIF), strengthening corporate governance, improving financial transparency and increasing their investment appeal.

Additionally, the discussions covered preparations for IPOs of selected companies, access to international capital markets and ways to attract institutional investors. The parties also considered opportunities to apply international expertise to these processes.

The meeting addressed measures to improve investment efficiency, introduce corporate governance practices aligned with international standards and build long-term investment cooperation.

Both sides expressed interest in continuing dialogue, exploring cooperation in priority areas and considering potential joint initiatives.

World.title: Caspian Construction Week opens in Azerbaijan with five exhibitions
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 14. Caspian Construction Week is kicking off in Azerbaijan, covering sectors such as construction, the restoration of Karabakh, engineering and utility systems, the plastic and polymer industry, as well as road infrastructure and public transport, Trend’s correspondent reports from the event.

Four international exhibitions, alongside a concurrent international exhibition dedicated to road infrastructure and public transport, are being held at the Baku Expo Center from October 14 to 16.

Caspian Construction Week serves as a platform for companies representing various industrial sectors to showcase their products and solutions, for industry participants to come together, and for the establishment of professional connections. The event encompasses a wide range of areas, spanning from construction materials and heating and ventilation equipment to solutions for the restoration of Karabakh, the plastic and polymer industry, road infrastructure, and public transport. The exhibitions held during the week provide an opportunity for both local and foreign companies to showcase their products and technologies, keep up with market innovations, and discuss potential partnership opportunities.

One of the event's key components is the 31st Azerbaijan International Construction Exhibition - "BakuBuild." This exhibition covers the construction sector and serves as a showcase for industry-specific products, materials, and technologies. It facilitates the gathering of various construction market stakeholders, the establishment of business connections between companies, and the exploration of collaboration opportunities.

Another significant component is the 6th Azerbaijan International Exhibition for Restoration, Reconstruction, and Development of Karabakh - "Rebuild Garabagh." This exhibition provides a platform for companies to present solutions related to restoration and reconstruction processes in the liberated territories, as well as the development and infrastructure construction of these areas. The 18th International Exhibition for Heating, Ventilation, Air Conditioning, Water Supply, Plumbing, and Swimming Pools - "Aquatherm Baku" - covers building engineering and utility systems. It showcases products and technologies related to heating, ventilation, and air conditioning equipment, water supply and plumbing solutions, as well as swimming pools.

Another component of the industrial sector is the 5th anniversary Caspian International Plastics and Polymer Industry Exhibition - "Plastex Caspian." This exhibition is significant for enabling companies in the plastics and polymer industry to present their products and manufacturing solutions, and for facilitating networking among industry participants.

Held in parallel with Caspian Construction Week, the 14th Caspian International Road Infrastructure and Public Transport Exhibition - "Road & Traffic" - covers the fields of road infrastructure and public transport. Thus, alongside construction and industry, the event brings together solutions related to the development of transport systems in a single venue. In addition to exhibitions, the Caspian Construction Week features panel discussions, innovation sessions, and business presentations on various topics.

According to the event program, the participation, initiatives, and opportunities for youth in the reconstruction of Karabakh will be discussed on October 14. That day will also see an innovation session dedicated to eco-friendly construction materials and energy-efficiency solutions, as well as a panel discussion on the future of construction, innovations, and emerging trends.

Another part of the day's program is dedicated to the presentation of Russian-made agricultural machinery and equipment.

On October 15, a panel discussion will be held regarding the realities of Karabakh, as well as the potential and social impact of digital media. Furthermore, discussions will cover the role of university-industry collaboration in construction based on circular economy principles, and adapting to changing lifestyles in future interior and exterior design.

The role of education in the revival of Karabakh will also be a key focus on that day. The discussion on this topic will examine the contributions of education to regional development, human capital formation, and the sustainability of the reconstruction process.

On October 16, issues regarding architectural policy and the preservation of cultural heritage within the context of modern construction will be discussed. The day’s program also includes architectural discussions focused on reimagining urban spaces and the future of urban planning in Azerbaijan.

The event program also features bilateral B2B and B2G business meetings for exhibitors and invited companies. These meetings are organized to enable companies to discuss opportunities for collaboration with one another as well as with relevant institutions.

Thus, the three-day Caspian Construction Week brings together the construction, engineering, industrial, Karabakh reconstruction, architecture, and transport sectors. The exhibitions and business events offer companies the opportunity to showcase their products and technologies, stay abreast of industry innovations, and provide an opportunity to establish cooperative ties.

World.title: Cooperation of Presidents Ilham Aliyev and Shavkat Mirziyoyev: How CICA complements ties between Azerbaijan and Uzbekistan
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 14. Uzbek President Shavkat Mirziyoyev will visit Baku on October 14–15 to attend the 7th Summit of the Conference on Interaction and Confidence Building Measures in Asia (CICA), which Azerbaijan will host under its chairmanship on October 15, against the backdrop of expanding bilateral cooperation and joint regional initiatives.

Earlier, Uzbekistan's First Deputy Chairman of the Senate, Sodiq Safoev, exclusively told Trend about Mirziyoyev's planned visit on the sidelines of the 2026 CAMCA Regional Forum in Baku.

"As part of the visit, a package of agreements on economic cooperation and the joint development of Karabakh is scheduled to be signed," Safoev said, noting that the strategic partnership between Uzbekistan and Azerbaijan had reached an all-time high in recent years.

The upcoming visit will build on active political dialogue between the two countries, which gained fresh momentum in 2026. In August, Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev paid a state visit to Uzbekistan, during which the two sides signed a Treaty on Eternal Friendship and agreed to expand cooperation in trade, investment, energy, transport and other sectors. The leaders are now set to continue their engagement in Baku, including through multilateral diplomacy.

Economic cooperation remains one of the key pillars of the Azerbaijan-Uzbekistan partnership. President Ilham Aliyev previously highlighted that bilateral trade reached $795 million in 2025, a 3.2-fold increase from the previous year. In January-June 2026, mutual trade totaled approximately $170.3 million, up 30.8% year on year, according to Uzbekistan's Ministry of Investment.

At the third meeting of the Azerbaijan-Uzbekistan Supreme Interstate Council in Tashkent on August 23, President Shavkat Mirziyoyev noted that bilateral trade had tripled over the previous five years, while the combined portfolio of joint projects had exceeded $5 billion.

Baku and Tashkent have set a target of increasing bilateral trade to $1 billion by 2030. A corresponding program and roadmap were signed in August 2026. However, both presidents see this figure more as an interim milestone than a ceiling on economic cooperation.

"Today, however, we are talking about the goal of reaching $1 billion in trade turnover not as some distant dream, but as something we will probably achieve within a couple of years," President Ilham Aliyev said during his visit to Tashkent.

Growing trade is accompanied by increased investment activity. The Azerbaijan-Uzbekistan Investment Company, established in 2023 with a capital of $500 million, supports the implementation of joint projects. At the Supreme Interstate Council meeting, President Ilham Aliyev said that approximately $160 million from the fund had already been earmarked for project financing. The total value of planned investments and projects for which contracts have been signed, however, is significantly higher than the fund's capital.

"The volume of investments for the projects we have envisioned and already contracted significantly exceeds the capacity of the fund," President Ilham Aliyev noted, highlighting cooperation on tourism projects, hotels and residential complexes in Uzbekistan.

The overall portfolio of joint initiatives spans industry, energy, construction, agriculture, tourism and financial services. According to Uzbekistan's National Statistics Committee, 473 enterprises with Azerbaijani capital are operating in the country.

A joint automotive venture between Uzavtosanoat and AzerMash at Azerbaijan's Hajigabul Industrial Park is a practical example of industrial cooperation. The facility has already produced more than 10,000 Chevrolet vehicles and Isuzu buses. The two sides are also exploring a transition to a full production cycle, with investment exceeding $84 million.

Other promising areas include the development of oil and gas fields in Uzbekistan, construction and tourism projects, raw material processing and the production of industrial goods.

Another tangible outcome of closer economic ties is the entry of Azerbaijani bank ABB into the Uzbek market. The ABB Davr project was launched in Tashkent on August 23, with Presidents Ilham Aliyev and Shavkat Mirziyoyev participating online in an event marking the launch and groundbreaking of projects being implemented by Azerbaijan in Uzbekistan.

The project предусматривает ABB's acquisition of a controlling stake in Davr Bank, followed by operations in the Uzbek market under the ABB Davr brand. The relevant agreement was signed on August 22 by ABB Chairman of the Management Board Abbas Ibrahimov and Davr Bank Supervisory Board Chairman Lutfulla Ubaev on the sidelines of the fourth Uzbekistan-Azerbaijan Interregional Forum.

Entry into the Uzbek market is in line with ABB's geographic expansion strategy for 2026–2028. The bank plans to provide financial services to corporate and retail customers across Uzbekistan, using digital solutions, artificial intelligence-based technologies and tools to support small and medium-sized enterprises.

"It is a great honor for us that the first historic step in the implementation of ABB Bank's geographic expansion goal for the new strategic period was taken in brotherly Uzbekistan," Abbas Ibrahimov said.

He said the bank viewed the project as the beginning of a long-term presence in the country and aimed to become a financial partner for businesses and individuals. Bilateral cooperation is therefore extending beyond trade and industry to encompass financial services and digital solutions.

A separate area of cooperation concerns the reconstruction of Azerbaijan's liberated territories. President Ilham Aliyev has emphasized that Uzbekistan was the first country to provide practical assistance in this effort. A school named after Mirzo Ulugbek, designed to accommodate nearly 1,000 students, was built in Fuzuli, while a garment manufacturing facility was established in Khankendi with Uzbek participation.

"Naturally, creating jobs in the Karabakh region - especially for women - is currently of paramount importance. Once again, the first investment project to establish a modern production facility and create over 200 jobs is being implemented by the Uzbek side," President Ilham Aliyev said, thanking Mirziyoyev for his support for Karabakh's reconstruction.

These projects demonstrate that the bilateral partnership extends beyond trade and investment to include social infrastructure and job creation. In this context, the planned agreements on the joint development of Karabakh, announced by Safoev in comments to Trend, could build on initiatives already underway.

Energy is another important component of the bilateral agenda. Uzbekistan is seeking investment in gas projects, while Azerbaijan could become a partner in developing the relevant infrastructure. Both countries are also involved in advancing a green energy corridor designed to transmit electricity from Central Asia through Azerbaijan to Europe.

The Middle Corridor as a shared economic opportunity

Transport connectivity is another area where the interests of Baku and Tashkent directly converge. The development of the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route, known as the Middle Corridor, is creating opportunities to expand trade between Central Asia, the South Caucasus and European markets.

In 2025, transit freight between the two countries totaled 1.4 million tons, an increase of 6.7%. In the first half of 2026, the figure reached 675,000 tons, up 12.2% from the same period a year earlier.

Tashkent is also interested in developing Caspian port infrastructure and expanding logistics capacity. As Safoev previously told Trend, Uzbekistan intends to participate in the development of a designated section of the Port of Alat and the Middle Corridor infrastructure.

In August, Mirziyoyev stressed the need for joint efforts in this area. "We will jointly develop the potential of the Trans-Caspian Corridor, improve the efficiency of logistics infrastructure and promote freight transportation. To this end, we will step up efforts to establish a joint fleet in the Caspian Sea," he said.

At the Supreme Interstate Council meeting, the Uzbek president also proposed accelerating the launch of a joint Caspian fleet and considering the creation of a dedicated Uzbekistan-Azerbaijan corridor with a single operator. President Ilham Aliyev, in turn, noted the increase in freight traffic from Uzbekistan through Azerbaijan and the need to expedite the joint fleet project.

Transport cooperation is therefore gradually moving beyond the organization of individual shipments. Its development could help establish more resilient production and logistics chains, reduce dependence on a limited number of routes and strengthen economic ties across the region.

CICA as a platform for broader regional cooperation

Against this backdrop, the CICA summit takes on added significance. Azerbaijan has chaired the organization for 2024–2026, promoting an agenda focused on connectivity, digitalization and sustainable development in Asia. For Baku, the upcoming meeting will also provide an opportunity to consolidate the results of its chairmanship and further strengthen the organization's institutional role.

The agenda of the seventh summit includes peace and security, confidence-building among states, transport infrastructure, digitalization and sustainable economic growth. The adoption of the Baku Declaration and a package of decisions aimed at improving CICA's effectiveness is expected.

For Uzbekistan, participation in the summit offers an opportunity to advance its economic and transport priorities within a broader Asian framework. For Azerbaijan, Tashkent's support is important to the development of interregional ties and closer cooperation between Central Asia and the South Caucasus.

However, engagement between the two countries is not limited to CICA. At the October Consultative Meeting of the Heads of State of Central Asia and Azerbaijan in Awaza, Mirziyoyev proposed moving beyond conventional trade toward the joint production of finished goods.

"We have reached a point where ordinary trade with one another is no longer enough. We need to create finished products together. The formula 'six economies - one product' captures what we should be striving for," the Uzbek president said.

This approach also reflects the economic agenda pursued by Baku and Tashkent: the two countries aim not only to increase bilateral trade but also to establish joint ventures, deepen industrial cooperation and develop new transport and energy links.

Building a common agenda at the presidential level

The sequence of high-level meetings reflects the two countries' determination to translate political agreements into tangible economic results. The signing of the Treaty on Eternal Friendship in August was an important symbolic step, while joint investment and infrastructure projects are laying the practical foundations of the partnership.

Mirziyoyev has described Azerbaijan as a reliable ally, strategic partner and brotherly state, emphasizing the shared historical roots and cultural ties underpinning relations between the two countries. President Ilham Aliyev, in turn, has described Central Asia and Azerbaijan as a single geopolitical and economic region with significant growth potential.

Closer regional engagement has been another important outcome of the political dialogue. At the Supreme Interstate Council meeting, Mirziyoyev noted that Azerbaijan's accession to the Consultative Meeting of the Heads of State of Central Asia had opened up new opportunities for economic and humanitarian cooperation between the two regions. President Ilham Aliyev separately thanked his Uzbek counterpart for supporting Azerbaijan's full participation in the format.

"We always support each other in the bilateral format and across all international organizations in which we participate. This happens automatically," President Ilham Aliyev said.

Such coordination takes on added importance ahead of the CICA summit in Baku. While bilateral mechanisms help the two countries coordinate specific projects and investment priorities, multilateral platforms offer an opportunity to promote common approaches to transport connectivity, economic development and confidence-building across the wider region.

Mirziyoyev's participation in the summit will continue this pattern of engagement. Meetings on the sidelines are expected to give the two sides an opportunity to discuss bilateral projects and coordinate their positions on regional issues.

Further progress will depend on how consistently political agreements are translated into new investment, joint production and efficient transport routes. In this respect, cooperation within CICA complements the bilateral agenda by providing an additional platform for advancing initiatives that link the economic interests of Azerbaijan and Uzbekistan with the broader development priorities of Asia.

World.title: EBRD sees pathways to mobilize international capital in Turkmenistan (Exclusive)
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 14. The EBRD sees opportunities to bring more international capital and expertise to Turkmenistan through project financing, risk-sharing and private-sector support.

The European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD) Head of Turkmenistan Eric Livny said this in an exclusive interview with Trend, responding to questions about potential financing structures for international investors and measures to expand access to finance for privately owned micro, small and medium-sized enterprises (MSMEs) in the country.

Livny said direct project financing could provide a straightforward mechanism for supporting investment.

"The most straightforward approach is direct project financing, where the Bank provides long-term loans alongside sponsors and commercial lenders. The EBRD's participation can help reduce perceived risks and provide comfort to other investors considering entry into a new market," Livny said.

According to Livny, syndicated financing could further expand the pool of private capital involved in projects by allowing commercial banks and institutional investors to participate alongside the Bank.

"We can also support projects through syndicated financing structures, whereby part of an EBRD-financed loan is subsequently shared with commercial banks and institutional investors. This allows larger volumes of private capital to participate in projects than would otherwise be possible," he said.

Livny also identified equity investments, trade-finance instruments, guarantees and risk-sharing arrangements among the tools that could be used to support investors.

"In addition, the EBRD can support investors through equity investments, trade-finance instruments, guarantees and risk-sharing arrangements where appropriate. Technical cooperation is often equally important. By helping projects meet international environmental, governance and operational standards, we can increase their attractiveness to foreign investors and facilitate access to international financing," Livny said.

Livny said the EBRD’s role would ultimately go beyond providing its own funding.

"Ultimately, our objective is not simply to provide EBRD funding but to act as a catalyst that helps attract additional international capital and expertise to the country," he said.

Turning to the private sector, Livny said improving access to finance for privately owned MSMEs is among the key objectives of the EBRD’s planned engagement with Turkmenistan’s financial sector.

"Improving access to finance for privately owned micro, small and medium-sized enterprises is one of the key objectives of our planned engagement with the financial sector," Livny said.

According to Livny, a first step could be establishing partnerships with selected local banks that have a meaningful presence in the SME segment.

"Through these partnerships, the EBRD could provide dedicated credit lines targeted at export-oriented businesses and other private enterprises with strong growth potential," he said.

Livny noted that access to finance is not always the only challenge for private companies.

"We would therefore seek to complement financing with advisory support to help companies strengthen management systems, improve productivity, obtain international certifications and prepare for expansion into export markets. Combining finance with advisory services is one of the EBRD's most effective tools for supporting SME development," Livny said.

The EBRD also sees significant scope for expanding the use of trade-finance instruments, including guarantees and letters of credit.

"We also see significant scope to expand the use of modern trade-finance instruments, including guarantees and letters of credit. These products can help businesses manage commercial risks, reduce working-capital constraints and build relationships with international suppliers and buyers," Livny said.

In the longer term, Livny said the EBRD aims to contribute to the development of a more commercially oriented financial sector.

"Our longer-term objective is to contribute to building a more commercially oriented financial sector capable of serving the evolving needs of Turkmenistan’s fast-growing private businesses," Livny said.

For reference, the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD) has been working with Turkmenistan since 1992. Its engagement has focused on private-sector development, cooperation with financial institutions and support for private companies through financing and advisory services. The bank has also identified sectors such as transport, logistics, agribusiness, industry and commerce as areas with potential for further private-sector investment.

According to the EBRD, the bank has financed 87 projects in Turkmenistan, with cumulative investment reaching €322 million.

In July 2026, EBRD President Odile Renaud-Basso visited Turkmenistan, during which the sides signed five memorandums of understanding covering strategic cooperation for 2027-2032, the banking sector, sustainable energy, environmental protection and water resources, transport corridors, and Ashgabat’s participation in the EBRD Green Cities programme. The documents are intended to provide a framework for further cooperation.

World.title: Migration rhetoric 'harming' reputation in Asia, uni vice-chancellor says
World.content:
Australia's national debate on migration is harming the country's reputation in Asia, the University of Tasmania's vice-chancellor has warned.

"We are creating a generation who think Australia is becoming a closed, fearful, racist place," Rufus Black told a state parliamentary inquiry this morning in Hobart.

"That is not the truth.

"But it is becoming who we are projecting ourselves to be, and that's harming our international relations and probably will in the long run unless we turn this narrative around."

International students help finance Australian research capabilities, UTAS's vice-chancellor says. (Supplied: UTAS)

Professor Black was appearing at a scrutiny hearing into the University of Tasmania's most recent annual report by the government affairs committee of the state parliament's upper house, chaired by independent Rosemary Armitage MLC.

Ten days ago the federal opposition leader Angus Taylor announced the Coalition's new migration policy which included major cuts to net overseas migration, and specifically targeted the number of international students arriving in Australia.

Compare Labor, the Coalition and One Nation's migration cuts One Nation wants negative migration in its first years, the Coalition has promised to more than halve it, while Labor has announced measures to ensure migration actually falls to its target of 225,000.

Under the policy, which proposed what Mr Taylor described as "the biggest cuts to immigration in this country's history", the number of temporary migrant visas would be slashed by 650,000 over four years.

The number of international student commencements would be limited to 240,000 a year, down from Labor's current cap of 295,000, and the Coalition policy would abolish temporary graduate visas in the hope of reducing foreign student levels to 25 per cent.

Mr Taylor has also accused universities of selling migration pathways.

One Nation has proposed even deeper cuts to international student intakes, limited to 100,000 a year.

Under the Coalition and One Nation policies, international student numbers would be heavily reduced from current levels. (ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke)

Professor Black said universities could live with the level of foreign student intake allowed by the current federal government, but cuts proposed by the opposition parties would have an enormous economic impact.

"It would be a very, very troubling picture," Professor Black said, because Australia funds research through international students.

"That's the simple truth."

Cuts would impact uni research capabilities, Black says

Professor Black said the large research-intensive universities on the mainland, which provide the bulk of critical research and development in the country, were largely funded by foreign student levels of 40 per cent.

"If you were to cut what would literally be thousands and thousands of them … that is a phenomenally large amount of money," he said.

"Not only would you cause thousands of job losses right across the higher education system, you would take vast amounts of research funding that the nation needs out of our system with no clear way in which you would alternatively fund it.

"Now, in a service-intensive economy, which is a knowledge-intensive economy, to basically take out the engine of knowledge creation from the Australian economy, to damage it that badly, that quickly, I think would have generational consequences.

"We all know productivity is a major challenge for the nation. The best driver of productivity is knowledge intensity and high skill.

"So if you take out in a very short period of time, right across the nation, that amount of capacity, it'll take more than a generation to recover from it.

" There's a real need for a lot more attention on the fact that this is the engine of national prosperity and there are now proposals on the table to break it. "

Rufus Black says the rhetoric around migration is projecting Australia as "a racist place". (ABC News: Kate Nickels)

Professor Black also warned of the generational harm that could be done to perceptions of Australia in Asia.

"If you talk to international students I think the national debate is really harming Australia in Asia," he said.

" When you talk to those who are working with our students across Asia it is really harming us. "

International education sector alarmed Higher education stakeholders say sweeping migration changes will jeopardise an export industry worth $55 billion, with international students likely to choose other destinations.

He said Australia is "not being seen as the friendly, welcoming kind of partner that we need to be in Asia, and what really is worrying is this is generational".

"We remember the Colombo program generation, who are still around," he said.

"Their commitment to a long-term partnership with Australia is extraordinary because they saw Australia as a place that was a great partner to the region and supporting them."

The Coalition has been approached for comment.

World.title: Breaking: Mining giant BHP to cut hundreds of jobs at iron ore mines
World.content:
Mining giant BHP has confirmed job cuts at its iron ore operations in Western Australia.

The ABC understands around 300 jobs will be affected across BHP's South Flank, Mining Area C, Jimblebar and Newman operations in the state's Pilbara.

A BHP spokesperson said the miner would work directly with staff and seek to redeploy people into other roles where possible.
