World.title: Forcing gas producers to sell to Australia won't 'crash' prices, King says
World.content:
The resources minister says gas prices will not crash under national reservation laws, but refused to say how much they will fall as the industry warns the government is pushing too hard.

Madeleine King said she wanted the proposed laws to make prices fairer while ensuring new gas projects would still be profitable enough to proceed.

"Allow me to be clear: we need gas to support the rollout of renewables. We need gas to have a strong Australian manufacturing industry. We need gas to continue heating our homes," she said.

The legislation introduced to parliament this morning would force producers to sell up to a fifth of their gas slated for export to Australia, pushing down wholesale prices by sparing the country from having to compete with the international market for its own resource.

How much gas producers will be required to sell to Australia each year would be set by the energy regulator, with a target amount of 110 per cent of Australia's actual needs. The government says the "modest oversupply" will put downward pressure on prices for consumers.

But after being burned by its failure to meet a previous promise to cut home power bills by $275 through renewables, which was thrown off course by Russia's invasion of Ukraine driving up gas and fuel prices globally, the government has been reluctant to put a price tag on how much prices would be expected to fall under the scheme.

The resources minister told the National Press Club that the rules for gas producers had been carefully balanced, but that information was commercially sensitive.

"We have done a lot of study and a lot of analysis and, I might add, that so has just about everybody else in relation to this," Ms King said.

"A lot of the modelling that we have done, or the analysis that we have done, is commercial-in-confidence, so it is difficult."

She said the government would release an impact assessment related to its gas reservation laws, but did not commit to that including estimated impacts on wholesale gas prices.

"Our focus is on making sure there is this modest oversupply, and that demand calibration is really important, as well, in this," Ms King said.

"We all know having too little gas to firm renewables or provide for the manufacturing industry is as dangerous as having a massive oversupply which crashes the market, but also it can undermine investment in renewables, so it is a really fine balance we have got to achieve here."

The resources minister said the bill's focus was to make gas cheaper for heavy industry and energy generation, but added that an important element was ensuring cheaper gas prices "will be felt by the consumer".

'Sugar hit' will hurt in long-term, industry says

The gas industry has warned that the government's plan could force the sale of gas at rates that are cheaper than it costs to produce.

It says the scheme might provide a "sugar hit", but would make future gas projects unviable and dry up supply in the long-term.

"The government cannot expect industry to invest billions of dollars in new gas supply while introducing policies that fundamentally undermine the commercial viability of those investments," Australian Energy Producers chief executive Samantha McCulloch said.

Australia's last gas prize 'not needed at home' The Browse gas fields have been eluding oil and gas players for decades and new analysis argues it should stay that way.

The Coalition has indicated it will work with the federal government to create a national gas reservation scheme, but says "numerous questions" remain about how future supply and investment will be assured.

"Reserving gas on paper is one thing. Ensuring we have the supply, investment, and infrastructure to deliver affordable, reliable energy to Australians when and where they need it, is another," Shadow Resources Minister Susan McDonald said in a statement.

The gas reservation scheme is meant to provide a long-term fix to issues that emerged after the invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

Wholesale gas prices soared from their average of less than $10 a gigajoule to $60 a gigajoule amid the interruption to global supply.

The federal government rushed in temporary fixes, including a one-year cap of $12 per gigajoule on gas prices, but a government review of the gas market found those had not been "sufficient" to place downward pressure on prices, and longer-term answers were needed to give the industry confidence to continue investing.

It also noted that new production and infrastructure to get gas from the north to south-eastern Australia was "critical" to ensuring lower prices.

World.title: Speeds of 188km/h, skids, burnouts before crash that killed driver's friend
World.content:
Whispers and the occasional scoff rippled through a Queensland courtroom as loved ones heard how a driver was under the influence of alcohol and drugs when he crashed his car, killing his friend.

Zachary Robert Kolm, 26, was sentenced to nine years' jail after pleading guilty to manslaughter in the Supreme Court in Bundaberg on Wednesday.

He was behind the wheel of an unregistered and modified car, and had alcohol and MDMA in his system, when he crashed and killed his friend, 23-year-old Nicholas 'Joel' Wright.

Joel Wright was killed in a crash at Burnett Heads in August 2023. (Supplied)

The court heard five people were in the car as Kolm did burnouts and skids around the Bundaberg CBD in the early hours of the morning on August 5, 2023.

The car was then seen driving along Burnett Heads Road, with GPS data showing it was travelling at 188km/h, before it crashed into a sugarcane paddock, rolled and hit a power pole.

The courtroom, with standing-room only, was packed with more than 40 people for the sentencing, including supporters of both men.

Mr Wright's loved ones, wearing Justice for Joel T-shirts, shook their heads and commented to each other after the sentence was handed down that it was "f*****g b******t".

Skids, burnouts before crash

The court heard Kolm and Mr Wright spent time at a Bundaberg hotel in the evening before the crash, and had invited friends to do burnouts with them.

The court heard the car landed on its roof in the sugarcane field after Kolm failed to navigate a curve in the road.

Mr Wright was pinned underneath the car and died from mechanical asphyxiation.

Emotions ran high during and after the hearing. (ABC Wide Bay: Grace Whiteside)

When paramedics arrived, Kolm said someone else had been driving and they had left the scene.

The court heard he then lay on the road, shaking, and was later shaking in the ambulance, but a report by paramedics questioned if it was a genuine seizure.

Justice Graeme Crow described Kolm's actions at the scene of the crash as "disgraceful", saying there was not "a shred of decency" that night.

But he acknowledged Kolm was remorseful, as he had called Mr Wright's father the day after the crash and has confessed he was the driver, and apologised.

"I hope you understand the pain you have caused," Justice Crow said.

Defence lawyer Callan Cassidy said his client "wishes he could change places with the deceased".

Kolm will be eligible for parole in April 2029.

World.title: Trump's new press secretary faces questions about her legal credentials
World.content:
An inaugural, albeit short, White House press briefing offered a glimpse into how Trump's latest press secretary, Katie Zacharia, will approach the notoriously difficult role.

The 41-year-old spent much of the 14-minute appearance reading from prepared remarks before taking just three questions, all from conservative-leaning outlets.

Zacharia's debut comes after the departure of Karoline Leavitt, who became known for her combative and high-profile briefing style.

Here are the key moments.

Talks up Trump agenda

Zacharia, a conservative commentator named to the role on Friday, opened her first session by reading, at a notably slow pace, a lengthy list of what she described as achievements made by the "energetic" US President Donald Trump.

She highlighted Trump's recent campaign rallies and his policies on energy, tariffs, immigration and more since he returned to office.

"Everyday Americans are showing up in droves to attend rallies because of President Trump's America-first agenda of lower taxes, higher wages and one of my favourites, secure borders," Zacharia said.

"Attendance is at record highs as enthusiastic and hardworking Americans are lining up and packing arenas to support President Trump and Republicans.

"It's not hard to see why. President Trump is fighting and delivering for American workers every minute of every day."

Answers only three questions

Typically, a lengthy question-and-answer session follows a press secretary's opening remarks, often spanning dozens of questions from reporters.

But Zacharia took questions from just three reporters, starting with right-wing website Breitbart, an outlet frequently accused of misinformation.

The next questions went to Fox News and the Daily Mail.

Katie Zacharia only answered questions from conservative-leaning news outlets. (AP: Julia Demaree Nikhinson)

When asked by Fox whether the administration had stopped sharing intelligence with Ukraine, Zacharia was unable to provide an answer.

"I'll have to get back to you on that," she said.

Scrutiny over legal credentials

Zacharia raised eyebrows when she was asked about her legal qualifications on the White House South Lawn alongside Trump after the briefing.

"What state did she pass the bar exam in? You said she is an attorney. Where did she pass the bar exam? Which state?" the reporter asked.

Trump turned to Zacharia and repeated the question.

"When I moved to China," she answered.

Katie Zacharia was asked about her legal credentials before heading to Alaska. (Reuters: Kevin Lamarque)

A White House official later did not directly answer questions about whether Zacharia had passed a US bar exam, which is required in the US to practice law.

Her LinkedIn profile said she worked as an associate in the International Practice Team at Zhong Lun law firm in Beijing from 2011 to 2013, however non-citizens can not sit China's national bar exam and cannot engage in legal practice involving Chinese law.

Pepperdine University confirmed Zacharia graduated from its law school in 2011, but there has been no confirmation so far she passed the California bar exam.

Former officials question debut

The briefing drew criticism from several former White House officials, who questioned both its length and Zacharia's performance.

Former White House communications director Anthony Scaramucci joked on X: "The clock is running. Thus far 1/11th of a Scaramucci."

Scaramucci famously lasted 11 days in the role during Trump's first administration.

Sarah Matthews, who served as deputy White House press secretary during Trump's first term, described the debut as "rather underwhelming".

"Three questions, including one from the new media seat, and a heavy reliance on her notes. Not exactly in command of the briefing room," Matthews wrote on X.

Former Clinton administration press secretary Joe Lockhart told CNN it was "a little bizarre" to usher Zacharia into the briefing room for such a short appearance.

"I'm not sure what they were hoping to accomplish, but I don't think they built any confidence in her ability to go forward," he said.

Meanwhile, former Biden press secretary Jen Psaki described the briefing on X as "basically an SNL skit … except it wasn't".

Mistakenly calls her husband 'my president'

One of the lighter moments came when Zacharia accidentally referred to her husband as "my president" while discussing her family.

"The idea of not spending evenings with my kids is completely unacceptable. So my president, excuse me, my husband ‒ that's a good one," she said.

White House asks US envoy to Greece to resign In her first briefing since becoming White House press secretary, Katie Zacharia says the Trump-appointed US ambassador to Greece, Kimberly Guilfoyle, has been asked to resign.

Trump says she 'did excellent'

Speaking to reporters before his trip to Alaska, Trump praised his new press secretary's performance.

"I thought she did excellent. She did very good," he said.

The White House also issued a statement.

"Today, Katie Zacharia delivered a commanding inaugural press briefing as the 37th White House Press Secretary," the White House statement read.

"The briefing, which generated wall-to-wall coverage, served as a strong introduction to her tenure and highlighted the Trump Administration's record of delivering historic successes for the American people."

World.title: Rex grounds two routes 10 months after $60m rescue package
World.content:
Less than a year after it was sold with the aid of a federal government rescue package, embattled airline Regional Express (Rex) has grounded flights to two NSW destinations.

The carrier announced that flights to and from Sydney and Port Macquarie on the Mid North Coast and Orange in the Central West will be indefinitely halted from October 25.

Independent MP Andrew Gee, whose federal electorate takes in Orange, described the decision as a "real shock".

"It feels like a slap in the face or a kick in the guts for the whole region after everyone called for so much support and so much pressure was put on the government to deliver it," he said.

Andrew Gee says Rex's decision comes as a blow after the effort put into ensuring its survival. (ABC News: Nick Haggarty)

A Commonwealth bailout allowed the airline to keep flying its regional routes and, in late 2025, it was bought by US-based air services company Air T.

The sale was endorsed by the federal government, which backed the bid with a $60 million support package and an additional $108 million to help restructure existing Commonwealth debt.

In exchange for that support Air T made commitments to increase the number of aircraft in service, maintain an ongoing level of service to regional Australia, and increase frequencies of profitable flights across its network.

The ABC has contacted Air T for comment.

'Disappointing for many'

A spokesperson for Federal Transport Minister Catherine King issued a statement acknowledging the Rex decision would be "be disappointing for many".

"In return for support from the Australian Government, Air T agreed to a set of regional commitments aimed at maintaining Rex's services to regional Australia," the spokesperson said.

"Notwithstanding these changes, Rex continues to operate one of Australia's largest regional air networks.

"The Government continues to work closely with Rex to understand market challenges and to monitor Rex's compliance with regional commitments."

The statement noted that customers in both regional destinations would still be able to fly to and from Sydney on different carriers.

A spokesperson for Catherine King says the government is continuing to "work closely" with Rex. (ABC News: Ian Cutmore)

A statement issued by Rex said the suspensions were indefinite, and affected customers would be offered "refunds or re-bookings".

"The environment of entrenched high fuel prices driven by the ongoing conflict in the Middle East, together with lack of demand, do not make these routes commercially viable at this time," the statement said.

REX said it would monitor the situation and consider reinstating the routes "once fuel prices decrease to a level that makes it commercially viable for flights to resume".

The carrier said it remained "committed to serving regional and remote Australia".

In May, the airline cut two services in Tasmania and scaled back a service to Mildura in Victoria's north-west.

Rex has blamed soaring fuel costs for the suspension of the flights. (Supplied: Rex Airlines)

'Significant flow-on effect'

Port Macquarie Mayor Adam Roberts said the area's $700 million annual visitor economy would be hit by the Rex decision.

"The reality is that it has a significant flow-on effect to our community," he said.

"Living in a regional area, we absolutely need these vital services."

Cr Adams said whether airport staff would lose jobs remained unclear, but discussions were underway to mitigate impacts.

"The state and federal governments need to look at what's happening here and ask the question [whether] they could potentially help us stabilise our potential for travel," he said.

"If it's a grant fund or if it's a carrot to entice more airlines to use this airport, we're already having some peripheral conversations."

Orange Mayor Tony Mileto is pessimistic about the prospect of the service ever being reinstated.

"I don't think they'll be backflipping on the decision," he said.

Cr Mileto said there was clearly demand among the other airlines that serviced the airport, including Qantas and Link Airways.

"I think it's for Rex to answer as to why more people weren't taking up their flights," he said.

Cr Mileto said the council would request a meeting with those competitors to ensure their services were at least maintained.

"Air travel is vitally important to Orange and we want to ensure that people feel confident there will be flights available should they require them," he said.

Earlier this year, the Orange City Council received a slice of $4.8 million from the Commonwealth to cover Rex's unpaid debts to regional councils.

World.title: Calls for judge to be stood down after teen rapist avoids jail
World.content:
The ACT Director of Public Prosecutions will consider appealing against a controversial sentence handed to a teenage boy who pinned down and raped a young woman he met at a Canberra house party.

Warning: This story contains descriptions of sexual assault.

The teenager, who was 16 at the time of the rape, pleaded guilty in the ACT Children's Court to sexual intercourse without consent.

The now-18-year-old avoided jail time and instead received an 18-month suspended sentence upon entering a good behaviour order.

In sentencing last week, ACT Supreme Court Justice Andrew Muller accepted the teenager's "prior lack of sexual experience and inevitably limited insight into societal norms in Australia … are factors mitigating his moral culpability".

The teenager had moved to Canberra from Bhutan in February 2025, six months before the assault occurred.

He cannot be named because he was a minor at the time of the offence.

He has spent one night in custody since the offending in August 2025.

Petition to remove judge from position

The sentence has sparked fierce public backlash from parts of the Canberra community.

A petition calling for the removal of Justice Muller had on Wednesday received 4,000 signatures.

Petition organiser Joanne Matthews said she wanted the justice system to reconsider the sentence.

"They are supposed to reflect what society wants, and this is not what society wants," she said.

Ms Matthews, a Canberra resident, said she was disappointed the court considered the teen's short time in Australia to be a mitigating factor.

"Does this give permission for anyone coming in to say, 'Well, I'm ignorant of the law, I can commit these horrendous crimes and that's OK'?" she said.

Justice Andrew Muller handed the offender an 18-month suspended sentence. (Supplied: ACT government)

A separate petition sponsored by Canberra Liberals MLA Peter Cain was launched on Tuesday calling for a public inquiry into the ACT's sentencing framework for sexual violence.

"The community needs assurance that sentencing outcomes are justified, assessments of reoffending risk are rigorous, and mitigating factors do not diminish victims' entitlement to justice or community safety," the petition, which has received 170 signatures, said.

The office of ACT Attorney-General Tara Cheyne declined to comment on the case, saying any decision about an appeal was a matter for the Director of Public Prosecutions (DPP).

An ACT government spokesperson said the territory's legislative framework was designed to safeguard the independence of the DPP.

"Under the Director of Public Prosecutions Act 1990, the attorney-general may issue directions or guidelines to the director only on matters of a general nature and cannot direct how the DPP should act in a specific case," the spokesperson said.

'Unclear' what offender is sorry for: judge

During sentencing, the court heard the teen and his 18-year-old victim had met at a party in Holt where they kissed before he asked her to go for a walk a few houses away.

He then pinned her down, ripped her clothes, and repeatedly sexually assaulted her.

The victim, who also cannot be named, said she "just froze" and told the offender, "please stop, I don't want this".

She estimated the offending lasted for 20 minutes.

The victim told the court she wanted to run away but was scared the offender would hurt her.

Justice Muller said he acknowledged "troubling concerns" about the teen's insights.

"I have no doubt he feels sorry," he said.

"But whether he feels sorry because of the impact these charges have had in his own life, or whether he feels sorry because he realises what he did was wrong and recognises the abhorrence with which the community regards his wrongful behaviour, is a little unclear," he said.

The offender, who is currently completing year 12, had previously been issued a restraining order for punching another student at school and had admitted to photographing another student using the toilet.

Speaking broadly about sentencing in sexual assault cases, ACT Victims of Crime Commissioner Juliette Ford said the lifelong impact a crime had on victims was not always understood.

The commissioner said victims generally reported incidents "because they have faith in the criminal justice process and because they don't want what happened to them to happen to someone else."

"It is very important, then, that the outcomes do properly reflect the impact of the harm caused to them," she said.

World.content:

Columbus: A Democrat running in a local Indiana election has gone viral for a slurred television interview in which she lurched wildly between lines of thought, ranted about the MAGA movement and ended with the observation: “We have guns too.” Jaime West, a candidate for the Fayette County Council east of Indianapolis, appeared several days ago in a televised forum sponsored by local outlets TV3 and The Connersville News Examiner. Democrat Jaime West slurred her way through the television interview that has since gone viral in the US. YouTube West appeared confused from the start, when she was asked to deliver her opening statement and conceded she did not write one. Following a rambling monologue, it sounded as though someone on a mic loudly broke wind. At one point, West requested the interviewer to repeat the question. Asked for one thing she would do in office that might be unpopular with some voters, she said: “Firing all Republicans.”



West continued, appearing to slur heavily: “I don’t even talk to them. I don’t like ’em. I mean they voted against - our own state representative votes against her own party. I mean … what do you want me to say? I don’t like being around ’em. Related Article US election With a month to go, Republicans’ midterm prospects are ‘catastrophically bad’ “I mean, y’all did this to us. Y’all voted for us. You made this happen, this ICE coming into our communities, stealing people’s jobs. I mean – arghhh.” West then began speaking about members of President Donald Trump’s Make America Great Again coalition. “I’ve been threatened so many times to my face by ‘MAGA’, we’ll call them. Because there’s Republicans who actually get it, you know. There are good Republicans out there. But then there’s these MAGAs, who are just racist and aren’t very intelligent at all. They call you names.”



West claimed a sheriff’s nephew tried to “blow my head off”. It was not clear who or what she was referring to. Asked for a final message to the voters, West looked down the barrel of the camera and said: “We have guns too.” She then threw up both her hands. Asked for a final message to voters, West turned to the camera and said: “We have guns too.” She then threw up her hands. YouTube The interviewer – the Examiner’s managing editor Amy Graham-McCarty – maintained her composure throughout, and never inquired about West’s condition. The footage was uploaded to YouTube by TV3 and clips of the segment have been viewed millions of times on social media as the interview went viral.



West could not be immediately reached for comment, and it does not appear that she has spoken publicly since the interview. She is running against Republican Gary Keener Jr for the council seat. Voting takes place on November 3 along with statewide contests in the US midterm elections. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Larvotto rolls out first antimony shipment from NSW Hillgrove
World.content:

Larvotto Resources has officially joined the ranks of Australia’s critical minerals producers, shipping its first batch of antimony concentrate from the company’s Hillgrove antimony-gold mine in New South Wales to offtake partner Wogen Resources. The company says the first truck carrying 68 tonnes of antimony concentrate has left the site, initiating mine-gate offtake sales and making Larvotto Australia’s newest supplier of critical minerals. The first truckload of antimony concentrate leaves Larvotto Resources’ Hillgrove mine in New South Wales. Under the shrewdly structured mine-gate offtake agreement, partner Wogen Resources collected the high-grade concentrate directly from Hillgrove for an initial part-payment, allowing cash to start flowing without the long shipping delays and distant laboratory results that can often hamstring new producers. A second, final payment will follow once independent assays confirm final metal content. The major milestone follows an extensive redevelopment and plant upgrade program at Hillgrove, which is set to produce 4900 tonnes of antimony and 40,500 ounces of gold per year, making it one of the world’s largest antimony producers and giving it control of a staggering 7 per cent of global supply.



‘With the antimony circuit now operating at a steady rate, we will broaden our focus to optimise gold.’ Larvotto Resources managing director Ron Heeks Management says the production ramp-up is progressing well, with plant availability already exceeding schedule, daily processing tonnages increasing as planned and concentrate grades continuing to improve as the operational team fine-tunes plant performance. Larvotto Resources managing director Ron Heeks said: “As the first of the three products the plant produces, the focus has been on the antimony circuit. With the antimony circuit now operating at a steady rate, we will broaden our focus to optimise gold concentrate and gold doré production.” The Hillgrove project, 23 kilometres east of Armidale in northern NSW, already hosts a significant mineral resource of 1.7 million ounces of gold equivalent at an impressive grade of 7.4 grams per tonne (g/t) gold equivalent, ranking it among the world’s top ten antimony deposits and the biggest in Australia. With the antimony circuit now humming, Larvotto is turning its attention to Hillgrove’s precious metal streams. The company says preparations for a first gold concentrate shipment are now nearing completion, with the production of gold doré bars also on the near-term agenda.



And there’s a third string to Hillgrove’s bow in the form of tungsten, another critical mineral caught in a tightening global market. Hillgrove’s planned future tungsten stream is riding against a backdrop of Chinese supply dominance, increasing export controls and a rapidly appreciating price environment. Larvotto says ongoing metallurgical testwork on its tungsten mineralisation continues to deliver positive results, with the company now narrowing down its preferred processing equipment and flowsheet as it targets the start of tungsten production in 2027. The transition from developer to producer is a notoriously difficult path to navigate; however, with its first product out of the gate, cash flowing in and two more high-value commodities lining up behind it, Larvotto could be heading into the new year with serious momentum and plenty of production to ramp things up. World.title: TMK Energy steps on gas with fresh Mongolian drilling
World.content:
Sponsored BusinessCompaniesBulls N' Bears TMK Energy steps on gas with fresh Mongolian drilling Brought to you by BULLS N’ BEARS Murray Ward October 14, 2026 — 4:27pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. TMK Energy has fired up the engines on a 2026 work program at the company’s Gurvantes XXXV coal-bed methane pilot project in Mongolia, mobilising a workover rig and crane to kick off a well optimisation and drilling campaign. Set-up has now started at the 100 per cent-owned project, with the workover rig and a 70-tonne crane arriving on site last week. The first order of business was to remove the currently idle pump and production string from well LF-03, which is now being prepared for a cleanout and the first of three planned re-completions. A 70-tonne crane pulling the pump from well LF-03 as part of the workover at TMK Energy’s Gurvantes XXXV coal-bed methane project in Mongolia. The work is designed to optimise gas flow from existing wells. The plan involves installing a new, smaller 5.5-inch slotted liner inside the existing 7-inch liner, before running smaller tubing and pumps. TMK says the reduced-diameter spacing should boost production from the existing wellbores. The optimisation process will initially apply to wells LF-03, LF-02 and LF-06. Once the three workovers are in the bag, the company plans to spud a new well, dubbed LF-08. This will be drilled with a smaller hole size from the get-go to accommodate the 5.5-inch slotted liner.



‘As of today, the field has been averaging approximately 950 cubic metres per day a strong increase the gas rate achieved in September.’ TMK Energy chief executive officer Dougal Ferguson If the re-completion strategy proves successful in boosting gas flows, the company says it will undertake the same process on all its existing Lucky Fox wells in 2027. That includes LF-07, which remains the star performer in the pilot field. Across TMK’s well portfolio, September’s average output climbed eight per cent from August to 872 cubic metres a day, equivalent to 30,800 standard cubic feet per day (scfd). So far in October, the average has climbed dramatically from September to 950 cubic metres per day, or 33,549 scfd, suggesting the field may be rapidly closing in on commercial flow rates. TMK Energy chief executive officer Dougal Ferguson said: “I am pleased to advise that the 2026 Work Program has now commenced at the Pilot Well Project with the LF-03 pump replacement and re-completion being the first of many field-based operations over the coming two months. Returning LF-03 to production after several months of being idle should only add to the overall increasing production in the field.” Gurvantes XXXV sits less than 20 kilometres from China, one of the world’s largest energy markets and close to several mining operations in need of additional industrial power. The company’s 8400-square-kilometre project hosts an independently certified 2C contingent resource of 1.2 trillion cubic feet (Tcf) across 60 square kilometres. Although the classification covers potentially recoverable gas, further appraisal and development work is still required. In contrast, an additional 5.3 Tcf of best-estimate prospective resources hints at the scale of the prize across the wider project area.



Additionally, TMK has proposed a one-megawatt gas-to-power project with Mongolian partner Dashvaanjil Group, which would feed off the company’s gas and supply TMK’s operational power needs and nearby industrial users. Management says it intends to make a final investment decision before the end of October, subject to commercial arrangements. With its first well now under the microscope for optimisation and a new drill campaign on the horizon, TMK appears to be methodically turning up the heat at Gurvantes XXXV. In a region that is beginning to attract major energy players, proving a repeatable, optimised production model could be a shrewd move. Is your ASX-listed company doing something interesting? World.content:

The City of Perth has brought back a former chief executive to fill the vacant role left by Michelle Reynolds after she was sacked by the council. At a special meeting on Tuesday night, the council endorsed the 12-month appointment of Garry Hunt while the search for a permanent replacement progressed. Garry Hunt will take on a 12-month contract as chief executive at the City of Perth. City of Perth Lord Mayor Bruce Reynolds said the council was “pleased to appoint an experienced and capable leader” to guide the organisation. “Dr Hunt brings an exceptional depth of experience, a proven record of leadership and a strong understanding of the City of Perth, having previously led the organisation,” Reynolds said in a statement on Wednesday.



“With more than 30 years of experience as a local government CEO, including leading the cities of Perth, Joondalup and Melville, his ability to lead complex organisations and navigate periods of change makes him ideally suited to this role. Related Article City of Perth Tensions run high at Perth council meeting over former CEO’s sacking “Council is focused on moving forward, providing stability for our organisation and ensuring we continue delivering positive outcomes for the people of Perth.” Hunt said he was pleased to return to the City of Perth, having been in the position from 1994 to 2002. “I look forward to working with Council and staff, drawing on my experience to provide steady leadership and support the important work of the City during this transition period,” he said.



Hunt will start his role with the City on October 19. The position was recently held by Maria Cooke, who stepped into the acting role after Michelle Reynolds was suspended by the council in May. The decision came after a confidential meeting with Local Government Inspector Tony Brown to discuss a report into claims levelled against the chief executive.The council was also subsequently put on notice by Brown at the same meeting. Reynolds (no relation to Bruce Reynolds) was later sacked from her position on September 22 following an investigation into the claims against her – a decision she says she intends to challenge. “It is particularly concerning that a local council presently the subject of an inquiry into their own governance issues, breaches of confidentiality and outright dysfunction, and who have been the subject of no less than 25 complaints since the start of this year, were permitted to make such an egregious decision,” Reynolds told the meeting after her sacking.



“The allegations made against me are individually trivial in nature, however are alleged to collectively amount to serious misconduct. I disagree. “The allegations and subsequent investigation process have exposed the factionalism between the views of elected members with personal agendas and the effective function of the administration of local government as a multimillion-dollar business.” Just over a week before Reynolds was sacked, Brown announced the City would face yet another inquiry as it battled to overcome “fractured working relationships” and “ongoing governance issues” plaguing the council. He said the fresh inquiry would take about three months and cost about $120,000, however was confident it would be a “short and effective way of providing an outcome for the City of Perth community”. Carol Adams was appointed as a local government monitor on January 19 for a period of six months which culminated in a confidential report submitted to Brown.



Related Article Updated

Local government City of Perth faces yet another inquiry – this one, with teeth Unlike Adams’ report, the inquiry report will be made available to the public and could include recommendations for the council to implement. “We could recommend to the minister for local government that the council be dismissed, or certain individuals be dismissed,” Brown said last month. “So that’s the worst-case scenario, and I do not want to pre-empt what the inquiry will find.” Legislatively, Brown cannot take action on Adams’ monitor’s report, which paved the way for his inquiry.



Brown also listed breaches of confidentiality, a breakdown of public working relationships, and city officers “inundated with way too many questions and requirements” as issues raised during the monitor’s inquiry. Altogether, Adams’ report led to 12 actions that Brown made clear he expected the city to undertake. “The City of Perth is the flagship local government of Western Australia, so it needs to be the leader in governance,” Brown said. “I don’t think it’s there at the moment, so we’re going to work through that, and we want the City of Perth to be able to return to providing good governance for its community.”

The wife of one of the AFL’s most powerful executives says she is “struggling” to deal with North Melbourne’s contentious decision to trade for Nick Blakey, who remains involved in a Victoria Police investigation. Felicity Harley, an author and a prominent media publishing identity who founded Women’s Health magazine commented on an Instagram post by Not All Clubs Media which focuses on inequality in sport. Contentious recruit: Former Swan Nick Blakey in his new colours after joining North Melbourne. Nathan John, North Melbourne FC Harley was one of several women who endorsed Tuesday’s post and commentary which began with the comment that “being a woman in 2026 means watching a footy player linked to an alleged sexual assault investigation receive an $11-$12 million deal”. Harley responded to the post with the comment: “Struggling with this …”



Blakey was one of five Sydney players handed season-ending suspensions by the club for their part in a wild night of partying in August after the Swans’ victory over Essendon in round 23, just a fortnight from the start of the finals. A separate Victoria Police investigation is ongoing after three women, working as exotic dancers, variously alleged they were sexually assaulted and touched inappropriately without consent. Felicity Harley and husband Tom, the AFL’s second in charge, at this year’s Brownlow Medal count. AFL Photos No charges have been laid, and all five Swans who served the bans denied criminal wrongdoing. One of those players, Riley Bice, is no longer a subject of the investigation and is being treated as a witness. Tom Harley is second in charge at the AFL as its chief operating officer, and is seen as the successor to chief executive Andrew Dillon.



Related Article Analysis

AFL 2026 From Pullman to pulling power: How Nick Blakey profited from scandal and the AFL’s strange economy The AFL was contacted for comment. The Kangaroos on Tuesday effectively gave up two first-round picks and a future second-round selection in a complex trade to secure Blakey, an All-Australian defender two seasons ago who has signed with the Kangaroos on a deal worth up to $12 million. After the deal was struck, Blakey, in a statement, apologised for his role in the Pullman hotel scandal that hurt the Swans’ finals campaign. “I want to say that I’m sorry for the events that led up to my exit from Sydney,” Blakey said.



“I know I have to win back the trust of the broader community, football and otherwise. “Now I have the opportunity to move forward, and I want to thank North Melbourne for helping me find a fresh start. I’m grateful I have landed at a place that has such deep connections to me and my family. “There is so much potential in this group, and I’m looking forward to getting to work to help take North Melbourne forward.” When the Swans scandal broke in August, Harley also posted a comment on social media in reply to author and mental health advocate Jill Stark, who had posted that an AFL club’s on-field success had come before women’s wellbeing.



“I couldn’t agree more,” Harley said in response to Stark’s post. Harley been voted one of Australia’s 100 Women of Influence for her “I Support Women in Sport” campaign. Tom Harley, a Geelong premiership captain, was the Sydney Swans’ chief executive before accepting the offer to head to the AFL. Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

World.title: Wallabies beef up bench for Bledisloe Cup as star faces fitness test
World.content:
SportRugby UnionWallabies Wallabies beef up bench for Bledisloe Cup as star faces fitness test Christy Doran October 14, 2026 — 4:23pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Les Kiss has shifted star prop Angus Bell to the bench to ensure there is no second-half fade out in Saturday’s Bledisloe Cup rematch, but there is no room for electric halfback Tate McDermott. The news came as it emerged that Carter Gordon – the Wallabies’ first-choice playmaker – will have a fitness test in the next 48 hours to determine if he will be available for the Nations Championship campaign next month. Carter Gordon will undergo a fitness test to determine his fitness for the November Tests. Getty Images Gordon fractured his fibula during the Wallabies’ agonising 28-all draw with the Pumas in Argentina last month. The injury was expected to keep the Queensland star out for up to two months. Should the 25-year-old be declared fit, it is expected he will be one of three playmakers included in Kiss’ squad for the campaign. Uncapped Wallaby Harry McLaughlin-Phillips, who is in the squad to face the All Blacks, would then join Australia A for their two-match tour of the USA.



The Australia A squad – which includes former Wallabies coach Joe Schmidt as an assistant alongside head coach Stephen Larkham – gathered in Sydney on Wednesday and will fly to America this weekend. Already some of the selections for Saturday’s Bledisloe Cup clash are being viewed as part of the bigger picture, despite the Wallabies hoping to snap their 12-match losing streak against the All Blacks. Wallabies prop Angus Bell in action against the All Blacks. Getty Images Bell, the Wallabies’ world-class loose-head prop, will come off the bench, with Aidan Ross set to start against the nation he played a Test for in 2022. The decision is set to give the Wallabies some strike power in the second half, having been smashed 50-19 despite trailing by just three points at half-time last week at Eden Park.



In the same way that Allan Alaalatoa’s minutes have been managed throughout 2026, the Wallabies’ hierarchy are keen to keep the destructive ball-carrier fresh given there’s another four Tests in the next seven weeks. Bell is expected to be joined on the bench by lock Josh Canham, who returns from a hamstring injury, and flanker Carlo Tizzano. Kalani Thomas is set to play ahead of Queensland teammate Tate McDermott. Getty Images for ARU Following Len Ikitau’s concussion, Kiss is also expected to shift Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii to the midfield to join Isaac Henry, and promote Harry Potter to the wing. The other significant change is Kalani Thomas being included on the bench at the expense of McDermott, who struggled last week and has yet to find his best form since returning from a long-term hamstring injury.



Related Article Australian rugby Suaalii keen for swift Wallabies return of Marky Mark While McDermott’s axing will raise eyebrows, his omission is tied to the fact that the experienced halfback, who captained the Wallabies against the All Blacks in 2023, could miss part of the November campaign as he awaits the birth of his first child, according to informed sources unable to speak publicly. It is also why selectors are keen to give Thomas some game time despite being named in the Australia A squad on Monday. The halfback is likely to join the Wallabies on tour in November. Rising Waratahs halfback Teddy Wilson was a notable omission from the Australia A squad, but the 23-year-old is set for a maiden call-up to the Wallabies squad instead.

World.content:
WorldNorth AmericaUS election ‘We have guns too’: Democrat slurs her way through viral, car crash interview Michael Koziol October 14, 2026 — 4:53pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Columbus: A Democrat running in a local Indiana election has gone viral for a slurred television interview in which she lurched wildly between lines of thought, ranted about the MAGA movement and ended with the observation: “We have guns too.” Jaime West, a candidate for the Fayette County Council east of Indianapolis, appeared several days ago in a televised forum sponsored by local outlets TV3 and The Connersville News Examiner. Democrat Jaime West slurred her way through the television interview that has since gone viral in the US. YouTube West appeared confused from the start, when she was asked to deliver her opening statement and conceded she did not write one. Following a rambling monologue, it sounded as though someone on a mic loudly broke wind. At one point, West requested the interviewer to repeat the question. Asked for one thing she would do in office that might be unpopular with some voters, she said: “Firing all Republicans.”



West continued, appearing to slur heavily: “I don’t even talk to them. I don’t like ’em. I mean they voted against - our own state representative votes against her own party. I mean … what do you want me to say? I don’t like being around ’em. Related Article US election With a month to go, Republicans’ midterm prospects are ‘catastrophically bad’ “I mean, y’all did this to us. Y’all voted for us. You made this happen, this ICE coming into our communities, stealing people’s jobs. I mean – arghhh.” West then began speaking about members of President Donald Trump’s Make America Great Again coalition. “I’ve been threatened so many times to my face by ‘MAGA’, we’ll call them. Because there’s Republicans who actually get it, you know. There are good Republicans out there. But then there’s these MAGAs, who are just racist and aren’t very intelligent at all. They call you names.”



West claimed a sheriff’s nephew tried to “blow my head off”. It was not clear who or what she was referring to. Asked for a final message to the voters, West looked down the barrel of the camera and said: “We have guns too.” She then threw up both her hands. Asked for a final message to voters, West turned to the camera and said: “We have guns too.” She then threw up her hands. YouTube The interviewer – the Examiner’s managing editor Amy Graham-McCarty – maintained her composure throughout, and never inquired about West’s condition. The footage was uploaded to YouTube by TV3 and clips of the segment have been viewed millions of times on social media as the interview went viral.



West could not be immediately reached for comment, and it does not appear that she has spoken publicly since the interview. She is running against Republican Gary Keener Jr for the council seat. Voting takes place on November 3 along with statewide contests in the US midterm elections. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Larvotto rolls out first antimony shipment from NSW Hillgrove
World.content:
Sponsored BusinessCompaniesBulls N' Bears Larvotto rolls out first antimony shipment from NSW Hillgrove Brought to you by BULLS N’ BEARS Andrew Todd October 14, 2026 — 4:48pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Larvotto Resources has officially joined the ranks of Australia’s critical minerals producers, shipping its first batch of antimony concentrate from the company’s Hillgrove antimony-gold mine in New South Wales to offtake partner Wogen Resources. The company says the first truck carrying 68 tonnes of antimony concentrate has left the site, initiating mine-gate offtake sales and making Larvotto Australia’s newest supplier of critical minerals. The first truckload of antimony concentrate leaves Larvotto Resources’ Hillgrove mine in New South Wales. Under the shrewdly structured mine-gate offtake agreement, partner Wogen Resources collected the high-grade concentrate directly from Hillgrove for an initial part-payment, allowing cash to start flowing without the long shipping delays and distant laboratory results that can often hamstring new producers. A second, final payment will follow once independent assays confirm final metal content. The major milestone follows an extensive redevelopment and plant upgrade program at Hillgrove, which is set to produce 4900 tonnes of antimony and 40,500 ounces of gold per year, making it one of the world’s largest antimony producers and giving it control of a staggering 7 per cent of global supply.



‘With the antimony circuit now operating at a steady rate, we will broaden our focus to optimise gold.’ Larvotto Resources managing director Ron Heeks Management says the production ramp-up is progressing well, with plant availability already exceeding schedule, daily processing tonnages increasing as planned and concentrate grades continuing to improve as the operational team fine-tunes plant performance. Larvotto Resources managing director Ron Heeks said: “As the first of the three products the plant produces, the focus has been on the antimony circuit. With the antimony circuit now operating at a steady rate, we will broaden our focus to optimise gold concentrate and gold doré production.” The Hillgrove project, 23 kilometres east of Armidale in northern NSW, already hosts a significant mineral resource of 1.7 million ounces of gold equivalent at an impressive grade of 7.4 grams per tonne (g/t) gold equivalent, ranking it among the world’s top ten antimony deposits and the biggest in Australia. With the antimony circuit now humming, Larvotto is turning its attention to Hillgrove’s precious metal streams. The company says preparations for a first gold concentrate shipment are now nearing completion, with the production of gold doré bars also on the near-term agenda.



And there’s a third string to Hillgrove’s bow in the form of tungsten, another critical mineral caught in a tightening global market. Hillgrove’s planned future tungsten stream is riding against a backdrop of Chinese supply dominance, increasing export controls and a rapidly appreciating price environment. Larvotto says ongoing metallurgical testwork on its tungsten mineralisation continues to deliver positive results, with the company now narrowing down its preferred processing equipment and flowsheet as it targets the start of tungsten production in 2027. The transition from developer to producer is a notoriously difficult path to navigate; however, with its first product out of the gate, cash flowing in and two more high-value commodities lining up behind it, Larvotto could be heading into the new year with serious momentum and plenty of production to ramp things up. We reported earlier on Richmond securing pick five from Port Adelaide and the Tigers have made it clear they went hard after high picks in this year’s draft to avoid next year’s “compromised draft”.

The arrival of the Tasmania Devils will see them have picks 1,3, 5, 7,9, 11 and 13 plus the first pick in each subsequent round although picks 5, 7, 11 and 13 need to be traded to other clubs.

Blair Hartley speaks to the media. AFL Photos via Getty Images

Tigers football talent executive general manager Blair Hartley said that format was why side sought out picks in this year’s draft.

“To have the opportunity to pick two players at the very front end of this year’s draft is exciting for us and gives us a chance to further bolster the talent on our list before Tasmania’s concessions take over next year,” Hartley said.

“The 2027 draft is set to be significantly compromised, so it made strategic sense for us to take this approach.”

The Tigers hold picks 2, 5, 44 and 81 in this year’s draft on November 19.

World.title: TMK Energy steps on gas with fresh Mongolian drilling
World.content:
Sponsored BusinessCompaniesBulls N' Bears TMK Energy steps on gas with fresh Mongolian drilling Brought to you by BULLS N’ BEARS Murray Ward October 14, 2026 — 4:27pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. TMK Energy has fired up the engines on a 2026 work program at the company’s Gurvantes XXXV coal-bed methane pilot project in Mongolia, mobilising a workover rig and crane to kick off a well optimisation and drilling campaign. Set-up has now started at the 100 per cent-owned project, with the workover rig and a 70-tonne crane arriving on site last week. The first order of business was to remove the currently idle pump and production string from well LF-03, which is now being prepared for a cleanout and the first of three planned re-completions. A 70-tonne crane pulling the pump from well LF-03 as part of the workover at TMK Energy’s Gurvantes XXXV coal-bed methane project in Mongolia. The work is designed to optimise gas flow from existing wells. The plan involves installing a new, smaller 5.5-inch slotted liner inside the existing 7-inch liner, before running smaller tubing and pumps. TMK says the reduced-diameter spacing should boost production from the existing wellbores. The optimisation process will initially apply to wells LF-03, LF-02 and LF-06. Once the three workovers are in the bag, the company plans to spud a new well, dubbed LF-08. This will be drilled with a smaller hole size from the get-go to accommodate the 5.5-inch slotted liner.



‘As of today, the field has been averaging approximately 950 cubic metres per day a strong increase the gas rate achieved in September.’ TMK Energy chief executive officer Dougal Ferguson If the re-completion strategy proves successful in boosting gas flows, the company says it will undertake the same process on all its existing Lucky Fox wells in 2027. That includes LF-07, which remains the star performer in the pilot field. Across TMK’s well portfolio, September’s average output climbed eight per cent from August to 872 cubic metres a day, equivalent to 30,800 standard cubic feet per day (scfd). So far in October, the average has climbed dramatically from September to 950 cubic metres per day, or 33,549 scfd, suggesting the field may be rapidly closing in on commercial flow rates. TMK Energy chief executive officer Dougal Ferguson said: “I am pleased to advise that the 2026 Work Program has now commenced at the Pilot Well Project with the LF-03 pump replacement and re-completion being the first of many field-based operations over the coming two months. Returning LF-03 to production after several months of being idle should only add to the overall increasing production in the field.” Gurvantes XXXV sits less than 20 kilometres from China, one of the world’s largest energy markets and close to several mining operations in need of additional industrial power. The company’s 8400-square-kilometre project hosts an independently certified 2C contingent resource of 1.2 trillion cubic feet (Tcf) across 60 square kilometres. Although the classification covers potentially recoverable gas, further appraisal and development work is still required. In contrast, an additional 5.3 Tcf of best-estimate prospective resources hints at the scale of the prize across the wider project area.



Additionally, TMK has proposed a one-megawatt gas-to-power project with Mongolian partner Dashvaanjil Group, which would feed off the company’s gas and supply TMK’s operational power needs and nearby industrial users. Management says it intends to make a final investment decision before the end of October, subject to commercial arrangements. With its first well now under the microscope for optimisation and a new drill campaign on the horizon, TMK appears to be methodically turning up the heat at Gurvantes XXXV. In a region that is beginning to attract major energy players, proving a repeatable, optimised production model could be a shrewd move. Is your ASX-listed company doing something interesting? World.content:

The City of Perth has brought back a former chief executive to fill the vacant role left by Michelle Reynolds after she was sacked by the council. At a special meeting on Tuesday night, the council endorsed the 12-month appointment of Garry Hunt while the search for a permanent replacement progressed. Garry Hunt will take on a 12-month contract as chief executive at the City of Perth. City of Perth Lord Mayor Bruce Reynolds said the council was “pleased to appoint an experienced and capable leader” to guide the organisation. “Dr Hunt brings an exceptional depth of experience, a proven record of leadership and a strong understanding of the City of Perth, having previously led the organisation,” Reynolds said in a statement on Wednesday.



“With more than 30 years of experience as a local government CEO, including leading the cities of Perth, Joondalup and Melville, his ability to lead complex organisations and navigate periods of change makes him ideally suited to this role. Related Article City of Perth Tensions run high at Perth council meeting over former CEO’s sacking “Council is focused on moving forward, providing stability for our organisation and ensuring we continue delivering positive outcomes for the people of Perth.” Hunt said he was pleased to return to the City of Perth, having been in the position from 1994 to 2002. “I look forward to working with Council and staff, drawing on my experience to provide steady leadership and support the important work of the City during this transition period,” he said.



Hunt will start his role with the City on October 19. The position was recently held by Maria Cooke, who stepped into the acting role after Michelle Reynolds was suspended by the council in May. The decision came after a confidential meeting with Local Government Inspector Tony Brown to discuss a report into claims levelled against the chief executive.The council was also subsequently put on notice by Brown at the same meeting. Reynolds (no relation to Bruce Reynolds) was later sacked from her position on September 22 following an investigation into the claims against her – a decision she says she intends to challenge. “It is particularly concerning that a local council presently the subject of an inquiry into their own governance issues, breaches of confidentiality and outright dysfunction, and who have been the subject of no less than 25 complaints since the start of this year, were permitted to make such an egregious decision,” Reynolds told the meeting after her sacking.



“The allegations made against me are individually trivial in nature, however are alleged to collectively amount to serious misconduct. I disagree. “The allegations and subsequent investigation process have exposed the factionalism between the views of elected members with personal agendas and the effective function of the administration of local government as a multimillion-dollar business.” Just over a week before Reynolds was sacked, Brown announced the City would face yet another inquiry as it battled to overcome “fractured working relationships” and “ongoing governance issues” plaguing the council. He said the fresh inquiry would take about three months and cost about $120,000, however was confident it would be a “short and effective way of providing an outcome for the City of Perth community”. Carol Adams was appointed as a local government monitor on January 19 for a period of six months which culminated in a confidential report submitted to Brown.



Related Article Updated

Local government City of Perth faces yet another inquiry – this one, with teeth Unlike Adams’ report, the inquiry report will be made available to the public and could include recommendations for the council to implement. “We could recommend to the minister for local government that the council be dismissed, or certain individuals be dismissed,” Brown said last month. “So that’s the worst-case scenario, and I do not want to pre-empt what the inquiry will find.” Legislatively, Brown cannot take action on Adams’ monitor’s report, which paved the way for his inquiry.



Brown also listed breaches of confidentiality, a breakdown of public working relationships, and city officers “inundated with way too many questions and requirements” as issues raised during the monitor’s inquiry. Altogether, Adams’ report led to 12 actions that Brown made clear he expected the city to undertake. “The City of Perth is the flagship local government of Western Australia, so it needs to be the leader in governance,” Brown said. “I don’t think it’s there at the moment, so we’re going to work through that, and we want the City of Perth to be able to return to providing good governance for its community.”

The wife of one of the AFL’s most powerful executives says she is “struggling” to deal with North Melbourne’s contentious decision to trade for Nick Blakey, who remains involved in a Victoria Police investigation. Felicity Harley, an author and a prominent media publishing identity who founded Women’s Health magazine commented on an Instagram post by Not All Clubs Media which focuses on inequality in sport. Contentious recruit: Former Swan Nick Blakey in his new colours after joining North Melbourne. Nathan John, North Melbourne FC Harley was one of several women who endorsed Tuesday’s post and commentary which began with the comment that “being a woman in 2026 means watching a footy player linked to an alleged sexual assault investigation receive an $11-$12 million deal”. Harley responded to the post with the comment: “Struggling with this …”



Blakey was one of five Sydney players handed season-ending suspensions by the club for their part in a wild night of partying in August after the Swans’ victory over Essendon in round 23, just a fortnight from the start of the finals. A separate Victoria Police investigation is ongoing after three women, working as exotic dancers, variously alleged they were sexually assaulted and touched inappropriately without consent. Felicity Harley and husband Tom, the AFL’s second in charge, at this year’s Brownlow Medal count. AFL Photos No charges have been laid, and all five Swans who served the bans denied criminal wrongdoing. One of those players, Riley Bice, is no longer a subject of the investigation and is being treated as a witness. Tom Harley is second in charge at the AFL as its chief operating officer, and is seen as the successor to chief executive Andrew Dillon.



Related Article Analysis

AFL 2026 From Pullman to pulling power: How Nick Blakey profited from scandal and the AFL’s strange economy The AFL was contacted for comment. The Kangaroos on Tuesday effectively gave up two first-round picks and a future second-round selection in a complex trade to secure Blakey, an All-Australian defender two seasons ago who has signed with the Kangaroos on a deal worth up to $12 million. After the deal was struck, Blakey, in a statement, apologised for his role in the Pullman hotel scandal that hurt the Swans’ finals campaign. “I want to say that I’m sorry for the events that led up to my exit from Sydney,” Blakey said.



“I know I have to win back the trust of the broader community, football and otherwise. “Now I have the opportunity to move forward, and I want to thank North Melbourne for helping me find a fresh start. I’m grateful I have landed at a place that has such deep connections to me and my family. “There is so much potential in this group, and I’m looking forward to getting to work to help take North Melbourne forward.” When the Swans scandal broke in August, Harley also posted a comment on social media in reply to author and mental health advocate Jill Stark, who had posted that an AFL club’s on-field success had come before women’s wellbeing.



“I couldn’t agree more,” Harley said in response to Stark’s post. Harley been voted one of Australia’s 100 Women of Influence for her “I Support Women in Sport” campaign. Tom Harley, a Geelong premiership captain, was the Sydney Swans’ chief executive before accepting the offer to head to the AFL. Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

World.title: Wallabies beef up bench for Bledisloe Cup as star faces fitness test
World.content:
SportRugby UnionWallabies Wallabies beef up bench for Bledisloe Cup as star faces fitness test Christy Doran October 14, 2026 — 4:23pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Les Kiss has shifted star prop Angus Bell to the bench to ensure there is no second-half fade out in Saturday’s Bledisloe Cup rematch, but there is no room for electric halfback Tate McDermott. The news came as it emerged that Carter Gordon – the Wallabies’ first-choice playmaker – will have a fitness test in the next 48 hours to determine if he will be available for the Nations Championship campaign next month. Carter Gordon will undergo a fitness test to determine his fitness for the November Tests. Getty Images Gordon fractured his fibula during the Wallabies’ agonising 28-all draw with the Pumas in Argentina last month. The injury was expected to keep the Queensland star out for up to two months. Should the 25-year-old be declared fit, it is expected he will be one of three playmakers included in Kiss’ squad for the campaign. Uncapped Wallaby Harry McLaughlin-Phillips, who is in the squad to face the All Blacks, would then join Australia A for their two-match tour of the USA.



The Australia A squad – which includes former Wallabies coach Joe Schmidt as an assistant alongside head coach Stephen Larkham – gathered in Sydney on Wednesday and will fly to America this weekend. Already some of the selections for Saturday’s Bledisloe Cup clash are being viewed as part of the bigger picture, despite the Wallabies hoping to snap their 12-match losing streak against the All Blacks. Wallabies prop Angus Bell in action against the All Blacks. Getty Images Bell, the Wallabies’ world-class loose-head prop, will come off the bench, with Aidan Ross set to start against the nation he played a Test for in 2022. The decision is set to give the Wallabies some strike power in the second half, having been smashed 50-19 despite trailing by just three points at half-time last week at Eden Park.



In the same way that Allan Alaalatoa’s minutes have been managed throughout 2026, the Wallabies’ hierarchy are keen to keep the destructive ball-carrier fresh given there’s another four Tests in the next seven weeks. Bell is expected to be joined on the bench by lock Josh Canham, who returns from a hamstring injury, and flanker Carlo Tizzano. Kalani Thomas is set to play ahead of Queensland teammate Tate McDermott. Getty Images for ARU Following Len Ikitau’s concussion, Kiss is also expected to shift Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii to the midfield to join Isaac Henry, and promote Harry Potter to the wing. The other significant change is Kalani Thomas being included on the bench at the expense of McDermott, who struggled last week and has yet to find his best form since returning from a long-term hamstring injury.



Related Article Australian rugby Suaalii keen for swift Wallabies return of Marky Mark While McDermott’s axing will raise eyebrows, his omission is tied to the fact that the experienced halfback, who captained the Wallabies against the All Blacks in 2023, could miss part of the November campaign as he awaits the birth of his first child, according to informed sources unable to speak publicly. It is also why selectors are keen to give Thomas some game time despite being named in the Australia A squad on Monday. The halfback is likely to join the Wallabies on tour in November. Rising Waratahs halfback Teddy Wilson was a notable omission from the Australia A squad, but the 23-year-old is set for a maiden call-up to the Wallabies squad instead.

World.title: Fijian minister sparks debate after trying to justify MPs' salaries
World.content:
A Fijian cabinet minister's attempt to have an "honest" discussion about salary increases for members of parliament due to their various traditional and community commitments has divided opinions.

Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka's fisheries and forestry minister Alitia Bainivalu took it upon herself to "talk openly about the salaries we receive as government ministers" on her official Facebook page on Wednesday morning.

In the lengthy post, Bainivalu said that while the topic of salary increases for MPs was sensitive, "many people may not fully understand the financial expectations that come with holding public office".

Her comments sparked immediate debate, with social media users split between praising her honesty and harshly criticising her of being out of touch.

Fijian MPs voted to give themselves a significant salary increase in May 2024, with backbenchers receiving a 138 percent pay rise, bumping their base salaries from FJ$50,000 up to FJ$100,000.

Cabinet ministers had their salaries standardised upwards of FJ$200,000.

However, they subsequently voted in April 2026 to pull back those gains by implementing a mandatory 20 percent pay cut across the board largely due to the economic pressures of the global fuel crisis.

This reduction brought cabinet ministers down to the current FJ$160,000 rate and ordinary MPs down to FJ$76,000.

But Bainivalu said in Fiji's "culture of giving, helping and supporting one another", particularly within the iTaukei community, despite their higher salaries, "contributions add up very quickly".

"So when people look at a minister's salary, they often see the amount we earn, but they don't always see the financial obligations and expectations that come with the position," she wrote.

"A significant portion of what some of us earn can end up going straight back into our communities through these contributions."

Bainivalu said she was not stating that ministers deserved higher salaries because they attend community events.

"I will never pretend that the financial challenges faced by politicians are the same as those faced by families living from one payday to the next. I believe in supporting our churches, villages, schools and communities.

"I will continue doing so whenever I can."

She said that people were entitled to believe that ministers "are paid too much" and "to demand accountability".

"I know that nothing I say today will ever be enough to justify the increase in our salaries as government ministers, especially when so many of our people are struggling to make ends meet.

"And I'm not asking you to agree with me, defend me or even sympathise with me. All I'm asking is that you try to see things from my side, even if it's just for a moment."

She added that sometimes there were realities and responsibilities that ministers had that people did not see from the outside.

The national minimum wage in Fiji is FJ$5 per hour (approximately NZ$4), with close to 50 percent of the population living in poverty.
